### Decorative Endpaper

This page consists of a full-page decorative **marbled paper** pattern <term>marbled paper: a decorative paper created by floating pigments on a liquid surface to create stone-like or swirled patterns</term>, which serves as the book's endpaper <term>endpaper: the paper at the beginning or end of a book, used to attach the text block to the cover</term>. 

The design features a **stone** or **shell** marble pattern, characterized by swirling, organic shapes that mimic the appearance of natural minerals. The color palette includes:
*   Deep crimson red
*   Ochre yellow
*   Slate blue-grey
*   A light tan or off-white background

The patterns on this page range from large, bold blotches of color to fine, intricate veining and small "eyes" or droplets, showcasing the artisan's skill in traditional bookbinding techniques.

--- Page 8 ---
<meta>This page follows a fragmentary and heavily damaged preface. The text here is well-preserved and represents the formal dedication of the first printed edition of Euclid’s "Elements" (Venice, 1482), addressed by the printer Erhard Ratdolt to the Doge of Venice.</meta>

# ¶ Erhard Ratdolt of Augsburg, printer. To the most Serene Prince of the nurturing city of Venice, Giovanni Mocenigo. Greetings.

I used to wonder, most Serene Prince, when I thought to myself, what the reason might be that in this powerful and blessed city of yours, while various volumes of ancient and modern authors were being printed daily, almost nothing or only small and trivial things seemed to be printed in this field of mathematics—the most noble of all disciplines—despite the great abundance of printers who work in your city. As I discussed this with myself quite often, I found that it happened because of the difficulty of the task. For they had not yet discovered how geometric diagrams—with which mathematical volumes teem, and without which almost nothing in these disciplines can be perfectly understood—might be printed. 

And so, since this alone stood in the way of the common benefit derived from these works, I, through my industry and not without the greatest labor, brought it about that geometric figures might be produced with the same ease with which the letters of the alphabet are printed. <note>Ratdolt’s breakthrough was likely using shaped metal rules or woodcuts to print diagrams alongside movable type, a major technical milestone in the history of the book.</note> Therefore, I hope that by this invention of ours, these disciplines which the Greeks call *mathematics* <note>original: "mathemata"</note> will soon be made clear through an abundance of volumes, just like the other sciences. Regarding their praise and utility, I could bring forward many things at present collected by illustrious authors, were these things not already known to all scholars.

It is also clearly understood that the other sciences are imperfect and, as it were, "maimed" without mathematics. This indeed neither the Logicians <term>Dialecticians: practitioners of formal logic and argumentation</term> will deny, nor will the Philosophers refuse to admit; in their books many things are found which can by no means be understood without mathematical reasoning. How divine was that Plato! In order to grasp the secret of pure truth, he sailed to Cyrene to see Theodorus—the greatest mathematician of that time—and to the priests of Egypt.

What is more, without this single faculty, the very method of living is not perfectly established. For to say nothing of music—which seems to have been granted to us as a gift by nature herself to more easily endure our labors—and to pass over astronomy <note>original: "astrologia". In the 15th century, the terms astrology and astronomy were often used interchangeably to describe the scientific study of the heavens.</note>, by which we, having been refined, ascend to heaven itself as if by certain ladders and machines to know the true argument of nature; without arithmetic and geometry—of which one teaches numbers and the other measurements—how can we live in a civilized and comfortable manner?

But why do I linger on these matters which, as I said, are already better known to everyone than they could be when told by me? Therefore, Euclid of Megara <note>Renaissance scholars frequently confused Euclid of Alexandria, the mathematician who wrote the "Elements," with the philosopher Euclid of Megara. Ratdolt is dedicating the mathematical work.</note>, most Serene Prince, who most perfectly encompassed the entire system of geometry in fifteen books, and whom I have taken care to print with the highest care and diligence, omitting no diagram, may he go forth safe and favored under your name.

<summary>This page contains Erhard Ratdolt's dedication of his 1482 edition of Euclid’s Elements to the Doge of Venice, highlighting his technical achievement in printing geometric diagrams for the first time.</summary>
<keywords>Erhard Ratdolt, Giovanni Mocenigo, Euclid, Geometry, Venice, Printing History, Incunabula, Mathematics, Renaissance Science</keywords>

# The most illustrious book of the elements of the most clear-sighted Euclid: the art of Geometry begins most auspiciously:

A point is that which has no part. ¶ A line is length without breadth, whose extremities <note>original: "extremitates"</note> are two points. ¶ A straight line is the shortest extension from one point to another, receiving each of those points into its own extremities. ¶ A surface is that which has only length and breadth: whose boundaries <note>original: "termini"</note> are lines. ¶ A plane surface is an extension from one line to another receiving [its extremities]. ¶ A plane angle is the mutual inclination <note>original: "alternus otactus," literally "alternate contact"</note> of two lines; whose expansion is upon a surface and their meeting is not in a straight line. ¶ When, however, two straight lines contain the angle, it is called a rectilinear angle. ¶ When a straight line stands upon a straight line and the two angles on either side are equal, each of them shall be a right angle. ¶ And the line standing upon the other is called the perpendicular <term>perpendicular: a line that meets another at a right angle (90 degrees)</term> to the one upon which it stands. ¶ An angle which is greater than a right angle is called obtuse. ¶ An angle which is smaller than a right angle is called acute. ¶ A boundary is that which is the end of anything. ¶ A figure is that which is contained by a boundary or boundaries. ¶ A circle is a plane figure contained by a single line which is called the circumference: in the middle of which is a point from which all straight lines going out to the circumference are equal to one another. And this point is called the center of the circle. ¶ The diameter of a circle is a straight line which, passing through its center and applying its extremities to the circumference, divides the circle into two equal parts. ¶ A semicircle is a plane figure contained by the diameter of the circle and half of the circumference. ¶ A segment <note>original: "portio"</note> of a circle is a plane figure contained by a straight line and part of the circumference: either larger or smaller than a semicircle. ¶ Rectilinear figures are those which are contained by straight lines: some of which are trilateral (three-sided), being contained by three straight lines; some are quadrilateral, being contained by four straight lines; and some are multilateral, being contained by more than four straight lines. ¶ Of trilateral figures: one is the triangle having three equal sides <note>equilateral</note>. Another is the triangle having two equal sides <note>isosceles</note>. Another is the triangle of three unequal sides <note>scalene</note>. ¶ Likewise, among these: one is the right-angled triangle <note>original: "orthogoniū"</note>, having one right angle. Another is the obtuse-angled triangle <note>original: "ambligonium"</note>, having one obtuse angle. Another is the acute-angled triangle <note>original: "oxigonium"</note>, in which there are three acute angles. ¶ Furthermore, of quadrilateral figures: one is the square, which is equilateral and right-angled. Another is the rectangle <note>original: "tetragon⁹ lōg⁹"</note>, which is a right-angled figure but is not equilateral. Another is the rhombus <note>original: "helmuaym," a term derived from the Arabic "al-mu’ayyan"</note>, which is equilateral but is not right-angled.

¶ Another [figure] is similar to a rhombus <note>original: "belmuaym," a term derived from the Arabic word for rhombus used in medieval translations</note> which has equal opposite sides and equal opposite angles; however, it is contained neither by right angles nor by equal sides. ¶ Moreover, all quadrilateral figures besides these are called trapezoids <note>original: "riphe," a medieval term for irregular quadrilaterals or trapezoids</note>. ¶ Parallel lines <note>original: "equidistantes linee"</note> are those which, being located in the same plane and extended in either direction, do not meet, even if they are extended unto infinity.

[A set of geometric diagrams: at top left, a rhombus labeled "Similar to a rhombus"; to its right, the word "Parallels" next to two lines being intersected by a transversal; in the center, three concentric circles; below them, two nearly parallel lines being intersected by a transversal at an acute angle.]

<margin>And from each and every one of [...] [...] [...] </margin>

The Postulates <note>original: "Petitiones," literally "requests" or "demands" of the reader to grant as possible</note> are five: ¶ To draw a straight line from any point to any other point, and to extend a finite straight line continuously in a straight path as far as one wishes. ¶ To describe a circle around any center, occupying any amount of space [as a radius]. ¶ That all right angles are equal to one another. ¶ That if a straight line falls upon two straight lines and the two [interior] angles on one side are less than two right angles, those two lines, if extended in that same direction, will undoubtedly meet together. ¶ That two straight lines enclose no surface.

The Common Notions <note>original: "animi conceptiones," literally "conceptions of the mind"</note> are these: ¶ Things which are equal to the same thing are also equal to each other. ¶ And if equals are added to equals, the wholes will also be equal. ¶ And if equals are taken away from equals, those which remain will be equal. ¶ And if you take away equals from unequals, those which remain will be unequal. ¶ And if you add equals to unequals, those [the sums] will also be unequal. ¶ If two things are equal to one thing, they themselves will be equal to each other. ¶ If there are two things of which each is half of one and the same thing, each will be equal to the other. ¶ If any thing is placed upon another and applied to it, and one does not exceed the other, they will be equal to each other. ¶ The whole is greater than its part.

It must be known, however, that besides these common notions, Euclid passed over many others which are incomprehensible in number, of which this is one: ¶ If two equal quantities are compared to any third quantity of the same kind, they will both be either equally greater than that third, or equally smaller, or both equal at the same time. ¶ Likewise another: however great any quantity is to any other of the same kind, so great is any third to some fourth of the same kind in continuous quantities; this is universally true whether the leading terms are greater or smaller than the following terms. For magnitude decreases unto infinity. In numbers, however, it is not so; but if the first is a submultiple of the second, any third will be an equal submultiple of some fourth, since number increases unto infinity, just as magnitude is diminished unto infinity.

[A geometric diagram illustrating Euclid's Proposition 1: two intersecting circles with centers at points a and b, such that each circumference passes through the other center. An equilateral triangle abc is constructed with its vertices at the centers and one of the intersection points. Points are labeled a, b, c, d, f, and h.]

### Proposition One.

To construct an equilateral triangle upon a given straight line.
¶ Let the given straight line be **.a.b.** I wish to constitute an equilateral triangle upon it. Upon one of its extremities, namely at point **.a.**, I shall place the fixed foot of the compass; and the other movable foot I shall extend as far as **.b.**, and I shall describe, according to the quantity of the given line itself by the second postulate, the circle **.c.b.d.f.**

again, I will make its other extremity, namely point **b**, the center: and by the same postulate <note>original: "petitionem," referring to Postulate 3: to describe a circle with any center and distance</note> and according to the same quantity [as the first circle], I will draw circle **c. a. d. b.** These circles will intersect each other at two points, which shall be **c** and **d**. I will then connect one of the two intersections, such as intersection **d**, with both extremities of the given line by drawing lines **d. a.** and **d. b.** according to the first postulate <note>Postulate 1: to draw a straight line from any point to any point</note>. Since, therefore, from point **a**, which is the center of circle **c. b. d.**, the lines **a. d.** and **a. b.** are drawn to its circumference, they will be equal by the definition of a circle. Similarly also, because from point **b**, which is the center of circle **c. a. d. b.**, the lines **b. a.** and **b. d.** are drawn to its circumference, they will also be equal. Since, therefore, each of the two lines **a. d.** and **b. d.** is equal to line **a. b.**, as has been proved: they themselves will be equal to each other according to the <term>first common notion<note>The axiom stating that "things which are equal to the same thing are also equal to one another."</note></term>. Therefore, upon the given line, we have constructed an equilateral triangle, which is what was proposed. 

¶ If, however, one wishes to place the remaining two species of triangles upon the same line—namely, the triangle of two equal sides <note>an isosceles triangle</note> and the triangle of three unequal sides <note>a scalene triangle</note>—let line **a. b.** be extended in both directions until it meets the circumference of both circles at two points, **f** and **b** <note>The text likely implies points beyond the original segment</note>. And with the center placed at point **a** of the line, let circle **e. b. g.** be drawn according to the quantity of line **a. b.** Likewise, with the center placed at point **b** of the line, let circle **e. f. g.** be drawn according to the quantity of line **b. f.** These circles will intersect each other at two points, which are **e** and **g**. Let the extremities of the given line then be joined with one of the said intersections by two straight lines, which are **a. g.** and **b. g.** Because these lines **a. b.** and **a. f.** go out from the center of circle **c. d. f.** to its circumference, they will be equal. Similarly also, **a. b.** and **b. f.**, because they go out from the center of circle **c. a. d. b.** to its circumference, they will be equal. Since, therefore, each of the two lines **a. f.** and **b. f.** is equal to line **a. b.**, they will be equal to each other. Therefore, with **a. b.** placed as a common [base], **b. f.** will be equal to **a. b.**, but **b. f.** is equal to **b. g.** because both go out from the center of circle **e. f. g.** to its circumference. Similarly also, **a. b.** is equal to **a. g.**, and each of them is greater than **a. b.** because each of the two lines **b. f.** and **a. f.** is greater than **a. b.** <note>The logic here describes constructing an isosceles triangle by using an extended radius.</note> Wherefore, upon the given line, we have constructed a triangle of two equal sides.

¶ We shall also construct a triangle of three unequal sides upon the same line: if we choose any point existing on the circumference of either of the two larger circles that is not at either of the two [previous] intersections, and which point **f. b.** does not meet when extended continuously and directly in either direction, and we join it by two straight lines with both extremities of the given line. Let point **k** be marked on the circumference of circle **e. f. g.**, and let it not be at either of the [previous] intersections, nor let **f. b.** meet it when extended continuously and directly to its circumference. I will therefore draw lines **a. k.** and **b. k.** Line **a. k.** will cut the circumference of circle **e. b. g.**; let it cut it at point **l**. Then **b. k.** will be equal to **a. l.**, because **b. k.** is equal to **b. g.** and **a. l.** is equal to **a. g.** <note>This is a complex medieval addition to Euclid's text intended to show that all types of triangles can be constructed using these circular methods.</note> Wherefore **a. k.** is greater than **b. k.**, but **b. k.** is also greater than **a. b.** Therefore, triangle **a. b. k.** has three unequal sides. Thus, therefore, we have constructed all species of triangles upon the given line.

### Proposition 2

From a given point, to draw a straight line equal to any given straight line.

<margin>
<image-desc>Geometric diagram showing a large circle with an inscribed triangle and several auxiliary lines. Labeled points include f, b, a, c, and e. </margin>

¶ Let **a** be the given point and **b. c.** be the given line. I wish to draw from point **a** a single line equal to line **b. c.** in whichever direction it may fall. I will therefore connect point **a** with either extremity of line **b. c.** that I wish; and I will connect **a** with extremity **c** by line **a. c.**, upon which I will construct an equilateral triangle according to the teaching of the preceding [proposition], which shall be **a. c. d.** Then, at that extremity of the given line with which I connected the given point (namely, at extremity **c**), I will place the fixed foot of the compass and describe upon it a circle according to the quantity of the given line itself, which shall be circle **e. b.**... <note>The construction of Proposition 2 continues on the next page.</note>

<meta>This page continues the proof of the second proposition of Book I of Euclid’s "Elements" and proceeds through the proofs of Propositions 3, 4, and the beginning of 5. It maintains the logical progression from constructing lines to comparing triangles.</meta>

of the equilateral [triangle] which is opposite the given point. From the side **d. c.**, I will draw a line through the center of the described circle to its circumference; and let the whole line thus drawn be **d. c. e.** Based on its length, I will describe a circle with its center at **d**, which shall be circle **e. f.** Then I will extend the side **d. a.** to the circumference of this last circle, and let it meet its circumference at point **f**. I say, therefore, that **a. f.** is equal to **b. c.** For **b. c.** and **c. e.** are equal, because they go from the center of circle **c** to its circumference. Similarly also, **d. f.** and **d. e.** are equal because they go from the center of circle **e. f.** to the circumference. But **d. a.** and **d. c.** are equal because they are sides of an equilateral triangle. Therefore, if from **d. e.** and **d. f.** (which are equal) **d. a.** and **d. c.** are taken away, the remainders, which are **a. f.** and **c. e.**, will be equal. Since each of the two lines **a. f.** and **c. b.** is equal to **c. e.**, they are equal to each other. Wherefore, from point **a**, we have drawn line **a. f.** equal to **b. c.**, which is what was proposed.

### Proposition .3.

<margin>
<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing a line segment 'a-b' and a longer segment 'c-d'. A circle centered at 'c' with radius 'ce' (which is equal in length to 'ab') is drawn, intersecting the line segment 'c-d' at point 'f'.</image-desc>
</margin>
**Given two unequal lines, to cut off from the longer of them a part equal to the shorter.**
¶ Let the two lines be **a. b.** and **c. d.**, and let **a. b.** be the shorter. I wish to cut from **c. d.** a line equal to **a. b.** First, from point **c**, I draw a line equal to **a. b.**, which the previous proposition taught; let this be **c. e.** Therefore, with the center placed at point **c**, I will describe a circle based on the length of **c. e.**, which will cut line **c. d.** Let it cut it at point **f**. The line **c. f.** will be equal to line **c. e.** because both go from the center of the same circle to the circumference; and because each of the two lines **a. b.** and **f. c.** is equal to **c. e.**, they are equal to each other; which is what was proposed.

### Proposition 4

<margin>
<image-desc>Two identical triangles labeled 'a b c' and 'd e f'. Below them, a diagram illustrates the proof by superposition, showing the triangles placed one upon the other to demonstrate equality of sides and angles.</image-desc>
</margin>
**In all cases of two triangles where two sides of one are equal to two sides of the other, and the two angles contained by those equal sides are equal to one another: their remaining corresponding sides shall also be equal; and the remaining angles of one shall be equal to the remaining angles of the other; and the whole triangle shall be equal to the whole triangle.**
¶ Let there be two triangles **a. b. c.** and **d. e. f.**, and let side **a. b.** be equal to side **d. e.**, and side **a. c.** be equal to side **d. f.**, and angle **a** be equal to angle **d**. Then I say that the base **b. c.** is equal to the base **e. f.**, and angle **b** is equal to angle **e**. Also, angle **c** is equal to angle **f**. This is proven: let triangle **a. b. c.** be placed upon triangle **d. e. f.** such that angle **a** falls upon angle **d**, and side **a. b.** upon side **d. e.**, and side **a. c.** upon side **d. f.** It is clear through the penultimate <term>conception<note>Original: "p̄ceptionē" or "conceptionem." In medieval geometry, the "Common Notions" or axioms were often called "conceptions." The penultimate one refers to the fourth common notion: "Things which coincide with one another are equal to one another."</note></term> that neither the angles nor the sides will exceed each other, because angle **a** is equal to angle **d**, and the sides placed upon those which they cover are equal by the hypothesis. Therefore, points **b** and **c** will fall upon points **e** and **f**. If, therefore, line **b. c.** falls upon line **e. f.**, the proposition is clear: because when line **b. c.** is placed over line **e. f.**, it neither exceeds it nor is exceeded by it, it is equal to it by the converse of the penultimate conception. By the same reasoning, angle **b** will be equal to angle **e**, and angle **c** equal to angle **f**. If, however, line **b. c.** does not fall upon line **e. f.**, but falls inside the triangle like line **e. g. f.**, or outside like line **e. b. f.**, then two straight lines would enclose a surface <note>original: "superficiem"</note>, which is against the last <term>postulate<note>original: "petitionē." This refers to the axiom that two straight lines cannot enclose a space.</note></term>.

->Proposition .6.<-

**If two angles of any triangle are equal, the two sides subtending those angles will also be equal.**
¶ This is the converse of the previous [proposition] regarding its first part. For let there be a triangle **a. b. c.**, whose two angles **b.** and **c.** are equal. I say that side **a. b.** is equal to side **a. c.** For if they are not equal, one will be greater than the other. Let **a. b.** be the greater, which shall be cut off to match the length of **a. c.** by the third proposition, so that the excess is on the side of **a.**, and let it be cut at point **d.** Let **b. d.** be equal to **a. c.**, and let line **d. c.** be drawn.

I consider therefore the two triangles **a. b. c.** and **d. b. c.**, which I will prove to be equilateral and equiangular. For the two sides **d. b.** and **b. c.** of triangle **d. b. c.** are equal to the two sides **a. c.** and **b. c.** of triangle **a. b. c.**, and angle **b.** is equal to the whole angle **c.** by hypothesis <note>original: "ypothefim"; the starting assumption of the proof</note>. Therefore, base **d. c.** is equal to base **b. a.**, and angle **d. c. b.** is equal to angle **a. c. b.**—that is, the part equal to the whole—which is impossible.

**If two lines are drawn from the ends of a single line and meet at a point, it is impossible for two other lines, equal to the first two respectively, to be drawn from the same ends and meet at a different point on the same side.**

## Proposition 8

<image-desc>Geometric diagrams for Proposition 8. The first shows two separate triangles: one with vertices labeled a, b, c, and another with vertices d, e, f. The second diagram shows a shared base d-e with two triangles having vertices f and g respectively, used for a proof by contradiction.</image-desc>

**O**f any two triangles where two sides of one are equal to two sides of the other, and the base of one is equal to the base of the other: it is necessary that the two angles contained by the equal sides are also equal.

Let there be two triangles **a.b.c.** and **d.e.f.**, and let **a.c.** be equal to **d.f.**, and **b.c.** equal to **e.f.**, and **a.b.** equal to **d.e.** I say that angle **c.** is equal to angle **f.**, and angle **a.** to angle **d.**, and angle **b.** to angle **e.** I will place base **a.b.** upon base **d.e.**; since they are equal, neither will exceed the other according to the penultimate common notion <note>The "penultimate common notion" refers to Euclid's fourth axiom: "Things which coincide with one another are equal to one another."</note>: therefore, either point **c.** will fall upon point **f.**, or it will not. If it does: then because angle **c.** will be placed upon angle **f.**, neither of them exceeds the other: they are equal by the conversion of the aforementioned common notion. Similarly, argue that the remaining angles are equal. But if point **c.** does not fall upon **f.**, but upon any other point which we may call **g.**, then because **e.g.** is equal to **b.c.** (indeed, they are the same line), and likewise **d.g.** is equal to **a.c.**, then **e.g.** will be equal to **e.f.** and **d.g.** equal to **d.f.**, which is impossible by the preceding [proposition].

## Proposition 9

<image-desc>Geometric diagram for Proposition 9 showing a rhombus or diamond-shaped figure with vertices labeled a, b, c, d. A vertical line connects vertex b (top) to vertex d (bottom), bisecting the figure.</image-desc>

->To divide a given angle into two equal parts.<-

**G**iven the angle which must be divided: angle **a.b.c.** Along the lines containing it, which are **a.b.** and **b.c.**, I will set equal lengths by the third [proposition], and I will draw line **a.c.** Upon this, I will construct an equilateral triangle <note>A triangle where all three sides are equal.</note> **a.d.c.**, and I will draw the line **b.d.** I say that this line divides the given angle into equal parts. I consider the two triangles **a.b.d.** and **c.b.d.**; since the two sides **a.b.** and **b.d.** of triangle **a.b.d.** are equal to the two sides **c.b.** and **b.d.** of triangle **c.b.d.**, and the base **a.d.** is equal to the base **c.d.**, therefore, by the preceding [proposition], angle **a.b.d.** is equal to angle **c.b.d.**, which is what was proposed to be done.

## Proposition 10

<image-desc>Geometric diagram for Proposition 10 showing a triangle with vertices a, b, c. A vertical line segment is dropped from vertex c to point d on the base line a-b, bisecting the line.</image-desc>

->To divide a proposed straight line into two equal parts.<-

**G**iven a proposed straight line which must be divided into equal parts: line **a.b.** Upon this, I will construct an equilateral triangle **a.b.c.**, and I will divide angle **c.** into equal parts according to the instructions of the preceding [proposition] using line **c.d.** I say that line **c.d.** divides the given line **a.b.** into equal parts. For I consider the two triangles **a.c.d.** and **b.c.d.** and I argue thus: the two sides **a.c.** and **c.d.** of triangle **a.c.d.** are equal to the two sides **b.c.** and **c.d.** of triangle **b.c.d.**, and angle **c.** of one is equal to angle **c.** of the other; therefore, by the fourth [proposition], base **a.d.** is equal to base **d.b.**, which is what was proposed.

# From a given point marked on a straight line, to draw a perpendicular line supported on both sides by two equal and right angles.

¶ Let the given line be **a. b.**, in which there is a given point **c.**, from which it is necessary <note>original: "oportet"</note> to draw a perpendicular. I shall therefore make, by the third [proposition], line **b. c.** equal to line **a. c.**, and upon the whole [segment] **a. b.** I construct an equilateral triangle **a. b. d.**, and I draw the line **c. d.** I say that this line is perpendicular to line **a. b.** I consider the two triangles **a. c. d.** and **b. c. d.**; and because the two sides **a. c.** and **c. d.** of triangle **a. c. d.** are equal to the two sides **c. b.** and **c. d.** of triangle **c. b. d.**, and the base **a. d.** is equal to the base **b. d.**, then by the 8th [proposition], angle **a. c. d.** will be equal to angle **b. c. d.** Therefore, each of them will be a right angle by the definition of a right angle; and line **c. d.** is perpendicular to line **a. b.** by the definition of a perpendicular line: which is what was proposed. **Proposition 12.** <note>Note that in this edition, the proposition number follows the text of the preceding proof; this is actually Euclid's Proposition 11.</note>

# From a point marked outside, to drop a perpendicular to a given line of indefinite length.

¶ Let **a.** be a point marked outside the line **b. c.**, from which it is necessary to drop a perpendicular. I shall therefore extend the line **b. c.** in both directions as much as is pleasing, and upon point **a.** I shall describe a circle **b. c.** <note>The author uses 'b. c.' to label the points where the circle intersects the line.</note> such that it cuts the given line at points **b.** and **c.** I then draw the lines **a. b.** and **a. c.**, and I divide the angle **b. a. c.** into two equal parts by the line **a. d.** using the 9th [proposition]. I say that **a. d.** is perpendicular to line **b. c.** I consider the two triangles **a. b. d.** and **a. c. d.**; because the two sides **a. b.** and **a. d.** of triangle **a. b. d.** are equal to the two sides **a. c.** and **a. d.** of triangle **a. c. d.**, and the angle **a.** of one is equal to the angle **a.** of the other, then by the 4th [proposition], the base **b. d.** will be equal to the base **d. c.**, and angle **a. d. b.** will be equal to angle **a. d. c.** Therefore, each of them is a right angle, and line **a. d.** is perpendicular to line **b. c.** by the definition of a right angle and a perpendicular line: which is what was proposed. **Proposition 13.** <note>This is Euclid's Proposition 12.</note>

# For every straight line standing upon a straight line, the two angles on either side are either right angles or equal to two right angles.

¶ Suppose that line **a. b.** stands upon line **c. d.** If it is perpendicular to it, it will make two right angles by the converse of the definition. <note>original: "per conversionem diffinitionis"</note> But if it is not perpendicular to it, let there be drawn from point **b.** a line **b. e.** perpendicular to **c. d.** by the eleventh [proposition]; then the two angles **e. b. c.** and **e. b. d.** will be right angles by the converse of the definition. Because, therefore, the two angles **d. b. a.** and **a. b. c.** are equal to angle **d. b. e.** together with angle **c. b. e.**, they will be equal to two right angles. This is because the three angles which are **d. b. a.**, **a. b. e.**, and **e. b. c.** are equal to two right angles; but angle **e. b. a.** <note>The author likely means the composite angle c. b. a.</note> is equal to the two angles **e. b. c.** and **e. b. a.** Therefore, the two angles **c. b. a.** and **a. b. d.** are equal to two right angles: which is what was proposed. From this it is clear <note>original: "poretet" (patet)</note> that the entire space that surrounds any point in any plane surface is equal to four right angles. **Propositio 14.** <note>This is Euclid's Proposition 13.</note>

# If two lines from a point of one line extend in different directions and make the two angles around themselves right or equal to two right angles, those two lines are joined directly to each other and are one line.

¶ Suppose that from point **b.** of line **a. b.**, two lines go out in opposite directions, which are **b. c.** and **b. d.**, and they make two angles, **c. b. a.** and **d. b. a.**, equal to two right angles. Then I say that the two lines **c. b.** and **d. b.** are directly joined to each other and are one line. This is, as it were, the converse of the previous [proposition]. If it were not one line, then let **c. b.** be extended in a continuous and straight [direction]. Because it is not one line with **d. b.**, it will pass above it like **b. e.** or below it like **b. f.** Because, therefore, the line **a. b.** falls upon the straight line which is **c. b. e.**, the angles **c. b. a.** and **e. b. a.** will be equal to two right angles by the preceding [proposition]. And because all right angles are equal to one another by the 5th petition <note>The 5th Postulate in the medieval numbering.</note>, and the angles **c. b. a.** and **d. b. a.** are also equal to two right angles by the hypothesis, then the two angles **c. b. a.** and **e. b. a.** will be equal to the two angles **c. b. a.** and **d. b. a.** Therefore, by subtracting the common angle **c. b. a.**, the angle **e. b. a.** will be equal to the angle

### Proposition 15

For any two lines intersecting each other: all angles placed opposite one another are equal. From this, it is manifest that when two straight lines intersect each other, the four angles that are made are equal to four right angles. <note>These are known today as "vertical angles."</note>
Let there be two lines **a. b.** and **c. d.** intersecting each other at point **e.** I say that angle **d. e. b.** is equal to angle **a. e. c.** and angle **b. e. c.** is equal to angle **a. e. d.** For by the 13th [proposition], the two angles **a. e. c.** and **c. e. b.** will be equal to two right angles. Likewise, the two angles **c. e. b.** and **d. e. b.** are equal to two right angles by the same [proposition]. Therefore, the first two are equal to the last two because all right angles are equal to one another by the 4th postulate. <note>The 4th postulate of Euclid states that all right angles are equal.</note> Therefore, by taking away the common angle which is **c. e. b.**, the angle **a. e. c.** will be equal to angle **d. e. b.** In the same way, it will be proven that angle **c. e. b.** is equal to angle **a. e. d.**, which is what was proposed.

<image-desc>Geometric diagram for Proposition 16 showing a triangle abc with its base extended toward d. A point e is marked on the side opposite the vertex a, and line ae is extended to point f. Internal point g and extension point k are also labeled.</image-desc>

### Proposition 16

If any of the sides of a triangle is extended straight out, it will make an exterior angle greater than either of the two interior angles of the triangle opposite to it.
Let the side **a. b.** of triangle **a. b. c.** be extended as far as **d.** I say that angle **d. b. c.** is greater than either of the two interior angles opposite to it, which are **b. a. c.** and **b. c. a.** For I shall divide line **c. b.** into [two] equal [parts] at point **e.** by the 10th [proposition], and I shall extend **a. e.** as far as **f.**, so that **e. f.** is made equal to **a. e.**, and I shall draw line **f. b.** I consider the two triangles **c. e. a.** and **b. e. f.** Because the two sides **a. e.** and **e. c.** of triangle **a. e. c.** are equal to the two sides **f. e.** and **e. b.** of triangle **f. e. b.**, and the angle **e.** of the one is equal to the angle **e.** of the other by the preceding [proposition] <note>Proposition 15</note> because they are opposite angles; then by the 4th [proposition], angle **e. c. a.** will be equal to angle **e. b. f.** Therefore, angle **e. b. d.** <note>The exterior angle</note> will be greater than angle **b. c. a.** Similarly, it will also be proven that it is greater than angle **c. a. b.** For I shall divide **a. b.** into equal [parts] at point **g.** by the 10th [proposition], and I shall draw line **c. g.** equal to line **c. g.** <note>The text likely means extending the line to a point h</note> by the 3rd [proposition]. Afterward, I shall draw **b. k.**, and there will be two triangles **a. g. c.** and **b. g. h.** <note>The text reads 'b.g.b.', likely a scribal error for 'b.g.h.' or 'b.g.k.'</note>. The two sides **a. g.** and **g. c.** of the first are equal to the two sides **b. g.** and **g. h.** of the second, and angle **g.** of one to angle **g.** of the other by the 15th [proposition]. Therefore, by the 4th [proposition], angle **g. c. a.** is equal to angle **g. b. h.**, and therefore by the 15th [proposition] to angle **k. b. d.** And because angle **c. b. d.** is greater than angle **k. b. d.**, it will also be greater than angle **b. a. c.**, which is what was proposed.

<image-desc>Geometric diagram for Proposition 17 showing a triangle abc with base extended to point d.</image-desc>

### Proposition 17

In every triangle, any two angles are less than two right angles.
Let there be triangle **a. b. c.** I say that any two of its angles are less than two right angles. For I shall extend one of its sides, such as **b. c.**, as far as **d.** By the preceding [proposition], the exterior angle **c.** <note>original: "e." - likely a typo for the exterior angle at vertex c</note> will be greater than **a.** and greater than **b.** But the exterior **c.** with the interior **c.** is equal to two right angles by the 13th [proposition]. Therefore, the interior angles **b.** and **c.**, or the interior angles **a.** and **c.**, are less than two right angles. Similarly, if I extend side **b. a.**, it will be proven that the two angles **a.** and **b.** are less than two right angles: which is what was proposed.

<image-desc>Geometric diagram for Proposition 18 showing a triangle abc with a segment bd drawn within it, meeting side ac at point d.</image-desc>

### Proposition 18

In every triangle, the longer side is opposite the greater angle.
Let it be that in triangle **a. b. c.**, angle **a.** is greater than angle **c.** I say that side **c. b.** will be greater than side **a. b.** For if it were equal, then by the 5th [proposition], angle **a.** would be equal to angle **c.**, which is contrary to the hypothesis. But if **a. b.** were greater, let it be cut down to be equal to **c. b.** by the 3rd [proposition], and let **d. b.** be equal to **c. b.** Therefore, by the 5th [proposition], angle **d. c. b.** will be equal to angle **b. d. c.** But **b. d. c.** is greater than angle **b. a. c.** by the 16th [proposition]. Therefore, **b. c. d.** is greater than **b. a. c.**, and therefore it is much more strongly greater than **a. c. b.**, being the part compared to the whole: which is impossible.

Let there be any triangle **a. b. c.** whose side **a. c.** is longer than side **a. b.** I say, therefore, that angle **a. b. c.** is greater than angle **a. c. b.**
Let there be cut from the longer [side] **a. c.** a length equal to **a. b.** by the 3rd [proposition], and let **b. d.** be joined. Because, therefore, the two sides **a. b.** and **a. d.** are equal, the angles at the base, **a. b. d.** and **a. d. b.** <unclear>are</unclear> <unclear>equal</unclear> to each other. Angle **a. b. d.** is smaller than angle **a. b. c.** because it is a part of it. But because angle **a. d. b.** of triangle **b. d. c.** is an exterior angle, it is greater than the interior angle which is opposite to it, namely angle **a. c. b.** But since it has been shown that angle **a. b. d.** is <unclear>equal</unclear> to angle **a. d. b.**, therefore angle **a. b. c.** is much greater than angle **a. c. b.**, which was proposed: the longer side subtends the greater angle.

<meta>This page continues the sequence of Euclid’s first book of "Elements." While the previous page ended at Proposition 15, this transcription picks up at Proposition 19. It covers fundamental rules about the relationship between the sides and angles of triangles, including the famous triangle inequality (that any two sides together must be longer than the third).</meta>

<margin>
19 In any triangle, the greater angle is opposite the longer side.
</margin>

### Proposition 19

**In every triangle, the longer side is opposite the greater angle.**
Let there be a triangle **a. b. c.** where side **b. c.** is larger than side **a. b.** I say that angle **a.** will be greater than angle **c.** This is the converse <note>A converse is a mathematical statement where the "if" and "then" parts are swapped.</note> of the preceding proposition. For if the angles were equal, then by the 6th proposition, side **a. b.** would be equal to side **b. c.**, which contradicts our hypothesis. If angle **c.** were larger, then by the preceding proposition, side **a. b.** would be larger than side **b. c.**, which also contradicts our hypothesis. Thus, the proposition is established.

### Proposition 20

**In every triangle, any two sides joined together are longer than the remaining side.**
Let there be a triangle **a. b. c.** I say that the two sides **a. b.** and **a. c.** are together longer than side **b. c.** Extend the line **b. a.** to point **d.** so that **a. d.** is equal to **a. c.**, and draw the line **c. d.** By the 5th proposition, angle **a. c. d.** will be equal to angle **d.** Therefore, the whole angle **b. c. d.** is greater than angle **d.** <note>Because the part is always smaller than the whole.</note> Thus, by the 18th proposition, the side **b. d.** is longer than side **b. c.** But since **b. d.** is equal to the sum of **a. b.** and **a. c.**, it follows that **b. a.** and **a. c.** joined together are greater than **b. c.**

### Proposition 21

**If from the two endpoints of one side of a triangle, two lines are drawn meeting at a single point inside the triangle, these lines will be shorter than the two remaining sides of the triangle but will contain a greater angle.**
Let there be a triangle **a. b. c.** From the ends of side **b. c.**, let two lines **b. d.** and **c. d.** meet at point **d.** inside the triangle **a. b. c.** I say that these joined together are shorter than the two lines **a. b.** and **a. c.** joined together, and that angle **d.** is greater than angle **a.** For extend **b. d.** until it cuts side **a. c.** at point **e.** By the 20th proposition, **b. a.** and **a. e.** joined together are greater than **b. e.** Therefore, **b. a.** and the whole side **a. c.** are greater than **b. e.** and **e. c.** Furthermore, **d. e.** and **e. c.** joined together are greater than **d. c.** by the same proposition. Therefore, **b. e.** and **e. c.** are greater than **b. d.** and **d. c.** Since **b. a.** and **a. c.** were shown to be greater than **b. e.** and **e. c.**, it follows by even stronger reason <note>original: "multo fortius"</note> that they are greater than **b. d.** and **d. c.**, which is the first thing proposed. And since angle **b. d. c.** is greater than angle **d. e. c.** by the 16th proposition, and angle **d. e. c.** is greater than angle **e. a. b.** by the same, it follows that angle **b. d. c.** is much more so greater than angle **b. a. c.**, which is the second thing proposed.

### Proposition 22

**Given three straight lines, any two of which joined together are longer than the remaining one, to construct a triangle from three other lines equal to them.**
Let there be three given straight lines **a.**, **b.**, and **c.**, where any two joined together are longer than the third—otherwise, a triangle could not be constructed from three such lines according to the 20th proposition. Since I wish to construct a triangle from these three, I take a straight line **d. e.** of indefinite length starting from **e.** From this line, by the 3rd proposition, I take **d. f.** equal to **a.**, **f. g.** equal to **b.**, and **g. h.** equal to **c.** Using point **f.** as the center, I describe a circle **d. k.** with a radius equal to line **f. d.** Similarly, using point **g.** as the center, I describe a circle **k.** with a radius equal to line **g. h.** These circles will intersect each other at two points, one of which we shall call **k.** If they did not intersect, it would mean one of the lines was equal to or greater than the other two combined, which contradicts our premise. I then draw the lines **k. f.** and **k. g.** Thus, triangle **k. f. g.** is constructed from three lines equal to the given lines **a.**, **b.**, and **c.** For **f. d.** and **f. k.** are equal because they are radii from the center to the circumference, so **f. k.** is equal to **a.** Likewise, **g. h.** and **g. k.** are equal as radii, so **g. k.** is equal to **c.** And since **g. f.** was taken as equal to **b.**, the proposition is clearly proven.

### On a given straight line and at a point on it, to construct an angle equal to any proposed angle.

¶ Let the given line be **f. e.**, which is in the upper figure; and let the lines **b.** and **a.** contain the given angle, which the base **c.** subtends <note>In geometry, to "subtend" means to be opposite to an angle or arc.</note>. At point **f.** of the line **e. f.**, it is required to create an angle equal to the given angle. To the line **e. f.**, let **f. d.** be joined equal to line **a.**; and from **f. e.** I take **f. g.** equal to **b.**; and from **g. c.** I take **g. h.** equal to **c.** Upon points **f.** and **g.**, I describe two circles, **d. k.** and **r. k. h.**, according to the lengths of the two lines **f. d.** and **g. h.**, intersecting each other at point **k.**, just as the preceding [proposition] taught. Once the lines **k. f.** and **k. g.** are drawn, the two sides **k. f.** and **f. g.** of triangle **k. f. g.** will be equal to the two sides **a.** and **b.** of triangle **a. b. c.**, and the base **g. k.** will be equal to the base **c.** Therefore, by Proposition 8 <note>original: "ꝓ. 8."; Euclid's 8th proposition states that if three sides of one triangle equal three sides of another, their angles are also equal.</note>, angle **k. f. g.** will be equal to the angle contained by **a.** and **b.**, which is what was proposed.

### Proposition 24.

**Of any two triangles where two sides of one are equal to two sides of the other: if the angle contained by those equal sides is greater in one than the other, the base of that triangle will also be greater than the base of the other.**

¶ Let there be two triangles, **a. b. c.** and **d. e. f.**, and let the two sides **a. b.** and **a. c.** be equal to the two sides **d. e.** and **d. f.**, each to its corresponding side—right to right and left to left. Let angle **a.** be given as greater than angle **d.** I say that the base **b. c.** will be greater than the base **e. f.** For I shall make, according to the teaching of the preceding proposition, [the angle] **e. d. g.** equal to angle **a.** Angle **e. d. f.** will be a part of it. I shall set **d. g.** equal to **a. c.** and draw **e. g.**, which will either pass above **e. f.** so that it cuts line **d. f.**, or [fall] upon **e. f.** so that it is one and the same line with it, or fall below it. Let it first pass above: and because sides **a. b.** and **a. c.** of triangle **a. b. c.** are equal to sides **e. d.** and **d. g.** of triangle **e. d. g.**, and the total angle **a.** is equal to angle **d.**; by Proposition 4 <note>The text likely means Proposition 4, though it reads 8; Prop 4 covers Side-Angle-Side equality.</note>, the base **b. c.** will be equal to the base **e. g.** Yet since **d. g.** and **d. f.** are equal (for both are equal to **a. c.**), by Proposition 5, angle **d. f. g.** will be equal to angle **d. g. f.** Therefore, **d. f. g.** will be greater than **f. g. e.**, which is [only a part] of **f. g. d.**; and much more so is it greater than that same **f. g. e.** By Proposition 18, the side **e. g.** is longer than side **e. f.**; therefore, **b. c.** is also greater than **e. f.**, which is what was proposed. If, however, **e. g.** passes over **e. f.** and is the same line with it, then **e. f.** will be a part of **e. g.**, and by the last axiom <note>Common Notion 5: The whole is greater than the part.</note>, the proposition is proven. If, however, **e. g.** passes below **e. f.**, let the two lines **d. f.** and **d. g.** (which are equal, as proven) be extended to **k.** and **h.** By the second part of the fifth proposition, the angles under the base **f. g.**—namely **k. f. g.** and **f. g. h.**—will be equal. Therefore, angle **e. f. g.** will be greater than angle **f. g. e.** Thus, by Proposition 18, side **e. g.** is longer than side **e. f.**; therefore **b. c.** is greater than **e. f.**, which is what was proposed. This last part could also be proven by Proposition 21; for in that arrangement, the two lines **d. g.** and **e. g.** would be greater than the two lines **d. f.** and **f. e.** And since **d. g.** is equal to **d. f.** because both are equal to **a. c.**, it follows that **g. e.** is greater than **e. f.**, and thus **b. c.** is greater; which is what was proposed. Nevertheless, it is better to demonstrate it in the prior way, so that in every arrangement it is argued by the fifth [proposition].

### Proposition 25.

**Of any two triangles where two sides of one are equal to two sides of the other: if the base of one is greater than the base of the other, the angle of the larger triangle contained by those equal sides will also be greater than the corresponding angle of the other.**

¶ Let there be two triangles, **a. b. c.** and **d. e. f.**, and let the two sides **a. b.** and **a. c.** of the first be equal to the two sides **d. e.** and **d. f.** of the second, each to its corresponding side. Let the base **b. c.** be greater than the base **e. f.** I say that angle **a.** will be greater than angle **d.** This is the converse <note>A converse statement flips the "if" and "then" parts of a previous rule.</note> of the preceding [proposition]. Indeed, it will not be equal; for if so, by Proposition 4, base **b. c.** would be equal to base **e. f.**, which contradicts the hypothesis <note>The hypothesis is the set of conditions we agreed upon at the start: that the bases are NOT equal.</note>. But neither will it be smaller, because then angle **d.** would be greater, and thus by the preceding proposition, base **e. f.** would be greater than base **b. c.**, which is contrary to the proposal. Therefore, it must be greater, and thus the proposition is established.

Of all two triangles in which two angles of one are equal to two angles of the other, each corresponding to the other, and one side of one is also equal to one side of the other; and should that side be between the two equal angles or opposite one of them: then the remaining two sides of the one will also be equal to the remaining two sides of the other triangle, each corresponding to each; and the remaining angle of the one will be equal to the remaining angle of the other.

<image-desc>Geometric diagram showing two triangles, labeled a-b-c and d-e-f. A third triangle g-e-f is drawn overlapping d-e-f to demonstrate the proof of Proposition 26.</image-desc>

Let there be two triangles, **a.b.c.** and **d.e.f.**, and let angle **b.** be equal to angle **e.**, and angle **c.** be equal to angle **f.** Furthermore, let side **b.c.** be equal to side **e.f.**, or let one of the other two sides, **a.b.** or **a.c.**, be equal to one of the two sides **d.e.** or **d.f.**, such that **a.b.** is equal to **d.e.** or **a.c.** is equal to **d.f.** I say that the remaining two sides of the one will be equal to the remaining two sides of the other, and the remaining angle equal to the remaining angle: namely, angle **a.** to angle **d.**

First, I shall suppose that side **b.c.**, upon which angles **b.** and **c.** lie, is equal to side **e.f.**, upon which angles **e.** and **f.** lie, which were set as equal to angles **b.** and **c.** Then I say that side **a.b.** is equal to side **d.e.**, side **a.c.** to side **d.f.**, and angle **a.** to angle **d.** For if side **a.b.** is not equal to side **d.e.**, one will be greater. Let **d.e.** be the greater, which I shall cut to be equal to **a.b.**; let **g.e.** be equal to **a.b.**, and I shall draw line **g.f.** By the 4th Proposition <note>Euclid’s 4th Proposition is the Side-Angle-Side (SAS) theorem.</note>, angle **g.f.e.** will be equal to angle **a.c.b.**; therefore it is also equal to angle **d.f.e.**, the part being equal to the whole, which is impossible. Therefore, **d.e.** must be equal to **a.b.** Thus, by the 4th Proposition, **d.f.** is equal to **a.c.** and angle **d.** is equal to angle **a.**, which is the first part of the proposed division.

Again, let there be as before two angles **b.** and **c.** equal to two angles **e.** and **f.**, and let side **a.b.** (which is opposite angle **c.**) be equal to side **d.e.** (which is opposite angle **f.**), to which angle **c.** was set as equal. I say that side **b.c.** will be equal to side **e.f.**, side **a.c.** to side **d.f.**, and angle **a.** to angle **d.** For if side **e.f.** were not equal to side **b.c.**, one would be greater. Let **e.f.** be greater; thus let **e.h.** be set equal to **b.c.**, and I shall draw line **d.h.** By the 4th Proposition, angle **d.h.e.** will be equal to angle **a.c.b.**, and therefore to angle **d.f.e.**—specifically, the exterior angle would equal the interior angle <note>This refers to a triangle formed by the intersection; an exterior angle cannot equal an opposite interior angle.</note>, which is impossible by the 16th Proposition. Therefore, **e.f.** must be equal to **b.c.** Thus, by the 4th Proposition, side **d.f.** is equal to side **a.c.**, and the total angle **d.** is equal to angle **a.**, which is the second part of the proposed division; whereby the whole is clearly proven.

->### Proposition 27.<-

<image-desc>Geometric diagram for Proposition 27. Two horizontal lines c-d and e-f are crossed by a transversal a-b at points g and h. The lines extend to meet at a point k on the left side, illustrating a triangle for the proof by contradiction.</image-desc>

If a straight line falls upon two straight lines and makes the two alternate angles equal to each other, those two lines will be parallel <note>original: "equidistantes". Euclidean geometry uses "equidistant" to mean lines that never meet.</note>.

Let it be that line **a.b.** falls upon two lines **c.d.** and **e.f.**, and cuts line **c.d.** at point **g.** and line **e.f.** at point **h.** Let angle **d.g.h.** be equal to angle **e.h.g.** I say that lines **c.d.** and **e.f.** are parallel. For if they are not, they will meet <note>original: "concurrant"</note> either on the side of **c.e.** at point **k.**, or on the side of **d.f.** at point **l.** Whichever occurs, an impossibility will result by the 16th Proposition <note>The 16th Proposition states that an exterior angle of a triangle is greater than either of the remote interior angles.</note>: namely, that an exterior angle is equal to an interior one. For one of the said alternate angles which were set as equal would be an exterior angle and the other an interior one. Since, therefore, it is impossible for them to meet on either side when extended, they will, by definition, be parallel; which is what was proposed.

If a straight line comes upon two straight lines, and its interior angle is equal to the opposite exterior angle, or if two interior angles on one side are equal to two right angles, those two lines will be parallel.

Let it be that line **a.b.** cuts two lines **c.d.** and **e.f.** at points **g.** and **h.** Let the exterior angle **g.** be equal to the interior angle **h.** taken on the same side; or let the two interior angles **g.** and **h.** taken on the same side be equal to two right angles...

...right [angles]: I say that the two lines **c.d.** and **e.f.** are parallel. Therefore, let the first angle **d.g.a.** be equal to angle **f.h.g.**; and by Proposition 15 <note>Proposition 15 proves that vertical/opposite angles are equal.</note>, angle **e.g.h.** will be equal to that same angle **f.h.g.**; wherefore by the preceding [proposition], **c.d.** and **e.f.** are parallel. Let it be again that two angles **d.g.h.** and **f.h.g.** are equal to two right angles; and because by Proposition 13, the two angles **d.g.h.** and **c.g.h.** are similarly equal to two right angles, then angle **c.g.h.** will be equal to angle **f.h.g.** Wherefore, by the preceding, **c.d.** and **e.f.** will be parallel: which is what was proposed.

# Proposition 29.

<image-desc>
A geometric diagram illustrating Proposition 29. Two horizontal lines, a-b and c-d, are intersected by a diagonal transversal line e-f-g-h. A point k is shown far to the right, indicating where the lines would eventually meet if they were not parallel. Letters a, b, c, d, e, f, g, h, k are placed at various intersections and endpoints.
</image-desc>

**I**f a line falls upon two <term>parallel lines</term> <note>original: "equidistantibus"; lines that never meet no matter how far they are extended.</note>, the two <term>alternate angles</term> <note>Angles on opposite sides of the transversal, like the inner corners of a Z-shape.</note> will be equal; and the exterior angle will be equal to the interior and opposite angle on the same side. Likewise, the two interior angles on the same side will be equal to two right angles.

Let there be two parallel lines **a.b.** and **c.d.** upon which falls the line **e.f.**, cutting them at points **g.** and **h.** I say that the alternate angles **g.** and **h.** are equal; and that the exterior angle **g.** is equal to the interior and opposite angle **h.** taken on the same side; and that the interior angles **g.** and **h.** taken on the same side are equal to two right angles; and this is the converse of the two preceding propositions. 

The first part is proved thus: For if angle **h.g.b.** is not equal to angle **c.h.g.**, one of them will be greater. Let angle **c.h.g.** be the greater. Since the two angles **c.h.g.** and **h.g.b.** [together with their adjacent angles] are equal to two right angles, then by Proposition 13, the two angles **h.g.b.** and **d.h.g.** will be less than two right angles. Therefore, by the <term>fourth postulate</term> <note>In this edition, the "fourth petition" refers to the famous Parallel Postulate, which states that lines inclined toward each other at less than 180 degrees must eventually meet.</note>, the two lines **a.b.** and **c.d.**, if extended, will meet on the side of **b.** and **d.** at some point, such as **k.** Therefore they are not parallel by the definition, which contradicts the hypothesis; and because this is impossible, the two alternate angles **h.g.b.** and **c.g.h.** will be equal, which is the first part proposed. 

From this, the second part is clear: for by Proposition 15, angle **h.g.b.** is equal to angle **a.g.e.**; therefore angle **a.g.e.** will be equal to angle **c.h.g.** (the exterior to the interior), which is the second part proposed. From this again, the third part is clear: for by Proposition 13, the two angles **a.g.e.** and **a.g.h.** are equal to two right angles. Therefore, the two angles **a.g.h.** and **c.h.g.** will also be equal to two right angles, which are the two interior angles taken on the same side: which is the third part proposed.

# Proposition 30.

<image-desc>
A geometric diagram for Proposition 30 showing three horizontal parallel lines stacked vertically, labeled a-b (top), e-f (middle), and c-d (bottom). A transversal line g-h intersects all three at points k, l, and m.
</image-desc>

**I**f two lines are parallel to the same line, they will also be parallel to each other.

Let there be two lines **a.b.** and **c.d.**, each of which is parallel to the line **e.f.** I say that those two lines, namely **a.b.** and **c.d.**, are parallel. This is universally true whether the two lines **a.b.** and **c.d.** are in the same <term>plane</term> <note>original: "superficie"; a flat two-dimensional surface.</note> with line **e.f.** or not; however, here it is only understood according to the condition that all are in one plane; for that they are parallel when in different planes is proved in the ninth [proposition] of the 11th book. Therefore, let them all be in one plane. Let a line **g.h.** be drawn cutting the lines **a.b.**, **e.f.**, and **c.d.** at points **k.**, **l.**, and **m.** 

Since **a.b.** is parallel to **e.f.**, angle **h.k.l.** will be equal to angle **e.l.k.** by the first part of the preceding [proposition], as they are alternate angles. And since **c.d.** is parallel to **e.f.**, the exterior angle **k.l.e.** will be equal to the interior angle **l.m.c.** by the second part of the preceding. Therefore, angle **h.k.l.** is equal to angle **c.m.l.** Since these are alternate angles, the lines **a.b.** and **c.d.** will be parallel by Proposition 27: which is what was proposed.

</image-desc>

**T**o draw a line parallel to a given line through a given point outside it.

A point given outside a line is understood as one through which the line does not pass, even if the line is extended in both directions. Therefore, let **a.** be the given point outside line **b.c.**, from which it is necessary to draw a line parallel to **b.c.** I shall draw a line **a.d.** in whatever way it may happen [to fall upon **b.c.**], and upon point **a.**, which is the endpoint...

...line **a.d.**, I construct angle **c.a.d.** by the method of Proposition 23 <note>Proposition 23 explains how to construct an angle equal to a given angle on a given line.</note>, equal to angle **b.d.a.**, its <term>alternate angle</term> <note>original: "coalterno"; angles on opposite sides of a line crossing two others.</note>; and **a.c.** will be parallel to **b.c.** by Proposition 27, which is what was proposed.

### Proposition 32.

<image-desc>Five geometric diagrams positioned in the right margin:
1. A triangle labeled a, b, c, with its base line bc extended to a point d. A line cf is drawn from vertex c parallel to side ab.
2. A quadrilateral divided into two triangles by a diagonal line.
3. A pentagon labeled a, b, c, d, e, with lines drawn from vertex a to vertices c and d, dividing the interior into three triangles.
4. A pentagon with a central point n connected by lines to each of the five vertices, creating five interior triangles.
5. A pentagon with each of its sides extended outward at the vertices (labeled f, g, h, k, l) to demonstrate exterior angles.</image-desc>

**I**n every triangle, an exterior angle is equal to the two interior and opposite angles; furthermore, it is necessary that all three of its angles are equal to two right angles.
¶ Let there be a triangle **a.b.c.** whose side **b.c.** is extended to **d**. I say that the exterior angle **c** is equal to the two interior and opposite angles **a** and **b** joined together; and that the three angles of triangle **a.b.c.** joined together are equal to two right angles.
From point **c**, I will draw **c.f.** parallel to **a.b.** following the method of the preceding proposition; angle **f.c.a.** will then be equal to angle **a**, because they are alternate angles by the first part of Proposition 29; and the exterior angle **f.c.d.** is equal to the interior angle **b** by the second part of the same proposition. Therefore, the entire exterior angle **a.c.d.** is equal to the two interior and opposite angles **a** and **b**: which is the first part. And because the two angles **a.c.b.** and **a.c.d.** are equal to two right angles by Proposition 13, the three interior angles **a**, **b**, and **c** will be equal to two right angles: which is the second part proposed. 
¶ From this it is evident that for all <term>polygonal figures</term> <note>original: "figure poligonie"; shapes with many sides and angles.</note>, all the angles taken together are equal to twice as many right angles as the rank by which the shape is removed from the first figure. In this order, the triangle is the first of polygonal figures—for if a figure were made of only two lines, since a figure is an enclosure of lines, then two straight lines would enclose a surface, which is impossible by the last <term>postulate</term> <note>original: "petitionem"; this refers to Euclid's common notion that two straight lines cannot enclose a space.</note>. The quadrilateral is the second; the pentagon is the third; and similarly, any figure will be at a certain rank in order according to the number of its sides or angles, after subtracting two from that number. 
I say, therefore, that for the triangle, which is the first, all angles are equal to two right angles. For the quadrilateral, which is the second, it will be equal to four right angles, and for the pentagon, which is the third, they will be equal to six right angles. 
This is manifest from the fact that any such figure can be resolved into as many triangles as its distance from the first, by drawing straight lines from any of its angles to all opposite angles; and since all the angles of every triangle are equal to two right angles, all the angles of a many-sided figure will be equal to twice as many right angles as its rank from the first: which is what was proposed. 
For example, let there be a pentagon **a.b.c.d.e.** From its angle **a**, I will draw lines to the opposite angles **c** and **d**; thus the whole pentagon is resolved into triangles **a.b.c.**, **a.c.d.**, and **a.d.e.** Since the angles of each of these are equal to two right angles, the angles of the pentagon will be equal to six right angles; which is double the number by which it is distant from the first, or double the number of its angles or sides after subtracting two <note>Modern formula: (n-2) × 180 degrees.</note>.
¶ We can also propose the same thing another way, saying that all the angles of any polygonal figure taken together are equal to as many right angles as double the number of its angles, minus four. By marking any point **n** within the figure and drawing lines from it to each angle, the figure itself will be resolved into as many triangles as it has angles. Because all the angles of all those triangles taken together will be equal to as many right angles as double the number of angles of the figure; and since all the angles of the triangles into which it was resolved that surround the middle point are equal to four right angles by Proposition 13, the proposition is clearly established.
¶ Similarly, it is also evident that all the <term>exterior angles</term> of any polygonal figure are equal to four right angles. For the interior and exterior angles together are equal to twice as many right angles as there are angles, by Proposition 13. But the interior angles are equal to twice as many right angles as there are angles minus four; therefore the exterior angles must be equal to four right angles: which is what was proposed. 
For example: let the sides of the proposed pentagon be extended so that exterior angles are formed. Let **a.b.** be extended to **f**, **b.c.** to **g**, **c.d.** to **h**, **d.e.** to **k**, and **e.a.** to **l**. By Proposition 13, the two angles at **a** (the interior and the exterior) will be equal to two right angles; and by the same reasoning, the two angles at **b** (interior and exterior); and so on...

<summary>This page presents Proposition 32, proving that the sum of the angles in any triangle equals 180 degrees (two right angles) and extending this principle to calculate the sum of interior and exterior angles for all polygons.</summary>

...the rest; wherefore the angles **a, b, c, d, e**, both interior and exterior, are equal to ten right angles. Therefore, by subtracting the interior angles, which are equal to six right angles <note>The sum of interior angles for any polygon is $(n-2) \times 180^{\circ}$. For a five-sided pentagon, this is $3 \times 180^{\circ} = 540^{\circ}$, or six right angles.</note>, the exterior angles—namely **b.a.l, c.b.f, d.c.g, e.d.b,** and **a.e.k**—will be equal to four right angles. 

¶ It is also clear that in every pentagon where each side intersects two of the others <note>This refers to a "star pentagon" or pentagram, as shown in the image description.</note>, the five angles at the points are together equal to two right angles. Let such a pentagon be **a.b.c.d.e**, and let side **a.c** intersect side **b.e** at point **g**, and side **a.d** intersect the same side **b.e** at point **f**. Angle **a.f.g** will be equal to the two angles **b** and **d**, since it is an exterior angle to them in triangle **f.d.b** <note>Following the rule from the first part of Proposition 32, that an exterior angle equals the sum of the two opposite interior angles.</note>. Likewise, angle **f.g.a** will be equal to the two angles **c** and **e**, since it is exterior to them in triangle **g.c.e**. But the two angles **a.f.g** and **f.g.a**, together with angle **a**, are equal to two right angles <note>Because they form the three angles of the interior triangle **a.f.g**.</note>; therefore, the four angles **b, d** and **c, e**, together with angle **a**, are equal to two right angles, which is what was proposed.

### Proposition 33.

<image-desc>Geometric diagram for Proposition 33. Above, two equal and parallel horizontal lines labeled a-b. Below, a parallelogram with vertices a, b (top) and c, d (bottom) connected by a diagonal line from a to d.</image-desc>

**I**f at the ends of two lines of equal length and parallel to each other, two other lines are joined, those lines will also be equal and parallel.
¶ Let there be two lines **a.b** and **c.d** that are equal and parallel, whose endpoints I join by the lines **a.c** and **b.d**, which I say are also equal and parallel. I will draw line **a.d** <note>This is the "diameter" or diagonal.</note>; and because lines **a.b** and **c.d** are parallel, angle **b.a.d** will be equal to angle **a.d.c** by the first part of Proposition 29. Therefore, the two sides **a.b** and **a.d** of triangle **a.b.d** are equal to the two sides **d.c** and **d.a** of triangle **d.c.a**, and angle **a** of the first is equal to angle **d** of the second. Therefore, by Proposition 4 <note>The "Side-Angle-Side" theorem for triangle congruence.</note>, the base **b.d** of the first is equal to the base **a.c** of the second, and angle **a.d.b** of the first is equal to angle **d.a.c** of the second. And because these are <term>alternate angles</term> <note>original: "coalterni"; angles on opposite sides of a transversal crossing two lines.</note>, the lines **b.d** and **a.c** will be parallel by Proposition 27; and since it was previously proven that they are equal, both parts of the proposition are clear.

### Proposition 34.

<image-desc>Geometric diagram for Proposition 34. A parallelogram with vertices a, b (top) and c, d (bottom) and a diagonal line drawn from vertex a to vertex d.</image-desc>

**E**very <term>equidistant surface</term> <note>original: "superficies equidistantibus"; what we now call a parallelogram.</note> has its opposite sides and angles equal to one another, and its <term>diameter</term> <note>original: "diametro"; the diagonal line of a quadrilateral.</note> divides it through the middle.
¶ Let there be a surface **a.b.c.d** of parallel sides, such that line **a.b** is parallel to **c.d**, and **a.c** is parallel to **b.d**. I say that the two lines **a.b** and **c.d**, and likewise the two lines **a.c** and **b.d**, are equal. Similarly, I say angle **a** is equal to angle **d** <note>Referring here to the opposite internal angles of the parallelogram.</note>, and angle **b** is equal to angle **c**. I will draw the diameter **a.d**, which will also divide that surface through the middle. Since **a.b** and **c.d** are parallel, the angles **b.a.d** and **c.d.a**, which are alternate, will be equal by Proposition 29. And because **a.c** and **d.b** are also parallel, the angles **c.a.d** and **b.d.a**, which are alternate, will be equal by the same proposition. I consider the two triangles **a.d.b** and **d.a.c**; since two angles **a** and **d** of triangle **a.d.b** are equal to two angles **d** and **a** of triangle **d.a.c**, and the side **a.d** upon which those angles lie is common to both triangles, it follows by Proposition 26 that side **a.b** is equal to side **c.d**, side **a.c** is equal to side **b.d**, and angle **b** is equal to angle **c**. And because it is clear that the whole angle **a** is equal to the whole angle **d** by the second <term>common notion</term> <note>original: "concepteōez"; the axiom that "if equals are added to equals, the wholes are equal."</note>, the entire proposition with its corollary is evident.

### Proposition 35.

<image-desc>Geometric diagram for Proposition 35. Multiple parallelograms sharing a common base c-e and situated between the same parallel lines. Points on the top parallel are labeled a, g, f, h, b; points on the bottom are c, e, d. An interior intersection is labeled k.</image-desc>

**A**ll parallelograms set upon the same base and within the same parallel lines are proven to be equal to one another.
¶ Let there be two parallel lines **a.b** and **c.d**, between which is formed the parallelogram **a.c.f.e** upon the base **c.e**. Upon the same base and between the same lines, let there be another parallelogram **g.c.b.e**. I say that these two aforementioned surfaces are equal, which is proven thus: for either the line **c.g** will intersect line **a.b** at some point on line **a.f**, or at point **f**, or at some point on line **b.f**. Suppose first it intersects at some point on line **a.f**, as appears in the first figure. Because each of the two lines **a.f** and **g.b** is equal to the line **c.e** by the preceding proposition, one of them will be equal to the other...

Therefore, when the common line **f.g** is taken away, there will remain **a.g** equal to **f.b**. Because, by the preceding [proposition], **a.c** is also equal to **f.e**, and angle **b.f.e** is equal to angle **g.a.c** by the second part of Proposition 29—namely, that an exterior angle is equal to its corresponding interior angle—then by Proposition 4 <note>This refers to the "Side-Angle-Side" theorem: if two triangles have two sides and the included angle equal, the triangles are equal.</note>, triangle **a.c.g** will be equal to triangle **f.c.b**. Consequently, if the irregular quadrilateral figure **g.c.f.e** is added to both, the surface **a.c.f.e** will be equal to the surface **g.c.b.e**, which is what was proposed. 

Now, let the line **c.g** intersect the line **a.b** at point **f**, as appears in the second diagram. By an argument similar to the first, the two triangles **a.c.f** and **f.e.b** will be equal; wherefore, by adding triangle **f.c.e** to both, the proposition is clear. 

In a third way, let the line **c.g** intersect line **a.b** between the two points **f** and **b**, as appears in the third diagram; it will intersect the line **f.e** at a point **k**. Because by an argument similar to the first, line **a.f** is equal to line **g.b**, and by making line **g.f** common to both, **a.g** will be equal to **f.b**, and triangle **a.g.c** will be equal to triangle **f.c.b**. Therefore, by adding triangle **c.k.e** to both and subtracting triangle **f.k.g** from both, the surface **a.c.f.e** will be equal to the surface **g.c.b.e**, which is what was proposed.

### Proposition 36
It is necessary that all parallelograms established on equal bases and between the same lines be equal.

A parallelogram is defined as a surface of equidistant <note>original: "equidistantiū"; in modern geometry, we use the term "parallel."</note> sides. Let there be two surfaces of parallel sides, **a.b.c.d** and **e.f.g.b**, established between two parallel lines **a.f** and **c.b**, and upon equal bases **c.d** and **g.b**. I say that they are equal. For I shall draw two lines, **c.e** and **d.f**, and by Proposition 33, the surface **c.d.e.f** will be a parallelogram because **e.f** is equal and parallel to **c.d**, for each of them is equal to **g.b**. Because, according to the previous propositions, each of the two surfaces **a.b.c.d** and **e.f.g.b** is equal to the surface **c.d.e.f**, they will therefore be equal to each other; which is what was proposed.

### Proposition 37
All triangles that are established upon the same base and between two parallel lines are equal to one another.

Let there be two triangles, **a.b.c** and **d.b.c**, established upon the base **b.c** between two lines **a.e** and **b.f** which are parallel. I say they are equal. For I shall draw **c.g** parallel to **a.b**, and **c.h** parallel to **d.b**, by Proposition 31. The two surfaces **a.b.c.g** and **d.b.c.h** will be equal by Proposition 35. And because the said triangles are half of them, according to the corollary of Proposition 34, they will be equal by the common notion <note>original: "cōez sciam" (communem scientiam); this refers to Euclid's Axioms or Common Notions, specifically that halves of equals are equal.</note> that things which are halves of equals are themselves equal; and thus the proposition is clear.

### Proposition 38
If two triangles fall upon equal bases and between two parallel lines, it is necessary that they be equal.

Let there be two triangles, **a.b.c** and **d.e.f**, established upon equal bases **b.c** and **e.f** and between parallel lines **a.g** and **b.h**. I say they are equal. For I shall draw **c.k** parallel to **a.b**, and **f.l** parallel to **e.d**. The two surfaces **a.b.c.k** and **d.e.f.l** will be equal by Proposition 36. And because the said triangles are half of them, according to the corollary of Proposition 34, they will be equal by the aforementioned common notion.

### Proposition 39
If any two triangles are equal and fall upon the same base and on the same side, they will be between two parallel lines.

Let there be two triangles, **a.b.c** and **d.b.c**, established upon the base **b.c** on one and the same side; and let them be equal. I say they are between parallel lines; and this is the converse of Proposition 37. From point **a**, I shall draw a line parallel to line **b.c**; if this passes through point **d**, the proposition is clear. If, however, it passes above or below: let it first pass above and be [line] **a.e**, and I shall extend **b.d** until it intersects...
