line **a.e** at point **e**, and I will draw line **e.c**. Since triangle **c.b.e** is equal to triangle **a.b.c** by Proposition 37, and triangle **d.b.c** was stated to be equal to triangle **a.b.c**, then triangle **d.b.c** would be equal to triangle **e.b.c**—the part being equal to the whole, which is impossible <note>This is a fundamental rule of logic in Euclid’s geometry: a smaller part of a shape cannot be equal in size to the entire shape.</note>. Therefore, the line drawn from point **a** parallel to **b.c** will not pass above **d**. Suppose, then, it passes below, and let **a.f** be the line cutting line **d.b** at point **f**. I will then draw line **f.c**. Since by Proposition 37 triangle **f.b.c** is equal to triangle **a.b.c**, it would also be equal to triangle **d.b.c**—again, the part being equal to the whole, which is impossible. Therefore, since the line from point **a** parallel to **b.c** cannot pass anywhere except through point **d**, the proposition is proven. 

¶ From this and the preceding proof, note that if any straight line cuts two sides of any triangle into equal parts, that line will be parallel to the third side, which is proven thus: Let there be a triangle **a.b.c** whose two sides **a.b** and **a.c** are cut equally by line **d.e**—side **a.b** at point **d** and **a.c** at point **e**. I say that line **d.e** is parallel to **a.c**. For if I draw the diagonals **a.e** and **d.c** in the quadrilateral **a.c.e.d**, then by Proposition 38 triangle **a.e.d** will be equal to triangle **d.e.b** because line **a.d** was stated to be equal to line **d.b**. Likewise, by the same proposition, triangle **c.e.d** will be equal to that same triangle **d.e.b** because line **c.e** was stated to be equal to line **e.b**. Since triangle **a.e.d** is equal to triangle **c.e.d**, and they are established upon the same base—namely, line **e.d**—and on the same side, they will be between parallel lines according to this Proposition 39. Therefore, line **d.e** is parallel to line **a.c**, a conclusion which will be useful to you for the fifth [proposition] of the fourth [book].

<margin>Corollary</margin>
<image-desc>Geometric diagram showing a triangle with vertices a, b, c. An internal line de is drawn parallel to the base, and additional lines extend to a point b forming multiple related triangles.</image-desc>

<image-desc>Geometric diagram showing several triangles sharing bases and heights between parallel lines. Points are labeled a, b, c, d, e, f, g, h along the horizontal bounds.</image-desc>

**I**f two equal triangles are established upon equal bases on one and the same line and on the same side, it is necessary that they be contained between two parallel lines. 
¶ Let two equal triangles **a.b.c** and **d.e.f** be established on two bases **b.c** and **e.f**. On the same side, I say they are between two parallel lines. This is the converse of Proposition 38, and it is proven by it just as the preceding was by Proposition 37. From point **a**, let a line be drawn parallel to line **b.f**. If it passes through point **d**, the proposition is proven. If, however, it passes above, as line **a.g**, let **e.d** be extended to it at point **g**, and let line **g.f** be drawn. Then, by Proposition 38, triangle **a.b.c** would be equal to triangle **g.e.f**, wherefore triangle **d.e.f** would also be equal to triangle **g.e.f**—the part being equal to the whole, which is impossible. Therefore, it does not pass above; let it then pass below, cutting line **d.e** at point **h**, and let line **f.h** be drawn. Then, by Proposition 38, triangle **b.e.f** <note>The text likely means a.b.c or d.e.f here</note> would be equal to triangle **a.b.c**, and therefore to triangle **d.e.f**—the part to the whole, which is impossible. Therefore, since it can only pass through point **d**, the proposition is proven.

---

<image-desc>Geometric diagram showing a rectangle (parallelogram) with diagonals. Points are labeled a, b, c, d, e.</image-desc>
<margin>Corollary</margin>

<image-desc>Geometric diagram showing a rectangle with a diagonal ad and external points e, f forming triangles that share the same base bd as the rectangle.</image-desc>

**I**f a parallelogram and a triangle are established on the same base and within the same alternating lines, it is appropriate that the parallelogram be double the triangle. 
¶ Let there be a parallelogram **a.b.c.d** and a triangle **e.b.d** on the base **b.d** and between the lines **a.e** and **b.d**, which are parallel. I say the parallelogram is double the triangle. I will draw the diagonal **a.d** in the parallelogram; triangle **a.b.d** will be half of the parallelogram by Proposition 34. And because triangle **c.b.d** <note>original: "c.b.d" - likely a scribal error for e.b.d</note> is equal to triangle **a.b.d** by Proposition 37, it is clear that triangle **e.b.d** is half of the parallelogram **a.b.c.d**, which is what was proposed. Similarly, it can also be proven that if a parallelogram and a triangle are established on equal bases and between parallel lines, the parallelogram will be double the triangle. Euclid did not set this down separately because it is easily clear as a corollary from this preceding [proposition] and Proposition 38, by dividing the parallelogram by a diagonal into two triangles, or [by placing them] upon the base of the parallelogram between the same parallel lines.

## Proposition 42

<image-desc>A geometrical diagram for Proposition 42. A triangle b-c-d has a line b-e bisecting its base at point e. A horizontal line b-f is drawn from vertex b parallel to the base. A parallelogram g-e-d-f is constructed on half the base e-d, with an interior line g-e forming an angle with the base.</image-desc>

To construct a parallelogram <note>Original: "equidistantium laterum superficiem," literally a "surface of parallel sides."</note> whose angle is equal to a given angle, and the surface itself is equal to a given triangle.
¶ Let there be a given angle **a** and a given triangle **b.c.d**. I wish to describe a parallelogram equal to triangle **b.c.d** where each of the two opposite angles is equal to angle **a**. I divide the base **c.d** in half at point **e**, and I draw line **b.e**, and from point **b** I draw **b.f** parallel to **c.d**. By Proposition 38, triangle **b.e.d** will be equal to triangle **b.e.c**; therefore triangle **b.e.d** is half of the total triangle **b.c.d**. Therefore, at point **e** on line **d.e**, I construct angle **d.e.g** equal to angle **a**, and I complete the parallelogram **g.e.d.f**. Since, by the preceding proposition, it is double the triangle **b.e.d**, it will also be equal to triangle **b.c.d** by this common notion <note>Euclid's "common notions" are basic mathematical axioms. This refers to the axiom that "things which are doubles of the same thing are equal to each other."</note>: those whose halves are equal are themselves equal. For triangle **b.e.d** is the half of both; therefore we have described the parallelogram **g.e.d.f** equal to triangle **b.c.d**, whose two opposite angles **g.e.d** and **d.f.g** are equal to angle **a**, which was proposed.

## Proposition 43

<image-desc>A geometrical diagram for Proposition 43 showing a large parallelogram a-b-c-d with a diagonal c-b. Inside, horizontal line e-f and vertical line g-k intersect at point h on the diagonal. This division creates four internal parallelograms: two along the diagonal (e-h-c-g and k-h-f-b) and two "complements" (a-e-h-g and k-h-d-f).</image-desc>

In any parallelogram, the complements <note>The "complements" are the two smaller parallelograms created within a larger one that do not have the main diagonal passing through them.</note> of those parallelograms which are situated around the diagonal are necessarily equal to each other.
¶ Let there be a parallelogram **a.b.c.d** in which I draw the diagonal **b.c**, and I draw **e.f** parallel to both sides **a.b** and **c.d**, which cuts the diagonal at point **h**. From that point I will draw **k.g** parallel to the remaining two sides **a.c** and **b.d**, and extend it until it cuts both sides **a.b** and **c.d**, making the whole line **g.k**. The whole parallelogram **a.b.c.d** will be divided into four parallelograms, two of which—namely **e.h.c.g** and **h.f.b.k**—are said to lie "about the diagonal" because the diagonal **c.b** passes through their middle. The remaining two, namely **a.e.h.g** and **h.f.d.k**, are called the "complements." It is said that these two complements are equal. For the two triangles **a.b.c** and **c.d.b** are equal by the conclusion of Proposition 34 <note>This proposition establishes that a diagonal bisects a parallelogram into two equal triangles.</note>. Similarly, the two triangles **g.h.b** and **f.h.b** are equal by the same conclusion of Proposition 34. Likewise, the two triangles **c.e.h** and **h.k.c** are equal by the same conclusion. Therefore, by taking away the two triangles **b.g.h** and **e.h.c** (which are equal) from the total triangle **a.b.c**, and the two remaining triangles **b.f.h** and **h.d.c** from the other total triangle **c.d.b**, the remainders will be equal by common knowledge <note>Common Notion 3: "If equals be subtracted from equals, the remainders are equal."</note>. These remainders are the two aforementioned complements, which is what was proposed.

## Proposition 44

<image-desc>A complex geometrical diagram for Proposition 44 showing the construction of a parallelogram on a given line a-b equal to a given triangle d-e-f. The construction involves extending lines below the main horizontal base to find the intersection points necessary to complete the parallelogram.</image-desc>

Given a straight line, to construct upon it a parallelogram whose angle is equal to a given angle, and whose surface is equal to a given triangle.
¶ To construct a parallelogram upon a certain line means to make that line one of the sides of the shape. Let there be a given line **a.b**, a given angle **c**, and a given triangle **d.e.f**. Upon line **a.b**, I wish to construct a parallelogram such that line **a.b** is one of its sides, each of its two opposite angles is equal to angle **c**, and its total surface is equal to triangle **d.e.f**. This differs from Proposition 42 because here a side of the parallelogram to be described is specified (line **a.b**), whereas there, none was given. When I wish to do this, I join the line **a.g**...

## Proposition 45

<image-desc>A diagram showing a square labeled with points a and b at the bottom corners and c and d at the top corners.</image-desc>

To describe a square from a given line.
**Let** the given line be **a.b**, from which I wish to describe a square. From points **a** and **b** of line **a.b**, I draw by Proposition 11 the lines **a.c** and **b.d** perpendicular to line **a.b**. These will be parallel by the last part of Proposition 28. I set each of them equal to the same **a.b** by the second proposition, and I draw line **c.d**. This will be equal and parallel to line **a.b** by Proposition 33. And because each of the two angles **a** and **b** is a right angle, each of the two angles **c** and **d** will be a right angle by the last part of Proposition 29. Therefore, by definition, **a.b.c.d** is a square, which is what was proposed. The same can be done otherwise: let **a.c** be perpendicular to line **a.b** by Proposition 11, and let it be equal to it as before. From point **c**, by Proposition 31, let **c.d** be drawn parallel to **a.b**, and let it be set equal to it. Let line **d.b** be drawn, which by Proposition 33 will be equal and parallel to **a.c**, and all angles are right angles by the last part of Proposition 29. Therefore, by definition, we have the proposed result.

**I**f the product of one side of a triangle multiplied by itself <note>Original: "in seipsum ducto," literally "led into itself," a standard phrase for squaring a number or line.</note> is equal to the two squares which are described from the two remaining sides, the angle which that side opposes is a right angle.
¶ To "lead a line into itself" is to describe its square. ¶ Let there be triangle **a.b.c**, and let the square of side **a.c** be equal to the squares of the two sides **a.b** and **b.c** joined together. It will be, by the preceding [proposition], that the square of **d.c** is equal to the two squares of the two lines **d.b** and **b.c**. And because **b.d** was set equal to **b.a**, it will be by common knowledge (that the squares of equal lines are equal) that the squares of the two lines **a.b** and **b.d** are equal. Wherefore, the square of **d.c** will be equal to the square of **a.c**. Therefore, by another common knowledge, which is the converse of the previous one—namely, that lines whose squares are equal are themselves equal—**d.c** will be equal to **a.c**. Wherefore, by Proposition 8, <note>The SSS (Side-Side-Side) congruence theorem.</note> angle **b** of triangle **a.b.c** is a right angle, which is what was proposed.

# Here begins the second book.

<margin>
<image-desc>A geometric diagram consisting of a large square ABCD divided by a diagonal AD. A point K on the diagonal marks the intersection of a horizontal line EF and a vertical line GH. This illustrates the definition of a gnomon and supplements within a parallelogram.</image-desc>
</margin>

Every rectangular parallelogram is said to be contained under the two lines that form the right angle.
¶ A parallelogram is a surface of parallel sides. <note>Original: "equidistantiũ laterum".</note>
¶ A rectangular parallelogram is one having all its angles as right angles; it is produced from one of its two sides that enclose one of its angles [multiplied] into the other, and therefore it is said to be "contained" under those two lines.

In every parallelogrammatic space, those parallelograms which the diagonal <note>Original: "diameter". In Euclidean geometry, the term diameter is often used for the diagonal of a parallelogram.</note> cuts through the middle are said to consist about the same diagonal. Of those parallelograms which consist about the same diagonal, any one of them along with the two supplements is named a **gnomon**. <term>Gnomon<gloss>An L-shaped geometric figure formed by removing a smaller similar parallelogram from a corner of a larger one.</gloss></term>
¶ Which parallelograms are said to consist about the diagonal, and which are the supplements, was explained above in the demonstration of Proposition 43 of the first book. ¶ For let there be a parallelogram **a.b.c.d.** whose diagonal is **a.d.**; let two lines **e.f.** and **g.h.** be drawn parallel to the opposite sides of the said parallelogram, intersecting each other on the diagonal **a.d.** at point **k**. The parallelogram itself will be divided into four parallelograms, and each of the two parallelograms—which are **a.g.e.k.** and **k.f.b.d.**—which the diagonal cuts through the middle, is said to consist about the diagonal. The remaining two, which the diagonal does not cut, are called **supplements**. These two supplements, along with either of the said parallelograms consisting about the diagonal, compose a certain figure called a **gnomon**. This gnomon lacks one remaining parallelogram consisting about the diagonal to complete the original parallelogram; if that remainder were added upon the diagonal of the total composite, it would fit and be similar to the whole. Hence, although a parallelogram grows by the addition of a gnomon, its shape is not altered, just as Aristotle said in the *Categories*. <note>Original: "predicamentis". This refers to Aristotle's work on the ten categories of being, where he uses the gnomon to illustrate how quantity can increase without changing quality (shape).</note>

### Proposition 1.

<margin>
<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing a large rectangle AFBG. The base line AB is divided into segments AD, DE, and EB. Vertical lines DH and EK are drawn to the top line FG, dividing the large rectangle into three smaller ones. A separate vertical line segment labeled C is shown to the left, representing the common height.</image-desc>
</margin>

If there be two lines, one of which is divided into any number of parts, the rectangle produced by the multiplication of the undivided line into the divided line will be equal to the rectangles produced by the multiplication of the undivided line into each of the individual parts of the divided line. <note>This is the geometric proof of the distributive law of multiplication: a(b+c+d) = ab + ac + ad.</note>
¶ To "lead" one line into another line <note>Original: "Lineam in aliam lineam ducere", meaning to multiply the lengths geometrically.</note> is to erect two lines perpendicularly <note>Original: "orthogonaliter".</note> at the endpoints of one of them, equal to the other line, and to complete the rectangular surface of parallel sides, which by definition is said to be "contained" under those two lines. ¶ Let there be two lines **a.b.** and **c.**, one of which—namely **a.b.**—is divided into any number of parts, which are **a.d.**, **d.e.**, and **e.b.** I say that the rectangle formed by the multiplication of **c.** into the whole of **a.b.** is equal to those rectangular parallelograms joined together which are formed from **c.** into **a.d.**, and into **d.e.**, and into **e.b.** ¶ At points **a.** and **b.**, I shall erect lines **a.f.** and **b.g.** perpendicular to line **a.b.**, each of which is equal to line **c.**, and I shall complete the rectangular surface **a.f.b.g.** by drawing line **f.g.**, which by definition is produced from **c.** into **a.b.**, and is said to be contained under them. I shall also draw from points **d.** and **e.** the lines **d.h.** and **e.k.** parallel to the sides **a.f.** and **b.g.** Each of them will be equal to **c.** according to Proposition 34 of the first book, as each of them is equal to **a.f.** By definition, therefore, the rectangle **a.d.f.h.** is produced from **c.** into **a.d.** and is said to be contained under them; and the rectangle **d.h.e.k.** <note>Original: "d.h.z.e.k.", likely a scribal error for the rectangle formed by the points.</note> is produced from **c.** into **d.e.**; and the rectangle **e.k.b.g.** is produced from **c.** into **e.b.** And because these rectangles joined together are equal to the total rectangle **a.f.b.g.**, it is clear that the proposition is true.

<meta>This page continues the opening of Book II of Euclid’s Elements, which focuses on "geometric algebra." ### Proposition 2
**I**f a line is divided into parts, the area produced by multiplying the whole line by itself <note>Original: "ex ductu totius linee in seipsam." This refers to the area of a square with sides equal to the whole line.</note> will be equal to the two areas produced by multiplying that same whole line by each of its parts.
¶ Let the line **a.b.** be divided at points **c.** and **d.** into segments **a.c.**, **c.d.**, and **d.b.** I say that the area produced by the whole line **a.b.** multiplied by itself—which is the square **a.e.b.f.**—is equal to the areas formed by the whole line multiplied by each of the said parts, as will be clearly evident. This is shown by drawing lines **c.g.** and **z.** <note>The letter z likely refers to a point on the side of the square not explicitly labeled in the text but present in the geometric logic.</note> and **d.b.** parallel to **a.e.** and **z.b.f.** ¶ Alternatively, let a line **k.** be taken equal to line **a.b.**; then, by the previous proposition <note>Proposition 1 of Book II.</note>, the area produced by multiplying **k.** by the whole line **a.b.** is equal to the area produced by multiplying **k.** by all the parts of **a.b.** And because the product of **k.** and **a.b.** is the same as the product of **a.b.** by itself, and the product of **k.** and all the parts of **a.b.** is the same as **a.b.** multiplied by all its parts, it is clear that the proposition is true because **k.** and **a.b.** are equal.

### Proposition 3
**I**f a line is divided into two parts, the area produced by the whole line multiplied by either one of the parts will be equal to the area produced by that same part multiplied by itself added to the product of the two parts. <note>Algebraically, this is expressed as $a(a+b) = a^2 + ab$.</note>
¶ Let line **a.b.** be divided into **a.c.** and **c.b.** I say that the area produced by the whole line **a.b.** multiplied by its part **a.c.** is equal to the square of that same part **a.c.** and the area produced by that same part **a.c.** multiplied by **b.c.** Let the square of line **a.c.** be formed, which is **a.c.d.f.**, and let the surface **a.b.d.e.** be completed; the proposition will then be clear. ¶ Alternatively, let **g.** be taken equal to **a.c.**; since the product of **a.b.** and **a.c.** is the same as **a.c.** and **a.b.** conversely, and the product of **a.c.** by both **a.b.** and **c.b.** and by itself is the same as **g.** multiplied by those same segments. Since **g.** multiplied by the whole **a.b.** is the same as the product of **g.** and **a.c.** plus **g.** and **c.b.** (according to the first proposition of this book), the proposition is clear. Thus, **a.c.** multiplied by **a.b.** is equal to the square of itself plus the product of **a.c.** and **c.b.**, which is what we wished to demonstrate.

### Proposition 4
**I**f a line is divided into two parts, the area produced by the whole line multiplied by itself is equal to the squares of each of the two parts multiplied by themselves, plus twice the area of one part multiplied by the other. <note>This is the geometric proof of the identity $(a+b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2$.</note> From this it is manifest that in every square, the two surfaces that the diagonal <note>Original: "diameter."</note> cuts through the middle are both themselves squares.
¶ Let line **a.b.** be divided into **a.c.** and **b.c.** I say that the square of the whole line **a.b.** is equal to the two squares of the two lines **a.c.** and **b.c.** plus double the area produced by multiplying one by the other. I shall describe the square of one of the parts, which is **c.d.b.e.**, the square of line **c.b.**; to this I shall join a gnomon <gloss>An L-shaped area remaining after a smaller square is removed from a larger one.</gloss> according to the direction of the other line, namely **a.c.** I shall do this in this manner: in the described square I shall draw the diagonal **b.d.**, and from point **a.** I shall draw a perpendicular line to line **a.b.**, which is **a.k.**; I shall extend **a.k.** and the diagonal **b.d.** until they meet at point **f.** From point **f.** I shall draw **f.h.** parallel to line **a.b.**, and I shall extend **f.h.** and **b.e.** until they meet at point **g.**, and I shall extend **c.d.** to **h.** and **z.c.d.** to **k.** And because the two sides **d.e.** and **e.b.** of the triangle **d.e.b.** are equal, then by the 5th proposition of the first book, the two angles **e.d.b.** and **e.b.d.** are equal. And because angle **e.** is a right angle, by the 32nd proposition of the first book, each of them is half of a right angle <note>45 degrees.</note>. By the same reasoning, each of the two angles **c.d.b.** and **c.b.d.** will be half of a right angle. Therefore, by the second part of the 29th proposition of the first book, each of the four angles **b.f.d.**, **b.d.f.**, **k.f.d.**, and **k.d.f.** is half of a right angle. Therefore, by the 6th proposition of the first book, **f.g.** and **g.b.** are equal. Similarly, **f.a.** and **a.h.** are equal; by the same reasoning **f.h.** and **h.d.**, and likewise **f.k.** and **k.d.** are equal. Therefore, both of the two surfaces **a.h.g.f.** and **k.d.h.f.** are squares, and the total square **a.b.f.g.** (which is the square of line **a.b.**) consists of two squares that lie about the diagonal (which are the squares of the two lines **a.c.** and **b.c.**) and of two supplements <note>Original: "supplementis." The rectangles that fill out the square.</note>, each of which is produced by multiplying **a.c.** by **b.c.** Thus our proposition is clear. ¶ Alternatively, let line **a.b.** be divided into **a.c.** and **c.b.** as before.

...and according to the second proposition of this book, it follows that the area produced by the whole line **a.b.** multiplied by itself is equal to the area produced by the same line multiplied by **a.c.** and **c.b.**; but from that line multiplied by **a.c.** alone, as much is produced as from **a.c.** by itself and from **a.c.** by **b.c.**, according to the third proposition of this book. ### Proposition .5.

<margin>
<image-desc>A geometric diagram for Proposition II.5. It features a horizontal line segment AB divided equally at C and unequally at D. A square is constructed on the half-segment CB (labeled CBEF). A diagonal is drawn from C to B (within the square). Rectangles and smaller squares are constructed within this framework, labeled with points a, b, c, d, e, f, g, h, i, k, l, m. To the left of the main construction is a separate rectangle labeled with points a, c, d, i, k.</image-desc>
</margin>

**I**f a straight line is cut into two equal and two unequal parts, the rectangle <note>Original: "rectangulũ." In Greek geometry, "the rectangle contained under two lines" means the area formed by a rectangle with those two lines as sides.</note> contained under the unequal segments of the whole, together with the square described on the segment between the points of section, is equal to the square described on the half of the whole line.
¶ Let the line **a.b.** be divided into equal parts at point **c.** and into unequal parts at point **d.** I say that the square of **c.b.** is equal to the area produced by **a.d.** multiplied by **d.b.** and the square of **c.d.** ¶ I shall describe the square of **c.b.**, which shall be **c.b.f.e.**, in which I shall draw the diagonal **c.b.** and I shall draw **d.g.** parallel to **b.f.**, which cuts the diagonal **c.b.** at point **b.** <note>The letter "b" is repeated here in the original Latin transcription for a point on the diagonal; in modern editions, this intersection is often labeled 'h'.</note>, and from point **b.** I shall draw a line parallel to the line **a.b.**, which shall be **h.k.**, cutting the line **b.f.** at point **m.** and the line **c.e.** at point **l.**, and I shall draw **a.k.** parallel to **c.e.** It will then be, by the corollary of the previous proposition, that both of the two surfaces **l.g.** and **d.m.** are squares; and by the 43rd proposition of the first book <note>Euclid I.43 proves that the "complements" of parallelograms about a diagonal are equal.</note>, the two supplements **c.b.** and **b.f.** are equal. Therefore, by adding the square **d.m.** to both, the parallelogram **c.m.** will be equal to the parallelogram **d.f.**; and because **a.l.** is equal to **c.m.** by the 36th proposition of the first book, **a.l.** will be equal to the gnomon <note>A "gnomon" is the L-shaped area remaining after a smaller square is removed from a larger square in the corner.</note> which stands around the square **l.g.** Therefore, by adding the square **l.g.** to both, **a.d.** <note>This refers to the rectangle formed by the segments.</note> together with the square **l.g.** will be equal to the square **e.f.**, which is what was proposed.

### Proposition .6.

<margin>
<image-desc>A geometric diagram for Proposition II.6. It shows a line segment AB bisected at C, with a segment BD added in line. A square is constructed on the segment CD, with internal constructions and a diagonal, similar in style to the previous diagram. Labels include points a, b, c, d, e, f, g, h, i, k, l, m.</image-desc>
</margin>

**I**f a straight line is divided into two equal parts and another line is added to it in a straight line, the rectangle formed by the whole composed line and the added line, together with the square of the half, is equal to the square described on the line composed of the half and the added line.
¶ Let line **a.b.** be divided into equal parts at point **c.**, and let line **b.d.** be added to it. I say that the square of **c.d.**, which shall be **c.d.e.f.**, is equal to the area produced by the whole **a.d.** multiplied by **b.d.** and the square of **c.b.** ¶ I shall produce the diagonal **d.e.** in the aforesaid square and draw line **b.g.** parallel to **d.f.**, which cuts the diagonal **d.e.** at point **h.**, from which I shall draw a line parallel to line **a.b.**, which shall be **h.k.**, cutting **d.f.** at point **m.** and **c.e.** at point **l.**, and I shall produce **a.k.** parallel to **c.l.** It will be, by the 36th proposition of the first book, that **a.l.** is equal to **c.h.** But **c.h.** will be equal to **b.f.** by the 43rd proposition of the first book; therefore **a.l.** is equal to **b.f.** Thus, by adding **c.m.** to both, **a.m.** will be equal to the entire gnomon standing around **l.g.**; wherefore, by adding **l.g.** to both, **a.m.** with **l.g.** will be equal to the whole square **c.f.** And because both of the two surfaces **l.g.** and **b.m.** are squares: by the corollary of the 4th proposition of this book, the proposition is clear.

### Proposition .8.

<image-desc>Geometric diagram for Proposition 8. A large square is divided by horizontal and vertical lines (c-g, b-h, p-q, m-o) and a diagonal line (e-b). Points are labeled: e, g, h, f (top); r, q, p (side); k, l (on diagonal); m, n (on interior intersections); a, c, b, d (bottom).</image-desc>

**I**f a line is divided into two parts, and a line equal in length to one of those parts is added to it: the square produced by the whole composite line multiplied by itself will be equal to four times the area produced by the first line multiplied by the added part, plus the square produced by the other dividing part. <note>In modern algebra, this relates to the identity: $(a+b)^2 = 4ab + (a-b)^2$.</note>

Let **a.b.** be divided at point **c.** in whatever way it happens: to which **b.d.** is added, being equal to **c.b.** I say that the square of the whole line **a.d.**, which is **a.d.e.f.**, is equal to four times the area produced by **a.b.** multiplied by **b.d.**, together with the square of **a.c.** This will be clear by drawing the diameter **d.e.** and the lines **c.g.** and **b.h.** parallel to line **d.f.** and intersecting the diameter at points **k.** and **l.** Through these points, let **p.q.k.r.** and **m.n.l.o.** be drawn parallel to **a.d.** For, by the corollary of the 4th proposition of this book, each of the areas **r.g.**, **n.q.**, and **b.m.** will be squares; and because **c.b.** was set equal to **b.d.**, both of the areas **c.l.** and **l.p.** will be squares. There will be four equal squares dividing the square **c.p.**, and because the whole <term>gnomon (the L-shaped area remaining when a smaller square is removed from a larger one)</term> surrounding the square **r.g.** is four times the area produced by **a.b.** multiplied by **b.d.**, which is four times the area **a.l.**, the proposition is proven.

**I**f a line is divided into two equal and two unequal parts: the squares produced by the unequal sections multiplied by themselves, taken together, are double the squares produced by the half [of the line] and the segment between the two points of division, taken together. <note>Algebraically: $AD^2 + DB^2 = 2(AC^2 + CD^2)$.</note>

Let line **a.b.** be divided into equal parts at **c.** and into unequal parts at **d.** I say that the square of **a.d.** and the square of **d.b.** joined together are double the square of **a.c.** and the square of **c.d.** joined together. Upon line **a.b.**, I erect the line **c.e.** perpendicular and equal to each of the lines **a.c.** and **c.b.**, and I draw **a.e.** and **e.b.** By the 32nd proposition of the first book, each of the angles **a.** and **b.**, and each of the partial angles at **e.**, will be half of a right angle; therefore the whole angle at **e.** is a right angle. I draw **d.f.** parallel to **c.e.** and perpendicular to line **a.b.**; each of the angles at **d.** will be a right angle, and the angle **d.f.b.** will be half of a right angle by the 32nd proposition of the first book (or by the second part of the 29th of the first book). Therefore, by the 6th proposition of the first book, **d.f.** and **d.b.** are equal. From point **f.** I draw **f.g.** parallel to **a.b.**; by the second part of the 29th proposition of the first book, each of the angles at **g.** will be a right angle, and the angle **e.f.g.** is half of a right angle. Therefore, by the 6th proposition of the same book, the sides **e.g.** and **g.f.** are equal. Since, by the <term>penultimate proposition (the Pythagorean Theorem, Book I, Prop. 47)</term> of the same book, the square of **e.f.** is equal to the square of **e.g.** and the square of **g.f.**, it will be double the square of **g.f.**, and therefore double the square of **c.d.** Likewise, by the same theorem, the square of **e.a.** is equal to the square of **a.c.** and the square of **c.e.**; it will be double the square of **a.c.** Because the square of **a.f.** is equal to the square of **e.f.** and **a.e.** by the same theorem, it will be double the square of **a.c.** and the square of **c.d.** But the square of **a.f.** is also equal, by the same theorem, to the square of **a.d.** and the square of **d.f.** Therefore, the square of **a.d.** and the square of **d.f.** are double the square of **a.c.** and the square of **c.d.** And because the square of **d.f.** is equal to the square of **d.b.**, the squares of the two lines will be double...

### Proposition .10.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram for Proposition 10 illustrating a line segment a-c-b-d with point c as the midpoint of ab. A perpendicular ce is drawn from c, equal to ac and cb. **If** a line is divided into two equal parts, and another line is added to it in a straight line: the square that is described from the whole [original line] with the added part, and the square from the part that was added—both squares taken together—must be double the square from the half [of the original line] and the square produced by the line consisting of the half and the added part, both squares taken together. <note>In modern algebraic terms, this states that $(2a+b)^2 + b^2 = 2(a^2 + (a+b)^2)$.</note>

¶ Let line **a.b.** be divided equally at **c.** and let line **b.d.** be added to it. I say that the two squares of the two lines **a.d.** and **b.d.** taken together are double the two squares of the two lines **a.c.** and **c.d.** taken together. ¶ I erect **c.e.** perpendicular to line **a.b.** and equal to each of the lines **a.c.** and **c.b.**, and I complete the triangle **a.e.b.** by drawing lines **a.e.** and **e.b.** It will be as in the previous [proposition] that each of the angles **a.** and **b.**, and each of those which are at **e.**, is half of a right angle <note>45 degrees</note> by Proposition 32 of the first book: and the whole angle **e.** is a right angle. From point **e.** I draw **e.f.** equal and parallel to **c.d.**, and I draw **f.d.** and **e.b.** until they meet at point **g.**, and I draw line **a.g.** By the last part of Proposition 29 of the first book, angle **c.e.f.** will be a right angle, but angle **c.e.b.** is half a right angle. Therefore angle **b.e.f.** is likewise half a right angle. And because by Proposition 33 of the same [book] **f.d.** is parallel to **c.e.**, by Proposition 34 of the same, angle **f.** will be a right angle. Therefore by Proposition 32 of the same, angle **e.g.f.** will be half a right angle. And likewise by the same, angle **d.b.g.** is similarly half a right angle, because angle **b.d.g.** is a right angle. Therefore by Proposition 6 of the same, the two sides **e.f.** and **f.g.** are equal. And likewise the two sides **d.b.** and **d.g.** are equal. Therefore by the penultimate proposition of the same <note>original: "penultimam eiusdem", referring to the Pythagorean Theorem, Proposition 47 of Book I</note> the square of **e.g.** is double the square of **e.f.**, and therefore [double] the square of **c.d.** ¶ And likewise by the same, the square of **a.e.** is double the square of **a.c.** And because the square of **a.g.** is by the same [theorem] equal to the squares of **a.e.** and **e.g.**, and similarly also to the squares of **a.d.** and **d.g.** But because the square of **d.g.** is equal to the square of **b.d.**, the two squares of the two lines **a.d.** and **b.d.** taken together will be double the two squares of the two lines **a.c.** and **c.d.** taken together, which is what was proposed. This, and all previous [propositions], hold true for numbers just as they do for lines.

### Proposition .11.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram for Proposition 11 depicting a square abdc. Point e is the midpoint of the side bd. **To cut** a given line so that the rectangle contained under the whole and one portion is equal to the square that is made from the remaining section. <note>This construction is used to find the "Golden Ratio."</note>

¶ Let the given line be **a.b.**, which we wish to divide thus: so that the [area] produced from the whole and its smaller portion is equal to the square of the larger part. ¶ I describe the square of it, which is **a.b.c.d.**, and I divide the side **b.d.** equally at **e.**, and I draw **a.e.** and I extend **e.b.** as far as **f.**, so that **e.f.** is equal to **a.e.** From the outer portion **b.f.**, I describe a square which cuts off from side **a.b.** a portion equal to **b.f.**, which is **b.h.**, and let the described square be **b.f.h.g.** I say that **a.b.** is thus divided at point **h.** so that the [area] which is made from the whole **a.b.** multiplied by its portion **b.h.** <note>The text here contains a common scribe's error or labeling variation; geometrically, this usually refers to the rectangle formed by the whole line and the smaller segment being equal to the square of the larger segment.</note> is equal to the square of **b.h.** I extend **g.b.** as far as **k.**, which will be parallel to **a.c.** And therefore line **d.b.** is divided equally at **e.**, and the line **b.f.** is added to it. By Proposition 6 of this book, the [area] made from **d.f.** multiplied by **b.f.**, with the square of **e.b.**, will be equal to the square of **e.f.**, and therefore to the square of **e.a.** Therefore by the penultimate [proposition]...

## Proposition .12.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing an obtuse triangle with vertices labeled b, a, and c. The angle at vertex a is obtuse. The side ba is extended to the left to a point d. From vertex c, a perpendicular line is dropped to meet the extended base line at point d, forming a right-angled triangle cda.</image-desc>

### In those triangles which have an obtuse angle: the square of the side which faces the obtuse angle is greater than the squares of both remaining sides which contain the obtuse angle by as much as twice the rectangle contained under one of those sides and the line added to it externally between the obtuse angle and the perpendicular. <note>This is a geometric version of the Law of Cosines: $c^2 = a^2 + b^2 + 2ax$, where $x$ is the external extension.</note>

¶ Let there be a triangle **a.b.c.** having an obtuse angle at **a.** From point **c.**, let a perpendicular line be drawn to line **b.a.**, which will necessarily fall outside the triangle **a.b.c.**; otherwise, the obtuse angle would be a right angle or less than a right angle by the 16th proposition of the first book. Therefore, let **c.d.** be the perpendicular upon line **a.b.** extended to **d.** I say that the square of side **b.c.** (which faces the obtuse angle) is greater than the two squares of the two lines **a.b.** and **a.c.** (which surround the obtuse angle) by twice the rectangle produced from **b.a.** multiplied by **a.d.** For the "power" of a line is considered in respect to its square; hence any line is said to be "able" <note>original: "poſſe" - the Latin "potentia" (power) refers to the area of the square a line can "produce."</note> to do as much as the area it produces when multiplied by itself. For by the 4th proposition of this book, the square of **b.d.** will be equal to the two squares of the two lines **b.a.** and **a.d.** and double the rectangle produced from **b.a.** multiplied by **a.d.** And because the square of **b.c.** (by the second to last proposition of the first book <note>The Pythagorean Theorem, Book I, Prop. 47.</note>) is equal to the square of **b.d.** and the square of **d.c.**, it will itself be equal to the squares of the three lines **b.a.**, **a.d.**, and **d.c.**, and double the rectangle produced from **b.a.** multiplied by **a.d.** But by that same proposition, the square of **a.c.** is equal to the squares of **a.d.** and **d.c.** Therefore, the square of **b.c.** is equal to the squares of the two lines **b.a.** and **a.c.** and double the rectangle produced from **b.a.** multiplied by **a.d.** Wherefore **b.c.** is "able" to do more than the two lines **b.a.** and **a.c.** by as much as double the rectangle produced from **b.a.** multiplied by **a.d.** For we have already said that any line is said to be "able" to do as much as it produces when multiplied by itself, which is what was proposed.

## Proposition .13.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing an acute-angled triangle with vertices a (top), b (bottom left), and c (bottom right). A vertical perpendicular line is dropped from vertex a to the base line bc, meeting it at point d.</image-desc>

### In every acute-angled triangle <term>origonij: from the Greek "oxygonios," meaning acute-angled</term>, the square of the side which faces an acute angle is less than the squares of both sides containing that acute angle by as much as twice the rectangle contained under one of those sides (upon which the perpendicular stands) and the segment of it that lies between the perpendicular and the acute angle.

¶ What is proposed here concerning the side facing any acute angle in an acute-angled triangle holds true for the side facing any acute angle in any triangle, whether it be right-angled <term>orthogonius: a triangle with one right angle</term>, obtuse-angled <term>ambligonius: a triangle with one obtuse angle</term>, or acute-angled. ¶ Let there be, therefore, in triangle **a.b.c.** (of whatever kind of triangle it may be) an acute angle at **c.** If it is an acute-angled triangle, let a perpendicular be drawn from either of the angles **a.** or **b.** to either base **b.c.** or **a.c.**, because in such a case the perpendicular always falls inside the triangle. But if it is obtuse-angled or right-angled, let the perpendicular be drawn from the obtuse or right angle to the opposite side, which clearly falls inside the triangle. And to speak simply, since in every triangle there are two acute angles, one of the remaining angles (which are **a.** and **b.**) will necessarily be acute. I will therefore draw the perpendicular to that line which...

...lies between the acute angles. Let it be then that in triangle **a.b.c.**, angle **b.** is also acute. I shall therefore draw the perpendicular **a.d.** to the base **b.c.**, which, as has been said, falls within the triangle. I say therefore that the square of **a.b.**, which faces the acute angle **c.**, is less than the two squares of the two lines **a.c.** and **c.b.** by as much as twice the area formed by **b.c.** multiplied by **d.c.** And I also say that the square of **a.c.**, which also faces angle **b.** (which we have set as acute, regardless of what angle **a.** might be), is less than the two squares of the two lines **a.b.** and **b.c.** by as much as twice the area formed by **c.b.** multiplied by **b.d.** 

For, by the 7th [proposition] of this book <note>Euclid II.7 relates the square of a whole line to the squares of its segments and the rectangles formed by them.</note>, the square of **b.c.** with the square of **d.c.** is equal to twice the area formed by **b.c.** multiplied by **d.c.** and the square of the other part, namely **b.d.** Therefore, by adding the square of **a.d.** to both sides, the square of **b.c.** along with the squares of the two lines **a.d.** and **d.c.** will be equal to the squares of the two lines **a.d.** and **d.b.** and twice the area formed by **c.b.** multiplied by **c.d.** 

And because, by the penultimate [proposition] of the first [book] <note>original: "penultimam primi." This refers to Euclid I.47, the Pythagorean Theorem.</note>, the square of **a.c.** is equal to the squares of the two lines **a.d.** and **d.c.**, then the square of **b.c.** with the square of **a.c.** will be equal to the squares of the two lines **a.d.** and **d.b.** and twice the area formed by **b.c.** multiplied by **c.d.** But by the same penultimate [proposition] of the first [book], the square of **a.b.** is equal to the squares of the two lines **a.d.** and **b.d.** Therefore, the square of **b.c.** with the square of **a.c.** is equal to the square of **a.b.** and twice the area formed by **b.c.** multiplied by **c.d.** Wherefore, the square of **a.b.** is less than the two sides **b.c.** and **a.c.** by exactly twice the area formed by **b.c.** multiplied by **c.d.**, which is what was proposed. In a similar way, you will prove that the side **a.c.**, which faces the acute angle **b.**, is less than the two sides **a.b.** and **b.c.** by twice the area formed by **c.b.** multiplied by **b.d.**

¶ It should be noted that through this [proposition], the preceding one, and the penultimate of the first [book]: once the sides of any triangle are known, its area is known; and with the help of tables of chords and arcs <note>An early form of trigonometric tables.</note>, every one of its angles is known.

## Proposition .14.

->To describe a square equal to a given triangle.<-

**G**iven a triangle **a.**, for which we wish to describe an equal square. I will designate a surface of parallel sides and right angles <note>A rectangle.</note> equal to the given triangle, according to what the 42nd [proposition] of the first book teaches. Let that surface be **b.c.d.e.** If its sides are equal, we have what we seek, for it will be a square by definition. But if the sides are unequal, then I shall join the smaller of the sides to the larger in a straight line. Let the line **c.f.** be equal to the smaller of the two sides, which is **c.e.**, joined to the larger, which is **b.c.**, in a straight line. I shall divide the whole line **b.f.** into two equal parts at point **g.**, and with **g.** as the center upon line **b.f.**, according to the length of line **g.b.**, I shall describe a semicircle **b.h.f.** I shall then extend the side **e.c.** until it cuts the circumference at point **h.** I say that the square of line **c.h.** is equal to the given triangle. 

I shall draw the line **g.h.** Since line **b.f.** is divided into equal parts at **g.** and into unequal parts at **c.**, then by the 5th [proposition] of this book, the area formed by the multiplication of **b.c.** by **c.f.** with the square of **c.g.** will be equal to the square of **g.f.**, and therefore equal to the square of **g.b.** Consequently, by the penultimate [proposition] of the first [book], it is equal to the two squares of the two lines **g.c.** and **c.h.** Therefore, by taking away the square of **c.g.** from both sides, the area formed by **b.c.** multiplied by **c.f.** (which is equal to the surface **b.c.d.e.** because **c.f.** is equal to **c.e.**) will be equal to the square of line **c.h.** Wherefore, the square of line **c.h.** is equal to triangle **a.**, which is what was proposed.

And note that by this method is found the <term>tetragonal side</term> <note>The side of a square equal in area to another shape; effectively the square root of the area.</note> of any rectangle and, simply put, of every figure contained by straight lines, whatever it may be. For we shall resolve every such figure into triangles, and we shall find the tetragonal side of each of those triangles according to the teaching of this [proposition]. Then, by the penultimate [proposition] of the first [book], we shall find one single line that can [form a square] equal to all the tetragonal sides found. For example, I wish now to find the tetragonal side of the irregular rectilinear figure **a.b.c.d.e.f.** I resolve it into three triangles which are...

**a.b.f.c.d.e.z.c.f.e.** I also find, according to the teaching of this [proposition], the three square sides <note>Latin: *latera tetragonica*. In this context, these are the sides of squares whose areas are equal to the three triangles mentioned previously.</note> of those three triangles, which are **g.b.**, **b.k.**, and **k.l.**; and I erect **b.k.** perpendicularly upon **g.b.** and extend **g.k.** and by the penultimate [proposition] of the first [book] <note>The Pythagorean Theorem, Euclid I.47, which states that the square of the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares of the other two sides.</note>, **g.k.** will be equal to the squares of the two lines **g.b.** and **b.k.** Then I erect the third side **k.l.** perpendicularly upon the line **g.k.** and extend the line **g.l.**; and by the penultimate [proposition] of the first [book], **g.l.** will be the square side <note>The side of a square equal in area to the whole figure.</note> of the entire rectilinear figure proposed.

Circles whose diameters are equal are themselves equal. Those whose [diameters] are larger are larger, and those whose [diameters] are smaller are smaller. ¶ A line is said to touch <term>tangent</term> <note>Latin: *pertingere* / *tangere*</note> a circle if, when it touches the circle and is extended in either direction, it does not cut the circle. ¶ Circles are said to touch one another which, while touching each other, do not intersect. ¶ Straight lines in a circle are said to be equally distant from the center when the perpendiculars drawn from the center to them are equal. ¶ That line is said to be further from the center upon which the longer perpendicular falls. ¶ A straight line containing the parts of a circle is called a **chord** <note>Latin: *corda*</note>. ¶ A part of the circumference is called an **arc** <note>Latin: *arcus*</note>. ¶ The angle of a segment <note>Latin: *portio*</note> is that which is contained by the chord and the arc. ¶ An angle is said to stand upon an arc when it is contained by two straight lines starting from any point on the arc to the endpoints of the chord. <term>inscribed angle</term> ¶ A **sector** of a circle is a figure contained by two lines drawn from the center and the arc which is intercepted by them. ¶ The angle enclosed by those lines is said to stand at the center. <term>central angle</term> ¶ Similar segments of circles are those in which the angles standing upon the arc are equal to one another. ¶ Arcs are also similar which subtend equal angles in the manner previously described.

## Proposition 1.

To find the center of a given circle. From which it is manifest that if two straight lines in the same circle are terminated at the circumference, neither of them bisects the other at right angles unless it passes through the center.
¶ Let the proposed circle be **a.b.c.**, the center of which we wish to find. I draw in the circle any line **a.c.** and divide it equally at point **d.** From which [point **d.**] I draw a perpendicular to line **a.c.**, which I extend to the circumference on both sides; let it be **e.d.b.** Which [line **e.b.**] I again divide equally at point **f.**, which I say is the center of the circle. For if it is not, it will be either elsewhere, or on the line **e.b.**, or outside it. Not on line **e.b.**; for if it were on it, as at point **g.**,
<margin>equal</margin>
the line **c.f.** would be greater than line **e.g.**, namely a part [being equal] to the whole, which is impossible. <note>The author uses a "reductio ad absurdum" argument here: if the center were anywhere else, it would contradict the definition of a circle where all radii are equal.</note> But if it were outside line **e.b.**, as at point **h.**, let lines **h.a.**, **h.d.**, and **h.c.** be drawn. And because sides **h.d.** and **d.a.** of triangle **h.d.a.** are equal to sides **h.d.** and **d.c.** of triangle **h.d.c.**, and base **h.a.** is [equal] to base **h.c.**, by the 8th [proposition] of the first [book] <note>Euclid I.8, the SSS congruence theorem.</note> angle **h.d.a.** will be equal to angle **c.d.h.**, since both are right angles; and since angle **a.d.b.** was also a right angle, **a.d.b.** would be equal to **a.d.h.** by the 3rd postulate <note>Referring to the common notion that "the whole is greater than the part."</note> of the first [book], namely the part [equal] to the whole, which is impossible. Therefore, the center of the given circle is nowhere else than at point **f.**, which was to be demonstrated.

## Proposition 2.

**I**f two points are marked on the circumference of a circle, the straight line drawn from one to the other must cut the circle. <note>This proposition proves that any straight line connecting two points on a circle—what we call a "chord"—must lie entirely inside the circle, rather than curving outside it.</note>

¶ Let there be a circle $a.b.$, the center of which is $c$, and let two points be marked, which are $a$ and $b$. I say that the straight line joining one with the other will cut the circle. Otherwise, it would fall outside the circle: let $a.e.b$ be that straight line, if possible. I shall draw the lines $c.a$ and $c.b$. By the 5th [proposition] of the first [book], <note>Euclid I.5: In isosceles triangles, the angles at the base are equal.</note> the angles $c.a.b$ and $c.b.a$ will be equal. I shall also draw the line $c.e$, which cuts the circumference at point $d$. By the 16th [proposition] of the first [book], <note>Euclid I.16: An exterior angle of a triangle is greater than either of the opposite interior angles.</note> the angle $a.e.c$ is greater than the angle $c.b.e$. Therefore, it is greater than angle $c.a.e$. Because of this, by the 18th [proposition] of the same [book], <note>Euclid I.18: In any triangle, the side opposite the greater angle is longer.</note> the side $a.c$ is greater than side $c.e$. And since $c.d$ is equal to $c.a$ <note>Because both are radii of the same circle.</note>, then $c.d$ is greater than $c.e$—the part is greater than the whole, which is impossible. Therefore, because the line joining the two points $a$ and $b$ does not pass outside the circle, it must cut it, which is what was proposed.

## Proposition 3.

**I**f a line placed within a circle does not pass through the center, and another line coming from the center bisects it <term>cuts it into equal parts</term>, then it must stand upon it **orthogonally** <term>perpendicularly</term>. And if it stands upon it orthogonally, it must divide it into equal parts.

¶ Let there be a line $a.b$ placed within a circle $a.b$, the center of which is $c$. Let the line $c.d$, coming from the center, divide it into equal parts. I say that it divides it orthogonally. And conversely, namely: if it divides it orthogonally, it divides it into equal parts. I shall draw the lines $c.a$ and $c.b$. First, I assume that it divides it into equal parts: therefore, the two sides $c.d$ and $d.a$ of triangle $c.d.a$ are equal to the two sides $c.d$ and $d.b$ of triangle $c.d.b$, and the base $c.a$ is equal to the base $c.b$ <note>Radii of the same circle are always equal.</note>. Therefore, by the 8th [proposition] of the first [book], <note>Euclid I.8: The SSS (Side-Side-Side) congruence theorem.</note> the angle $d$ of one is equal to the angle $d$ of the other. Thus, each is a right angle; therefore $c.d$ is perpendicular to $a.b$, which is what was proposed.
¶ Again, I assume that $c.d$ is perpendicular to $a.b$, and I will show that it divides $a.b$ into equal parts. Because of this assumption, each of the angles at $d$ is a right angle, and therefore one is equal to the other. And because by the 5th [proposition] of the first [book] the angle $c.a.d$ is equal to the angle $c.b.d$, and side $c.a$ is equal to side $c.b$, then by the 26th [proposition] of the same first [book], <note>Euclid I.26: The AAS (Angle-Angle-Side) congruence theorem.</note> the line $a.d$ will be equal to the line $d.b$, which is what was proposed.

## Proposition 4.

**I**f two lines inside a circle intersect each other and do not pass through the center, they cannot both be bisected at the point of intersection.

¶ Let there be a circle $a.b.c.d$, the center of which is $e$. Let two lines $a.c$ and $b.d$ intersect each other at point $f$. Let both of them, or at least one of them, not pass through the center. I say that they do not divide each other into equal parts, such that each is bisected by the other.
¶ If this were possible: let it be so, and first assume that neither passes through the center. From the center $e$ I shall draw the line $e.f$. By the most recent previous proposition [Prop. 3], each of the angles $a.f.e$, $e.f.c$, $b.f.e$, and $e.f.d$ would be a right angle, which is impossible; for in that case, a right angle would be smaller than a right angle. <note>In the geometric configuration, the angles would be nested inside one another.</note>
¶ Now let one of them pass through the center and the other not. Let $b.d$ pass through the center. I still say they do not divide each other into equal parts. If they did, then by the first part of the previous proposition: since $b.d$ is drawn from the center and divides $a.c$ into equal parts, it must divide it orthogonally. Thus $a.c$ would also divide $b.d$ orthogonally. And because it [the line $a.c$] divides $b.d$ into equal parts as the opponent <note>original: *adversarius*. This refers to the hypothetical person arguing for the impossible case in a proof by contradiction.</note> claims, it would have to pass through the center by the corollary of the first [proposition] of this book. Thus both would pass through the center, which is against the **hypothesis**.

### ->Proposition .5.<-

**T**hat the centers of circles intersecting one another are different.
¶ Let there be two circles, $a.c.b.$ and $a.d.b.$, intersecting each other at two points, $a$ and $b$. I say that their centers are different. ¶ For if they were to have the same center, that point would, by definition, be within the portion common to both circles; let that center be $e$. Let the lines $e.a$ and $e.f.c$ be drawn. By definition, the two lines $e.a$ and $e.f$ will be equal. <note>Because they are both radii of the first circle.</note> ¶ Likewise, by definition, the two lines $e.a$ and $e.c$ are equal. <note>Because they are both radii of the second circle.</note> Therefore, $e.f$ is equal to $e.c$, since each of them is equal to $e.a$. This would mean a part is equal to the whole, which is impossible. <note>original: "pars videlicet toti quod est impossibile." This relies on the common notion that the whole is always greater than its parts; here, the segment $e.f$ is clearly only a part of the longer line $e.c$.</note>

**I**t is necessary that the centers of circles touching one another be different.
¶ Let there be two circles, $a.b.$ and $a.c.$, touching each other at point $a$. I say that their centers are different. For if they were to have the same center, it would, by definition, be within the smaller of them, since the smaller is placed inside the larger. Let that center be $d$, and let the lines $d.a$ and $d.b.c$ be drawn. By definition, each of the two lines $d.b$ and $d.c$ would be equal to $d.a$, which is impossible. <note>As in the previous proof, the radius of the smaller circle cannot be the same length as the radius of the larger circle if they share a center and a touching point.</note> ¶ Regarding circles that touch externally—where one is outside the other—it is manifest by the definition of a center that they do not have the same center.

**I**f a point other than the center is marked on the diameter of a circle, and many lines are drawn from it to the circumference: that which passes through the center will be the longest of all. That which completes the diameter will be the shortest of all. Those lines closer to the center will be longer than the others. ¶ And it follows that the further they are from the center, the shorter they will be. ¶ Furthermore, it is necessary that two lines on either side of the shortest line, standing at equal distances, be equal to each other.
¶ Let it be that on the diameter $a.f$ of the circle $a.b.c$, the center of which is $h$, there is a marked point $k$ other than the center, from which many lines are drawn to the circumference: $k.a, k.b, k.c, k.d, k.e, k.f, k.g$. Let $a.k$ pass through the center $h$, and let $k.f$ be the remainder of the diameter. Let it be that $k.e$ and $k.g$ are equidistant from $k.f$—that is to say, the angle $e.k.f$ is equal to the angle $f.k.g$. I say that $k.a$ is the longest of all, and $k.f$ is the shortest of all; the others are longer the closer they are to the center: thus $k.b$ is longer than $k.c$, and $k.c$ is longer than $k.d$, and $k.d$ is longer than $k.e$. And $k.e$ and $k.g$ are equal.
For in the triangle $h.k.b$, the two sides $h.b$ and $h.k$ (by the 20th [proposition] of the first [book]) <note>Euclid I.20: Any two sides of a triangle are greater than the third side.</note> are together greater than side $b.k$. Since $h.b$ and $h.a$ are equal <note>as radii</note>, then $a.k$ <note>which is $h.a + h.k$</note> will be greater than $b.k$. By the same reasoning, it is greater than all the others; and this is the first part.

Therefore they will be greater than line $h.f$. If the common line $h.k$ is taken away, there remains $k.e$, which is greater than $k.f$. By the same reasoning, any of the others will be greater than it; and this is the second part.

### Proposition .8.

<image-desc>Two geometrical diagrams are printed to the left of the main text column. The upper diagram shows two circles, one contained within the other, and multiple radii (labeled k-b, k-c, k-d, k-e, k-f, k-g) extending from a shared interior point 'k' to the circumferences. The lower diagram, corresponding to Proposition 8, depicts a circle with center 'n' and an external point 'a'. Several lines radiate from point 'a' through the circle: a central line 'a-k-n-b' passing through the center 'n', and lateral lines such as 'a-g-c' and 'a-f-d'. Labels 'h', 'o', 'l', and 'm' denote various intersections and points along these lines.</image-desc>

**I**F a point is marked outside a circle, and from it many lines are drawn to the circumference, cutting through the circle: that which passes through the center will be the longest of all. ¶ Moreover, those closer to the center are longer than those more remote. ¶ Regarding the line segments applied to the circumference from the outside <note>i.e., the segments between the external point and the near side of the circle</note>: indeed, the one that lies in a straight line with the diameter is the shortest of all. ¶ Those closer to it are shorter than those more remote. ¶ And two such lines that are equally close to the shortest one on either side are equal.

¶ Let there be a point $a$ outside a circle $b.c.d$, the center of which is $n$. Let many lines be drawn to the circumference, cutting the circle, namely $a.k.n.b$, $a.g.c$, $a.d$, and $a.e$ <note>The OCR lists these as a.b.c, a.g.d, and a.f.e, but the logic follows the diagram's labels</note>. I say that $a.b$, which passes through the center, will be the longest of all, and that $a.c$ is greater than $a.d$, and $a.d$ greater than $a.e$. Also, that $a.k$ is the shortest of all exterior segments; and that $a.b$ <note>This is likely a typo for $a.k$ in the source</note> is shorter than $a.g$, and $a.g$ is shorter than $a.f$. Finally, I say that if $a.l$ is drawn so that it and $a.b$ <note>Again, likely a typo for $a.g$ or similar</note> are equally distant from $a.k$—that is, the angle $k.a.b$ is equal to angle $k.a.l$—then they themselves will be equal.

¶ I shall draw lines $n.c, n.d, n.e, n.f, n.g,$ and $n.b$ from the center $n$. By the 20th [proposition] of the first [book] <note>The triangle inequality: any two sides of a triangle are greater than the third.</note>, the two sides $a.n$ and $n.c$ of triangle $a.n.c$ are greater than $a.c$. Since $n.c$ is equal to $n.b$ <note>both are radii</note>, the line $a.b$ <note>which is $a.n + n.b$</note> is greater than $a.c$. By the same reasoning, it will be greater than all others, which is the first part. And because the two sides $a.n$ and $n.c$ of triangle $a.n.c$ are equal to the two sides $a.n$ and $n.d$ of triangle $a.n.d$, and angle $a.n.c$ is greater than angle $a.n.d$, it follows by the 24th [proposition] of the first [book] that base $a.c$ is greater than base $a.d$. By the same reasoning, $a.d$ is greater than $a.e$, which is the second part. ¶ Also, because in triangle $a.n.b$ <note>meaning any triangle formed with the center</note>, two sides $a.k$ and $n.k$ <note>Original text says $a.b$ and $n.b$</note> are greater than $a.n$ by the 20th [proposition] of the first [book]. Since $n.b$ is equal to $n.k$, it follows by a common notion that $a.b$ is greater than $a.k$. In the same way, any other exterior line will be greater than $a.k$, which is the third part. ¶ Furthermore, because by the 21st [proposition] of the first [book], two lines $a.b$ and $b.n$ are smaller than two lines $a.g$ and $g.n$ <note>Euclid I.21: lines drawn to a point inside a triangle are shorter than the other two sides of the triangle</note>, and $b.n$ is equal to $g.n$, it follows by a common notion that $a.g$ is greater than $a.b$ <note>This $a.b$ refers to the exterior segment $a.k$</note>. In the same way $a.f$ will be greater than $a.g$, which is the fourth part. ¶ Finally, if $a.l$ were not equal to $a.b$ <note>the corresponding exterior segment</note> despite being equally distant from $a.k$, one would be larger. Let it be $a.l$. I will set $a.m$ equal to $a.b$ and extend the line $n.o.m$. Since the two sides $m.a$ and $a.n$ of triangle $m.a.n$ are equal to the two sides $b.a$ and $a.n$ of triangle $b.a.n$, and angle $m.a.n$ is equal to angle $b.a.n$, then by the 4th [proposition] of the first [book], base $m.n$ is equal to base $n.b$. And since $m.o$ <note>the full radius</note> is equal to $n.b$, then $n.o$ would be equal to $n.m$—that is, a part would be equal to the whole, which is impossible. And this is the fifth part.

### Proposition .9.

<meta>This page continues the third book of Euclid’s Elements, which focuses on the geometry of circles. Following the previous discussion on the lengths of lines drawn from points inside or outside a circle, this section establishes how to identify the center of a circle and defines the limits of how circles can intersect or touch one another.</meta>

->III<-

# Proposition .9.

If, from a point marked within a circle, more than two lines drawn to the circumference are equal, it is necessary that that point is the center of the circle.
¶ Let there be a point marked **a** within the circle **b.c.d**, from which three lines **a.b**, **a.c**, and **a.d** are drawn to the circumference, which I posit to be equal. I say that point **a** is the center of the circle. I shall draw two lines <note>These are "chords," lines segmenting the circle.</note> **c.b** and **d.c**, and I shall divide each of them into two equal parts: **c.b** at point **e**, and **d.c** at point **f**. Then I shall draw lines **e.a** and **f.a** and extend them to the circumference on both sides. By the 8th [proposition] of the first [book] <note>The SSS (Side-Side-Side) congruence theorem.</note>, each of the angles at **a.e.b** will be equal to the other. Therefore, by the 13th [proposition] <note>which states that if a line stands on another line, the adjacent angles are either two right angles or equal to two right angles</note>, each will be a right angle. Likewise, by the same reasoning, each of the angles at **a.f.d** is a right angle. Therefore, by the corollary of the first [proposition] of this book <note>Proposition III.1 states that the perpendicular bisector of a chord passes through the center.</note>, because **a.e** divides **c.b** equally and perpendicularly, it passes through the center. Similarly, **a.f** also passes through the center because it divides **d.c** equally and perpendicularly. Therefore, **a** is the center, which is what was proposed.

<image-desc>A circular diagram labeled for Proposition 9. Inside circle b-c-d, a point 'a' is connected by three lines to the circumference. Chords c-b and d-c are drawn, each intersected by perpendicular lines originating from 'a' at points 'e' and 'f'.</image-desc>

# Proposition .10.

If a circle cuts another circle, it is necessary that it cuts it in only two places.
¶ If it were possible, let two circles cut each other in more than two places, specifically at three points **a**, **b**, and **c**. I shall draw lines **a.b** and **a.c**, which I shall divide into equal parts at points **d** and **e**. From point **e**, I shall draw line **e.f** perpendicular to line **a.c**; and from point **d**, line **d.f** perpendicular to line **a.b**. Let these two lines **e.f** and **d.f** intersect at point **f**. By the corollary of the first [proposition] of this book, point **f** would be the center of both circles, which is impossible according to the 5th [proposition] of this book <note>Proposition III.5 states that circles which cut one another cannot have the same center.</note>.

<image-desc>A diagram for Proposition 10 showing the intersection of two circles, forming a lens-like shape. Three points 'a', 'b', and 'c' are marked where the circles supposedly meet. Lines and perpendiculars intersect at a central point 'f'.</image-desc>

# Proposition .11.

If a circle touches another circle <note>This refers to tangency, where circles meet at a single point.</note>, and a line passes through their centers, it is necessary that the line reaches the point of contact.
¶ If the line passing through the centers of two circles **c.e** and **d.c** that touch each other—either internally or externally—does not go to the point of contact, let it cut the circumference of each. Let **a** be the center of circle **e.d** and **b** be the center of circle **e.c**. Let the straight line **a.b.c.d** be drawn cutting the circumference of both. Let lines be drawn from point **e** (which is the point of contact) to the centers, which are **e.a** and **e.b**. In the case of internal contact, by the 20th [proposition] of the first [book] <note>The Triangle Inequality: any two sides of a triangle are together greater than the third side.</note>, the two lines **e.b** and **b.a** are longer than **e.a**, and therefore longer than **a.d** <note>because a.e and a.d are both radii of the same circle</note>. And since **b.c** is equal to **e.b** (because **b** is the center of circle **e.c**), the lines **e.a** and **c.b** would be longer than **a.b**. Consequently, **a.d** and **c.b** would be greater than the whole line **a.b**, which is false.

<image-desc>A diagram for Proposition 11 depicting a small circle tangent to the interior of a larger circle at point 'e'. A line segment passes through the centers 'a' and 'b' towards the point of contact.</image-desc>

# Proposition .12.

If a circle touches another circle, whether internally or externally, it is necessary that it touches in only one place.
¶ If it were possible for a circle to touch another in two places, let circle **a.b.c** be touched by circle **a.b.e** internally at two points **a** and **b**, or externally by circle **c.d.f** at two points **c** and **d**. When we draw a straight line **a.b** and **d.b**, if it falls outside the internal circle **a.b.e**, it contradicts the second [proposition] of this book <note>Proposition III.2 states that a line segment connecting two points on the circumference of a circle falls inside that circle.</note>. If the line falls inside it, when we divide it equally and draw a perpendicular from the point of division to the circumference on both sides, it would pass through the center of both circles. This would lead to a contradiction of the previous [proposition] <note>Proposition III.11</note>. Regarding the circle touching externally at points **c** and **d**, if we draw a straight line from point **c** to point **d**, a contradiction of the 2nd [proposition] of this book necessarily follows. Therefore, both are impossible.

<image-desc>Two sets of diagrams for Proposition 12. The top set shows internal tangency of two circles at two points 'a' and 'b' to prove impossibility. The bottom set shows external tangency of two circles at points 'c' and 'd'.</image-desc>

### Proposition .13.

<image-desc>A circular geometric diagram labeled with the number 13. A circle with center 'e' contains two equal, parallel horizontal chords. The top chord is labeled 'a-f-b' and the bottom chord is labeled 'd-g-c'. Perpendicular lines 'ef' and 'eg' connect the center to the midpoints of the chords. Radii connect the center 'e' to the endpoints 'a', 'b', 'c', and 'd', forming several triangles within the circle.</image-desc>

**E**qual straight lines in a circle are at an equal distance from the center; and if they are at an equal distance from the center, it is necessary that they are equal.
Let there be a circle **a.b.c.d** whose center is **e**, and let two lines **a.b** and **c.d** be equal. I say that they are equally distant from the center and vice versa. Let the lines **e.f** and **e.g** be drawn from the center **e** perpendicular to **a.b** and **c.d**. By the second part of the third [proposition] of this book <note>Proposition III.3 states that a line from the center bisecting a chord is perpendicular to it, and vice-versa.</note>, **a.b** is divided into two equal parts at **f**, and **c.d** at **g**. Therefore, because the two sides **e.d** and **d.a** of triangle **e.d.a** are equal to the two sides **e.c** and **c.b** of triangle **e.c.b**, and the base **e.a** is equal to the base **c.b** <note>The text here uses the vertices of the triangles to demonstrate equality of the radii.</note>, by the 8th [proposition] of the first [book] <note>The SSS (Side-Side-Side) congruence theorem.</note>, angle **d** is equal to angle **c**. And since the two sides **e.d** and **d.f** of triangle **e.d.f** are equal to the two sides **e.c** and **c.g** of triangle **e.c.g**—for **d.f** is equal to **c.g** because the whole line **a.d** <note>The text here shifts to calling the chords **a.d** and **b.c**.</note> was posited as equal to **b.c**—and angle **d** is equal to angle **c**, then by the 4th [proposition] of the first [book] <note>The SAS (Side-Angle-Side) congruence theorem.</note>, the base **e.f** is equal to the base **e.g**. And because these are the perpendiculars coming to them from the center, it is clear by the definition (or by the 4th [proposition] of this book) that they are at an equal distance from the center. **¶** Another way for the same thing: For the square of **e.d**, by the second-to-last [proposition] of the first [book] <note>original: "per penultimam primi"; this refers to Proposition I.47, the Pythagorean theorem.</note>, is worth the squares of the two lines **e.f** and **f.d**; and the square of **e.c** is worth the squares of the two lines **e.g** and **c.g**. Because the square of **d.e** is equal to the square of **e.c**, and the square of **d.f** is equal to the square of **g.c**, then the square of **e.f** will be equal to the square of **e.g**, whereby **e.f** is equal to **e.g**. Thus the same point is clear. Therefore, let **e.f** be equal to **e.g**, which means they are at an equal distance from the center. I say then that **a.d** is equal to **b.c**. For when the squares of the two equal lines **e.f** and **e.g** are subtracted from the squares of the two equal lines **e.d** and **e.c**, there remains (by the second-to-last [proposition] of the first book) the squares of the two lines **f.d** and **g.c**. By common knowledge, these must be equal; therefore **f.d** is equal to **g.c**. Thus, the double of **f.d**, which is **a.d**, is equal to the double of **g.c**, which is **b.c**. This is the second part of the proposition.

### Proposition .14.

<image-desc>A circular geometric diagram labeled with the number 14. A circle contains a horizontal diameter 'a-e-d' with center 'e'. Chords 'ab' and 'ac' extend from point 'a'. Two other chords, 'fg' and 'bk', are drawn in other parts of the circle. Radii from center 'e' connect to points 'f' and 'g' to form triangle 'efg'.</image-desc>

**I**f several straight lines are placed within a circle, the diameter is the longest of all of them; and it is necessary that those closer to the center are longer than those further away.
Let there be a circle **a.b.c** whose center is **e**, and let many lines fall within it, which are **a.b**, **a.c**, **a.d**, **f.g**, and **b.k**; and let **a.e.d** be the diameter. I say that the diameter itself is the longest, and the others are greater the closer they are to it. Let lines be drawn from the center **e** to the endpoints of all of them, which are **e.b**, **e.c**, **e.f**, **e.g**, and **e.k**. By the 20th [proposition] of the first [book] <note>The triangle inequality theorem: any two sides of a triangle added together are greater than the third side.</note>, the two sides **e.f** and **e.g** of triangle **e.f.g** are longer than **f.g**. Because these are equal to [the radii making up the diameter] **a.d**, then **a.d** is greater than **f.g**. By the same reasoning, it will be greater than **a.c**, because **a.e** and **e.c** are greater than **a.c** and equal to **a.d**; therefore **a.d** is greater than **a.c**. Likewise it is also greater than **b.k** and greater than **a.b**. That **f.g** is greater than **b.k**, **a.c**, and **a.b** is also clear. Because by the 24th [proposition] of the first [book] <note>The "Hinge Theorem," which relates the size of the included angle to the length of the opposite side in two triangles with two equal sides.</note>, since the two sides **f.e** and **e.g** of triangle **f.e.g** are equal to the two sides **b.e** and **e.k** of triangle **b.e.k**, and angle **f.e.g** is greater than angle **b.e.k**, the base **f.g** will be greater than the base **b.k**. Similarly, because **a.e** and **e.c** are equal to **a.e** and **e.b**, and angle **a.e.c** is greater than angle **a.e.b**, the base **a.c** will be greater than the base **a.b**. Thus is the proposition.
