...it is impossible. Moreover, it is necessary that the angle contained by the tangent and that circumference is the narrowest of all acute angles. Conversely, the interior angle contained by the diameter and the circumference <note>This is the "angle of the semicircle," the curved angle formed where the diameter meets the arc.</note> must be the widest of all acute angles. From this, it is also manifest that every straight line drawn perpendicularly from the end of any diameter of a circle touches that circle <note>original: "contingere," meaning to be tangent to.</note>.

<image-desc>A circular geometric diagram. A circle is centered at point d. A vertical diameter connects a and c (c is off-screen below). A horizontal tangent line e-a-e touches the circle at the top point a. Another line a-f-b cuts into the circle, and a line d-g is drawn from the center perpendicular to a-f-b.</image-desc>

Suppose that from the endpoint **a** of the diameter **a.c** of the circle **a.b.c**, whose center is **d**, a line is drawn perpendicularly. I say that this line falls outside the circle, and that no other straight line can be inserted between that line and the circumference; and that the angle which the line and the circumference contain is smaller than any rectilinear angle <note>An angle formed by two straight lines.</note>; and that the angle contained by the diameter and the circumference is greater than any acute rectilinear angle.

For if the line **a.b**, drawn perpendicularly to line **a.c** at point **a**, could fall inside the circle, let that line be **a.b**, and let the line **d.b** be drawn. Then, by the 5th [proposition] of the first [book] <note>Proposition I.5: In isosceles triangles, the angles at the base are equal.</note>, the angle **d.a.b** will be equal to the angle **d.b.a**. And because angle **d.a.b** is a right angle by hypothesis, the triangle **a.b.d** would have two right angles, which is impossible by the 32nd [proposition] of the first [book] <note>Proposition I.32: The sum of the three interior angles of a triangle is equal to two right angles.</note>.

Therefore, the line falls outside; let it be **a.e**. Now, if a straight line could be intercepted between it and the circumference, let that line be **a.f**, to which a perpendicular **d.g** is drawn from the center. And because the angle **d.g.a** is a right angle, by the 18th [proposition] of the first [book] <note>Proposition I.18: In any triangle, the greater side subtends the greater angle.</note>, line **a.d** would be longer than line **d.g**, which is impossible <note>Since d.a is a radius and g is a point on a line supposedly outside the circle, d.g should be longer than the radius, not shorter.</note>. Therefore, no straight line can be intercepted between the tangent and the circumference.

Because of this, it is clear that the angle contained by **e.a** and the circumference—which is called the <term>angle of contingency</term> <note>original: "angulum contingentie"; also known as a 'horn angle' (angulus cornicularis). Historically, this was a point of great debate because it is an 'infinitesimal' quantity—greater than zero but smaller than any straight-lined angle.</note>—is smaller than any angle contained by two straight lines. For if any rectilinear angle were equal to the angle of contingency, or smaller than it, since every such angle can be divided into equal parts according to the teaching of the 9th [proposition] of the first [book] <note>Proposition I.9: To bisect a given rectilinear angle.</note>, a straight line could then be inserted between the line **a.e** and the circumference, which we have shown to be impossible. By this, it is clear that the angle contained by the diameter and the circumference is greater than all acute rectilinear angles, because it differs from a right angle only by the angle of contingency, which we have shown to be smaller than any rectilinear angle.

The **Corollary** is clear from the first part. Since the line **a.e**, extended in both directions, does not cut the circle and touches it at point **a**, it is a <term>tangent</term> <note>original: "contingens"; a line that touches a curve at a point but does not cross it there.</note> by definition.

From this, it should be noted that the following argument is not valid: "This thing passes from a smaller to a larger state, and through all intermediate stages; therefore, it passes through the 'equal' stage." Nor is it valid to say: "It is possible to find a thing greater than this and smaller than the same; therefore, it is possible to find one equal to it." This is shown as follows: Let there be a circle **a.b** on center **c**, whose diameter is **a.c.b**, and let line **a.d** be drawn perpendicularly from its endpoint **a**; it will be tangent to the circle by the corollary of this proposition.

<image-desc>A diagram showing a smaller circle with center c and diameter a-b. A larger circle with center a and radius a-b is drawn, creating an arc b-e-d. A vertical line a-d is tangent to the smaller circle at point a. The arc b-e-d represents the path of a moving line pivoting around point a.</image-desc>

Again, let a circle **b.c.d** be described around point **a** according to the quantity of the diameter **a.b**, and imagine line **a.b** moving upon point **a** through the circumference of the arc **b.c.d**, so that point **b** marks all points of the arc **b.e.d** until it reaches line **a.d** and covers it. And because the angle **b.a.d** is a right angle, it would seem that there is no acute angle which the line **a.b** does not form with the diameter **a.c.b** of the smaller circle as it moves toward the right angle, passing through the positions of all acute angles. It is manifest that some of these are smaller than the angle of the semicircle contained by the semi-circumference **a.b** and the diameter **a.c.b**, while the right angle is clearly greater than it. I say that in the transition from the smaller acute angles to the greater right angle, no intermediate stage was equal to it [the angle of the semicircle]. For if there were one, let it be the one formed by line **a.b** when point **b** was at point **e** of the arc **b.e.d**. Because then the angle...

By common conception, the angle **f.a.b** will be wider than the angle **e.a.b**; thus there would be something wider than the widest, which is impossible. ¶ Or like this: since angle **e.a.b** is equal to the angle of the semicircle, as is posited, and the angle of the semicircle together with the <term>angle of contingency</term> <note>Also called the "horn angle," this is the infinitely small space between the curved arc and the tangent line.</note> is equal to one right angle; similarly, because the angle **e.a.b** together with the angle **e.a.d** is equal to one right angle: then angle **e.a.d** will be equal to the angle of contingency. But because the angle of contingency is the narrowest of all acute angles by the 3rd part of this [proposition]: then angle **e.a.d**, being equal to it, will likewise be the narrowest of all acute angles. But angle **e.a.f** is narrower than it by common conception: therefore there would be something narrower than the narrowest, which is impossible. ¶ Therefore, a rectilinear angle will not be equal to the angle of a semicircle, because the transition from the smaller to the greater does not occur through equality. Likewise, because it is possible to find something smaller than it and larger than it: an instance is evident against both aforementioned arguments, wherefore it must be responded to by interruption.

### Proposition 16

**From a given point, to draw a tangent line to a given circle.**
Let the given circle be **a.b**, whose center is **c**, and let the given point be **d**. I wish, therefore, to draw from point **d** a line touching <note>original: "contingentem," meaning tangent to.</note> circle **a.b**. I draw the line **d.c**, intersecting the circumference of circle **a.b** at point **a**, upon which I describe circle **d.e** according to the length of line **d.c**, concentric with circle **a.b**. And from point **a**, I draw line **a.e** perpendicular to line **d.c**, which intersects the circumference of circle **d.e** at point **e**. Then I draw line **e.c**, intersecting the circumference of circle **a.b** at point **b**. Finally, I draw line **d.b**, which will be the tangent to circle **a.b**. For since the two sides **a.c** and **c.e** of triangle **a.c.e** are equal to the two sides **b.c** and **c.d** of triangle **b.c.d**, and angle **c** is common to both, then by the 4th [proposition] of the first, angle **e.a.c** will be equal to angle **d.b.c**. But angle **e.a.c** is a right angle; therefore, angle **d.b.c** is a right angle. Thus, by the corollary of the preceding [proposition], line **d.b** will be tangent to circle **a.b**, which is what was proposed.

### Proposition 17

**If a straight line touches a circle, and a straight line is drawn from the contact point to the center, it is necessary that it be perpendicular to the tangent line.**
Let line **a.b** be tangent to circle **c.e**, whose center is **d**, at point **c**, which is joined to the center by line **c.d**. I say that this [line] is perpendicular to the tangent line. For if it is not perpendicular to it, let **d.f** be the perpendicular to the same, which intersects the circumference of the circle at point **e**. Each of the angles at **d.f** will be a right angle, and therefore by the 18th [proposition] of the first, line **c.d** is greater than line **d.f** <note>In a right triangle, the hypotenuse must be longer than the legs. If d-f were the perpendicular, d-c would be the hypotenuse.</note>, which is impossible: it is established, therefore, that **d.c** is perpendicular to **a.b**, which is what was proposed.

## Proposition 18

<image-desc>Geometric diagram showing a circle with a horizontal tangent line at the top point 'c'. A vertical line segment 'ce' is drawn from the contact point through the center 'd' (labeled 'd' in the center). Points 'a' and 'b' are marked on the tangent line.</image-desc>

If a straight line touches a circle, and from the point of contact a line is drawn <term>orthogonally</term> <note>At a right angle, or perpendicular.</note> into the circle, the center must necessarily be on that line.
¶ Let there be, as before, a line **a.b** <term>contingent to</term> <note>original: "contingens"; meaning tangent to or touching at a single point.</note> the circle **c.c** at point **c**. From the contact point, let the line **c.e** be drawn inside the circle perpendicular to line **a.b**. I say that the center of the circle is on line **c.e**. This is the <term>converse</term> <note>A theorem that reverses the hypothesis and conclusion of a previous one.</note> of the previous proposition. For if the center were not on line **c.e**, let it be anywhere else it might happen to be; let it be **d**. Draw the line **d.c**. By the previous proposition, **d.c** would be perpendicular to line **a.b**, which is impossible since **e.c** was already placed perpendicular to it. Therefore, the proposition is clear.

## Proposition 19

<image-desc>A vertical series of three circular diagrams illustrating the relationship between central and inscribed angles:
1. The inscribed angle 'abc' and central angle 'adc' sharing arc 'ac', where the center 'd' is inside the inscribed angle.
2. The same elements, but one side of the inscribed angle passes through the center 'd'.
3. The same elements, but the center 'd' is outside the inscribed angle.</image-desc>

If an angle within a circle stands upon the center, and another angle standing upon the circumference has the same base, the lower angle <note>The central angle.</note> will be double the upper angle <note>The inscribed angle.</note>.
¶ Let there be a circle **a.b.c** whose center is **d**. Let angle **a.d.c** be formed at the center and angle **a.b.c** at the circumference. Let both angles have the same base, which is arc **a.c**. I say that angle **a.d.c** is double angle **a.b.c**. This is proved as follows: either the two lines **a.b** and **b.c** include the two lines **a.d** and **d.c** <note>Meaning the center is inside the inscribed angle.</note>, or one of them forms a single line with one of the others <note>Meaning the center lies on one of the sides of the inscribed angle.</note>, or one of the first lines cuts the other of the latter lines <note>Meaning the center is outside the inscribed angle.</note>.
¶ First, let them include them as appears in the first figure. Let line **b.d.e** be extended. By the 32nd proposition of the First Book, the <term>extrinsic</term> <note>Exterior.</note> angle **a.d.e** is equal to the two intrinsic angles **b.a.d** and **a.b.d**. And because these [sides **da** and **db**] are equal <note>As radii of the same circle.</note>, by the 5th proposition of the same book, angle **a.d.e** will be double angle **a.b.d**. Similarly, angle **e.d.c** will be double angle **d.b.c**. Therefore, the whole angle **a.d.c** is double the whole angle **a.b.c**, which is what was proposed.
¶ If one of the two lines **a.b** and **b.c** forms a single line with one of the lines **a.d** and **d.c**, as appears in the second figure: the proposition is evident by the same means and in a similar manner as before.
¶ If one of the first two lines cuts the other of the last two, as appears in the 3rd figure, where line **a.b** cuts line **d.c**: let line **b.d.e** be extended. By the same principles we assumed before and in a similar manner, angle **c.d.a** is double angle **d.b.a**, and the whole angle **e.d.c** is double the whole angle **d.b.c**. Therefore, [by subtraction] angle **d.b.c** is double angle **a.b.c**, which is what was proposed.

## Proposition 20

<image-desc>A circle showing two inscribed angles 'c' and 'e' sharing the same base arc 'ab'. Lines are drawn from the center 'f' to points 'a' and 'b'.</image-desc>

If angles in one <term>portion</term> <note>A segment of a circle.</note> of a circle stand upon the [same] arc, it is necessary that those angles be equal to one another.

By the previous proposition, angle **f** standing at the center will be double each of them; therefore, they are all equal to each other, which is what was proposed.

->Proposition 22<-
<note>In many editions, this is Book III, Proposition 23.</note>

**I**t is impossible for two <term>similar</term> <note>original: "similes"; in geometry, similar segments are those that contain equal angles.</note> and unequal <term>segments</term> <note>original: "portiones"; a part of a circle cut off by a straight line (a chord).</note> of a circle to be constructed upon one assigned straight line on the same side.
¶ Let the assigned straight line be **a.b**, upon which let there be a segment of a circle **a.c.b**. I say that upon the same line, on the same side, there shall not be made another segment which is similar to this one, whether it be greater or smaller. ¶ For if it were possible, let there be a segment **a.d.b** that is greater than it, but which is nonetheless similar to it. Let there be an angle **a.c.b** in the smaller segment, and an angle **a.d.b** in the larger. It will then be that the lines **a.d** and **d.b** include the lines **a.c** and **c.b**, as is seen in the first figure; or that one of the first lines becomes the same as one of the last, as in the second; or that one cuts the other, as in the third. ¶ If it were in the first way, by the 21st [proposition] of the First Book <note>Usually a reference to the exterior angle theorem or triangle inequality.</note>, angle **c** would be greater than angle **d**. Therefore, they are not similar segments by definition. If in the second way, angle **c** would still be greater than angle **d** by the 16th [proposition] of the same [book]. Thus, even so, the segments will not be similar. But if in the third way, let it be that line **a.d** cuts line **c.b** and cuts the circumference of the smaller segment at point **e**. Let line **e.b** be drawn. By the same 16th [proposition] of the First Book, the angle **a.e.b**—which stands in the segment **a.c.b**—is greater than angle **d**. But **e** is equal to **c** by the 20th [proposition] of this book <note>original: "p.20.b9" likely "per 20 huius"; referring to the property that angles in the same segment are equal.</note>; wherefore **c** is greater than **d**. Thus, in no way are they similar. ¶ In a similar way, you will prove that upon the line **a.b** there shall not be made a segment similar to segment **a.c.b** that is smaller than it, by placing **c** in the place of **d** and **d** in the place of **c** in the aforesaid figures. For by the previous [propositions], namely by the 21st and 16th of the First Book, and in the manner previously described, angle **d** in all configurations will be greater than angle **c**; wherefore the segments will not be similar. ¶ And note that although it is proposed that similar unequal segments cannot be made on one line from the same side, it is also true that they cannot be made from different sides. For although it is permitted to prove it for the smaller which is on one side by supposing it against the larger on the other, it will necessarily be exceeded by the larger according to <term>common notion</term> <note>original: "communem sciam" (communem scientiam); a self-evident mathematical truth or axiom.</note>. Therefore, they are not similar, according to this 22nd [proposition].

->Proposition 23<-
<note>In many editions, this is Book III, Proposition 24.</note>

**I**f similar segments of circles are placed upon equal lines, it is necessary that those segments are equal to one another.
¶ Let there be two equal lines **a.b** and **c.d**, upon which are two segments of circles **a.e.b** and **c.f.d** which are similar. I say that they are equal. For if they are not equal, one of them, when placed upon the other, will exceed it, the greater over the smaller. But line **a.b** will not exceed line **c.d**, nor be exceeded by it, since they are equal. Wherefore, the contrary of the previous [proposition] would occur, which is impossible. For lines **a.b** and **c.d** will be as one line.

¶ The intent of this conclusion is to complete the circle from any given arc or from any given segment of a circle. Let there be, therefore, any arc **a.b**...

III

...from which I wish to complete the circle, I shall draw in it two lines in whatever way they happen to fall, which let be **a.c.** and **b.d.** These I shall divide into equal parts: **a.c.** indeed at point **e.**, and **b.d.** at <margin>f.</margin> point **f.** And I shall draw **e.g.** perpendicular to **a.c.** and **f.h.** perpendicular to **b.d.**, which intersect each other at point **k.** It will be, by the <term>corollary</term> <note>original: "conel." – an abbreviation for "corollarium." This refers to the corollary of Book III, Proposition 1, which states that the perpendicular bisector of a chord passes through the center.</note> of the first [proposition] of this book, that the center of the circle is on both of the lines **e.g.** and **f.h.**; therefore, the center is point **k.** If, however, **e.g.** does not intersect **f.h.** but they are one and the same line—as will happen if the two lines **a.c.** and **b.d.** are parallel—then that line will meet the circumference of the given arc on both sides. Therefore, that line being divided in the middle at point **k.**, the center of the circle will be there by the same corollary. Moreover, **e.g.** and **f.h.** will not be parallel [in the first case] because since the center of the circle is on both by the said corollary, the same circle would have two centers <note>Euclidean geometry assumes a circle has only one unique center; having two would be a contradiction.</note>. Thus it can be demonstrated generally for every arc or every <term>portion</term> <note>original: "portione." In this context, a "portion" refers to a circular segment.</note> how the circle may be completed from it. ¶Because, however, the author <note>Likely referring to the commentator Campanus of Novara, whose version of Euclid was standard in the Middle Ages.</note> sees fit to vary this conclusion according to the different types of arcs, by enumerating the types of all portions: we shall demonstrate separately by types how the circle is completed from every given portion. 

Let there be first a given portion **a.b.**, which is a semicircle. By the definition of a semicircle, the line **a.b.** will be the diameter. Therefore, that line being divided in the middle at point **c.**, **c.** will be the center of the circle. ¶Again, let the portion **a.c.b.** be greater than a semicircle, whose <term>chord</term> <note>original: "corda." The straight line connecting the ends of an arc.</note> is **a.b.**, which I divide into equal parts at point **d.** From this point I lead **d.c.** perpendicular to it, which will pass through the center by the corollary of the first [proposition] of this book. And I shall draw the line **a.c.** And because the line **a.b.** is less than the diameter since **a.c.b.** is a portion greater than a semicircle, **a.d.** will be less than the semi-diameter <note>The radius.</note>. But **d.c.** is greater than the semi-diameter. Therefore, **d.c.** is greater than **a.d.** Therefore, by the 19th [proposition] of the First Book <note>Euclid I.19: In any triangle, the greater side is opposite the greater angle.</note>, angle **c.a.d.** is greater than angle **a.c.d.** Let there be made, therefore, by the 23rd [proposition] of the First Book, an angle **c.a.e.** equal to angle **a.c.d.**, by drawing the line **a.e.** which intersects the line **c.d.** at point **e.** And it will be, by the 6th [proposition] of the First Book <note>Euclid I.6: If two angles of a triangle are equal, the sides opposite them are also equal.</note>, that line **a.e.** is equal to line **e.c.** Let the line **e.b.** then be drawn, and it will be, by the 4th [proposition] of the First Book, that line **e.b.** is equal to line **a.e.** Wherefore the three lines **e.a.**, **e.b.**, and **e.c.** are equal. Therefore, by the 9th [proposition] of this book, **e.** is the center of the circle. 

¶Again, let **a.c.b.** be a portion less than a semicircle, whose chord is **a.b.**, which I divide into equal parts at point **d.** From there I draw the line **c.d.e.** perpendicular to the line **a.b.**, which intersects the circumference at point **c.** It is manifest that this passes through the center by the corollary of the first [proposition] of this book. I draw again the line **a.c.** Angle **a.c.d.** will be greater than angle **c.a.d.** If it were equal, the portion **a.c.b.** would be a semicircle; and if it were less, it would be greater than a semicircle. But it is established that it is less. I draw, therefore, the line **a.e.** which, with line **a.c.**, makes an angle equal to angle **c.**, and it intersects the line **e.f.** at point **e.** It is manifest that point **e.** falls outside the given portion. And I draw the line **e.b.** And because the total angle **a.** is equal to angle **c.**, by the 6th [proposition] of the First Book, line **c.a.** <note>The text likely means e.a. here to match the logic of the previous paragraph.</note> will be equal to line **e.c.** And because, by the 4th [proposition] of the First Book, line **e.b.** is equal to line **e.a.**, point **e.** will be the center of the circle by the 9th [proposition] of this book. Wherefore the proposition is clear according to all types of portions of a circle.

### Propositio 25.
<note>In modern editions of Euclid, this is Book III, Proposition 26.</note>

**I**f, in equal circles, equal angles stand either at the centers or at the circumferences, it is necessary that they fall upon equal arcs.
> ¶Let there be two equal circles **a.b.c.**, whose center is **d.**, and **e.f.g.**, whose center is **h.** And let there be made at their centers two angles, **a.d.c.** and **e.h.g.**, which are set as equal. <image-desc>Five geometric diagrams arranged vertically on the left side of the page. Each diagram depicts a circle with various inscribed triangles, arcs, and chords. By the definition of equal circles, the radii <note>original: "semidiametri"</note> are equal. And because the two angles **d.** and **b.** are equal, it follows from the 4th [proposition] of the first [book] <note>Book I, Proposition 4 is the Side-Angle-Side (SAS) theorem, proving triangles are congruent if two sides and the included angle are equal.</note> that line **a.c.** is equal to line **e.g.** Furthermore, by the 19th [proposition] of this book, angle **b.** will be equal to angle **f.** Since angle **d.** is equal to angle **b.**, therefore by the definition of similar segments <note>In geometry, "similar segments" of circles are those that contain equal angles.</note>, the two segments **a.b.c.** and **e.f.g.** are similar. And because they stand upon equal lines **a.c.** and **e.g.**, they will be equal to each other by the 23rd [proposition] of this book. Wherefore, the arcs **a.b.c.** and **e.f.g.** are equal. If the angles **b.** and **f.** which are on the circumference are assumed to be equal, the segments will be similar by definition, and the angles **d.** and **b.** will be equal by the 19th [proposition] of this book. Because the circles are equal by hypothesis, the two lines **a.c.** and **e.g.** will be equal by the 4th [proposition] of the first [book]. Wherefore, as before, the segments are equal by the 23rd [proposition] of this book, since they are similar and stand upon equal lines. Therefore, the arcs are also equal, which is what was proposed.

### Proposition 26

If in equal circles equal arcs are taken, the angles formed within them—whether they are placed at the centers or at the circumferences—must necessarily be equal.
Let there be, as before, two circles: **a.b.c.** with center **d.**, and **e.f.g.** with center **b.** Let the two arcs **a.b.c.** and **e.f.g.** be equal. Let two angles be formed at the center upon these arcs, which are **d.** and **b.**, by drawing lines **a.d.**, **c.d.**, **e.b.**, and **g.b.** Likewise, let two other angles be formed on the circumferences upon the same arcs, which are **b.** and **f.**, by drawing lines **a.b.**, **c.b.**, **e.f.**, and **g.f.** I say that the two angles **d.** and **b.** are equal to one another, and likewise the two angles **b.** and **f.** are equal to one another. This is the converse of the previous [proposition]. For if the angles **d.** and **b.** are not equal to one another, let **b.** be the larger, from which is cut an angle **k.b.g.** that is equal to angle **d.** By the preceding proposition, the arc **k.e.f.g.** <note>This refers to the arc subtended by the newly created angle.</note> would be equal to arc **a.b.c.** But the two arcs **a.b.c.** and **e.f.g.** were stated to be equal. Thus, it would happen that a part is equal to the whole, which is impossible. <note>This is a fundamental "Common Notion" in Euclidean geometry: the whole is always greater than the part. If a part of arc e.f.g. were equal to the whole arc a.b.c., and a.b.c. is equal to e.f.g., then a part would equal the whole.</note> Therefore, the total angles **d.** and **b.** are equal. In a similar way, you will prove angles **b.** and **f.** to be equal. Or, if you prefer, having proven that angles **d.** and **b.** are equal, it follows that **b.** and **f.** are equal by the 19th [proposition] of this book, and vice versa.

---

### Proposition 27

If in equal circles equal lines <note>The text uses "lineae" to mean chords, the straight lines connecting two points on a curve.</note> cut off arcs, the arcs will also be equal. However, if the lines are unequal, the arcs will also be unequal; and it is necessary that the larger arc be cut off by the larger line, and the smaller arc by the smaller.
Let there be two equal circles: **a.b.c.** with center **d.**, and **e.f.g.** with center **b.** Let the chord **a.c.** be equal to chord **e.g.** I say that the two arcs **a.b.c.** and **e.f.g.**, which the said chords cut from the said circles, are equal. Furthermore, if chord **e.g.** is assumed to be larger than chord **a.c.**, I say that arc **e.f.g.** is larger than arc **a.b.c.** The first part is proved thus: let lines be drawn from the centers to the ends of the chords, which are **d.a.**, **d.c.**, **b.e.**, and **b.g.** Because the circles are stated to be equal, these radii <note>original: "semidiametri"</note> will be equal. And because line **a.c.** is stated to be equal to line **e.g.**, the angle **d.** will be equal to the total angle **b.** by the 8th [proposition] of the first [book]. Wherefore, by the 25th [proposition] of this book, arc **a.b.c.** will be equal to arc **e.f.g.**, and thus the first part is clear. The second part is proved thus: let **e.g.** be larger than **a.c.** By the 25th [proposition] of the first [book], angle **b.** will be larger than angle **d.** Therefore, let an angle **f.b.g.** be made equal to angle **d.** By the 25th [proposition] of this book, arc **f.g.** will be equal to arc **a.b.c.** Wherefore, arc **e.f.g.** is larger than arc **a.b.c.**, which is the second part proposed.

# Proposition .28.

**In equal circles, equal arcs must necessarily have equal chords.**

<image-desc>Two identical circles displayed side-by-side. The left circle contains points a, b, and c on its circumference, with center point d. Lines from d to a and d to c form a central angle and a triangle with chord ac. The right circle is identical but labeled with points e, f, g on the circumference and center point h.</image-desc>

Let there be two equal circles **a.b.c.** (the center of which is **d.**) and **e.f.g.** (the center of which is **h.**). Let arc **a.b.c.** be equal to arc **e.f.g.** I say that chord **a.c.** is equal to chord **e.g.** This is the converse of the first part of the previous [proposition]. ¶ Let lines **d.a.**, **d.c.**, **h.e.**, and **h.g.** be drawn. By the 26th [proposition] of this book, the angles **d.** and **h.** will be equal. Therefore, by the 4th [proposition] of the first [book] <note>Book I, Proposition 4 is the Side-Angle-Side (SAS) theorem, which proves that if two sides and the included angle of one triangle are equal to those of another, the triangles are congruent.</note>, line **a.c.** will be equal to **e.g.**, which is what was proposed. Furthermore, whatever properties <note>original: "passiones"</note> have been proven regarding different equal circles, understand that they are even more certainly true regarding the same circle.

# Proposition .29.

**To divide a given arc into two equal parts.**

<image-desc>A diagram of a circle with an arc labeled a, b, c. A chord ac is drawn, and a perpendicular line from the chord's midpoint d extends upward to point b on the circumference. Chords ab and bc are drawn to show the arc has been bisected.</image-desc>

Let there be a given arc **a.b.c.**, subtended by chord **a.c.** Let this chord be divided into two equal parts at point **d.** From this point, let a perpendicular line be drawn to the chord, which shall be **d.b.**, cutting the circumference of the given arc at point **b.** I say that this point divides the given arc into two equal parts. For if lines **b.a.** and **b.c.** are drawn, they will be equal by the 4th [proposition] of the first [book]. Therefore, by the first part of the 27th [proposition] of this book <note>This refers to the rule that in equal circles (or the same circle), equal chords cut off equal arcs.</note>, arc **a.b.** will be equal to arc **b.c.**, which is what was proposed.

# Proposition .30.

<image-desc>Four separate diagrams illustrating the geometry of angles in circles: 1. A circle with an inscribed angle in a semicircle. 2. A circle with an inscribed angle in a segment larger than a semicircle. 3. A circle with an inscribed angle in a segment smaller than a semicircle. 4. A more complex diagram showing a circle with several intersecting chords and triangles, labeled with points a, b, c, d, and e, used to prove the properties of angles in different segments.</image-desc>

**If a rectilinear angle in a semicircle stands upon an arc, it is a right angle. If, however, it is in a segment smaller than a semicircle, it is greater than a right angle. But if it is in a segment larger than a semicircle, it is less than a right angle. Likewise, the angle of any segment greater than a semicircle will necessarily be greater than a right angle, and the angle of a segment smaller than a semicircle will be less than a right angle.**

¶ Let there be, as in circle **a.b.c.** (the center of which is **d.** and the diameter **a.d.c.**), a semicircle **a.b.c.** On the circumference of this semicircle, let angle **a.b.c.** be formed by drawing lines **a.b.** and **b.c.** I say that this angle is a right angle. Let line **b.d.** be drawn from the angle itself to the center. By the 5th [proposition] of the first [book] <note>This theorem states that the base angles of an isosceles triangle are equal.</note>, angle **a.b.d.** will be equal to angle **a.**, and angle **d.b.c.** will be equal to angle **c.** And because angle **c.d.b.** is equal to the two angles **d.b.a.** and **a.** by the 32nd [proposition] of the first [book] <note>Book I, Proposition 32 states that the exterior angle of a triangle is equal to the sum of the two opposite interior angles.</note>, it will itself be double the angle **d.b.a.** By the same reasoning, angle **a.d.b.** will be double the angle **d.b.c.** Therefore, the two angles **c.d.b.** and **a.d.b.** are double the total angle **a.b.c.** But those two angles are equal to two right angles by the 13th [proposition] of the first [book]. Therefore, the total angle **a.b.c.** will be half of two right angles; wherefore it is a right angle, which is the first thing proposed. ¶ The same is shown otherwise: let **b.c.** be extended to **e.** By the 32nd [proposition] of the first [book], angle **a.b.e.** will be equal to the two angles **a.** and **c.** Since angle **a.** is equal to angle **a.b.d.** and angle **c.** to angle **c.b.d.**, angle **a.b.e.** will be equal to the total angle **a.b.c.** Therefore, each of them is a right angle by definition <note>Euclid's definition of a right angle: when a straight line standing on another straight line makes the adjacent angles equal to one another, each of the equal angles is a right angle.</note>. ¶ The second part is clear as follows: let there be in circle **a.b.c.** (center **d.**) a segment <term>portio<gloss>segment of a circle</gloss></term> **a.b.c.**, the chord of which **a.c.** is greater than a semicircle <note>This likely means the segment itself is larger than a semicircle.</note>. Let angle **a.b.c.** be formed on its circumference by drawing lines **b.a.** and **b.c.** I say that this angle is less than a right angle. For let the diameter **a.d.e.** and line **e.b.** be drawn. By the first part of this [proposition], the total angle **b.** <note>Referring to the angle inscribed in the semicircle constructed using the diameter ae.</note> is a right angle. Therefore, angle **a.b.c.** will be less than a right angle by common knowledge <note>original: "communem scientiam," referring to the common notion that the part is less than the whole.</note> since it is a part of it. Thus the second part is clear. ¶ The third part follows: again, let there be in circle **a.b.**

<image-desc>A circular diagram in the middle left showing a circle with center d. A line a-b is tangent to the circle at point a. A secant line a-f is drawn from the point of tangency into the circle. Point c is marked on the circumference.</image-desc>

two final parts, note also the counter-example <note>original: "instantia"</note> against those two arguments for which we brought a counter-example in the 15th [proposition] of this book. For there is a transition from the angle of a segment smaller than a semicircle (which is less than a right angle by the last part of this [proposition]) to the angle of a segment larger than a semicircle (which is greater than a right angle by the penultimate part of this [proposition]). However, this does not pass through an "equal" state. For since every segment of a circle is either a semicircle, or greater than a semicircle, or less than a semicircle: let both the angle of a semicircle (by the first part of the 15th) and the angle of a smaller segment (by the last part of this) be less than a right angle; while the angle of the larger segment is greater than a right angle. And yet, there will not be an angle of any segment, nor simply any angle contained by a circumference and a straight line, that is either a right angle or equal to a right angle. To make this more clear, let there be a circle **a.b.c.** with center **d.** and a line **a.b.** of undetermined length at end **b.**, cutting from it a segment smaller than a semicircle. By the last part of this, it will be less than a right angle. Let the diameter of this circle be **a.d.c.**, and imagine the line **a.b.** moving toward part **c.** upon point **a.** As long as it is short of **c.**, or at **c.** itself coinciding with the diameter **a.d.c.**, it will form an angle with the arc that is less than a right angle. But at every point beyond **c.**, such as at **e.**, it will form an angle greater than a right angle by the penultimate part. Therefore, it passes from a lesser to a greater state without passing through equality. And just as in rectilinear angles <note>Angles formed by straight lines.</note> one can find an angle greater or less than the angle of a semicircle, yet not equal to it (as shown in the 15th of this book), so in the angles of a segment one can find an angle greater or less than a right angle, yet not equal to it, as is clear from this demonstration.

## Proposition 32

<image-desc>Three geometric diagrams are placed in the right margin. The top diagram shows a circle with a horizontal diameter marked 'a' and 'b', and an inscribed triangle with vertex 'c' on the circumference. The middle diagram depicts a circle for Proposition 32, showing various chords, a tangent line 'd-a-g', a perpendicular 'a-e', and points labeled 'a, b, c, d, e, f, g, h, k'. The bottom diagram illustrates Proposition 33, showing a circle with a tangent 'd-a-e' and a chord 'a-b'.</image-desc>

**Upon** a given line, to describe a segment of a circle containing an angle equal to a given angle, whether that angle be a right angle, or greater than a right angle <term>obtuse<note>An angle greater than 90 degrees.</note></term>, or less than a right angle <term>acute<note>An angle less than 90 degrees.</note></term>.

**Let** **a.b.** be the given line and **c.** the given angle. Upon the line **a.b.**, I wish to describe a segment of a circle that receives on its circumference a rectilinear angle equal to angle **c**. If, therefore, angle **c** is a right angle, I shall divide **a.b.** in the middle and describe a semicircle upon it; and the task will be done, according to the first part of Proposition 30 of this book. If, however, it is obtuse, I shall draw line **d.a.** so that it contains an angle equal to angle **c** with line **b.a.**, and from point **a** I shall draw line **a.e.** perpendicular to line **a.d.**; and upon point **b**, according to Proposition 23 of the first book, I shall make an angle equal to angle **e.a.b.**, which is the amount by which an obtuse angle exceeds a right angle. Having drawn line **b.f.** to meet the perpendicular **a.e.**, lines **f.a.** and **f.b.** will be equal according to Proposition 6 of the first book. Thus, with point **f** as the center of the circle, I shall describe a circle **a.b.b.** according to the length of line **f.a.**; and by the corollary of Proposition 15 of this book, line **a.d.** will be tangent to the circle. Therefore, by the preceding proposition, the angle formed in the segment **a.b.b.** is equal to angle **d.a.b.**, and thus also to angle **c**, which is what was proposed. If, however, angle **c** is acute, I shall produce line **a.g.** containing an angle equal to angle **c** with line **a.b.**; and from point **a** I shall draw **a.e.** perpendicular to line **a.g.**; and upon point **b** I shall make an angle equal to angle **e.a.b.**, which is the amount by which a right angle exceeds an acute angle. Having drawn line **b.f.** to the perpendicular **a.e.**, lines **f.a.** and **f.b.** will be equal according to Proposition 6 of the first book. Thus, having made point **f** the center of the circle, I shall describe the circle **a.k.b.** according to the length of line **f.a.**; and by the corollary of Proposition 15 of this book, line **a.g.** will be tangent to the circle. Therefore, by the preceding proposition, the angle formed in the segment **a.k.b.** is equal to angle **g.a.b.**, and thus also to angle **c**, which is what was proposed.

## Proposition 33

**From** a given circle: to cut off a segment containing an angle equal to a given angle.

**Let** **a.b.** be the given circle and **c.** the given angle. I wish, therefore, to cut off from circle **a.b.** one segment containing an angle equal to angle **c**. I draw line **d.a.e.** tangent to the given circle at point **a**, from which I draw line **a.b.** into the circle, containing an angle equal to angle **c** with line **a.e.**; and according to Proposition 31 of this book, the segment **a.b.** existing on the side of line **a.d.** will receive an angle equal to angle **c**, which is what was proposed.

# Proposition 34

<margin>
<image-desc>
A vertical sequence of four circular diagrams illustrating Proposition 34 of Euclid's Book III:
1. A circle with two chords, ac and bd, intersecting at point e exactly in the center.
2. A circle with diameter bd and chord ac intersecting at point e. The center is labeled f. Auxiliary lines fa and fc form a triangle.
3. A circle with diameter bd and chord ac intersecting at point e. A perpendicular line fg is dropped from the center f to chord ac. There is a faded handwritten marginal note "equal" next to this figure.
4. A circle with two chords ac and bd intersecting at point e away from the center. A diameter gefb is drawn passing through the point of intersection e.
</image-desc>
<gloss>equal</gloss> <note>original: "equali"</note>
</margin>

If two straight lines cut one another within a circle, the rectangle produced by the two parts of one of them is equal to the rectangle contained by the two parts of the other line. <note>In Euclidean geometry, "the rectangle produced by two parts" refers to the area of a rectangle whose sides are the lengths of those two line segments. Essentially: segment AE × EC = BE × ED.</note>

¶ Let there be two lines, **a.c.** and **b.d.**, cutting each other in the circle **a.b.c.d.** at point **e.** I say that the rectangle formed by **a.e.** and **e.c.** is equal to that formed by **b.e.** and **e.d.** For either both lines **a.c.** and **b.d.** will pass through the center of the circle, or only one of them, or neither. ¶ If both pass through the center, **e** will be the center of the circle and all four lines will be equal <note>As they would all be radii of the circle.</note>; therefore the proposition is clear. ¶ But if only one of them passes through the center, let that be **b.d.**, and let the center of the circle be **f.** Then **b.d.** will cut **a.c.** either into equal parts or into unequal parts. Therefore, let it first cut it into equal parts: and by the first part of the 3rd proposition of this book, it will cut it perpendicularly. <note>Proposition 3 of Book III states that a diameter bisecting a chord is perpendicular to it.</note> Let line **f.c.** be drawn; then by the 5th proposition of the second book, the rectangle formed by **b.e.** and **e.d.** together with the square of **e.f.** is equal to the square of line **f.d.**, and therefore also to the square of line **f.c.** <note>Since f.d. and f.c. are both radii.</note> Therefore, by the penultimate proposition of the first book <note>This is Proposition 47, known today as the Pythagorean Theorem.</note>, it is equal to the squares of the two lines **f.e.** and **e.c.** Subtracting the square of **e.f.** from both sides, the rectangle formed by **b.e.** and **e.d.** will be equal to the square of line **e.c.**; and because **e.c.** is equal to **a.e.**, the proposition is evident. ¶ But if **b.d.**, passing through the center, cuts **a.c.** into unequal parts, let **f.g.** be drawn from the center **f** perpendicular to **a.c.** By the second part of the third proposition of this book, **a.g.** will be equal to **g.c.** Let line **f.c.** be drawn. By the 5th proposition of the second book, the rectangle formed by **b.e.** and **e.d.** together with the square of **f.e.**—and therefore, by the penultimate proposition of the first book, together with the squares of the two lines **f.g.** and **g.e.** because angle **f.g.e.** is a right angle—is equal to the square of line **d.f.**, and therefore to line **f.c.** Consequently, by the penultimate proposition of the first book, it is equal to the squares of the two lines **f.g.** and **g.c.** Subtracting the square of line **f.g.** from both sides, the rectangle formed by **b.e.** and **e.d.** together with the square of line **g.e.** will be equal to the square of line **g.c.** But by the 5th proposition of the second book, the rectangle formed by **a.e.** and **e.c.** together with the square of line **g.e.** is equal to that which is formed by **b.e.** and **e.d.** together with the square of that same **g.e.** Subtracting the square of line **g.e.** from both sides: the rectangle formed by **b.e.** and **e.d.** will be equal to that formed by **a.e.** and **e.c.**, which is what was proposed. ¶ But if neither of them passes through the center, whether one divides the other into equal or unequal parts, I shall produce line **g.f.e.b.** as the diameter of the circle passing through the point of their intersection. And if one divides the other into equal parts, such as **b.d.** and **a.c.**, then **g.b.** also divides **a.c.** into equal parts; therefore it does so perpendicularly by the third proposition of this book. Therefore, by the second method of this conclusion, the rectangle formed by **g.e.** and **e.b.** is equal to that formed by **a.c.** and **e.c.**, and by the third method of this, the rectangle formed by **g.e.** and **e.b.** is equal to that formed by **b.e.** and **e.d.** Therefore, the rectangle formed by **a.e.** and **e.c.** is equal to that formed by **b.e.** and **e.d.**, which is what was proposed. ¶ But if neither divides the other into equal parts, it will be by the third method of this conclusion that the rectangle formed by **g.e.** and **e.b.** is equal to each of those formed by **a.e.** and **e.c.** and **b.e.** and **e.d.**, wherefore one of them will be equal to the other: which is what was proposed.

If a point is marked outside a circle, and from it two straight lines are drawn to the circle, one cutting it <term>secant</term> and the other touching it <term>tangent</term>, the rectangle contained by the whole secant and its external part is equal to the square described by the touching line.

Let **a.** be the point marked outside the circle **b.c.d.**, whose center is **e.** From which...

# Book III

<margin>
<image-desc>
Three geometric diagrams in the right margin illustrating theorems on circles.
1. The top diagram shows a circle with center **e**. A tangent line **ab** touches at **b**. A secant **acd** passes through the center. Lines **ae** and **be** are drawn.
2. The middle diagram shows a circle with center **e**, a tangent **ab**, and a secant **acd** that does not pass through the center. A line **afeg** passes through the center, and a perpendicular **eh** is drawn to the secant **acd**.
3. The bottom diagram shows a circle with center **e** and an external point **a**. Two tangents **ab** and **ad** are drawn from point **a**. Radii **eb** and **ed** are shown, along with lines **ae** and the chord **bd**.
</image-desc>
</margin>

Let two lines be drawn to a circle: **a.b.** being a <term>tangent</term><note>A line that touches the circle at exactly one point.</note> and **a.c.d.** being a <term>secant</term><note>A line that intersects the circle at two points.</note>. I say that the rectangle formed by **a.c.** and **d.a.** is equal to the square of line **a.b.** Either the line **a.d.c.** passes through the center, or it does not. Therefore, first let it pass through the center, which is **e**, and let line **e.b.** be drawn, which by the 17th proposition of this book <note>original: "17. huius"; likely referring to Book III, Proposition 18 in modern numbering, which states that a tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact.</note> will be perpendicular to line **a.b.** And because line **d.c.** is divided equally at point **e** and the line **d.a.** is added to it, then by the sixth proposition of the second book <note>original: "sextam secundi"</note> it follows that the rectangle formed by **c.a.** and **a.d.**, together with the square of line **e.d.** (and therefore with the square of line **e.b.**, since they are radii), is equal to the square of line **e.a.** And thus, by the penultimate proposition of the first book <note>original: "penultimam primi"; this is the Pythagorean Theorem (Book I, Prop. 47).</note>, this is equal to the squares of the two lines **e.b.** and **b.a.**, because angle **b** is a right angle. Therefore, by subtracting the square of **e.b.** from both sides, the rectangle formed by **c.a.** and **a.d.** will be equal to the square of line **a.b.**, which is what was proposed.

¶ Now, if the line **a.d.c.** does not pass through the center, let **a.f.e.g.** be taken passing through the center, and let lines **e.d.** and **e.b.** be drawn, and let **e.h.** be perpendicular to **a.d.c.** By the 3rd proposition of this book, **d.h.** will be equal to **h.c.** Because line **d.c.** is divided equally at point **h** and line **a.d.** is added to it, then by the 6th proposition of the second book, the rectangle formed by **c.a.** and **a.d.** together with the square of **d.h.** is equal to the square of line **a.h.** <note>The text here condenses several steps of geometric algebra common in medieval copies of Euclid.</note> Since lines **e.h.**, **e.b.**, and **e.f.** are related <note>Specifically, eb and ef are radii and thus equal.</note>, adding the square of **h.e.** to both sides makes the sum equal to the square of line **a.e.** by the penultimate proposition of the first book (Pythagoras). But since by the 6th of the second book the rectangle formed by **g.a.** and **a.f.** together with the square of **f.e.** is also equal to the square of line **a.e.**, then both expressions—the one involving **c.a.** and **a.d.** and the one involving **g.a.** and **a.f.**—must be equal to each other when the square of line **e.f.** is included. Therefore, by subtracting the square of line **e.f.** from both sides, the rectangle of **c.a.** and **a.d.** will be equal to the rectangle of **g.a.** and **a.f.** But the rectangle of **g.a.** and **a.f.** is equal to the square of line **a.b.** by the previous method; therefore, the rectangle of **c.a.** and **a.d.** is equal to the square of line **a.b.**, which is what was proposed.

¶ And from this, note that if any number of secant lines are drawn from a point marked outside the circle, the rectangles contained by the whole lines and their external segments are equal to one another, because they are all equal to the square of the tangent line. 

¶ Note also that if two tangent lines are drawn from any point marked outside the circle to the circle itself, they will be equal to each other. For the square of each of them will be equal to the rectangle formed by a secant line drawn from that same point into the circle and its external part. This, however, is more clearly evident through the penultimate proposition of the first book (Pythagoras). 

¶ Let **a.** be a point marked outside the circle **b.c.d.**, the center of which is **e**, and from it let two lines **a.b.** and **a.d.** be drawn tangent to the circle at points **b** [and **d**]. I say that these are equal. For I shall extend lines **e.a.**, **e.b.**, and **e.d.** By the 17th of this book, both angles **b** and **d** will be right angles. Wherefore, by the penultimate of the first book, the square of **a.e.** will be equal to the two squares of the two lines **a.b.** and **b.e.** Similarly, it is also equal to the two squares of **a.d.** and **d.e.** Therefore, the squares of the two lines **a.b.** and **b.e.** are equal to the squares of the two lines **a.d.** and **d.e.** And because the squares of the two lines **b.e.** and **e.d.** are equal <note>Because they are radii of the same circle.</note>, the squares of the two lines **a.b.** and **a.d.** will be equal. Therefore, **a.b.** is equal to **a.d.**, which is what was proposed. 

¶ Alternatively, let line **b.d.** be drawn. By the 5th proposition of the first book, angle **e.b.d.** is equal to angle **e.d.b.** because line **e.b.** is equal to line **e.d.** And because each of the two angles **b** and **d** <note>referring to the angles formed by the tangents and radii</note> is a right angle, then by common knowledge the remaining angle **a.b.d.** will be equal to the remaining angle **a.d.b.** Therefore, by the 6th proposition of the first book, line **a.b.** is equal to line **a.d.**

<summary>This page presents Proposition 36 of Euclid's Book III, proving that the square of a tangent is equal to the rectangle of the segments of a secant from the same point, and further proves that two tangents from the same point are equal in length.</summary>

# BOOK III

<margin>
<image-desc>A geometric diagram in the left margin consisting of a circle with several lines. A point 'a' lies outside the circle. A secant line 'abd' passes through the circle, and a potential tangent line 'ac' meets the circle at point 'c'. Point 'e' marks the center, and point 'f' is another point on the circumference.</image-desc>
</margin>

### Proposition 36.

If a point is marked outside a circle, and from it two lines are drawn to the circumference—one cutting the circle <note>a secant</note> and the other meeting the circumference <note>a potential tangent</note>—and if the <term>rectangle</term><note>The product of the lengths, often referred to as "the space created by the multiplication."</note> formed by the whole cutting line and its external part is equal to the square of the line meeting the circumference: then the line meeting the circumference must necessarily be a <term>tangent</term><note>A line that touches the circle at exactly one point without cutting through it.</note> to the circle.

Let **a** be the point marked outside the circle **b.c.d.**, whose center is **e**. From this point, let the line **a.b.d.** be drawn cutting the circle, and the line **a.c.** meeting the circumference. Let the rectangle formed by **d.a.** and **a.b.** be equal to the square of **a.c.** I say that the line **a.c.** is a tangent, and this is the <term>converse</term><note>A theorem that reverses the "if-then" parts of a previous theorem.</note> of the previous one. For if it is not a tangent, let the line **a.f.** be a tangent. Then, by the preceding proposition, the rectangle formed by **d.a.** and **a.b.** would be equal to the square of line **a.f.** Consequently, the square of line **a.f.** is equal to the square of line **a.c.**; therefore **a.c.** is equal to **a.f.**, which is impossible <note>original: "impossibile"</note> by the 8th proposition of this book. Therefore, **a.c.** must be the tangent, which is what was proposed.

The same will be proven directly: let the prior arrangement and <term>hypothesis</term><note>The given conditions of the proof.</note> remain. If the line **a.b.d.** passes through the center, let line **c.e.** be drawn. By the 6th proposition of the second book, the rectangle formed by **d.a.** and **a.b.** together with the square of **e.b.** (and thus with the square of **c.e.**) is equal to the square of **a.e.** But the rectangle formed by **d.a.** and **a.b.** was stated to be equal to the square of **a.c.** Therefore, the square of **a.c.** together with the square of **c.e.** is equal to the square of **a.e.** Thus, by the last proposition of the first book <note>The Pythagorean Theorem, Book I, Prop 47.</note>, the angle **a.c.e.** is a right angle. Therefore, by the 15th conclusion of this book <note>original: "concl⁹ 15.huius"</note>, the line **a.c.** is tangent to the circle, which is what was proposed. 

However, if **a.b.d.** does not pass through the center, let a line be drawn from point **d** passing through the center. Since the rectangle formed by this whole line and its external part is equal to the rectangle formed by **d.a.** and **a.b.** by the preceding proposition, it will also be equal to the square of line **a.c.**; whereby, as before, **a.c.** will be tangent to the circle.

**Book Three ends. Book Four begins.**

<image-desc>Two diagrams in the left margin. The upper diagram shows an equilateral triangle with a smaller triangle inscribed within it, created by connecting the midpoints of the sides. The lower diagram shows two intersecting circles, with a horizontal line segment passing through centers 'd' and 'f' and meeting the outer circumference at 'c'. Points 'a', 'b', 'e', 'g', and 'h' are also labeled.</image-desc>
</margin>

A figure is said to be **inscribed** within another figure when the one being inscribed touches the sides of the one in which it is inscribed with each of its angles from the inner side. 

Conversely, a figure is said to be **circumscribed** about another figure whenever the figure that is circumscribed touches all the angles of the inner figure with all of its sides.

### Proposition 1.

Within a given circle, to fit a straight line equal to a given straight line, provided that the given line is not longer than the <term>diameter</term><note>The longest straight line that can fit inside a circle, passing through the center.</note>.

Let the given line be **a.b.** and the given circle be **c.d.e.**, whose diameter is **c.d.**, which line **a.b.** is not greater than. I wish to fit a line equal to **a.b.** within the given circle. If **a.b.** is equal to the diameter, the goal is already achieved. If it is smaller, let a length **d.f.** equal to it be taken from the diameter. Using point **d** as the center and the length of line **d.f.** as the radius, let the circle **f.e.g.** be described, cutting the given circle at points **g** and **e**. Let a line be drawn from point **d** to either of these, such as **d.e.** or **d.g.** Either of these will be equal to line **a.b.**, because both are equal to line **d.f.** by the definition of a circle; thus we have achieved what was proposed.

<meta>This page continues the transition into Book IV of Euclid's Elements. The previous page ended with the final theorem of Book III (the converse of the tangent-secant theorem). ### Proposition 2.

**To inscribe a triangle in a given circle that is <term>equiangular</term><note>Having the same angles as another figure, even if the side lengths differ.</note> to a given triangle.**

To inscribe a triangle in a given circle that is equiangular to a given triangle. Let **a.b.c.** be the given triangle, and **d.e.f.** be the given circle. I wish to place within this circle a triangle that has the same angles as triangle **a.b.c.** It is not necessary for it to be <term>equilateral</term><note>Having all sides of equal length.</note>, though it is possible. I draw the line **g.d.h.** <term>tangent</term><note>A line that touches the circle at only one point.</note> to the circle at point **d**. Upon this line, I create angle **b.d.h.** by drawing line **d.f.** equal to angle **c**, and angle **g.d.e.** by drawing line **d.e.** equal to angle **b**. I then draw line **e.f.** By the 31st proposition of the third book, angle **e** will be equal to angle **c**, because both are equal to angle **b.d.h.**—the first by construction and the second by the 31st proposition of the third book. By the same reasoning, angle **f** will be equal to angle **b**. Therefore, by the 32nd proposition of the first book, the third angle **d** will be equal to the third angle **a**. Thus, we have achieved what was proposed.

<image-desc>Geometric diagram for Proposition 2: A circle contains an inscribed triangle with vertices d, e, and f. A tangent line g-h touches the circle at vertex d. Above and to the left of the circle is a separate reference triangle with vertices a, b, and c.</image-desc>

### Proposition 3.

**To <term>circumscribe</term><note>To draw a figure around another so that they touch but do not intersect.</note> a triangle about a given circle that is equiangular to a given triangle.**

To circumscribe a triangle about a given circle that is equiangular to a given triangle. Let the given triangle be **a.b.c.** and the given circle be **d.e.f.** with its center at **g**, as before. I wish to describe around this circle a triangle equiangular to triangle **a.b.c.** Again, it is not necessary for it to be equilateral, though it is possible. I shall extend the base **b.c.** in both directions to form two <term>exterior angles</term><note>The angle between one side of a triangle and the extension of an adjacent side.</note>. From the center **g**, I draw the line **g.d.** to the circumference, and I shall establish angle **d.g.e.** (by drawing line **g.e.**) equal to the exterior angle at **b**, and angle **d.g.f.** (by drawing line **g.f.**) equal to the exterior angle at **c**. From points **d, e,** and **f**, I shall draw lines in both directions at right angles <note>orthogonaliter</note>, which by the 15th conclusion of the third book will be tangent to the circle. I shall extend these tangents until they meet at points **h, k,** and **l**, for it is necessary that they meet. Since both angles at **d** and both at **e** are right angles, if line **d.e.** is understood to be drawn, the two angles on the side of **b** will be less than two right angles. Therefore, by the second-to-last <term>postulate</term><note>original: "petitionem"; referring to Euclid's Parallel Postulate, which states that lines will eventually meet if the interior angles are less than 180 degrees.</note>, the lines **l.d.h.** and **k.e.h.** will meet when extended. By the same reasoning, the lines **h.d.l.** and **k.f.l.** will meet, since both angles at **f** are also right angles. Because in the quadrilateral **h.d.g.e.** the two angles **d** and **e** are right angles, the two angles **g** and **h** together must equal two right angles; for the four angles of any quadrilateral are equal to four right angles, as was shown above in the 32nd proposition of the first book. And because the two angles at **b** (interior and exterior) are likewise equal to two right angles by the 13th proposition of the first book, and the exterior angle **b** was set equal to angle **d.g.e.**, it follows that the interior angle **b** is equal to angle **h**. By similar reasoning, the interior angle **c** will be equal to angle **l**. And because the two interior angles **h** and **l** are less than two right angles by the 32rd proposition of the first book, the lines **h.e.** and **l.f.** will meet at point **k** when extended, according to the second-to-last postulate. Thus, triangle **h.k.l.** is formed. Since angle **h** is equal to the interior angle **b**, and angle **l** is equal to the interior angle **c**, then by the 32nd proposition of the first book, angle **k** must be equal to angle **a**. Thus, we have achieved what was proposed.

A large triangle h-k-l is circumscribed around the circle, tangent at points d, e, and f. To the left is a reference triangle a-b-c with its base extended to the right.</image-desc>

- **Triangle:** A three-sided polygon.

- **Equilaterally:** Having all sides of equal length.

# To describe a circle within a given triangle.

Let **a.b.c.** be the assigned triangle. I wish to describe a circle within it; this is, as it were, the converse of the second proposition. For I divide its two angles, **a.** and **b.**, by the [9th] proposition <note>Euclid's method for bisecting an angle</note>: one bisector being the line **a.d.** and from **b.** the line **b.d.**, which meet at point **d.** From this point, I shall draw perpendiculars to its three sides: **d.e.** to **a.b.**, **d.f.** to **b.c.**, and **d.g.** to **a.c.** Because in the two triangles **e.a.d.** and **g.a.d.**, the angle **a.** of one is equal to angle **a.** of the other, and both angles **e.** and **g.** are right angles, and the side **a.d.** is common to both, then by the 26th proposition of the first book <note>The Angle-Angle-Side congruence theorem</note>, the line **d.e.** will be equal to the line **d.g.** By the same reasoning, since in the two triangles **e.b.d.** and **f.b.d.**, the angle **b.** of one is equal to angle **b.** of the other, and both angles **e.** and **f.** are right angles, and the side **d.b.** is common, then by the same proposition, line **e.d.** will be equal to line **d.f.** Wherefore the three lines **d.e.**, **d.f.**, and **d.g.** are equal. Therefore, with the center placed at **d.** and a circle described according to the length of one of them, it will pass through the ends of the other two by the 9th proposition of the third book. And because, by the 15th conclusion of the third book, each of the lines **a.b.**, **b.c.**, and **c.a.** will be <term>tangent</term><note>Touching the circle at only one point without crossing into it.</note> to the circle, it is clear that the proposal has been accomplished.

## Proposition 5.

### To describe a circle around an assigned triangle, whether it be <term>right-angled</term><note>Latin: Orthogonium; a triangle with one 90-degree angle.</note>, <term>obtuse-angled</term><note>Latin: Ambligonium; a triangle with one angle greater than 90 degrees.</note>, or <term>acute-angled</term><note>Latin: Oxigonium; a triangle where all angles are less than 90 degrees.</note>.

About the assigned triangle **a.b.c.**, I wish to describe a circle; this is, as it were, the converse of the third proposition. I divide its two sides, **a.b.** and **a.c.**, into equal parts: **a.b.** at point **d.** and **a.c.** at point **e.** From these points, I produce perpendiculars to the lines **a.b.** and **a.c.**, which I extend until they meet at point **f.**; let these be **d.f.** and **e.f.** They will surely meet because, since both angles **d.** and **e.** are right angles, if the line **d.e.** is understood to be drawn, the two interior angles on the side they are extended will be less than two right angles; therefore they will meet by the <term>penultimate postulate</term><note>The 5th Postulate, or the Parallel Postulate, which states that if two lines meet a third such that the interior angles are less than 180 degrees, the lines must eventually intersect.</note>. Therefore, from point **f.**, which is the point of intersection and which I say is the center of the sought circle, I shall draw lines to each of the angles, which are **f.a.**, **f.b.**, and **f.c.** And because in triangle **a.d.f.**, the two sides **a.d.** and **d.f.** are equal to the two sides **b.d.** and **d.f.** of triangle **b.d.f.**, and angle **d.** of one equals angle **d.** of the other (since both are right angles), it will be by the 4th proposition of the first book that **f.a.** is equal to **f.b.** By the same reasoning, **f.a.** will be equal to **f.c.**, comparing the sides and angles of the two triangles **a.e.f.** and **c.e.f.** Therefore, by the 9th proposition of the third book, point **f.** will be the center of the sought circle. This is the universal demonstration for all types of triangles. ¶ However, since the author seems to wish to vary the method by distinguishing between the right-angled, obtuse-angled, and acute-angled, each of them must be demonstrated individually. ¶ Let the proposed triangle be right-angled, and let angle **a.** be the right angle. I divide the side **b.c.**, which faces this right angle, into equal parts at point **f.** From this point, which I say is the center of the circle, I draw the line **f.d.** to the midpoint of one of the two remaining sides, let it be **d.** And because the line **f.d.** divides two sides (**a.b.** and **b.c.**) of triangle **a.b.c.** into equal parts, it will be <term>parallel</term><note>Latin: equidistans.</note> to the third side, namely line **a.c.** This was demonstrated above in the 39th proposition of the first book. And because angle **a.** was set as a right angle, by the second and third parts of the 29th proposition of the first book, both angles at **d.** will be right angles. Let line **f.a.** be drawn; then by the 4th proposition of the first book, line **a.f.** will be equal to line **b.f.**, by comparing the sides and angles of triangles **a.d.f.** and **b.d.f.** to one another. And since line **b.f.** is equal to line **c.f.**, the three lines **b.f.**, **a.f.**, and **c.f.** will be equal to one another. Wherefore, by the 9th proposition of the third book, **f.** will be the center of the sought circle. ¶ Let the triangle **a.b.c.** again be obtuse-angled, and let angle **a.** be [the obtuse angle]...

A line cutting two sides of a triangle into equal parts is parallel to the third side. <note>original: "Linea ſecans duo latera tr'angli p[er] eq[ua]lia 3^a. est equidistans"</note>

the side **b.c.** facing this obtuse angle. I divide it into equal parts at point **b.** <note>The text likely refers to the midpoint of the base, though the letter labels follow the diagram's logic</note> from which, to the midpoints of the two remaining sides which are **d.** and **e.**, I draw lines **b.d.** and **b.e.** Then **d.b.** will be parallel to **a.c.** and **e.b.** parallel to **a.b.** because of what was demonstrated above in the 39th [proposition] of the first [book] <note>Euclid, Elements I.39</note>: namely, that a line cutting two sides of any triangle into equal parts is parallel to the third side. Therefore, by the second part of the 29th [proposition] of the first [book], each of the two angles **b.d.b.** and **c.e.b.** will be equal to angle **a.**, and therefore each is obtuse. 

Thus, having drawn the perpendiculars **d.f.** to line **a.b.** and **e.f.** to line **a.c.** until they meet at point **f.**, I declare this point to be the center of the circle. It is clear that they meet for the reason previously stated. Each of them will cut line **b.c.** which faces the obtuse angle, and they meet outside the triangle **a.b.c.** Therefore, from point **f.**, which is their point of intersection, I draw lines **f.a.**, **f.b.**, and **f.c.**, which by the 4th [proposition] of the first [book] applied twice, will be equal—first by comparing the sides and angles of the two triangles **a.d.f.** and **b.d.f.**, and then the other two, **a.e.f.** and **c.e.f.** Wherefore, by the 9th [proposition] of the third [book], **f.** is the center of the sought-after circle. 

Let it be again that triangle **a.b.c.** is an <term>acute-angled triangle<gloss>oxigonius</gloss></term>. All its sides having been divided into equal parts: namely, side **a.b.** at point **d.**, side **a.c.** at point **e.**, and **b.c.** at point **h.** I draw lines **d.e.**, **d.h.**, and **e.h.** Then **d.h.** will be parallel to **a.c.** and **e.h.** to **a.b.** because of what was demonstrated in the 39th [proposition] of the first [book]. Wherefore, by the second part of the 39th [proposition] of the first [book], each of the angles **b.d.b.** and **c.e.h.** will be equal to angle **a.**, and therefore acute. Thus, having drawn the perpendiculars **d.f.** to line **a.b.** and **e.f.** to line **a.c.**, it is manifest that they meet inside the triangle **a.b.c.** Let the point of intersection be **f.**, which I say is the center of the circle. For I draw lines **f.a.**, **f.b.**, and **f.c.**, which by the 4th [proposition] of the first [book], applied twice as before, will be equal. Wherefore, by the 9th [proposition] of the third [book], **f.** will be the center of the sought-after circle. 

From the aforesaid, it is clear that if the triangle is <term>right-angled<gloss>orthogonius</gloss></term>, the center of the circumscribing circle will fall in the middle of the side which is opposite the right angle <note>the hypotenuse</note>. If it is <term>obtuse-angled<gloss>ambligonius</gloss></term>, the center will fall outside the triangle. If, however, it is <term>acute-angled<gloss>oxigonius</gloss></term>, it will fall inside the triangle.

->Proposition .6.<-

### To describe a square within a given circle.

Within a given circle **a.b.c.d.**, whose center is **e.**, I wish to describe a square. I draw within it two diameters, **a.c.** and **b.d.**, cutting each other <term>perpendicularly<gloss>orthogonaliter</gloss></term> at the center **e.** I join the ends of these by drawing lines **a.b.**, **b.c.**, **c.d.**, and **d.a.**, which I say contain the sought-after square. For they themselves will be equal to one another, by the 4th [proposition] of the first [book] applied three times, because the four lines **e.a.**, **e.b.**, **e.c.**, and **e.d.** are equal. And the four angles at **e.** are right angles. Also, each of the four angles **a.**, **b.**, **c.**, and **d.** is a right angle by the first part of the 31st [proposition] of the third [book] <note>The OCR says "30. tertii", but Euclid's 3.31 proves angles in a semicircle are right</note>, because each of them is in a semicircle. Therefore **a.b.c.d.** will be a square by definition, which is what was proposed.

...orthogonally through the center **e.**, and from its endpoints I draw lines in both directions orthogonally <term>orthogonally</term><note>Meaning at right angles, or perpendicularly</note> until each of them meets with the two lateral lines. Let the points of intersection be **f.**, **g.**, **h.**, and **k.** <note>The transcription lists 'ca.e.f.g.b.k.', but the geometric logic and diagrams typically use f, g, h, k for the outer vertices.</note> By the 15th [proposition] of the third [book], each of the angles at the four points **a.**, **b.**, **c.**, and **d.** is a right angle. Therefore, because in the quadrilateral **a.f.b.e.** three angles **a.**, **b.**, and **c.** are right angles, the fourth angle **f.** must also be a right angle; for every quadrilateral has four angles equal to four right angles, as was demonstrated above in the 32nd [proposition] of the first [book]. By the same reasoning, each of the angles **g.**, **h.**, and **k.** will be a right angle. Therefore, by the second part of the 28th [proposition] of the first [book], the two lines **f.g.** and **k.h.** and the two lines **f.k.** and **g.h.** are parallel. Thus, by the 34th [proposition] of the first [book], **f.k.** is equal to **g.h.** and **f.g.** to **k.h.** And because by the same [proposition] **f.k.** is equal to **b.d.** and **f.g.** to **a.c.**, and since **b.d.** is equal to **a.c.**, the four lines **f.k.**, **g.h.**, **f.g.**, and **k.h.** will be equal. Furthermore, since the four angles **f.**, **g.**, **k.**, and **h.** are right angles, as was proved before, **f.g.h.k.** is a square by definition. This is what was proposed.

### Proposition 8.

<margin>
<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing a circle inscribed within a square labeled 'a', 'b', 'c', 'd'. Midpoints of the sides are labeled 'f' (top), 'g' (left), 'e' (right), and 'h' (bottom), with lines connecting them intersecting at the center 'k'.</image-desc>
</margin>

**T**o describe a circle within a given square.
Let the given square be **a.b.c.d.** I wish to describe a circle inside it. This is essentially the converse of Proposition 6. I divide each of its sides into equal parts: **a.d.** at point **f.**, **b.a.** at point **g.**, **c.b.** at point **h.**, and **d.c.** at point **e.** I then draw the lines **e.g.** and **f.h.**, which intersect at point **k.**, which I claim is the center of the circle. Indeed, **f.b.** will be parallel and equal to **a.b.** <note>The author likely means a segment within the square parallel to the side</note> per the 33rd [proposition] of the first [book], because **a.f.** and **d.b.** are equal and parallel. Similarly, by the same reasoning, **e.d.** [is parallel to] **a.b.** And because all the halves of the four sides of the square are equal to each other, by the 34th [proposition] of the first [book], the four lines **k.e.**, **k.f.**, **k.g.**, and **k.h.** will be equal. Therefore, by the 9th [proposition] of the third [book], **k.** is the center of the required circle.

---

### Proposition 9.

<margin>
<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing a circle circumscribing a square with vertices 'a', 'b' (top) and 'd', 'c' (bottom). Two diagonal lines intersect at the central point 'e'.</image-desc>
</margin>

**T**o describe a circle around a given square.
Let the square be **a.b.c.d.** I wish to describe a circle around it. This is essentially the converse of Proposition 7. I draw two diameters <term>diameters</term><note>Here the author refers to the diagonals of the square</note> **a.c.** and **b.d.** within it, which intersect at point **e.**, which I claim is the center of the circle. Since the lines **a.d.** and **a.b.** are equal, by the 5th [proposition] of the first [book], the angles **a.d.b.** and **a.b.d.** will be equal. And since the whole angle **a.** is a right angle, by the 32nd [proposition] of the first [book], each of those angles will be half of a right angle. In the same way, it will be proved that each of the small angles formed by the aforementioned diameters and the sides of the proposed square is half of a right angle. Because, therefore, angle **e.a.d.** is equal to angle **e.d.a.**, by the 9th [proposition] of the first [book] <note>The author likely refers to the proposition that sides opposite equal angles are equal, which is I.6 in standard Euclid</note>, line **e.a.** will be equal to line **e.d.** For the same reason, **e.a.** will be equal to **e.b.**, and **e.c.** will be equal to **e.d.** Thus, since the four lines **e.a.**, **e.b.**, **e.c.**, and **e.d.** are equal, by the 9th [proposition] of the third [book], **e.** is the center of the required circle. This is what was proposed.
