### Proposition 10.

<margin>
This proposition is extracted from Book 13, Proposition 27. <note>original: "hac propositio extrahur 27 . f . 13"</note>
</margin>

**T**o construct an isosceles triangle <term>isosceles triangle</term><note>A triangle with at least two equal sides</note> in which each of the two angles at the base is double the remaining angle.
The intention is to describe a triangle with two equal sides and a third unequal side, such that each of the angles on the unequal side is double the third angle. To do this, take any line **a.b.** and divide it at point **c.** as taught in the 11th [proposition] of the second [book], so that the rectangle formed by **a.b.** and **b.c.** is equal to the square of **a.c.** <note>This "extreme and mean ratio" construction is the basis for the Golden Ratio, used here to find the proportions needed for a regular pentagon.</note>

It begins Proposition 10, which describes the construction of a specific isosceles triangle used in further complex polygons.</summary>

This specific triangle is the essential "building block" for constructing a regular pentagon.</meta>

And having made point **a.** the center, let a circle **b.d.e.** be described according to its [the line's] quantity <note>Original: "sm [secundum] ipsius quantitatem". This refers to using the length of a given line as the radius.</note>, within which, by the first [proposition] of this [book], let line **b.d.** be fitted equal to line **a.c.**, and let two lines **d.a.** and **d.c.** be produced. I say that triangle **a.b.d.** is such as was proposed. Let a circle, which shall be **d.c.a.**, be circumscribed <term>circumscribed</term><note>To draw a figure around another so they touch at the vertices</note> about triangle **d.c.a.** by the 5th [proposition] of this [book]. Since, therefore, line **d.b.** is equal to line **a.c.**, it will be that the rectangle produced from **a.b.** and **b.c.** <note>The text uses the phrase "quod fit ex... in..." to describe the area of a rectangle formed by two segments.</note> is equal to the square of line **b.d.** Wherefore, by the last [proposition] of the third [book], line **b.d.** is tangent to circle **d.c.a.**; and by the 31st [proposition] of the same, angle **c.d.b.** is equal to angle **c.a.d.** Therefore, with angle **c.d.a.** being made common, the whole angle **b.d.a.** will be equal to the two angles **c.a.d.** and **c.d.a.** But by the 32nd [proposition] of the first [book], angle **b.c.d.** is equal to those same [angles] because it is exterior to them. Therefore, angle **b.d.a.** is equal to angle **b.c.d.** And because angle **a.d.b.** is equal to angle **a.b.d.** by the 5th [proposition] of the first [book]—for the reason that sides **a.d.** and **a.b.** are equal <note>They are both radii of the same circle.</note>—angle **b.c.d.** will be equal to angle **c.b.d.** Therefore, by the 6th [proposition] of the first [book], line **c.d.** is equal to line **b.d.**, and thus also to line **a.c.** And by the 32nd [proposition] of the first [book], angle **c.a.d.** is equal to angle **c.d.a.** Since, therefore, each of the angles **c.d.b.** and **c.d.a.** is equal to angle **c.a.d.**, the whole angle **b.d.a.** will be double the angle **d.a.b.**; and therefore angle **a.b.d.**, being equal to it, is also double the angle **b.a.d.**, which is what was proposed.

¶ Perhaps an adversary <note>A common term in scholastic logic for a hypothetical person raising an objection to the proof.</note> will say that the circle **d.c.a.** circumscribed about the partial triangle cuts the circle **b.d.e.** at some point on the arc **b.d.**, so that it will simultaneously cut line **b.d.**, whereby that line would not be applied to the circle, as is supposed in the demonstration, but rather intersecting it. Let it be so, then, if it is possible as the adversary posits, and from point **b.** let a tangent **b.f.** be drawn to that smaller circle. Lines **f.a.** and **f.d.** shall be drawn, and by the penultimate [proposition] of the third [book], the rectangle of **a.b.** and **b.c.** will be equal to the square of **b.f.** Therefore, **b.f.** is equal to **b.d.** Wherefore, by the 5th [proposition] of the first [book], angle **b.f.d.** is equal to angle **b.d.f.** And because by the 31st [proposition] of the third [book], angle **b.f.a.** is equal to angle **a.d.f.**, angle **b.d.f.** would be greater than angle **a.d.f.**, which is impossible, since it [angle a.d.f.] is a part of it [angle b.d.f.].

¶ In another way we can refute this and show that the smaller circle will in no way cut line **b.d.**; for perhaps he might say that it cuts it without cutting arc **d.b.** of the larger circle. If indeed it is possible that it cuts it, let this be at point **b.**; then the rectangle of **a.b.** and **b.c.** would be equal to that which is made from **d.b.** and **b.b.** <note>A phrasing indicating the square of the segment.</note> For it was shown above the penultimate [proposition] of the third [book] that if from any point marked outside a circle any number of secant lines are drawn to the circle, the rectangles contained under the whole lines and their external portions are equal to one another. And because the rectangle of **a.b.** and **b.c.** is equal to the square of **b.d.**, then the rectangle of **d.b.** and **b.b.** would be equal to the square of **d.b.**, which is impossible by the second [proposition] of the second [book]. Wherefore the proposition is established.

¶ And note that the smaller circle will necessarily cut the larger and cut off from it one arc equal to arc **b.d.**, and the larger will similarly cut off from the same one arc equal to arc **d.c.** Which is proved thus: for if the smaller does not cut the larger, it then touches it at point **d.** And because by the 11th [proposition] of the third [book], the centers of circles touching each other and the point of contact are in one line, the center of the smaller circle will be on line **a.d.**, because the center of the larger and the point of contact are on it. Therefore, by the 17th [proposition] of the third [book], angle **a.d.b.** is a right angle, wherefore similarly angle **a.b.d.**, being equal to it, is a right angle; which is impossible by the 32nd [proposition] of the first [book]. Therefore, let it cut it at points **e.** and **d.** I say that arc **e.d.** of the larger is equal to arc **d.b.**, and arc **e.d.** of the smaller is equal to arc **d.c.** I produce lines **d.e.**, **c.e.**, and **e.a.** It will then be, by the 26th [proposition] of the third [book], that each of the four angles **d.e.c.**, **c.e.a.**, **d.a.c.**, and **a.d.c.** is equal to another for the reason that the two arcs **d.e.** and **e.a.** are equal by the 27th [proposition] of the same. Wherefore the whole angle **a.e.d.** is double the angle **b.a.d.**, and thus equal to both angles **a.b.d.** and **a.d.b.** And because angle **a.e.d.** is equal to angle **a.d.c.** by the 5th [proposition] of the first [book], because **a.e.** and **a.d.** are equal from the center to the circumference, the two angles **e.** and **d.** of triangle **a.e.d.** will be [equal].

->Proposition 11<-

### To describe an equilateral and equiangular pentagon within a given circle.

<image-desc>A circular diagram showing a circle with an inscribed pentagon. The vertices are labeled a, d, b, c, e. Chords connect the vertices to form the pentagon, and additional lines connect vertices across the circle and to the center. To the left of the circle is a separate triangle labeled with the number 2.</image-desc>

Let **a.b.c.** be the given circle; I wish to describe within it a pentagon that is both equilateral <term>equilateral</term><note>A shape where all sides are of equal length</note> and equiangular <term>equiangular</term><note>A shape where all interior angles are equal</note>. I designate a triangle of the kind that the previous [proposition] proposed, which shall be triangle **2.**; I describe another equiangular triangle within the given circle as the second [proposition] of this [book] teaches, which shall be **a.b.c.** Let each of the angles **a.b.c.** and **a.c.b.** be double the angle **c.a.b.** I divide each of those [base angles] into equal parts by drawing lines **b.e.** and **c.d.** By the 25th [proposition] of the third [book], the five arcs into which the five points **a., d., b., c., e.** divide the circle will be equal to one another, because the five angles that fall upon the said arcs are equal to one another. Therefore, having connected those five points with straight lines, which are **a.d., d.b., b.c., c.e.,** and **e.a.**, the pentagon **a.d.b.c.e.** will be inscribed in the given circle as proposed. For it is equilateral by the 28th [proposition] of the third [book], since the five arcs of which its five sides are chords are equal to one another; and it is also equiangular by the 26th [proposition] of the same [book], because the five arcs **d.a.e., a.c.e., c.b.d.,** and **b.d.a.**, upon which the angles of the pentagon itself fall, are equal to one another. Thus the proposition is established.

->Proposition 12<-

### To design an equilateral and equiangular pentagon around a given circle.

<image-desc>A circular diagram illustrating a circumscribed pentagon construction. An inscribed pentagon with vertices a, d, b, c, e is shown within the circle. Outside it, a larger pentagon with vertices g, h, k, l, m is circumscribed, with its sides tangent to the circle at the vertices of the inner pentagon. Lines connect the center f to both the inner vertices and the outer vertices.</image-desc>

Let **a.b.c.** be the proposed circle, whose center is **f.**; I wish to design an equilateral and equiangular pentagon around it. Upon the circumference of this circle, as if I had inscribed a pentagon according to the teaching of the previous [proposition], I will mark five angular points, which are **a., d., b., c., e.** To these I will draw lines from the center, **f.a., f.d., f.b., f.c., f.e.**, and from these same points I will draw perpendicular lines to these [radial] lines in both directions until they meet at points **g., h., k., l., m.** These lines will be tangent to the circle by the corollary of the 15th [proposition] of the third [book]. To these points of intersection, I will draw lines from the center: **f.g., f.h., f.k., f.l., f.m.** And because it was shown in the penultimate [proposition] of the third [book] <note>Original: "super penultimā tertii". This refers to Proposition III.36 in many editions, regarding tangents from a point.</note> that if two tangent lines are drawn to a circle from any point marked outside the circle, they will be equal, the line **g.a.** will be equal to line **g.d.**, and **h.d.** to **h.b.**, and so on for the rest. But since the five arcs into which the five points **a., d., b., c., e.** divide the circle are equal to one another, by the 26th [proposition] of the third [book], the five angles **a.f.d., d.f.b., b.f.c., c.f.e., e.f.a.** standing upon these arcs at the center **f.** will be equal to one another. Moreover, the two sides **a.g.** and **f.a.** of triangle **f.g.a.** are equal to the two sides **d.g.** and **f.d.** of triangle **f.g.d.**, and the side **g.f.** is common [to both]. Therefore, by the 8th [proposition] of the first [book], the two angles **a.f.g.** and **d.f.g.** are equal to one another. By the same reasoning, the two angles **d.f.h.** and **h.f.b.** are equal to one another. Similarly, each of the three remaining angles, which are **b.f.c., c.f.e., e.f.a.**, and each of the three [points] **k., l., m.**, are divided into equal parts by the [propositions] of the first [book]: the first by line **f.k.**, the second by line **f.l.**, and the third by line **f.m.** And because these three angles **b.f.c., c.f.e., e.f.a.** are equal to one another and equal to the other two, **a.f.d.** and **d.f.b.**, their halves will be equal, which are the ten angles made at the center **f.**...

...mutually equal. Since, therefore, the two angles of triangle **g.a.f.** are equal to the two angles of triangle **m.a.f.** <note>original: "a.z.f." - Likely a scribal shorthand for the specific angles at the vertex or base</note>, and the side **a.f.** is common, then by the 26th [proposition] of the first [book] <note>Proposition I.26 is a rule for triangle congruence (ASA or AAS): if two angles and one side are equal, the whole triangle is identical.</note>, the angle **g.** of one is equal to the angle **m.** of the other, and side **g.a.** is equal to side **a.m.** By the same reasoning, the angle **g.** in triangle **g.f.d.** will be equal to the angle **h.** in triangle **d.f.h.**, and side **g.d.** equal to side **d.h.** Because **g.a.** is half of **g.m.**, and **g.d.** is half of **g.h.**, and since **g.a.** and **g.d.** are equal, it follows by common knowledge <term>common knowledge</term><note>Referring to Euclid's "Common Notions," specifically that if equals are added to equals, the wholes are equal.</note> that their doubles, **g.m.** and **g.h.**, are equal. Similarly, we shall prove **g.m.** to be equal to **m.l.**, and **m.l.** to **l.k.**, and **l.k.** to **k.h.** Therefore, the pentagon **g.h.k.l.m.** is equilateral. But it is also equiangular; for since the two partial angles at **g.** are mutually equal, and the two at **m.** are likewise mutually equal, and the partial angle at **g.** is equal to the partial angle at **m.** (as both were proved before), it follows by that same common knowledge that the total angle **g.** is equal to the total angle **m.** By the same reasoning, you will prove equality in the remaining angles. Therefore, it is equiangular, and thus the proposition is established.

### Proposition 13.

### Within a given equilateral and equiangular pentagon, to describe a circle.

Let **a.b.c.d.e.** be the assigned equilateral and equiangular pentagon (as this is not necessarily possible for others). I wish to inscribe a circle within it. This is, as it were, the converse of the 11th [proposition]. I divide its two adjacent angles, **a.** and **e.**, into equal parts by drawing lines **a.f.** and **e.f.** until they meet at point **f.** within the pentagon, which I say is the center of the circle. They will indeed meet because half of the total angle **a.** and likewise half of the total angle **e.** is less than a right angle <note>In a regular pentagon, each interior angle is 108 degrees; half is 54 degrees, which is less than 90.</note>.
If they did not meet inside the pentagon, they would meet either outside the pentagon, or on a side of the pentagon, or at one of its angles opposite to the two different angles.
Suppose they first meet outside at point **f.** and the line **b.f.** is drawn. Because the two sides **e.a.** and **a.f.** of triangle **e.a.f.** are equal to the two sides **b.a.** and **a.f.** of triangle **b.a.f.**, and angle **a.** of the one is equal to angle **a.** of the other, then by the 4th [proposition] of the first [book] <note>Proposition I.4 is the SAS (Side-Angle-Side) congruence theorem.</note>, the base **e.f.** is equal to the base **f.b.** And because the partial angle **a.** is equal to the partial angle **e.** (since the total angle **a.** is equal to the total angle **e.**), then by the 6th [proposition] of the first [book], **f.a.** is equal to **f.e.** Therefore, **f.a.** is equal to **f.b.** Thus, by the 5th [proposition] of the first [book], the two angles of the total **b.** and the partial **a.** are equal <note>This refers to the angles at the base of an isosceles triangle being equal.</note>. Consequently, the partial angle **a.** would be equal as a part to the total angle **a.**, which is impossible.
Suppose they meet instead at point **f.** upon the side **b.c.** By arguing through the same premises and in the same manner, the partial angle **a.** would be equal to the total angle **a.**, which is impossible.
And if by chance they should meet at angle **c.**, then by the same means and in the same way, **c.b.** would be equal to **c.a.**, and therefore, as before, the partial angle **a.** would be equal to the total angle **a.**
Since none of these can be the case, let the point of meeting be **f.** inside the pentagon. From this point, I draw five perpendicular lines to its five sides, which shall be **f.g.**, **f.h.** <note>labeled "f.b." in the text, but the diagram implies "f.h." or similar</note>, **f.k.**, **f.l.**, and **f.m.** And to the two adjacent angles on either side of the angles divided into equal parts, which are **b.** and **d.**, I draw the lines **f.b.** and **f.d.** Because the two angles **a.** and **m.** of triangle **a.f.m.** are equal to the two angles **a.** and **g.** of triangle **a.f.g.**, and side **a.f.** is common, then by the 26th [proposition] of the first [book], **f.m.** is equal to **f.g.** By the same reasoning, you will prove **f.l.** equal to **f.m.** by taking the two triangles **z.f.m.** and **e.f.l.** <note>original: "z.f.m." likely refers to a segment of the base</note>. Because again the two sides **a.f.** and **a.b.** of triangle **a.f.b.** are equal to the two sides **a.f.** and **a.e.** of triangle **a.f.e.**, and the angle **a.** of the one is equal to the angle **a.** of the other, then by the 4th [proposition] of the first [book], the partial angle **b.** will be equal to the partial angle **e.** And because the total **b.** is equal to the total **e.**, and the total **e.** is divided into equal parts, the total **b.** will also be divided into equal parts. In the same way, you will prove the total **d.** is divided into equal parts because of the equality of partial **d.** and partial **a.** when triangles **e.a.f.** and **e.d.f.** are taken. Therefore...

...the two angles **g.z.b.** of triangle **g.f.b.** are equal to the two angles **b.z.h.** of triangle **b.f.h.**, and the side **f.b.** is common; therefore, by the 26th proposition of the first book <note>Euclid’s Proposition I.26 proves triangle congruence: if two angles and a side are equal, the triangles are identical.</note>, **f.b.** is equal to **f.g.** In the same way, you will prove that **f.h.** is equal to **f.l.** by taking triangles **l.f.d.** and **k.f.d.** Since, therefore, the five lines **f.g.**, **f.b.**, **f.k.**, **f.l.**, and **f.m.** are equal, **f.** will be the center of the circle, by the 9th proposition of the third book <note>Proposition III.9 states that if more than two equal lines can be drawn from a point to the circumference, that point is the center.</note>, which we shall draw according to the length of one of those lines. And this circle will touch all the sides of the pentagon because of the equality of those lines, and it will not cut through any of them, according to the first part of the 15th proposition of the third book <note>This refers to the property of tangents being perpendicular to the radius.</note>. ### Proposition 14.

<image-desc>A circular diagram showing a circle with an inscribed regular pentagon labeled a-b-c-d-e. The center of the circle is marked 'f', with lines radiating from the center to each vertex. The vertices are arranged with 'a' at the top, 'b' at the top right, 'c' at the bottom right, 'd' at the bottom left, and 'e' at the top left.</image-desc>

**To circumscribe a circle about a given pentagon that is equilateral and equiangular.**

Let the given pentagon be equilateral and equiangular, as before—for it is not necessary that this be possible for other types of pentagons—and let it be **a.b.c.d.e.** I wish to circumscribe a circle about it. This is, in a sense, the converse of the 12th proposition. I divide its two neighboring angles, which are **a.** and **e.**, into equal parts by drawing lines **a.f.** and **e.f.** until they meet within the pentagon at point **f.** They will indeed meet within the pentagon as was proved in the previous proposition. From the point of their meeting, I draw lines to the remaining angles, which are **f.b.**, **f.c.**, and **f.d.** Since the two sides **a.f.** and **a.b.** of triangle **a.f.b.** are equal to the two sides **a.f.** and **a.e.** of triangle **a.f.e.**, and the angle **a.** of one is equal to the angle **a.** of the other, then by the 4th proposition of the first book <note>Prop. I.4 is the Side-Angle-Side (SAS) theorem.</note>, **f.a.** is equal to **f.e.**, and the partial angle **b.** is equal to the partial angle **e.** And because the total angle **b.** is equal to the total angle **a.**, and the total angle **e.** has been divided into equal parts, so likewise the total angle **b.** will be divided into equal parts. In this same way, you will prove each of the angles **c.** and **d.** to be divided into equal parts, and that the five lines **f.a.**, **f.b.**, **f.c.**, **f.d.**, and **f.e.** are equal. Therefore, by the 9th proposition of the third book, **f.** will be the center of the circle. Thus the proposition is clear.

### Proposition 15.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing a large circle with an inscribed regular hexagon composed of six equilateral triangles. Points on the circumference are labeled a, f, b, c, d, g. Point 'a' is at the top, 'f' at top left, 'b' at middle left, 'c' at the bottom, 'd' at middle right, and 'g' at top right. The center point is 'e'. A second circle of the same radius is drawn with its center at point 'c', passing through the center 'e' and intersecting the main circle at points 'b' and 'd'.</image-desc>

**To inscribe an equilateral and equiangular hexagon within a given circle. From this it is also manifest that the side of a hexagon is equal to half the diameter of the circle in which it is inscribed.** <note>Today we would simply call "half the diameter" the radius.</note>

Let the given circle be **a.b.c.d.**, whose center is **e.** I wish to inscribe within it an equilateral and equiangular hexagon. I draw the diameter **a.e.c.**, and according to the length of the semi-diameter <term>semi-diameter</term><note>The radius.</note> **e.c.**, using point **c.** as the center, I describe a circle **e.b.d.** intersecting the first circle at two points, **b.** and **d.** From these points, I draw two diameters in the first circle, which are **b.e.g.** and **d.e.f.** I then join the ends of the three diameters with six lines, which are **a.f.**, **f.b.**, **b.c.**, **c.d.**, **d.g.**, and **g.a.**, which I say contain the sought-after hexagon. For as the first proposition of the first book demonstrates, each of the triangles **b.e.c.** and **c.e.d.** will be equilateral. Therefore, they are also equiangular by the 5th proposition of the same book. Thus, by the 32nd proposition of the first book <note>Prop. I.32 states the interior angles of a triangle sum to two right angles (180 degrees).</note>, the two angles **b.e.c.** and **c.e.d.**, together with one equal to one of them, are equal to two right angles, because each of them is a third of two right angles <note>Each angle is 60 degrees, and three of them make 180 degrees.</note>. But by the 13th proposition of the same book, these together with angle **d.e.g.** are equal to two right angles; therefore, angle **d.e.g.** is equal to each of them. Consequently, by the 15th proposition of the same book, the five angles <note>The text likely means the angles surrounding the center point **e**.</note> which are at **e.** are mutually equal. Therefore, by the 25th proposition of the third book, the arcs upon which they fall are equal; and thus their chords, by the 28th proposition of the same book, which are the sides of the hexagon itself, are equal. It is therefore equilateral. But it is also equiangular by the 26th proposition of the third book, because the six arcs into which the corner points of the hexagon divide the circle, when taken two by two, are mutually equal—as arc **a.f.b.** is equal to arc **f.b.c.**—and therefore angle **f.**, which stands upon the first, is equal to angle **b.**, which stands upon the second. The same holds for the others. Therefore, the proposition is established. From this, the **Corollary** is evident: that the half-diameter and the side of the hexagon are [equal]...

<meta>This page concludes the discussion of Proposition 15 regarding the hexagon and introduces Proposition 16, which details the construction of a fifteen-sided polygon (quindecagon). ...the sides of the same equilateral triangle, such as **e.c.**, **c.b.**, and **c.d.** And note that it is not explicitly proposed to designate an equilateral and equiangular hexagon <term>exagonum</term><note>a six-sided polygon</note> around the given circle. Nor is it proposed to describe such a hexagon within such a circle, or a circle around it, in the same way he did for the triangle, the square, and the pentagon. This is not because it is impossible or unnecessary, but because these three operations are performed by the same principles used for the equilateral and equiangular pentagon, and indeed for any equilateral and equiangular figure whatsoever. Therefore, whatever equilateral and equiangular figure we know how to inscribe in a circle, we can also describe that same figure outside the circle, and a circle inside and outside of it, using the same means by which we did these things for the pentagon.

¶ Note also that every equilateral figure inscribed in or circumscribed about a circle is also necessarily equiangular. In the case of an inscribed figure, this is clear through the 26th and 27th propositions of the third book <note>These propositions relate the equality of arcs to the equality of the angles and chords that subtend them.</note> by taking the arcs of the circle for which the sides of the inscribed figure are chords, two by two. For the angles of the figure itself fall upon these arcs. In the case of a circumscribed figure, however, by drawing lines from the center of the circle to all its angles and to the points of contact, you will easily prove this if a diligent understanding is applied to the fully understood demonstration of the 13th proposition of this book. For it will be seen that the lines coming from the center divide all the angles of the figure into equal parts. Thus, by taking any two of its adjacent sides along with the line to the angle contained by them, and with the two lines coming from the center to their extremities, you will prove that the two triangles contained by them are equiangular to each other by the 4th proposition of the first book <note>The Side-Angle-Side (SAS) theorem.</note>. And by doing this for all of them, it will be clear that they are equiangular by this common principle: those things whose halves are equal must themselves be equal.

## Proposition 16.

**T**o design an equilateral and equiangular quindecagon <term>quindecagonum</term><note>a fifteen-sided polygon</note> within a given circle. ¶ Then, to describe an equilateral and equiangular quindecagon around any assigned circle, and to describe a circle within a given quindecagon.

¶ Let the given circle be **a.b.c.** I wish to inscribe an equilateral and equiangular quindecagon within it; then also to circumscribe one, and to describe a circle within such a proposed quindecagon. It does not, however, propose to describe a circle *around* such a quindecagon, because it gives enough understanding of this through the other things it proposes. In the given circle, according to the teaching of the second proposition of this book, I draw the side of an equilateral triangle, which is **a.c.**, and according to the teaching of the second, the side of an equilateral and equiangular pentagon, which is **a.b.** And because the arc **a.c.** is a third of the whole circumference, and the arc **a.b.** is a fifth, the remainder between them—which is arc **b.c.**—will be two-thirds of a fifth, or two-fifths of a third; that is, two-fifteenths of the whole circumference. For in every whole, a third exceeds a fifth by two-thirds of that fifth, or by two-fifths of that third, or by two-fifteenths of the whole. This is clear in the third and fifth parts of the first number having both a fifth and a third, which is 15 <note>15 is the lowest common multiple of 3 and 5, making it the "first number" to demonstrate these fractions easily.</note>. For its third, which is 5, exceeds its fifth, which is 3, by two units; these are two-thirds of the three (the fifth), or two-fifths of the five (the third), or two-fifteenths of the 15 (the whole). Therefore, by dividing the arc **b.c.** into equal parts at **d**, it is clear that each of the two arcs **c.d.** and **d.b.** is a third of arc **a.b.**, or a fifth of arc **a.c.**, or a fifteenth of the whole circumference. Therefore, by subtending the chords **c.d.** and **d.b.** and fitting them continuously within the given circle equal to themselves by the first proposition of this book, the proposed figure will be completed. ¶ As for the other two things it proposes, along with the third which it implies—namely, a quindecagon in a circle...

# BOOK

...to circumscribe, and to inscribe a circle within a fifteen-sided polygon <term>quindecagono</term><note>a 15-sided regular polygon</note>, and also to circumscribe it, you will easily accomplish by fully understanding propositions 12, 13, 7, and 14 of this book. ¶ And note that for whatever equilateral figure we know how to inscribe in a circle, we also know how to inscribe and circumscribe a figure with double the number of sides in that circle, and a circle within that figure. For once the arcs subtended by the sides of the known inscribed figure have been divided into equal parts, and lines are drawn from the midpoints to the ends of the sides of that figure, there will be formed within the circle a figure with double the number of sides which will be equilateral according to the 28th proposition of the third book <note>original: "28. tertij"; referring to Euclid's Elements, where equal chords subtend equal arcs</note>. Therefore, it will also be equiangular; for this was demonstrated above in the 15th proposition of this book, which states that every equilateral figure inscribed in a circle is also equiangular. And because we know how to inscribe an equilateral triangle in this circle, we shall know through this how to inscribe a hexagon <term>exagonum</term><note>6 sides</note>, and through the hexagon a dodecagon <term>duodecagonū</term><note>12 sides</note>, and through the dodecagon a figure of 24 sides, and so on to infinity by doubling. And although a hexagon can be inscribed through a triangle as we have said, he nevertheless placed a specific demonstration for it here, from which follows a most powerful and useful conclusion. And similarly, because we know how to inscribe a square, we shall know through this how to inscribe every figure whose number of sides is even-times-even <term>pariter par</term><note>A number that can be divided by two repeatedly until reaching one, such as 4, 8, 16, etc.</note>. Through the pentagon <term>penthagonum</term> we shall also know the decagon <term>decagonum</term><note>10 sides</note>, and a figure of 20 sides, and so by continuing to double. Understand the same likewise for the fifteen-sided polygon <term>quindecagono</term>; for through it, figures of 30 and 60 sides, and all figures with a continually doubled number of sides, shall be known. ¶ However, the knowledge of other figures about which this [book] does not teach, or which cannot be found through these, is difficult and of little use, such as heptagons <term>eptagona</term><note>7 sides</note>, nonagons <term>nonagena</term><note>9 sides</note>, and undecagons <term>undecagona</term><note>11 sides</note>. But if we knew how to designate an isosceles triangle <note>original: "triangulū duū equaliū laterū"; literally 'a triangle of two equal sides'</note> in which each of the angles at the base was triple the remaining angle, we would know how to inscribe a heptagon in a circle, just as we inscribed the pentagon above. And if each [base angle] were quadruple the other, we would know the nonagon; and if quintuple, the undecagon. The same applies to other figures with an odd number of sides, by setting each of the angles at the base as a multiple of the remaining angle by that number which is half of the greatest even number contained beneath the odd number of sides of the figure itself.

To divide a given angle into three equal parts <note>This refers to the "Angle Trisection," one of the three famous problems of antiquity. While impossible with only a compass and straightedge, the author here describes a specific geometric construction/proof.</note>. Let the given angle be **a. c. b.** I wish to divide it into three equal angles, which I do as follows. First, I place **c** as the center, describing a circle in whatever way it happens to fall. And I extend the sides containing the given angle until they cut the circumference at points **a** and **b**. Then, from point **c**, which is the center of the circle, I draw line **c. d.** perpendicular to line **c. b.**, and on line **c. d.** I mark point **e**, from which I draw a line equal to **c. b.** until it cuts the circumference of the circle at point **f**, and I extend **e** toward **a**. Then I draw line **g. b.** parallel to **f. a.**; let this **g. b.** pass through the center. And I draw line **f. g.** parallel to line **c. e.**, and I extend line **c. b.** continuously and straight to **l**, which cuts line **f. g.** perpendicularly at point **o** and into two equal parts. I say, therefore, that arc **l. g.** is equal to arc **h. b.** because of this: that angle **l. g. c.** is equal to angle **h. c. b.**, since they are positioned opposite to each other. Since, therefore, arc **f. g.** is double arc **l. g.**, it will also be double arc **h. b.** But arc **f. g.** is equal to arc **a. b.**, since they are between two parallel lines, which are **f. a.** and **g. b.** Therefore, arc **b. a.** is double arc **h. b.** Therefore, angle **a. c. b.** is also double angle **h. c. b.** I shall therefore divide angle **a. c. b.** into two equal parts by line **c. m.**, and the proposition is clear.

# Definition 1.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'P' featuring intricate interlaced vine patterns within a square frame.</image-desc>
**A** part is a quantity of a quantity, the smaller of the larger, when the smaller measures the larger.

¶ "Part" is sometimes used in its proper sense: and this is that which, when taken a certain number of times, constitutes its whole precisely, without deficiency or excess; and it is said to "measure" its whole by that number according to which it is taken to constitute that same whole. Such a part, which we call **multiplicative**, is defined here. ¶ Sometimes it is used in a common sense, and this is any smaller quantity which, however many times it is taken, constitutes less or more than its whole. This we call **aggregative** <note>Also known as an "additive" part; a piece of a whole that is not an exact divisor, like 3 is a part of 7.</note> because it constitutes its whole together with another different quantity; but by itself, no matter how many times it is taken, it does not produce the whole.

# Definition 2.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'M' featuring interlaced foliate patterns within a square frame.</image-desc>
**A** multiple is the larger of the smaller when the smaller measures it.

¶ "Part" is spoken of in relation to the "whole": and their relationship to each other consists in these two extremes. Therefore, the definition here defines the larger extreme by the smaller. He calls it a **multiple** <term>multiplex</term><note>A quantity that contains another quantity some number of times exactly.</note> because the smaller, taken a certain number of times, constitutes it; therefore, "part" and "multiple" will be terms spoken of in relation to each other. For every part is a **submultiple** <term>submultiplex</term>, as is clear from its definition.

¶ Ratio is the relation of two things of the same kind to each other in that one of them is larger or smaller than the other, or equal to it. For ratio is found not only in quantities, but also in weights, powers, and sounds. In weights and powers, Plato <note>original: "plato"</note> maintains in the *Timaeus* <note>original: "thimeo"</note> that there is ratio, where he shows the number of elements; moreover, it is clear from music that ratio exists in sounds. For as Boethius <note>original: "Boecius"</note> maintains in his fourth book, if any string is divided into two unequal parts, there will be the same ratio between these parts and their sounds, in an inverse fashion. But in whatever things ratio is found, they participate in the nature and property of quantity; for it is not found in any two things except in that one of them is larger or smaller than the other, or equal to it. ¶ Now, it is the property of quantity to be called "equal" or "unequal" according to itself, as Aristotle <note>original: "Aristo"</note> maintains in the *Categories* <note>original: "predicamentis"</note>. From this it is clear that ratio is found primarily in quantity, and through quantity in all other things. Nor is there a ratio in any things to which a similar ratio does not exist in some quantities. For this reason, Euclid <note>original: "euclides"</note> rightly said that ratio exists simply in quantity when he defined it through the relation of two quantities of the same kind to each other. The understanding of this definition is: that ratio is the relation of two quantities to each other which is observed in that one of them is larger or smaller than the other or equal to it. By this it is clear that it is necessary for them to be of the same kind: such as two numbers, or two lines, or two surfaces, or two bodies, or two places, or two times. For one cannot...

<meta>This page continues the introduction to Book 5 of Euclid's Elements, moving from the definitions of "part" and "multiple" to the fundamental nature of ratios (proportions) and how they differ between the world of numbers (arithmetic) and the world of shapes (geometry). # BOOK 5

[A line] cannot be said to be greater or smaller than a surface, nor a body [greater or smaller] than a time or a place; rather, a line [is compared] to a line, and a surface to a surface. For only univocal <note>original: "vniuoca"; things belonging to the same category or species, such as two lengths or two areas.</note> things are comparable. ¶ When he says a "certain relationship," you should not understand this as something already known or discovered, but as something determined: so that the meaning is: Proportion is the determined relationship <term>habitudo</term> of two quantities; it is determined in the sense that it is this specific relationship and no other. For it is not necessary that every relationship between two quantities be known to us, or even to nature. ¶ For some proportion belongs to discrete things, like numbers; other proportion belongs to continuous things. In numbers, the smaller is either a part <note>A divisor, like 2 is a part of 6.</note> or parts <note>A fraction, like 2 is two-thirds of 3.</note> of the larger, as is demonstrated in the seventh book; therefore, in all of them, the relationship is certain and known. But in continuous things, proportion is more broad: for in them, there are cases where the smaller quantity is a part or parts of the larger, and in all such cases, the proportion is known through the mediation of numbers; this is called **rational**. All such quantities are called **commensurable** <note>original: "comunicantes"</note> because one and the same measure necessarily measures both; thus, all numbers are commensurable, for unity measures them all. There is also the case where the smaller is not a part or parts of the larger, and in such cases, the proportion is not known, neither to us nor to nature. This is called an **irrational** proportion, and these quantities are **incommensurable** <note>original: "incómunicantes"</note>. Thus it follows that whatever proportion is found in numbers is also found in every kind of continuous thing—such as in lines, surfaces, bodies, and times—but not the other way around. For there are infinite proportions found in continuous things which the nature of numbers does not support. However, whatever proportion is found in one kind of continuous thing is found in all others. For in whatever way any line relates to any other, so too does any surface relate to some other, and any body to some other; and similarly for time. But this is not the case for any number in relation to any other; hence proportion is broader in continuous things than in discrete things. From this, it is manifest that geometric proportion is of a higher abstraction than arithmetic proportion; for every proportion with which arithmetic deals is rational, but geometry considers rational and irrational proportions equally.

### Definition 4.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing four horizontal line segments illustrating a discrete proportion. Line segment 'a' is associated with the number '4', and segment 'b' with the number '2'. Proportionality is the similarity of proportions. As if we were to say that the proportion of *a* to *b* is the same as that of *c* to *d*. The proportion between *a* and *b* is similar to that which is between *c* and *d*; this similarity resulting from these proportions is called **proportionality**.

### Definition 5.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram illustrating continuous proportion using a horizontal line with multiple marked points. The points and segments are labeled above and below. Points 'a' and '8' correspond to each other, followed by 'b' and '4', 'c' and '2', and 'd' and '1', representing the progression of a geometric series where each term is half of the previous one (8:4 = 4:2 = 2:1).</image-desc>

Quantities which are said to have **continuous proportionality** are those whose equal multiples are either equal or are added or subtracted from each other without interruption.
¶ Having assumed the division of proportionality into continuous and discontinuous, he defines the dividing members. And first, the continuous—or to speak more truly: having assumed the division of proportionals into those that are continuously proportional and those that are not, he defines not "continuous proportionality" nor "discontinuous," but rather "continuously proportional" and "incontinuously" <note>Today we would call "incontinuous" proportionality "discrete" proportionality (a:b = c:d).</note>. The definition of continuous and incontinuous proportionality is clear enough through the definition of continuous and incontinuous proportionals. Continuous proportionality is when, among any number of quantities of the same kind, the first antecedent <note>The first term in a ratio.</note> relates to the second as the second relates to the third, and the third to the fourth. As when we say: as *a* is to *b*, so is *b* to *c*, and *c* to *d*. Each of them will be both antecedent and consequent, except for the first, which is only an antecedent, and the last, which is only a consequent. And in this proportionality, it is necessary that all quantities be of the same kind because of the continuation of the proportion...

<meta>This page continues the discussion from the previous page regarding the comparability of quantities, specifically explaining why proportions only exist between things of the same kind (e.g., line to line, but not line to surface). It transitions into the formal definitions of continuous and discontinuous proportions.</meta>

proportions, because there is no proportion between quantities of different kinds; and this [continuous proportion] will be, at a minimum, established in three terms. ¶ **Discontinuous proportion**, however, is when there are four quantities, whether all of the same kind, or the first two are of one kind and the last two of another. In this, in whatever proportion the first precedes the second, in that same [proportion] the third precedes the fourth: as when we say as **.a.** is to **.b.**, so **.c.** is to **.d.** Any of these will be either only an **antecedent** <note>The first term in a ratio, such as "a" in a:b.</note> or only a **consequent** <note>The second term in a ratio, such as "b" in a:b.</note>. Nor is it necessary that all four be of the same kind, as was required in continuous proportionality; this is because the consequent of the first ratio is not continued as the antecedent of the second. Instead, it is possible for them to be of the same kind, and possible for them to be different. For just as it happens that a line can be found to be double or triple to another line, so can a surface to a surface, a body to a body, a time to a time, and a number to a number. ¶ Having seen what continuous and discontinuous proportionality is, let us explain the previously mentioned definition of continuous proportionals. He says: **Continuous proportional quantities** are those whose multiples are either equal to each other, or exceed or fall short of each other equally and without interruption. For example: Let there be three quantities of the same kind, **.a. b. c.**, and for these let multiples be taken, **.d. e. f.**, such that as **.d.** is a multiple of **.a.**, so **.e.** is a multiple of **.b.**, and **.f.** is a multiple of **.c.** All of these will be in the same kind. ¶ For multiples and sub-multiples are in the same kind. Let it be that **.d. e. f.** are either equal to each other, or they behave similarly in adding or subtracting, so that as **.d.** adds above **.e.** or is diminished from it, so **.e.** adds above **.f.** or is diminished from it. When these multiples behave in this way, I say the three quantities **.a. b. c.** will be **continuously proportional**. ¶ However, you should not understand "behaving similarly in adding or subtracting" in terms of the *amount of the excess* <note>The simple numerical difference, like the "1" that separates 2, 3, and 4.</note>, but in terms of the *proportion*; otherwise, the definition would be false. For if any quantities of the same kind exceed each other by equal differences, and equal multiples of them are taken, those multiples will also exceed each other by equal differences; thus they behave similarly in adding and subtracting regarding the amount of excess. Yet, those original quantities are not continuously proportional; rather, the proportion of the smaller ones is always greater. This happens because their multiples do not exceed each other similarly regarding the **proportion**, but only regarding the **amount of excess**; for even there, in the smaller multiples, the proportion is greater. For example: let three numbers be taken exceeding each other by equal differences, specifically in an immediate arithmetic sequence: such as **2, 3, 4**. All equal multiples of these three exceed each other equally: the doubles by two, the triples by three, and so on. Yet **2, 3, 4** are not continuously proportional; rather, the proportion of the smaller is greater: for the proportion of the first two is **sesquialter** <note>original: "sesquilatera"; a ratio of 3:2 or 1.5.</note>, and the proportion of the larger is **sesquitertial** <note>original: "sesquitertia"; a ratio of 4:3 or 1.33.</note>. Therefore, because there is no similarity of proportions between them, there will be no proportionality between them—neither continuous nor discontinuous. It is clear, then, that this "similarity of addition or diminution" is not understood as the amount of excess, but as the proportion. Thus, the sense of the previous definition will be: **Continuous proportionals** are those whose multiples are all continuously proportional. However, he did not wish to propose the definition in this form, because then he would be defining the same thing by itself <note>original: "diffiniret idem p idem"; circular reasoning.</note>; yet this is clearly interchangeable with his definition. Furthermore, the three quantities **.a. b. c.** must be of the same kind so that their multiples may be equal to each other, or behave similarly in adding or subtracting. For if **.a.** and **.b.** were of different kinds, then **.d.** and **.e.** (the multiples of **.a.** and **.b.**) would also be of those same different kinds; because multiples and sub-multiples are of the same kind, **.d.** would not be equal to **.e.**, nor greater, nor smaller. For quantities of different kinds are not comparable to one another.

->Definition 6<-

<meta>This page continues from the previous discussion on continuous proportion. It introduces the formal definition of what we now call "equal ratios" or "proportionality" for four quantities, which is famously known as Euclid’s fifth definition of Book V.</meta>

# BOOK

<margin>
A marginal diagram illustrating proportional magnitudes with labeled line segments and numerical values. 
Top line: a segment marked 12 starting at point **f** and a segment marked 8 ending at point **e**.
Middle segments: **c** with the value 6 and **a** with the value 4.
Lower middle segments: **d** with the value 3 and **b** with the value 2.
Bottom line: a segment marked 9 starting at point **h** and a segment marked 6 ending at point **g**.
These illustrate the application of equimultiples <note>Equimultiples are products of different numbers multiplied by the same factor (e.g., 2 and 4 are equimultiples of 1 and 2 if both are doubled).</note> in the definition of proportion.
</margin>

Quantities are said to be in the same proportion—the first to the second and the third to the fourth—when, if any equimultiples whatever are taken of the first and third, and any equimultiples whatever of the second and fourth, the multiples of the first and third alike exceed, are equal to, or fall short of the multiples of the second and fourth respectively, when compared in that order.

¶ Having previously set down the definition of continuously proportional quantities <note>Quantities where the middle term repeats, like a:b as b:c.</note>, he here sets down the definition of discontinuously proportional quantities <note>Also called "discrete proportion," where four distinct terms are used, like a:b as c:d.</note>. It states that for any four quantities, if equal multiples are taken of the first and third, and likewise equal multiples are taken of the second and fourth, and if the multiple of the first relates to the multiple of the second in terms of exceeding, falling short, or being equal exactly as the multiple of the third relates to the multiple of the fourth, then the proportion of the first to the second is the same as the third to the fourth. 

For example: Let there be four quantities **a, b, c, d**. Let equimultiples be taken of the first and third, which are **a** and **c**—for instance, the doubles, which shall be **e** and **f**. Likewise, for the second and fourth, which are **b** and **d**, let other equimultiples be taken—for instance, the triples, which shall be **g** and **h**. Now let these four multiples, thus taken, be compared to one another according to the order of the four primary quantities; that is, **e** is compared to **g**, and **f** to **h**. We do not compare **e** to **f**, or **g** to **h**. If they are similar in exceeding, falling short, or being equal—meaning that if **e** is greater than **g**, then **f** must also be greater than **h**; or if **e** is less than **g**, then **f** must also be less than **h**; or if **e** is equal to **g**, then **f** must be equal to **h**—then the proportion of **a** to **b** is the same as **c** to **d**. 

This similarity in adding or diminishing should be understood here as it was in the definition of continuous proportionals: not in terms of the specific amount of the excess, but in terms of the relationship of the proportion. Furthermore, when he says "taken in the same order," it should be understood as explained: that the multiples are not compared to each other based on the order of the quantities they were multiplied from (such as comparing the multiple of the first to the multiple of the third), but rather they are compared according to the original order of the four quantities: the multiple of the first to the multiple of the second, and the multiple of the third to the multiple of the fourth. 

The meaning of this definition, therefore, is this: four quantities are discontinuously proportional because the ratio of the first to the second is the same as the third to the fourth, since when equimultiples are taken of the first and third, and equimultiples of the second and fourth, the ratio of the first multiple to the second will be the same as the ratio of the third multiple to the fourth. However, Euclid did not define it in this exact form for the reason mentioned before <note>original: "propter causam predictam," referring to the difficulty of defining "ratio" generally across different types of magnitudes like lines and times.</note>, even though in reality it is the same thing. 

It is not necessary for the four quantities **a, b, c, d** to be of the same kind, because **b** and **c** do not form a continuous proportion; rather, the first two can be of one kind (such as lines) and the following two of another (such as surfaces). From this, it is clear that the multiple of the first must be compared to the multiple of the second, and the multiple of the third to the multiple of the fourth. We do not compare the multiple of the first to the multiple of the third, nor the second to the fourth, because the first and third (or second and fourth) are not always of the same kind. It was necessary to take equimultiples for the first and third, and likewise for the second and fourth, rather than for the first and second, because without this method of taking multiples, there would be no way to connect the terms of the first ratio with the terms of the second ratio to show that **a** is to **b** as **c** is to **d**.

Quantities whose proportion is the same are called proportionals.

¶ After defining continuous and discontinuous proportionality, he defines "proportional" quantities in a general sense, and the definition is self-evident.

<meta>This page transitions from the definition of equal ratios (proportionality) to the definition of unequal ratios (improportionality). It specifically addresses Euclid’s Seventh Definition of Book V, which explains how to determine if one ratio is "greater" than another using the method of equimultiples.</meta>

# When equimultiples of the first and third [are taken], and likewise equimultiples of the second and fourth [are taken], and the multiple of the first exceeds the multiple of the second, but the multiple of the third does not exceed the multiple of the fourth: then the first is said to have a greater ratio to the second than the third has to the fourth.

<margin>note ^</margin>Having defined proportional quantities, he now defines unproportional quantities. Unproportionality—where there is a lack of similarity between ratios—occurs in two ways: either because the ratio of the first to the second is greater than that of the third to the fourth, or because it is lesser. Therefore, there are two species of it. The first is when the ratio of the first to the second is greater than the third to the fourth; this is called "greater unproportionality." <margin>note ^</margin>The second is when the ratio of the first to the second is lesser than the third to the fourth; this is called "lesser unproportionality." He defines those between which there is a greater ratio (greater unproportionality), but he does not provide a separate definition for those with a lesser ratio, as that definition is evident from the other. Therefore, when there are four quantities where equimultiples <note>Equimultiples are products of different numbers multiplied by the same factor; for example, if you double both 5 and 10, the results—10 and 20—are equimultiples.</note> are taken of the first and third, and equimultiples of the second and fourth, if the multiples of the first and second do not relate to each other in the same way as the multiples of the third and fourth in terms of exceeding, falling short, or being equal, those four quantities will be unproportional. This occurs if the multiple of the first is equal to the multiple of the second, while the multiple of the third is less than the multiple of the fourth. <margin>^</margin> Or if the multiple of the first is greater than the multiple of the second, while the multiple of the third is equal to or less than the multiple of the fourth. Or if the multiple of the first is greater than the multiple of the second, and similarly the multiple of the third is greater than the multiple of the fourth, but the multiple of the first exceeds the multiple of the second by a larger proportion (not necessarily by a larger quantity) than the third exceeds the fourth. Or if the multiple of the first is less than the multiple of the second, and similarly the third is less than the fourth, but the first falls short by a smaller proportion (not a smaller quantity) than the third falls short of the fourth. In any of these four ways, there will be a greater ratio of the first to the second than the third to the fourth. Conversely, in the four opposite ways, there will be a lesser ratio. Clear examples of all these can be taken from numbers. That "exceeding" of the multiple of the first over the multiple of the second—while the multiple of the third does not exceed the fourth—of which the author speaks in the definition, has a broad application to these four modes and encompasses them. Whence the sense of this definition is: when multiples are taken as proposed, <margin>thus</margin> if the ratio of the multiple of the first to the multiple of the second is greater than the multiple of the third to the multiple of the fourth, then the ratio of the first [quantity] to the second will be greater than the third to the fourth. He did not define it in this exact form for the reason mentioned above. Or we can say that the "exceeding" of the multiple of the first over the multiple of the second—and not the third over the fourth—as spoken of in the premise of the definition of greater unproportionality, is taken literally as the words sound. It only explicitly extends to the second of the four aforementioned modes, although in truth, in any of those four modes, there is a greater ratio of the first to the second than the third to the fourth. <margin>thus</margin> Hence the sense of that definition is: when such multiples are taken, if the multiple of the first is greater than the multiple of the second, it is not necessary that the multiple of the third be greater than the multiple of the fourth; in such a case, the ratio of the first to the second is greater than the third to the fourth. He did not include the other three modes of "exceeding" in the definition because this one is the clearest of all and sufficient for the definition. Never...

# BOOK

...indeed, the ratio of the first of four quantities to the second is greater than the third to the fourth: whenever it happens that certain equimultiples <note>Equimultiples are products of different numbers multiplied by the same factor; for example, if you double both 3 and 5, the results—6 and 10—are equimultiples.</note> are found for the first and third, which, when related to certain equimultiples of the second and fourth, show the multiple of the first to be greater than the multiple of the second, but the multiple of the third not greater than the multiple of the fourth. Nor does it ever happen that this is found without the ratio of the first to the second being greater than the third to the fourth, as we shall demonstrate below after the tenth [proposition] of this book. These unproportional quantities can be of different kinds, just as quantities in a discrete proportion <note>original: "incontinua" - also known as a disconnected or "disjoined" proportion.</note> can be, if there is a discrete unproportionality between them: as if it were said that the ratio of **a** to **b** is greater than **c** to **d**. However, if there is a continuous unproportionality, they will all necessarily be of the same kind, just as they are in a continuous proportion; as if it were said that the ratio of **a** to **b** is greater than **b** to **c**.

->Definition 9.<-

->**Proportionality is established among at least three terms.**<-

<margin>
<image-desc>Diagram featuring three horizontal line segments. The top line is labeled "a". The second line is shorter, labeled "b", with the numeral "4" written above its right extremity. The third line is the shortest, labeled "c", with the numeral "2" written above its center. There are faint traces of other lines and numbers in the surrounding space.</image-desc>
</margin>

After the author defined ratio, proportionality, and proportional and unproportional quantities, he now shows the minimum number of terms among which a proportionality can exist. He does not set a maximum number, however, because it is not possible to reach one; any ratio can be continued through infinite terms, whether it be a rational or irrational ratio. For a proportionality, at least two similar ratios are required, because proportionality is a similarity of ratios. Every ratio has an antecedent <note>The "leading" or first term in a ratio.</note> and a consequent <note>The "following" or second term in a ratio.</note>. Therefore, every proportionality has at least two antecedents and two consequents. This is impossible to achieve in fewer than three terms, in which the middle term becomes both a consequent [to the first] and an antecedent [to the third]. In this way, the proportionality will be small; therefore, a continuous proportionality will be established in at least three terms. A discrete <note>original: "Incontinua"</note> proportionality, however, will not exist in fewer than four terms, because in such a case every term is either only an antecedent or only a consequent. Understand the same regarding the minimum number of terms for unproportionality: if it is continuous, it will be among at least three terms; if discrete, among at least four.

->Definition 10.<-

**If there are three continuous proportional quantities, the ratio of the first to the third is called the duplicate ratio of the first to the second.**

He defines the ratio that exists between the extreme terms of a continuous proportionality established in three terms. He says that if the ratio of the first to the second is as the second is to the third, the ratio of the first to the third will be as the duplicate ratio of the first to the second—that is, composed of two such ratios. Or, what is the same thing: the ratio of the first to the third will be as the first to the second "duplicated," which is to say, multiplied by itself. For example: in numbers, let there be 3 continuous proportional numbers, and let them be continuously double, such as 2, 4, 8. The ratio of the first to the third [2 to 8] will be as the ratio of the first to the second [2 to 4] multiplied by itself. The ratio of the first to the second is "double"; "double" multiplied by itself produces "quadruple" <note>In modern terms, if the ratio is 1:2, the duplicate ratio is (1:2) squared, which is 1:4.</note>. Hence, the ratio of the extremes is quadruple—namely, the double of the double. Or, according to the earlier explanation, the ratio of the extremes is as the ratio of the first to the second duplicated, because a quadruple ratio consists of two double ratios.

->Definition 11.<-

**When there are four continuous proportional quantities, the ratio of the first to the fourth is called the triplicate ratio of the first to the second.**

# V

<image-desc>A geometric diagram located in the right margin, consisting of four horizontal line segments labeled 'a', 'b', 'c', and 'd' from top to bottom. <margin>
To add ratios here is not by [simple] addition but by multiplying them with each other, the antecedent of one by the antecedent of the other <note>In a ratio a:b, 'a' is the antecedent and 'b' is the consequent.</note>, and that the ratio of two [ratios], when the antecedents are gathered, then of the two... and as they are gathered... just as a ratio of 3 to 2 with a ratio of 4 to 3, when combined, make a ratio of 12 to 10 <note>original: "12 ad 10". Mathematically, compounding 3:2 and 4:3 should result in 12:6 (or 2:1). The text "10" may be an error for "6" in the original manuscript or OCR.</note>. Similarly, a ratio... in a ratio is the same as dividing, and in this one number is multiplied by the antecedent... one quotient by the remaining number of the other through the antecedent and that which is gathered becomes the quotient. A ratio such as 3 to 4(?) and... to 1, the residue or quotient is a ratio of 3 to 1.
</margin>

He defines the ratio which exists between the extreme terms of a continuous proportionality in four established terms: and he says that if there are four quantities in continuous proportion, the ratio of the first to the fourth will be as the ratio of the first to the second **triplicated** <note>In modern mathematics, a "triplicate ratio" refers to cubing the ratio (n³). For example, if the ratio is 3:1, the triplicate ratio is 27:1.</note>; this means it is composed of three such [ratios] because such are found in it. Or, which is the same thing: the ratio of the first to the fourth will be as the first to the second triplicated; that is, multiplied by itself, then multiplied again by the product. For example, in numbers: Let there be four numbers in continuous proportion, and let them be continuously triple, such as 1, 3, 9, 27. The ratio of the first to the fourth will be as the ratio of the first to the second multiplied by itself, then multiplied by the product. Now, the ratio of the first to the second is **triple**; but triple multiplied by itself produces **ninefold** <note>original: "noncupla"</note>, and triple multiplied by ninefold produces **twenty-sevenfold** <note>original: "vigincupla septupla", literally twenty and sevenfold.</note>. Therefore, the ratio of the extremes will be twenty-sevenfold, which is the "triple of the triple" <note>This is an archaic way of saying 3 to the 3rd power.</note>. Or, according to the earlier explanation, the ratio of the extremes is like the ratio of the first to the second triplicated, because twenty-sevenfold consists of three triples. 

However, he does not define the ratio of extremes in a continuous proportionality consisting of more than four terms, for the reason that the **dimensions** found in natural things do not exceed the number three. ¶ Furthermore, the denomination of a ratio of two quantities between which no mean <note>A "mean" is an intermediate term in a sequence.</note> is placed has the nature of a **line**. But those between which one mean is placed in continuous proportionality have the nature of a **surface**, because it arises from the multiplication of the denomination of the first two by itself. For everything that is produced by the multiplication of a line by a line has the nature of a surface—if by itself, indeed, a square; if by another, an oblong <note>original: "altera longioris", literally 'longer than the other'.</note>. But the denomination of the ratio of those quantities in which two means are placed in continuous proportion has the nature of a **solid**; because it comes from the multiplication of the denomination of the first two first by itself—from which multiplication a surface is produced—then into the product, from which multiplication a solid or body arises. For everything produced by the multiplication of a line by a surface grows into a solid. 

¶ It is, therefore, as if he were saying: the ratio of two quantities is a single interval, having the nature of a simple dimension like a **line**; the proportionality of three terms is a double interval, having the nature of a double dimension like a **surface**; and the proportionality of four terms is a triple interval, having the nature of a triple dimension like a **solid**. And because dimensions do not proceed further, he therefore did not define the ratio contained between the extremes of proportionality in five or more terms; or, he did not define the ratio in these cases because their ratio is understood from the aforementioned definitions. For if in three terms the ratio of the extremes consists of the ratio of the first terms **duplicated** <note>Squared (n²).</note>, and in four terms it consists of the same **triplicated** <note>Cubed (n³).</note>, in five terms it consists of the same **quadruplicated**, and in six of the same **quintuplicated**. Wherefore, just as in three terms in continuous proportionality the ratio of the extremes contains the ratio of the first terms twice, and in four terms thrice, so in five terms it will contain it four times, and in six terms five times, and so on. Thus, the ratio of the extremes in terms of continuous proportionality always contains the ratio of the first terms as many times as there are total terms minus one. Similarly, also, if the ratio of the extremes of a continuous proportionality in three terms is that which is produced from the ratio of the first terms multiplied by itself once; and in four, multiplied by itself twice; in five terms, that which is produced from the ratio of the first terms multiplied by itself three times; and in six terms, four times; and so always, the terms will be two more than the number of multiplications—or, the multiplications are equal to the means.

-> Thus the ratio of the extremes will be held by the ratio of the first terms as many times as there are terms in continuous proportion minus one. <-

...with the extremes placed between. And note that even in continuous proportionality <note>A series where the consequent of one ratio is the antecedent of the next, e.g., a:b = b:c = c:d.</note>, the ratio of the **extremes** is produced from all the intermediate ratios. ¶ From the aforesaid, it appears that the ratio of the extremes in a continuous proportionality consisting of **three terms** is named by the **square**; but in one consisting of **four terms**, it is named by the **cube**. The "side" of these squares and cubes is the denomination <note>The value or quotient of the ratio.</note> of the ratio of the first to the second. For example, in numbers: let there be four numbers in continuous proportionality which are continuously triple: 3, 9, 27, 81. The ratio of the first to the second is named by three, for it is triple. The ratio of the first to the third is named by nine, which is the square of three; for that ratio is ninefold. But the ratio of the first to the fourth is named by 27, which is the cube of the denomination of the first to the second (namely, of three); for that ratio is twenty-sevenfold. ¶ And the ratio of the extremes of a continuous proportionality consisting of **three terms** [where the ratios are not equal] is named by a **non-square surface**, the sides of which are the denominations of those ratios. In four terms, it is named by a **non-cube solid**, whose three sides are the denominations of the three ratios. This is also clear in numbers: Let there be four numbers in "discontinuous" proportionality: 2, 4, 12, 48. In these, the ratio of the first to the second is double; the second to the third is triple; and therefore the first to the third is sixfold. The third to the fourth is quadruple; and therefore the first to the fourth is twenty-fourfold. Six, therefore, which is the denomination of the ratio of the first to the third, is a "surface" number <note>A plane number; the product of two factors.</note> whose sides are two and three (which are the denominations of the first two ratios). Twenty-four, however, which is the denomination of the ratio of the first to the fourth, is a "solid" number <note>The product of three factors.</note> whose sides are 2, 3, and 4 (the denominations of the three ratios existing between those four terms).

### Definition 12

<margin>
->[A diagram showing proportional lines. Line C-A (6 to 4) and line D-B (3 to 2). Brackets indicate they share the same ratio (1.5:1).]<-
</margin>

**Quantities** that are in one ratio—the antecedent to the consequent and the [other] antecedent to its [other] consequent—may be spoken of **inversely** <note>original: "econtrario"</note>, as the consequent to the antecedent is to the [other] consequent to its [other] antecedent. ¶ Likewise **alternately** <note>original: "permutatim"</note>, as the antecedent is to the [other] antecedent, so is the consequent to the [other] consequent. ¶ He defines the species of proportionality, which are six: namely, **converted**, **permuted**, **disjunct**, **conjunct**, **everted**, and **equal**. ¶ These species are, as it were, certain modes of arguing or reasoning. He first defines "converted" and "permuted" proportionality, in which the antecedents and consequents remain the same in substance <note>The terms themselves do not change, only their positions.</note>, which is not the case in disjunct, conjunct, or everted proportionality; and in which nothing is taken from outside, as in "equal" proportionality. He calls the "antecedent" the first extreme of a ratio, and the "consequent" the second. ¶ He intends by this definition that if there be a ratio of *a* to *b* as *c* is to *d*, and from this I conclude: therefore, *b* is to *a* as *d* is to *c* (namely, so that I make consequents out of antecedents and antecedents out of consequents), this mode of arguing is called **inverse** or **converted** proportionality. If, however, I argue thus: *a* is to *b* as *c* is to *d*, therefore *a* is to *c* as *b* is to *d* (namely, so that both antecedents of the original ratios become the first ratio, and both consequents become the second), he intends that this mode of arguing be called **permuted** proportionality. In this mode of arguing, the antecedent of the second ratio becomes the consequent [of the first], and the consequent of the first becomes the antecedent [of the second].

<note>original: "proportionalitas continua" (continuous proportionality), "quadratus" (square), "cubus" (cube), "superficialis" (surface/plane), "solidus" (solid), "antecedens" (antecedent), "consequens" (consequent), "conuersa" (converted), "permutata" (permuted), "disiuncta" (disjunct), "coniuncta" (conjunct), "euersa" (everted), "equa" (equal)</note>

**Connected** <note>Latin: *coniuncta*. In modern geometry, this is often called *componendo*.</note> proportionality is so-named whenever the ratio of the antecedent <note>The first term in a ratio.</note> combined with the consequent <note>The second term in a ratio.</note> to the consequent is the same as the [second] antecedent combined with the [second] consequent to its consequent.

<margin>This means that if the ratio is such that $a$ is to $b$ as $c$ is to $d$, I may conclude from this: therefore, the whole $a+b$ is to $b$ as the whole $c+d$ is to $d$. This mode of reasoning is called "connected proportionality."</note>
¶ He defines the "connected," "disconnected," and "inverted" types of proportions, in which no outside terms are added, but the existing terms are rearranged. They remain the same in substance.

### Proposition 14.
<image-desc>A horizontal diagram showing two lines: the top one labeled 'a' and 'b' with a total value of 8 and a subdivision at 4; the bottom one labeled 'c' and 'd' with a total of 6 and a subdivision at 3.</image-desc>

**Disconnected** <note>Latin: *disiuncta*. Also known as *dividendo*.</note> proportionality is called the equal comparison of the excesses of the antecedents over the consequents.

¶ This means that if there was a ratio of the whole $a+b$ to $b$ as the whole $c+d$ to $d$, and from this I conclude: "therefore, $a$ is to $b$ as $c$ is to $d$," then this mode of reasoning is called "disconnected proportionality."

**Inverted** <note>Latin: *euersa*. Also known as *convertendo*.</note> proportionality is called the similarity of the ratios of any antecedents to their own excesses over their consequents.

¶ This means that if $a+b$ is to $b$ as $c+d$ is to $d$, and from this I conclude: "therefore, $a+b$ is to $a$ as $c+d$ is to $c$," then this mode of reasoning is called "inverted proportionality."

### Proposition 16.
<image-desc>A complex diagram of proportions. On the left, a vertical arrangement of points representing values 8, 4, and 2. On the right, values 12, 6, and 3. **Equal** <note>Latin: *equa*. Also known as *ex aequali*.</note> proportionality is so-named when, given several quantities and another set equal in number to the first and proportional to them, the similarity of the ratios of the extremes remains once an equal number of middle terms has been removed from both sets.

¶ He defines "equal proportionality," which requires taking outside quantities to prove the point. It means that if any number of quantities are taken, such as $a, b, c$, and likewise as many others (whether they be of the same kind as the first or another), such as $d, e, f$; and if the second set are in the same ratio as the first, whether in the same order—as if it is said $a$ is to $b$ as $d$ is to $e$, and $b$ is to $c$ as $e$ is to $f$—or in reverse order—as if $a$ is to $b$ as $e$ is to $f$, and $b$ is to $c$ as $d$ is to $e$—and from this it is concluded: "therefore, $a$ is to $c$ as $d$ is to $f$," then this mode of reasoning is called "equal proportionality." The author [Euclid] proves four of these six modes of reasoning (which are called species of proportionality) later in the text of this 5th book. He proves **Permuted** <note>Latin: *permutatam*, or *alternando*.</note> proportionality in the 16th proposition of this book; **Disconnected** in the 17th; **Connected** in the 18th; and he demonstrates **Equal** proportionality in the 22nd and 23rd. However, in the 22nd, he treats the case where the quantities of the two orders are proportional in the same order, whereas in the 23rd, they are proportional in reverse order. But he does not demonstrate **Converse** <note>Latin: *conuersam*, or *invertendo*.</note> or **Inverted** proportionality because the converse is obvious from the definition of quantities in "discontinuous" proportion. The inverted type is clear from being permuted with one another in the 19th proposition, as we shall discuss regarding that proposition. Now, let us demonstrate how inverted proportionality is manifest from the definition of quantities in discontinuous proportion. ¶ Let there be, therefore, a ratio of $a$ to $b$ as $c$ is to $d$; I wish to demonstrate that $b$ will be to $a$ [as $d$ is to $c$]...

These logical tools allow a mathematician to transform one set of ratios into another while maintaining the truth of the proportion.</summary>
