...just as $d$ is to $c$. Let $e$ be taken in relation to $a$, and $f$ to $c$, as equimultiples <note>original: "eque multiplicia"; quantities multiplied by the same factor.</note>. Likewise also $g$ to $b$ and $h$ to $d$ as equimultiples. And it will be, through the conversion of the definition of quantities in / 
discontinuous proportion <note>original: "incontinue proportionalium"</note>, that as $e$ and $g$ relate, so also $f$ and $h$ relate in addition, 
subtraction, and equality. I understand then that $b$ is the first, $a$ the second, $d$ the third, and $c$ 
the fourth. $g$ and $h$ are taken as equimultiples to the first and third; likewise $e$ and $f$ 
are equimultiples to the second and fourth. And because the multiples of the first and second, which are $g$ and $e$, 
relate to each other in the same way as the multiples of the third and fourth, which are $h$ and $f$, in subtraction 
and equality: therefore, by the said definition, the proportion of $b$ (the first) to $a$ (the second) is 
as $c$ (the third) to $d$ (the fourth), which is what was proposed. Thus the mode of reasoning called 
**inverted proportionality** <note>original: "conuersa proportionalitas"; if $a:b = c:d$, then $b:a = d:c$.</note> is established. 
¶ The principles of this fifth book, however, seem to most people to be 
exceedingly difficult, and they seem further removed from the intellect because of certain 
conclusions which he demonstrates from them. For nothing seems to adhere more immediately to the intellect 
than that any two equal quantities have one and the same proportion to any third quantity. 
Yet, the seventh proposition of this fifth book demonstrates this from the definition of discontinuous 
proportionality, which at first seems very far removed from the intellect. For who 
would not more easily grant that the proportion of two equal quantities to some third is the same, 
than grant that four quantities are in proportion if the multiples of the first and third, taken equally, 
relate to the multiples of the second and fourth, taken equally, in addition, 
subtraction, and equality? 
Again, if we look closely, it will be clearly established that it is impossible for the intellect to see 
that the proportion of two equal quantities to a third is the same, except through 
the knowledge of *what it is* for a proportion to be the same <note>The author argues that we cannot rely on "common sense" to prove equality; we must use Euclid's rigorous definition of "same ratio."</note>. For if one is ignorant of what it is for one 
proportion to be the same as another, how shall he know that two equal quantities 
have the same proportion to a third? Therefore, without a doubt, the intellect 
requires—before it can grasp that proposition which seemed so easily conceivable—a 
cognition of this matter which is held through its definition. Afterward, one must examine 
whether that definition applies to two equal quantities compared to a third. 
If the definition is found to apply to those quantities, the 
proposition is concluded. If not, then the opposite. Therefore, it is not an "immediate" proposition, even though 
superficial apprehension judged it to be immediate. 
¶ Similarly, the first apprehension indicates more immediately to the intellect that of two unequal quantities, the 
proportion of the larger to a third is greater than the proportion of the smaller to the same third—which the 8th 
proposition of this book demonstrates—than it indicates that of four quantities, there is a greater proportion of the first to the second than the third to 
the fourth when, with multiples of the first and third taken equally, and 
others to the second and fourth likewise taken equally, the multiple of the first exceeds the multiple of the 
second, but the multiple of the third does not exceed the multiple of the fourth. From this, the aforesaid 
proposition is demonstrated; but similarly, it cannot be understood except through "what it is" to be 
a greater proportion. 
Therefore, it was necessary for Euclid to define which quantities are called 
proportional and which are non-proportional. Proportional quantities are those 
whose proportion is one [the same]; and non-proportional are those whose proportions are different. Thus 
he defined quantities whose proportion is one, and those in which the 
extremes are connected without the means being separated, which he called **continuous proportionals**. 
And he said this proportionality exists in three terms at least, because one mean must be taken 
at least twice; and those in which an interruption of the means occurs, and these are **discontinuous proportionals**; 
and this proportionality requires at least four terms because of the taking of another mean...

<meta>This page continues the technical justification for Euclid’s definitions in Book V of the *Elements*. Having previously discussed inverted proportionality, the author now explains why Euclid had to rely on a complex system of "multiples" to define equal ratios, rather than simply "naming" the ratios as one does in arithmetic. This is due to the existence of irrational (incommensurable) magnitudes in geometry.</meta>

# BOOK V

And he also defined quantities that are disproportionate <note>original: "inproportionales"</note>, in which one ratio is greater than another. If every ratio were "known" <note>meaning expressible as a ratio of whole numbers</note> or rational, then it would be easy for the intellect to recognize which ratios were the same and which were different. Those that had the same denomination <note term="denomination">The "denomination" (denominatio) of a ratio is the number or fraction that expresses its value; for example, the denomination of a 4:2 ratio is 2.</note> would be the same, and those with different denominations would be different. This ease is manifest in arithmetic, since the ratio of all numbers is known and rational. Hence, Jordanus <note>Jordanus de Nemore, a 13th-century mathematician</note>, in the second book of his *Arithmetic*, when defining which ratios are the same and which are different, says that those which receive the same denomination are the same. A greater ratio is one that receives a greater denomination, and a smaller ratio a smaller one. 

But there are infinite irrational ratios whose denomination is not knowable. Therefore, since Euclid considers proportional things in this book in a general way—not restricting himself to rational or irrational quantities, because he considers the proportion found in continuous magnitudes <note>such as lines or areas, which can be incommensurable</note> which is common to both—he could not define the identity of ratios through the identity of denominations as the arithmetician does. This is because, as was said, the denominations of many ratios are simply unknown. However, a definition must be made from known things; thus, the "difficulty" <note>original: "malicia," literally the "wickedness" or troublesome nature</note> of irrational ratios compelled Euclid to set down such definitions.

Because, therefore, he could not (as is clear from what was said) define proportionality or the identity of ratios through the identity of the relationships or denominations of the terms themselves—due to the irrationality of the relationships and the incommensurability of the terms—he was forced to resort to the multiples of the terms. He sought a definition by considering the relationships of those multiples in terms of excess <note>being greater than</note> and equality, taking equal sets of multiples <note term="equimultiples">Quantities multiplied by the same factor; for example, if you have A and B, their equimultiples might be 3A and 3B.</note> through which they are reduced to a state of "rationality." For in any kind of inequality, nothing is more identical to the terms than their multiples, nor is anything more identical to the relationships of the terms than the relationship of their multiples.

And because a ratio is a certain relationship of two quantities of the same kind, considered in terms of whether they are equal or one is greater, the identity of ratios existing between the first of four quantities to the second, and the third to the fourth, is a similar equality of the first to the second and the third to the fourth; or a similar "greater-than-ness," or a similar "less-than-ness." This similar equality, greater-than-ness, or less-than-ness exists among any four quantities when it exists among all their equal multiples.

Therefore, regarding what he says in the **fifth definition**: *quantities which are said to have continuous proportionality*, and so on—it is as if he were saying: I call all those quantities "continuously proportional" when they are similarly equal, similarly greater, or similarly smaller across all their equimultiples. That is, their multiples are also continuously proportional; if this relationship fails anywhere among the multiples, I say they are not continuously proportional.

Regarding what he says in the **sixth definition**: *quantities which are said to be according to one ratio, the first to the second and the third to the fourth*, and so on—it is as if he were saying: I call all four quantities "discontinuously proportional" <note>also known as discrete proportion</note> when the first relates to the second as the third relates to the fourth. This means the first to the second and the third to the fourth behave similarly in equaling, exceeding, or falling short, when all equimultiples of the first and third are compared to all equimultiples of the second and fourth. They must behave similarly in equaling, adding, or subtracting; that is, the multiples of the first relate to the multiples of the second in the same ratio as the multiples of the third relate to the multiples of the fourth. If this fails anywhere among the multiples, I say there is no proportion.

<summary>This page explains why Euclid defines proportionality using the comparison of "multiples" rather than simple numerical values. This method is necessary to account for "irrational" ratios in geometry that cannot be expressed as simple whole numbers or fractions.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Euclid’s Book V, specifically focusing on the logic behind the definitions of proportionality. # BOOK V

...of the first to the second is as the third is to the fourth. What was said previously in the fifth definition is as if he had said: I call it a "greater proportion" of four quantities—of the first to the second than of the third to the fourth—when some multiple of the first exceeds some multiple of the second, while some multiple of the third (taken according to the same multiplication as the first) does not exceed some multiple of the fourth (taken according to the same multiplication as the second). <note>This explains Euclid's rigorous definition of why one ratio is "larger" than another by comparing their multiples—a necessary tool for dealing with numbers that cannot be written as simple fractions.</note> This is the same as saying the ratio of the multiple of the first to the multiple of the second is greater than the ratio of the multiple of the third to the multiple of the fourth.

¶ However, there are some who have tried to prove these definitions. Among them, Ametus, son of Joseph <note>original: "Ametus filius Joseph"; this refers to the Egyptian mathematician Ahmed ibn Yusuf (c. 835–912), whose work on proportions was highly influential in the Middle Ages</note>, attempted to demonstrate the cause in his letter which he composed on proportion and proportionality. He accepted three points by way of assumption, as if they were principles that are self-evident and do not require proof.

¶ The first of these is that if there are four quantities where the ratio of the first to the second is as the third to the fourth, then conversely, the ratio of the second to the first will be as the fourth to the third. This is the mode of arguing which Euclid previously called "inverse proportionality" <note>original: "conuersam proportionalitatē"</note>. But he was in error who said this proposition is self-evident, since its "antecedent" and "consequent" <note term="antecedent and consequent">In a ratio $a:b$, $a$ is the antecedent and $b$ is the consequent. In a logical proof, the antecedent is the starting assumption and the consequent is what follows.</note> are unknown. For it is unknown what it means for the ratio of the first quantity to the second to be the same as the third to the fourth; therefore, if this is unknown, it is impossible to understand what follows from it. Likewise, as long as the consequence is unknown, it is impossible to understand what leads to it.

¶ His second principle was: if there are four quantities where the ratio of the first to the second is as the third to the fourth, if the first is greater than the second, the third will be greater than the fourth; if less, then less; and if equal, then equal.

¶ The third was: if there are four quantities where the ratio of the first to the second is as the third to the fourth, then the first will be to any multiple of the second as the third is to an equal multiple of the fourth. And he fell into the same error in these two principles as he did in the first. For he accepted unknown things as known in all of them; therefore, he did not truly demonstrate them. He also erred in his second demonstration, and in the third and fifth, in each of which he argues from Proposition 5 as if from Proposition 10 of this book, which are themselves proved from the definition of continuous proportionality. 

He argues thus: if the ratio of $A-B$ to $C$ is greater than $G$ to $D$, let the ratio of some part of $A-B$ (let it be $U-B$) to $E$ be as $G$ to $D$. By this, he appears to suppose that for two unequal quantities ($A-B$ and $U-B$) related to $E$, the greater quantity has the greater proportion and the lesser has the lesser; or that a quantity having a smaller proportion to $E$ than $A-B$ has will be smaller than $A-B$. The first of these is demonstrated in Proposition 8 of this book, and the second in Proposition 10. For when you wish to take a quantity that relates to $E$ in the same ratio as $G$ to $D$, I could give you one greater, smaller, or equal to $A-B$ indifferently, just as I please. Therefore, he does not demonstrate the premise first; instead, he falls into "circular reasoning" <note>original: "circulus"</note>, and his principles are more obscure than his conclusions. Therefore, the principles must be assumed with Euclid as being known, and they should not be proven from conclusions; rather, the conclusions must be demonstrated from them.

¶ Let there be any number of quantities, which are $A$, $B$, and $C$, and as many others, which are $D$, $E$, and $F$. Let each of the first be an "equimultiple" <note term="equimultiple">Quantities that are multiplied by the same number; for example, if $A=2D$, $B=2E$, and $C=2F$, then $A, B, C$ are equimultiples of $D, E, F$.</note> to its counterpart, or let each be equal to each, in such a way that...

# BOOK V.

Because just as *a* is a multiple of *d*, so *b* is a multiple of *e*, and *c* a multiple of *f*; or if *a* is equal to *d*, then similarly *b* is equal to *e* and *c* is equal to *f*. I say that just as *a* relates to *d*, so the sum <note>original: "aggregatū"</note> of all those which are *a, b, c* relates to the sum of all those which are *d, e, f*. ¶ If the individual quantities are equal to one another, the proposition is clear through this common notion <term>commune sciam</term>: "if equals be added to equals, the wholes will also be equal" <note>This is Euclid’s second common notion, or axiom, used here to show that sums of equal parts remain equal.</note>. But if they are all equal multiples of their corresponding parts, by dividing them according to the quantity of their sub-multiples: the sum of the first part of *a*, the first of *b*, and the first of *c* will be equal to the sum of *d, e, f* by the aforementioned common notion, aided by this one: "things which are equal to the same thing are equal to each other." ¶ Similarly, the sum of the second parts of the quantities *a, b, c* will be equal to the sum of *d, e, f*, and so on for the rest. Since this can be done as many times as *d* is contained in *a*, it will follow that an equal sum of *d, e, f* is contained in the sum of *a, b, c* as many times as *d* is contained in *a*. Because however many times *d* measures *a*, so many times the sum of *d, e, f* measures the sum of *a, b, c*. It is clear that just as *a* is a multiple of *d*, so the sum of *a, b, c* is a multiple of the sum of *d, e, f*, which is what was proposed.

## Proposition .2.

If there are six quantities, of which the first is the same multiple of the second as the third is of the fourth; and the fifth is the same multiple of the second as the sixth is of the fourth: then the sum of the first and fifth to the second, and the sum of the third and sixth to the fourth, will be equally multiple.

<image-desc>
A diagram for Proposition 2 consisting of line segments with labels and numerical values. 
Top set: a (length 8) over b (length 4); c (length 12) over d (6). 
Bottom set: a (length 4) and b (length 2); d (length 6) and f (length 3); c (length 2) and e (length unknown).
Handwritten calculations in the right margin include numbers like 14, 16, 32, and 40.
</image-desc>

¶ Let there be six quantities: *a* the first, *b* the second, *c* the third, *d* the fourth, *e* the fifth, and *f* the sixth. Let *a* and *c* be equal multiples of *b* and *d*; likewise, let *e* and *f* be equal multiples of those same quantities. I say that just as the whole sum of *a* and *e* is a multiple of the quantity *b*, so the whole sum of *c* and *f* is a multiple of the quantity *d*. For because the number of times *b* is contained in *a* is equal to the number of times *d* is contained in *c*; and similarly the number of times *b* is contained in *e* is equal to the number of times *d* is contained in *f*; then by the common notion which is "if equals be added to equals, etc.," the number of times *b* is contained in the sum of *a* and *e* will be equal to the number of times *d* is contained in the sum of *c* and *f*. Therefore, just as the sum of *a* and *e* is a multiple of *b*, so the sum of *c* and *f* is a multiple of *d*, which is what was proposed.

## Proposition .3.

If the first is the same multiple of the second as the third is of the fourth, and if equal multiples are taken of the first and the third: then the multiple of the first to the second and the multiple of the third to the fourth will be equally multiple. <note>In modern terms: if a = nb and c = nd, then m(a) is the same multiple of b as m(c) is of d (i.e., both are mn times the base quantity).</note>

¶ Let there be six quantities: *a* the first, *b* the second, *c* the third, *d* the fourth, *e* the fifth, and *f* the sixth. Let *a* to *b* and *c* to *d* be equally multiple; and likewise *e* to *a* and *f* to *c* be equally multiple. I say that just as *e* is a multiple of *b*, so *f* is of *d*. For let *e* be divided according to the quantity of *a* (its multiples), and *f* according to the quantity of *c*. Because of the equality of the parts of *e* to *a* and the parts of *f* to *c*, any of the parts of *e* will be the same multiple of *b* as any of the parts of *f* is of *d*. Since, therefore, the first part of *e* is the same multiple of *b* as the first part of *f* is of *d*; and likewise the second part of *e* is the same multiple of *b* as the second of *f* is of *d*; then by the preceding proposition, the sum of the first two parts of *e* will be the same multiple of *b* as the sum of the first two parts of *f* is of *d*. And because again the third part of *e* (if there is a third part) is the same multiple of *b* as the third part of *f* is of *d*, it will follow by the same reasoning that the whole sum of the first three parts of *e* is the same multiple of *b* as the whole sum of the first three parts of *f* is of *d*. ¶ And so, if there are more parts of *e* and *f*, by always combining the following part with the sum of the previous ones, you conclude...

...just as *e* is a multiple of *b*, so *f* is a multiple of *d*, by the previously taken premise as many times as there were parts in *e* or in *f* minus one: and thus the proposition is clear.

## Proposition 4.

<image-desc>A diagram illustrating Proposition 4. It shows two sets of proportional magnitudes. On the left, a column of line segments labeled k (48), e (24), a (12), b (3), g (18), and m (54). On the right, a corresponding column labeled l (64), f (32), c (16), d (4), h (24), and n (72). The diagram visually demonstrates how taking equal multiples of terms in a proportion maintains the same ratio.</image-desc>

**If** there be a ratio of a first magnitude to a second as of a third to a fourth: and if equal multiples be assigned to the first and the third, and likewise equal multiples be assigned to the second and the fourth, then the assigned multiples will be proportional in the same order.

¶ Let the ratio of the first *a* to the second *b* be as the third *c* to the fourth *d*. And let *e* be taken as a multiple of *a*, and *f* as an equal multiple of *c*. Likewise, let *g* be a multiple of *b*, and *h* an equal multiple of *d*. I say that the ratio of *e* to *g* is as *f* to *h*. Let us take *k* as a multiple of *e*, and *l* as an equal multiple of *f*. Likewise, *m* as a multiple of *g*, and *n* as an equal multiple of *h*. And because *e* and *f* are equal multiples of *a* and *c*, and likewise *k* and *l* are equal multiples of *e* and *f*, they will be—by the previous proposition—equal multiples of *a* and *c*. By the same reasoning, *m* and *n* will be equal multiples of *b* and *d*. Wherefore, by the conversion of the definition of discrete proportionality <term>incontinuae proportionalitatis</term> <note>Euclid distinguishes between "continuous" proportions (a:b = b:c) and "discrete" or "incontinuous" proportions (a:b = c:d).</note>, *k* to *m* and *l* to *n* will behave similarly in adding, subtracting, and equaling. Therefore, since *k* and *l* are equal multiples of *e* and *f*, and *m* and *n* are equal multiples of *g* and *h*, it will be—by the definition of discrete proportionality—that the ratio of *e* to *g* is as *f* to *h*, which is what was proposed.

## Proposition 5.

<margin>if the part is a part for which also an aliquot part is subtracted</margin>
<margin>similar</margin>

<image-desc>A diagram for Proposition 5 using semi-circular arcs to represent magnitudes. A large arc is labeled 32. Below it, arcs c and f (labeled 24) and arc g (labeled 8) show how the whole is composed of parts. Further down, smaller arcs a and e (6) and b (2) relate to the larger segments, illustrating the subtractive property described in the text.</image-desc>

**If** there be two quantities of which one is a part of the other, and the same part is subtracted from each of them, the remainder will be the same multiple of the remainder as the whole is of the whole.

¶ Or thus: if it be an aliquot part <term>aliquota</term> <note>An "aliquot part" is a part that measures its whole exactly, such as 2 being an aliquot part of 6 because it fits exactly three times.</note>, the remainder of the remainder will be the same part as the whole is of the whole. Let the quantity *a.b.* be the same part of the quantity *c.d.* as *e.b.* is of *a.b.* And let *a.b.* be subtracted from the quantity *c.d.*, and let the remainder be *f.c.*; then *f.d.* will be equal to *a.b.* Similarly, let *e.b.* be subtracted from the quantity *a.b.*, and let the remainder be *e.a.* I say that whatever part the quantity *a.b.* is of the quantity *c.d.*, the quantity *a.e.* is that same part of the quantity *c.f.* Since *f.d.* is equal to *a.b.*, *f.d.* will be the same multiple of *e.b.* as *c.d.* is a multiple of *a.b.* I shall therefore place *d.g.* as the same multiple of *a.e.* as *f.d.* is of *e.b.* By the first [proposition] of this book, the quantity *f.g.* will be the same multiple of *a.b.* as *f.d.* is of *e.b.* And because *c.d.* was the same multiple of *a.b.* as *f.d.* was of *e.b.*, each of the two quantities *c.d.* and *f.g.* are equal multiples of the quantity *a.b.* Wherefore, by common knowledge <note>original: "communem scientiam," referring to a common notion or axiom.</note>, *c.d.* and *f.g.* are equal to one another. Therefore, when the quantity *f.d.* is taken from each of them, *c.f.* will be equal to *d.g.* And because *d.g.* was the same multiple of *a.e.* as *f.d.* was of *e.b.* (and thus as *a.b.* was of *e.b.*), then just as *c.d.* is to *a.b.*, *c.f.* will be the same multiple of *a.e.* as the whole *c.d.* is of the whole *a.b.*, which is what was proposed.

## Proposition 6.

**If** there be two quantities which are equal multiples of two others, and two smaller quantities, being equal multiples of those same two, are subtracted from the larger ones, the two remainders will either be the same multiples of them, or equal to them.

¶ Let the quantities *a.b.* be to *c.* and *d.e.* to *f.* equally multiple <note>original: "eque multiplices"; meaning they are the same multiples of their respective bases</note>: and let *c.* be subtracted from *a.b.* and *f.* from *d.e.* and let the remainders be: from *a.b.* indeed *a.g.* and from *d.e.* *d.h.* and let *g.b.* be equal to *c.* and *h.e.* equal to *f.* I say that the two remainders *a.g.* and *d.h.* will be equal to the two quantities *c.* and *f.* or equally multiple of them. Therefore, let first *a.g.* be equal to *c.* I say that *d.h.* is equal to *f.* For I will take the quantity *e.k.* equal to *f.* and it will be, by the previous hypotheses, that as many times as *f.* is in *h.k.* so many times is *c.* in *a.b.* wherefore just as *a.b.* is a multiple of *c.* so *b.k.* <note>The text likely means *h.k.*</note> is a multiple of *f.* but since *d.e.* was also a multiple of the same *f.* it will be, therefore, by common knowledge <note>original: "cōem scientiam"; referring to the Common Notions or Axioms of geometry</note> that *h.k.* is equal to *d.e.* thus, the common quantity *h.e.* being removed, *d.h.* will be equal to *e.k.* and therefore equal to *f.* which is what was to be shown. ¶ If, however, *a.g.* be a multiple of *c.* I will set *e.k.* to be an equal multiple of *f.* and it will be as before, that as many times as *f.* is in *h.k.* so many times is *c.* in *a.b.* But it was also there as many times in *d.e.* therefore, as before, *d.e.* will be equal to *h.k.* and *d.h.* to *e.k.* wherefore just as *a.g.* is a multiple of *c.* so *d.h.* is a multiple of *f.* which is what was to be shown. Alternatively, the same is true since the quantity *a.b.* contains the quantity *c.* according to the same number as the quantity *d.e.* contains the quantity *f.* and a unit being removed from it, there remains a unit or a number according to which *a.g.* contains *c.* and according to which *d.h.* contains *f.* it is clear that the quantities *a.g.* and *d.h.* are equal to or equally multiple of the quantities *c.* and *f.*

## Proposition 7.

**If two equal quantities are compared to any other third quantity, their ratio to that one will be the same; and likewise, the ratio of that third quantity to each of them is one and the same.**

<margin>
[handwritten mark]
</margin>
Let there be two equal quantities *a.* and *b.* which are compared to any third, such as *c.* I say that the ratio of *a.* to *c.* is the same as *b.* to *c.* and also that the ratio of *c.* to *a.* is the same as *c.* to *b.* The first part is proved thus: since *c.* is the <term>consequent</term> <note>the second term in a ratio</note> to the first *a.* and to the third *b.* it will be in the position of the second and fourth terms. I will take, therefore, *d.* as a multiple of the first *a.* and *e.* as an equal multiple of the third *b.* and I will take *f.* as any multiple of *c.* which is the second and fourth: and because *a.* and *b.* (of which *d.* and *e.* are equal multiples) are set as equal, it will follow that if *d.* is divided according to the quantity *a.* and *e.* according to the quantity *b.* the parts in both are equal in number and quantity: in number certainly by the hypothesis due to the equality of the multiplication in both: and in quantity by this common knowledge repeated as often as necessary: things which are equal to the same thing are equal to each other. Because, therefore, the first of the parts of *d.* is equal to the first of the parts of *e.* and the second to the second, and the rest to the rest; and there are as many parts in *d.* as there are in *e.* then by the first proposition of this book, *d.* is equal to *e.* wherefore by common knowledge <note>axiomatic reasoning</note>, if *d.* and *e.* are equal quantities and are compared to another third *f.* then either both quantities *d.* and *e.* are similarly greater than *f.* or similarly smaller, or equal to it. Therefore, from the definition of <term>discrete proportionality</term> <note>original: "incontinue proportionalitatis"; referring to the definition of four proportional terms (a:c :: b:c)</note>, the ratio which is of the first *a.* to the second *c.* is the same as the third *b.* to the fourth *c.* <note>OCR says "d." but logic dictates "c." or a placeholder for the second term</note> which is what was to be shown. ¶ The second part you will prove in the same way by reversing the order: let *c.* be placed as the first and third, *a.* indeed as the second, and *b.* as the fourth. Since the quantities *d.* and *e.* which are equal multiples of the first and third are either similarly greater than the quantities which are equal multiples of the second and fourth, or similarly smaller or equal to them; it will be by the same definition that the ratio of the first *c.* to the second *a.* is as the third *c.* to the fourth *b.* which is the second thing proposed.

->Proposition 8.<-

If two unequal quantities are compared to one <note>That is, a single third quantity used as a common reference</note> quantity, the greater quantity will have a greater ratio, while the lesser will have a lesser ratio. Conversely, the ratio of that third quantity to the lesser will be greater, and its ratio to the larger will be lesser.
¶ Let there be two unequal quantities, *a.* and *b.c.*, and let *b.c.* be the greater. Let them both be compared to the same quantity, which is *d.* I say that the ratio of *bc.* to *d.* is greater than that of *a.* to *d.*, and conversely, that the ratio of *d.* to *a.* is greater than that of *d.* to *b.c.* ¶ The first part is proved thus: I will set *e.b.* equal to *a.* and I will multiply *e.c.* <note>the excess of *b.c.* over *a.*</note> so many times that the resulting quantity is greater than *d.*. Let this be *f.g.*. I will also take *k.f.* as a multiple of *b.e.*, and similarly *h.* as a multiple of *a.*, in the same way that *f.g.* is a multiple of *e.c.* By the first proposition of this book, *h.* will be the same multiple of *a.* as *k.g.* is of *b.c.* <note>original: "per primam huius"; referring to Book V, Proposition 1, which states that multiples of parts are equimultiples of the whole</note>. Furthermore, *h.* is equal to *k.f.* because their submultiples <note>the base units from which the multiples were created</note>, which are *a.* and *b.e.*, were set as equal. I will also assume that *b.* is not less than *d.*, but equal or greater. For I will multiply each of the three quantities—*e.c.*, *b.e.*, and *a.*—equally so that *f.g.* (the multiple of *e.c.*) becomes greater than *d.*, and that *h.* (the multiple of *a.*) does not become less than it. Then I will multiply *d.* until it becomes a quantity greater than *b.c.*. Let *m.* be the first multiple of *d.* that is greater than *b.c.*. Below this, I will take the largest multiple of *d.* that is either less than it or equal to it; if *m.* is the first in the order of multiples of *d.*, let this previous one be *l.*. Thus, *l.* will not be greater than *b.c.*, and *m.* will consist of *d.* and *l.* because every multiple consists of the next lowest multiple plus the single unit (as a triple consists of a double plus the unit, except the first multiple <note>the double</note> which consists of twice the unit). ¶ Because *h.* is equal to *k.f.*, *k.f.* will not be less than *l.*. Therefore, *k.f.* and *d.* together will not be less than *l.* and *d.*. For this reason, they will not be less than *m.*. And because *f.g.* is greater than *d.*, *k.g.* will be greater than *m.*. ¶ I understand, therefore, the quantity *b.c.* as the first, *d.* as the second, *a.* as the third, and *d.* as the fourth. For the first and third, equimultiples have been taken—namely *k.g.* and *h.*. Similarly, for the second and fourth, equimultiples have been taken—indeed, the same multiple for both, which is *m.*. Since the multiple of the first (*k.g.*) exceeds the multiple of the second (*m.*), but the multiple of the third (*h.*) does not exceed the multiple of the fourth (*m.*), it follows by the definition of greater proportionality <note>original: "diffinitionem maioris improportionalitatis"; referring to Definition 7 of Book V, which defines how to identify a larger ratio</note> that the ratio of the first (*b.c.*) to the second (*d.*) is greater than that of the third (*a.*) to the fourth (*d.*). This is the first part. ¶ You will prove the second part by the same definition but in reverse order: so that *d.* is the first and third, *a.* is the second, and *b.c.* the fourth. For the multiple of the first (*m.*) exceeds the multiple of the second (*h.*), but the multiple of the third (*m.*) does not exceed the multiple of the fourth (*k.g.*). Therefore, the ratio of *d.* to *a.* is greater than the ratio of *d.* to *b.c.*, which is the second part. ¶ From this method of demonstration, the sufficiency of the definition of greater proportionality is clear, which the author <note>Euclid</note> placed at the beginning of this fifth book. For never is the ratio of the first of four quantities to the second greater than that of the third to the fourth, unless it happens that some equimultiples of the first and third can be found which, when compared to equimultiples of the second and fourth, show the multiple of the first exceeding the multiple of the second, while the multiple of the third does not exceed the multiple of the fourth. These multiples we shall find as we will demonstrate below, following the 12th proposition of this book.

### Proposition 9.

[Initial S]i If several quantities have the same ratio to a single quantity, those quantities are equal to each other. If, however, a single quantity has the same ratio to several others, it is necessary that those others be equal.
¶ Let there be two quantities, *a.* and *b.*, having one [and the same] ratio to *c.* I say they are equal. And if, conversely, there is the same ratio of *c.* to both of them, I still say they are equal. This is the converse of Proposition 7 <note>original: "conuersa .7."</note>. The first part is evident: for if they are not equal, but one of them is greater—suppose *a.*—then by the first part of the preceding proposition <note>Proposition 8</note> the ratio of *a.* to *c.* would be greater than the ratio of *b.* to *c.*, which is against the hypothesis <note>original: "contra ypothe."; meaning it contradicts what we assumed to be true</note>. The second part is also evident: because if *a.* is greater than *b.*, then by the second part of the preceding proposition, the ratio of *c.* to *b.* would be greater than the ratio of *c.* to *a.*, which is also against the hypothesis.

The top segment is marked with the number 9, the letter 'b', and another 9 (representing magnitude b=9). Below it, a segment is marked 'c' and the number 3 (representing the common reference magnitude c=3). To the right is a vertical segment marked 9 (representing magnitude a=9). This illustrates that if 9:3 is the same as 9:3, then the two '9s' must be equal.</image-desc>

->Proposition 10.<-

<margin>but of the other</margin>
[Initial S]i If the ratio of a quantity to some other quantity is greater, the [first] quantity is the greater. If, however, the ratio of one quantity to another is greater [than its ratio to a third], the [third] quantity must be the lesser.
¶ Thus, if the ratio of *a.* to *c.* is greater than the ratio of *b.* to *c.*, I say that *a.* is greater than *b.* And if the ratio of *c.* to *b.* is greater than that of *c.* to *a.*, I still say that *a.* is greater than *b.* This is the converse of Proposition 8. The first part is clear through the first part of Proposition 7 and the first part of Proposition 8: for by the first part of the seventh, *a.* will not be equal to *b.*, nor will it be lesser by the first part of the eighth. The second part is clear from the second parts of those same propositions.

->Proposition 11.<-

[Initial S]i If ratios are equal to the same ratio, it is necessary that those ratios also be equal to each other.
¶ Euclid, at the beginning of the first book, counted this among the common notions <note>original: "communes animi conceptiones"; these are self-evident axioms like "things equal to the same thing are equal to each other"</note>: that things which are equal to the same thing are also equal to each other. As that is understood regarding quantities, he demonstrates it here insofar as it is applied to ratios. Therefore, let each of two ratios—which are *a.* to *b.* and *c.* to *d.*—be equal to the ratio which is *e.* to *f.* I say that the ratios *a.* to *b.* and *c.* to *d.* are equal to each other. For I will take *g.*, *h.*, and *k.* as equal multiples <note>term: "eque multiplices"; quantities multiplied by the same factor</note> of *a.*, *c.*, and *e.* Likewise, let *l.*, *m.*, and *n.* be equal multiples of *b.*, *d.*, and *f.* And because by the hypothesis the ratio *e.* to *f.* is as *a.* to *b.*, and similarly as *c.* to *d.*, it will be (by the converse of the definition of discontinuous proportionality <note>term: "incontinue proportionalitatis"; this refers to a proportion between four terms, a:b = c:d, as opposed to a continuous proportion like a:b = b:c</note> taken twice): if *k.* is greater than *n.*, then *g.* is greater than *l.* and *h.* is greater than *m.* And if *k.* is less than *n.*, then *g.* is less than *l.* and *h.* is less than *m.* And if *k.* is equal to *n.*, then *g.* is equal to *l.* and *h.* is equal to *m.* Therefore, since *g.* to *l.* and *h.* to *m.* behave the same way in terms of exceeding, falling short, and equaling—by means of the intermediaries *k.* and *n.*—it follows by the definition of discontinuous proportionality that *a.* is to *b.* as *c.* is to *d.*, which is what was proposed.

First row: h=12, k=9, g=6. 
Second row: c=4, e=3, a=2. 
Third row: d=8, f=6, b=4. 
Fourth row: m=24, n=18, l=12. 
These numbers demonstrate the ratios: a:b (2:4) and c:d (4:8) both equal e:f (3:6). Their multiples (e.g., g, h, k being 3 times a, c, e) maintain the same comparative relationship to the multiples of their denominators (l, m, n being 3 times b, d, f).</image-desc>

...equal, whichever one of them it may be, the same will be greater than the rest. ¶ In the case of proportions, however, this is demonstrated: that if the ratio of *a* to *b* is as *c* to *d*, but the ratio of *c* to *d* is greater than that of *e* to *f*, then the ratio of *a* to *b* will also be greater than that of *e* to *f*. <note>This is Proposition 13: If a first ratio is equal to a second, and the second is greater than a third, the first is also greater than the third.</note> For I shall take *g* [as a multiple] of *a*, and *h* of *c*, and *k* of *e*, as equimultiples <term>equimultiples: quantities multiplied by the same factor, such as 10 and 20 being the five-fold multiples of 2 and 4</term>. Likewise, let *l* be a multiple of *b*, *m* of *d*, and *n* of *f*, as equimultiples. And because, by the hypothesis <note>original: "ypothesim"</note>, the ratio of *c* to *d* is as *a* to *b*, and greater than *e* to *f*, it will follow by the conversion of the definition of incontinuous proportionality <note>original: "incontinue proportionalitatis"; referring to discrete proportions between four distinct terms</note> that if *b* is added over *m* <note>meaning if the multiple of the second term exceeds the multiple of the fourth</note>, then *g* is added over *l*. And by the conversion of the definition of a greater proportion, it is not necessary for *k* to be added over *n*. Since, therefore, through the mediation of *b* and *m*, if *g* is added over *l* it is not necessary for *k* to be added over *n*, it will be (by the definition of a greater proportion) that the ratio of *a* to *b* is greater than the ratio of *e* to *f*, which is what was proposed. ¶ In a similar way, you will also prove that if *a* is to *b* as *c* is to *d*, and *c* to *d* is less than *e* to *f*, then *a* to *b* will be less than *e* to *f*. For since *c* to *d* is less than *e* to *f*, then *e* to *f* will be greater than *c* to *d*. Therefore, by the conversion of the definition of a greater proportion, if *k* is added over *n*, it is not necessary that *b* is added over *m*. But if *b* is not added over *m*, then *g* is not added over *l*. Therefore, if *k* is added over *n*, it is not necessary that *g* be added over *n* <note>OCR likely intended "l" here</note>. Therefore, by the definition of a greater proportion, the ratio of *e* to *f* will be greater than that of *a* to *b*. Therefore, conversely: *a* to *b* will be less than *e* to *f*, which is what was proposed.

Moreover, from the manner of the eighth demonstration of this [book] and this [one], it will be manifest that if the first of four quantities has a greater ratio to the second than the third to the fourth, it happens that some equimultiples of the first and third can be found which, when compared to some equimultiples of the second and fourth, the multiple of the first will be found to exceed the multiple of the second, but the multiple of the third will not exceed the multiple of the fourth. This is shown as follows: Let the ratio of *a* to *b* be greater than *d* to *e*. I will then set it so that the ratio of *af* to *c* is as *d* to *e*. It will then be, by this [Proposition] 12 and by [Proposition] 10, that *af* is less than *ab*. And let *r* be less by the quantity *fb*, which I shall multiply so many times that it produces a quantity greater than *c*, which let be *gb*, with this condition: that *d* multiplied just as many times produces a quantity not less than *e*, which let be *k*. Then I will set it so that *lg* is the same multiple of *af* as *gb* is a multiple of *fb* or *kd* is [of *d*]. By the first [Proposition] of this [book], *lb* will be the same multiple of *ab* as *kd* is of *d*. Then I will set *m* to be the first multiple of *e* which is greater than *k*, and I will set *n* to be the same multiple of *c* as *m* is of *e*. By the previous hypotheses and the conversion of the definition of incontinuous proportionality, the quantity *n* will be the first of the multiples of *c* that is greater than *lg*, nor will *lg* be less than *c*. I shall therefore take the greatest of the multiples of *c* below *n*, or equal to it if perhaps *n* is the first of its multiples, which let be *o*. It will be established that *n* consists of *o* and *c*. Because, therefore, *lg* is not less than *o*, and *gb* is greater than *c*, *lb* will be greater than *n*. Wherefore, since *k* is less than *m*, the proposition is clear. ¶ We can also demonstrate the converse of this: namely, that if it happens that some equimultiples of the first and third are found, where the multiple of the first exceeds some multiple of the second, and the multiple of the third does not exceed the multiple of the fourth, then the ratio of the first to the second will be greater than that of the third to the fourth. This is proven thus: Let there be four quantities: *a* the first, *b* the second, *cd* the third, and *e* the fourth. Let *f* be a multiple of *a* and *g* be a multiple of *cd* as equimultiples. Similarly, let *h* be a multiple of *b* and *k* be a multiple of *e* as equimultiples. And let *f* exceed *h*, but *g* does not exceed *k*. I say that the ratio of *a* to *b* is greater than the ratio of *cd* to *e*. For if it were equal, then by the conversion of the definition of incontinuous proportionality, *g* would exceed *k*, which is against the hypothesis. If, however, it were less, let *cd* to *e* be as *a* to *b*, and by the 10th [Proposition] of this [book], *cl* would be less than *cd*; let it be less by the quantity *ld*. I will then set *mn* to be the same multiple of *cl* and *np* the multiple of *ld* as *f* is a multiple of *a*...

...and by the first [proposition] of this [book], *m.p.* will be as many times a multiple of *c.d.* as *f.* is a multiple of *a.* Therefore, each of the two quantities *m.p.* and *f.g.* is equally a multiple of the quantity *c.d.* Thus, they are equal. For this inference was demonstrated in the 7th [proposition] of this [book]. And because *g.* is not greater than *k.*, then *m.p.* will not be greater than the same. But by the conversion of the definition of discrete proportionality <note>original: "incontinue proportionalitatis"; this refers to ratios between four distinct terms rather than a continuous series</note>, *m.n.* is greater than *k.* because *f.* is greater than *b.* Therefore, *m.n.* is greater than *m.p.*, which is impossible; therefore, the proposition remains as stated.

### Proposition 13

<note>In modern editions of Euclid, this is Proposition 12 of Book V.</note>

**I**f there be any number of magnitudes that have the same ratio to as many others, then as one is to one, so will all those [antecedents] taken together be to all those [consequents] taken together.

¶ Where he first proposed concerning multiples [in Proposition 1], here he proposes concerning all proportions. For this is a general rule: because every multiplicity is a proportion, but not vice versa. Let there be, therefore, one ratio of *a.* to *b.*, and of *c.* to *d.*, and of *e.* to *f.* I say that whatever the ratio of *a.* to *b.* is, the same is the ratio of the composite [sum] of *a. c. e.* to the composite of *b. d. f.* Let I take *g.* [as a multiple] of *a.*, and *h.* of *c.*, and *k.* of *e.* as equimultiples <term>equimultiples: quantities multiplied by the same factor, such as 12 and 18 being the three-fold multiples of 4 and 6</term>. Likewise, let *l.* be a multiple of *b.*, *m.* of *d.*, and *n.* of *f.* as equimultiples. By the first [proposition] of this [book], the composite of *g. h. k.* will be as many times a multiple of the composite of *a. c. e.* as *g.* is a multiple of *a.* Similarly, by the same [proposition], the composite of *l. m. n.* will be as many times a multiple of the composite of *b. d. f.* as *l.* is a multiple of *b.* And by the conversion of the definition of discrete proportionality, if *g.* exceeds *l.*, then *h.* exceeds *m.* and *k.* [exceeds] *n.*; and if it is less, it is less; and if equal, it is equal. Therefore, by common knowledge, if *g.* exceeds *l.*, the composite of *g. h. k.* exceeds the composite of *l. m. n.*; and if it is less, it is less; and if equal, equal. Therefore, by the definition of discrete proportionality, the ratio of *a.* to *b.* is as the composite of *a. c. e.* is to the composite of *b. d. f.*, which is what was proposed.

### Proposition 14

**I**f there are four proportional magnitudes, and the first is greater than the third, the second must be greater than the fourth; and if smaller, smaller; and if equal, equal.

¶ Let the ratio of *a.* to *b.* be as *c.* to *d.* I say that if *a.* is greater than *c.*, then *b.* will be greater than *d.*; if smaller, smaller; and if equal, equal. For if *a.* is greater than *c.*, then by the first part of the 8th [proposition] of this [book], the ratio of *a.* to *d.* is greater than that of *c.* to *d.* Therefore, the ratio of *a.* to *d.* will be greater than that of *a.* to *b.* Consequently, by the second part of the 10th [proposition] of this [book], *b.* will be greater than *d.*, which is what was proposed. If, however, *a.* is smaller than *c.*, then by the first part of the 8th, the ratio of *a.* to *d.* will be smaller than *c.* to *d.*; wherefore *a.* to *b.* will be greater than *a.* to *d.* By the second part of the 10th, therefore, *b.* will be smaller than *d.* If, however, *a.* is equal to *c.*, then by the first part of the 7th, *a.* is to *d.* as *c.* is to *d.*; wherefore *a.* is to *d.* just as it is to *b.* Thus, by the second part of the 9th, *b.* will be equal to *d.*, just as the proposition makes clear.

### Proposition 15

**I**f equimultiples are assigned to any magnitudes, there will be one ratio of those multiples as well as of the sub-multiples <term>sub-multiples: the original parts that make up a multiple; for example, if 20 is a multiple of 5, then 5 is the sub-multiple</term>.

¶ Let *c.* to *a.* and *d.* to *b.* be equimultiples. I say that whatever the ratio of *a.* to *b.* is, the same is the ratio of *c.* to *d.* Let *c.* be divided according to the quantity of *a.*, and *d.* according to the quantity of *b.* There are as many parts of *c.* as there are of *d.* And because any part of *c.* to any part of *d.* has itself as *a.* is to *b.*, then by the 13th [proposition] of this [book], *c.* is to *d.* as *a.* is to *b.*, which is what was proposed.

### Proposition 16

<margin>
e ———— 8 12
a —— 4 c —— 8
f —— 4 b — 6
b — 2 h ——— 6
d — 3 12
</margin>

**I**f there be four proportional quantities, they will also be proportional alternately. <note>In modern terms: if $a:b = c:d$, then $a:c = b:d$. This is often called "alternando."</note>
¶ Let the ratio of *a.* to *b.* be as *c.* to *d.* I say that *a.* will be to *c.* as *b.* is to *d.* And this is the mode of arguing which is called permuted proportionality <note>original: "proportionalitas permutata"</note>. The demonstration of this is evident as follows: Let I take *e.* as a multiple of *a.*, and *f.* as an equal multiple of *b.* Likewise, let *g.* be a multiple of *c.* and *h.* an equal multiple of *d.* By the previous [proposition], *e.* will be to *f.* as *g.* is to *h.* Wherefore, by the 14th [proposition], if *e.* exceeds *g.*, then *f.* exceeds *h.*; and if it is less, it is less; and if it is equal, it is equal. Therefore, by the definition of discrete proportionality <note>original: "incontinue proportionalitatis"; this refers to a proportion between four distinct terms</note>, *a.* will be to *c.* as *b.* is to *d.*, which is what was proposed. It is necessary, however, that in permuted proportionality all four quantities be of the same kind <note>original: "eiusdem generis"; you cannot alternate a proportion if the first two terms are lines and the second two are areas, as you cannot have a ratio between a line and an area</note>.

### Proposition 17

<margin>
g ———— 16 h k 12 p
a ———— 8 c 4 b
c — 4 f 3 e
l ———— 12 m n 9 q
a. b. f. e.
</margin>

**I**f quantities be proportional when combined, they will also be proportional when separated. <note>This is the "dividendo" rule: if $(a+b):b = (c+d):d$, then $a:b = c:d$.</note>
¶ He demonstrates by the mode of arguing called permuted proportionality; he demonstrates that which is called separated proportionality <note>original: "proportionalitas disiuncta"</note>. Let there be, therefore, the ratio of *a.b.* to *b.* as *d.e.* to *e.f.* I say that the ratio of *a.c.* to *c.b.* will be as *d.f.* to *f.e.* For let I take *g.b.* as a multiple of *a.c.*, and *h.k.* as an equal multiple of *c.b.* Likewise, let *l.m.* be a multiple of *d.f.* and *m.n.* an equal multiple of *f.e.* By the first [proposition] of this [book], *g.k.* is the same multiple of *a.b.* as *g.b.* is of *a.c.*, and *l.n.* is the same multiple of *d.e.* as *l.m.* is of *d.f.* And therefore, by the previously stated hypotheses, *g.k.* and *h.* <note>The text likely means the multiple of the whole</note> is the same multiple of *a.b.* as *l.n.* is of *e.* Let I further take *k.p.* as a multiple of *c.b.* and *n.q.* an equal multiple of *f.e.* By the second [proposition], *h.p.* will be to *c.b.* and *m.q.* to *f.e.* equal multiples. Therefore, by the conversion of the definition of discrete proportionality: if *g.k.* exceeds *h.p.*, then *l.n.* exceeds *m.q.*; and if it is less, it is less; and if it is equal, it is equal. Thus, by removing the common parts *h.k.* and *m.n.*, it will be by common knowledge <note>original: "communem scientiam"; referring to an axiom or common notion</note> that if *g.b.* exceeds *k.p.*, then *l.m.* exceeds *n.q.*; and if it is less, it is less; and if it is equal, it is equal. Therefore, by the definition of discrete proportionality, the ratio of *a.c.* to *c.b.* is as *d.f.* to *f.e.*, which is what was proposed.

### Proposition 18

<margin>
g ———— 16 h k 12 p
a ———— 8 c 4 b
c — 4 f 3 e
l ———— 12 m n 9 q
</margin>

**I**f quantities be proportional when separated, they will also be proportional when combined. <note>This is the "componendo" rule: if $a:b = c:d$, then $(a+b):b = (c+d):d$.</note>
¶ This demonstrates the mode of arguing called combined proportionality <note>original: "proportionalitas coniuncta"</note>, and it is the converse of the prior [proposition]. For its demonstration, let the arrangement of the previous [proposition] be taken up again, and let all its hypotheses remain, except that it is assumed that the ratio of *a.c.* to *c.b.* is as *d.f.* to *f.e.* I say that the ratio of *a.b.* to *b.c.* will be as *d.e.* to *f.e.* For it follows from this hypothesis and the other hypotheses of the previous [proposition] concerning equally taken multiples, by the conversion of the definition of discrete proportionality: if *g.b.* exceeds *k.p.*, then *l.m.* exceeds *n.q.*; and if it is less, it is less; and if it is equal, it is equal. Therefore, the common parts *h.k.* and *m.n.* having been placed [added], it follows by common knowledge that if *g.k.* exceeds *h.p.*, then *l.n.* exceeds *m.q.*; and if it is less, it is less; and if it is equal, it is equal. Wherefore, by the definition of discrete proportionality, the ratio of *a.b.* to *b.c.* will be as *d.e.* to *e.f.*, which is what was proposed. Otherwise, the same is proven indirectly thus: Since the ratio of *a.b.* to *c.b.* is as *d.f.* to *f.e.* <note>The text here contains a slight notation error, should be $a.c.:c.b.$</note>, if *a.b.* to *b.c.* were not as *d.e.* to *e.f.*, let the ratio of *d.e.* be to some other quantity as *a.b.* is to *b.c.* That quantity would be either greater than *e.f.* or less; for if it were equal to it, the proposition would be established.

### Proposition 19

<margin>
<image-desc>A geometric diagram with two horizontal lines. The top line has points a, e, b. The bottom line has points d, f. There are handwritten strokes and labels "dg", "af", "ge".</image-desc>

**I**f two portions are cut off from two wholes, and if the whole is to the whole as the portion cut off is to the portion cut off: then the remainder will be to the remainder as the whole is to the whole.

<margin>
<image-desc>A horizontal line labeled with points a, e, b and numbers 12 above ae and 4 above eb. Below it, another line labeled c, f, d with numbers 6 above cf and 2 above fd.</image-desc>
ab . cd . be . df
ae . eb . cf . fd

ab be cd df
</margin>

**I**f the fifth [proposition] proposed this concerning multiples, this one proposes it universally for all proportions; hence, this is as much more general than that one as proportion is more general than multiplicity. Therefore, let there be two quantities .a.b. and .c.d., from which two are cut off, which are .b.e. and .d.f. And let the proportion of the whole .a.b. to the whole .c.d. be as the cut-off .b.e. to the cut-off .d.f. I say that the ratio of the remainder .a.e. to the remainder .c.f. will be the same as that of the whole .a.b. to the whole .c.d. For since .a.b. is to .c.d. as .b.e. is to .d.f., by permutation <note>original: "permutatim"; the rule from Prop. 16 allowing the inner terms of a proportion to be swapped.</note> .a.b. will be to .b.e. as .c.d. is to .d.f. And by separation <note>original: "diiunctim"; referring to the "division" of ratios in Prop. 17.</note> .a.e. will be to .e.b. as .c.f. is to .f.d. And again by permutation, .a.e. will be to .c.f. as .e.b. is to .f.d. And since this was the ratio of .a.b. to .c.d., the proposition is clear. ¶ From this 19th and by permuted proportionality, the mode of arguing called everted proportionality <note>original: "proportionalitas euersa"; this refers to the ratio of a whole to its remainder.</note> is demonstrated. For example, if .a.b. is to .b.e. as .c.d. is to .d.f., I say that .b.a. will be to .a.e. as .c.d. is to .c.f. Because since .a.b. is to .b.e. as .c.d. is to .d.f., by permutation .a.b. will be to .c.d. as .b.e. is to .d.f. Therefore, by this 19th [proposition], .b.a. is to .d.c. as .a.e. is to .c.f. Therefore, by permutation, .b.a. is to .a.e. as .c.d. is to .c.f., which is what was proposed. ¶ Also, converted proportionality <note>original: "conuersa proportionalitas"; the inverse of a ratio, i.e., if a:b, then b:a.</note>, which we demonstrated from the definition of discrete proportionality in explaining the principles of this fifth book, can also be demonstrated here indirectly from permuted proportionality (the 5th of this book). For if the proportion of .a. to .b. is as .c. to .d., I say that .b. will be to .a. as .d. is to .c. If it were otherwise, let .d. be to .e. as .b. is to .a. And since .a. is to .b. as .c. is to .d., by permutation .a. will be to .c. as .b. is to .d. And because again .b. is to .a. as .d. is to .e., by permutation .b. will also be to .d. as .a. is to .e. Wherefore .a. will be to .c. as .d. is to .e. If therefore .e. is not equal to .c., an impossibility follows, contrary to the second part of the 9th [proposition]. But if they are equal, then .b. will be to .a. as .d. is to .c., which is what was proposed.

### Proposition 20

**I**f there be any number of quantities, and others equal to them in number, of which any two of the first set are in the same ratio as two of the latter set, then there is a necessity in the proportionality of equality <note>This refers to the "ex aequali" property. If a:b = d:e and b:c = e:f, then a:c = d:f.</note>: namely, if the first of the first set be greater than the last, then the first of the latter set will also be greater than the last. And if it be less, then less. If indeed equal, then equal.

**I**ntending to demonstrate the mode of arguing which is called equal proportionality <note>original: "equa proportionalitas"</note>—whether the quantities of two orders are proportioned directly or crosswise—Euclid premises two antecedents necessary for demonstrating the proposition. Through the first of these, he demonstrates equal proportionality when the quantities of two orders are proportioned directly; through the second, however, when they are proportioned crosswise. He proposes these two antecedents concerning quantities of two orders equal in number, however many they may be. <meta>This page continues the discussion of ratios and proportionality from Euclid’s Book V. The previous page concluded a proof concerning the comparison of two sets of magnitudes. This page critiques a common but flawed proof method used by other commentators before formally introducing and proving Proposition 21, which deals with "perturbed" or cross-wise proportions.</meta>

-># BOOK V<-

It is not necessary that we demonstrate these things except only in three <note>The author refers to three magnitudes in a series, which is the minimum required to establish the logic of the proof.</note>, for this alone is sufficient for the purpose. However, for more than three, it will be clear through equal proportionality <note>original: "equā ꝓportiõalitatē", referring to the *ex aequali* proposition (Euclid V.22), where if a:b = d:e and b:c = e:f, then a:c = d:f.</note> once it has been demonstrated.

¶ Let there be, therefore, three magnitudes, **a**, **b**, and **c**, and let there be three others, **d**, **e**, and **f**. Let the proportion of **a** to **b** be as **e** to **d**, and the proportion of **b** to **c** be as **f** to **e**. I say that if **a** is greater than **c**, then **f** will be greater than **d**; and if it is less, it will be less; and if equal, it will be equal. For if **a** is greater, then by the first part of [Proposition] 8, the proportion of **a** to **b** will be greater than **c** to **b**. Therefore, by [Proposition] 12 and by inverse proportionality, **c** to **d** will be less than **f** to **d**, and therefore by the first part of [Proposition] 10, **c** will be less than **f**, which is what was proposed. If, however, **a** is equal to **c**, then by the first part of [Proposition] 7, the proportion of **a** to **b** will be as **c** to **b**, and therefore by the second part of [Proposition] 11 and inverse proportionality, **c** to **d** will be as **f** to **d**, wherefore by the first part of [Proposition] 9, **c** is equal to **f**, which is what was proposed.

¶ Certain people, however, have demonstrated this conclusion through alternating proportionality <note>original: "permutatim", a geometric operation where the inner terms of a proportion are swapped: if a:b = c:d, then a:c = b:d.</note> in this way: the proportion of **a** to **b** is as **e** to **d**, therefore by permutation **a** is to **e** as **b** is to **d**. And since again **b** is to **c** as **f** is to **e**, by permutation **b** is to **f** as **c** is to **e**. But **b** was to **d** as **a** was to **e**, therefore by [Proposition] 11, **a** will be to **e** as **c** is to **f**. Thus, by [Proposition] 14, if the first **a** is greater than the third **c**, the second **e** will be greater than the fourth **f** <note>The author is following a logical chain to show that if the ratios are equal, the magnitudes must correspond in size.</note>; and if less, then less; and if equal, equal, which is what was proposed.

¶ These men, however, have erred in their demonstration; because if it were Euclid's intention to demonstrate it thus, it would not have been necessary for him to set forth this conclusion as a prerequisite for equal proportionality. For if one permutation of the proportionality is made again to which it has come—which is **a** to **c** as **e** to **f**—it follows that **a** is to **e** as **c** is to **f**, and this is equal proportionality. Furthermore, their conclusion does not follow unless all the quantities of both orders were of one kind. For if **a**, **b**, and **c** are lines, and **d**, **e**, and **f** are surfaces, or solids, or times, then it will not be possible to permute the proportions <note>This is a crucial point in Euclidian geometry: you cannot have a ratio between a line and a surface. The "alternated" proof only works if all six magnitudes are the same type, but Euclid’s Book V is designed to be universal across all types of magnitudes.</note>. Therefore, they sin by demonstrating particularly what is stated universally.

<margin>
<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing two sets of three magnitudes. On the left, a=12, b=6, c=3. On the right, d=16, e=8, f=4. Arrows show the "perturbed" relationship: a connects to e, and b to d; b connects to f, and c to e. This illustrates that 12:6 = 8:16 (which is 2:1 vs 1:2, a reversed proportion) and 6:3 = 4:8.</image-desc>
</margin>

### Proposition 21.

**I**f there be any number of magnitudes, and others equal to them in
number, which, when taken two by two in the former and
latter sets, are in the same ratio in a perturbed order <note>original: "peruersim comparate", referring to a perturbed proportion where a:b = e:f and b:c = d:e.</note>;
it is also necessary that if, in the proportionality of
equality, the first of the former magnitudes is greater than
the last, the first of the latter magnitudes will also be greater than the last; and if less, less; and if equal, equal.

<margin>
<image-desc>A diagram with six line segments. On the left: a=16, b=8, c=4. On the right: f=12, e=6, d=3. The diagram shows that a:b (16:8 = 2:1) is the same as e:d (6:3 = 2:1), and b:c (8:4 = 2:1) is the same as f:e (12:6 = 2:1). Since a > c (16 > 4), it follows that f > d (12 > 3).</image-desc>
</margin>

¶ According to the premise, let there be three magnitudes, **a**, **b**, and **c**, and let there be another three, **f**, **e**, and **d**. Let the proportion of **a** to **b** be as **e** to **d**, and **b** to **c** as **f** to **e**. I say that if **a** is greater than **c**, then **f** will be greater than **d**; and if less, less; and if equal, equal. This is proved by the same [propositions] and in the same manner as the preceding one: for if **a** is greater than **c**, the proportion of **a** to **b** will be greater than **c** to **b**. Wherefore **e** to **d** is greater than **c** to **b**, and therefore greater than **c** to **f**. Thus, **f** is greater than **d** by the second part of [Proposition] 10, which is what was proposed. If **a** is less than **c**, it will finally be that **c** to **d** is less than **f** to **f** <note>This "f to f" may be a transcription error in the original for a ratio involving d, but the logic holds that f would be less than d.</note>, wherefore by the same part of the same [proposition], **f** will be less than **d**. If, however, **a** is equal to **c**, it follows that the proportion of **c** to **d** is as **f** to **f**, therefore by the second part of [Proposition] 9, **f** will be equal to **d**, which is what was proposed.

<summary>This page discusses Euclid's Proposition 21 regarding "perturbed" proportionality, where the ratios of two sets of magnitudes are compared in a cross-wise order. The text also critiques previous mathematicians for using "alternated" proportions in their proofs, which fails when comparing different types of magnitudes like lines and surfaces.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the demonstration of proportionality in series of magnitudes, specifically focusing on the "ex aequali" theorem. ### Proposition 22.

If there are any number of quantities, and others equal to them in number, which when taken two by two are in the same proportion, they will also be in the same proportion through equal proportionality <note>This is the "ex aequali" theorem (Euclid V.22). It states that if a:b = d:e and b:c = e:f, then a:c = d:f.</note>.

¶ Having demonstrated the prerequisites for equal proportionality, he demonstrates it here; and first, when the quantities of the two series are directly proportional. It is not necessary to demonstrate this except when there are only three quantities in each of the two series. For from this it follows evidently when there are four quantities in each, and so on; and therefore also its antecedent <note>original: "añs" (antecedens)</note> did not need to be demonstrated except only when there are also three quantities in each series. ¶ Let there be, therefore, three quantities **a**, **b**, **e**, and let three others be taken which are **c**, **d**, **f**. And let the proportion of **a** to **b** be as **c** to **d**, and **b** to **e** as **d** to **f**. I say that **a** to **e** will be as **c** to **f**. For I shall take **g** as a multiple of **a**, and **h** as an equal multiple of **c**. Likewise, **k** of **b** and **l** of **d** as equal multiples, and again **m** of **e** and **n** of **f** as equal multiples. And by the 4th [proposition], **g** will be to **k** as **b** to **l**, and **k** to **m** as **l** to **n**. Therefore, by the 20th [proposition], if **g** is greater than **m**, then **h** will be greater than **n**; and if less, less; and if equal, equal. Therefore, by the definition of discontinuous proportionality <note>This refers to a proportion where the terms are compared in separate pairs (a:b = c:d) rather than a continuous chain (a:b = b:c).</note>, the proportion of **a** to **e** is as **c** to **f**, which is what was proposed. ¶ This can also be demonstrated by the 15th [proposition] of this book, by taking **g**, **k**, **m** as equal multiples to **a**, **b**, **e**, and **h**, **l**, **n** as equal multiples to **c**, **d**, **f**; for by the 15th, **g** will be to **k** as **b** to **l**, and **k** to **m** as **l** to **n**, with the rest carried out as before. ¶ If there should be more than three quantities in each series, for instance four: by adding **p**, **r**, **q** so that **e** is to **p** as **f** is to **q**, then again **a** will be to **p** as **c** to **q**. For **a** will be to **e** as **c** to **f**, as has been demonstrated. Therefore, by removing **b** and **d**, there will be three quantities **a**, **e**, **p** and three others **c**, **f**, **q** as proposed; wherefore **a** is to **p** as **c** to **q**. And thus it is demonstrated for 4 quantities by means of 3, by removing one middle term. In the same way, you will demonstrate it for 5 by means of 4, by removing two middle terms; and for 6 by means of 5, by removing three; and so for the rest.

<note>The diagram shows two sets of magnitudes (lines). On the left: g, k, m (multiples) above a, b, e, p (the primary quantities). On the right: h, l, n (multiples) above c, d, f, q. Brackets indicate how they are grouped to show the proportional steps from the first to the last term.</note>

### Proposition 23.

If there are any number of quantities, and others equal to them in number, which when taken two by two are in the same proportion but indirectly proportional <note>Also known as "perturbed" or "cross-wise" proportion. If a:b = e:f and b:c = d:e, then a:c = d:f.</note>, they will also be in equal proportionality.

¶ This demonstrates equal proportionality in quantities of two series that are indirectly or cross-wise <note>original: "puerſim" (perversely/perturbed)</note> proportional. Nor is it necessary that I demonstrate this except when there are only three quantities in each of the two series; for by this, it evidently follows for however many are placed in each series, just as was demonstrated in the preceding [proposition] concerning those directly proportional. Let there be, therefore, 3 quantities **a**, **b**, **e**, and let 3 others be taken which are **f**, **c**, **d**. And let the proportion of **a** to **b** be as **c** to **d**, and **b** to **e** as **f** to **c**. I say that **a** to **e** will be as **f** to **d**. For I shall take **g** as a multiple of **a**, and **h** of **c**, and **k** of **f** as equal multiples. Likewise, **l** of **b**, **m** of **e**, and **n** of **d** as equal multiples. And by the fourth [proposition], **g** will be to **l** as **b** to **n**, and by the 15th, **l** is to **m** as **k** is to **h**. Therefore, by the 21st [proposition], if **g** exceeds **m**, then **k** exceeds **n**; and if it is less, it is less; and if equal, equal. Therefore, by the definition of discontinuous proportionality, the proportion of **a** to **e** is as **f** to **d**, which is what was proposed. ¶ This can also be demonstrated by the 15th [proposition] of this book, by taking **g**, **l**, **m** as equal multiples of **a**, **b**, **e**, and **k**, **h**, **n** as equal multiples of **f**, **c**, **d**; for by the 15th, **g** will be to **l** as **b** to **n**, and **l** to **m** as **k** to **h**, with the rest carried out as before. However, these and the preceding are more conveniently demonstrated according to the first method. ¶ If there are more than three quantities in each series, for instance four: by adding **p**, **r**, **q** so that **a** is to **b** as...

<note>The second diagram mirrors the first but arranges the labels to show the "cross-wise" relationship: the ratios in the second set are inverted or shuffled relative to the first, yet the relationship between the first and last magnitudes remains constant.</note>

Thus it is demonstrated for four quantities by means of three by removing one middle term. In the same way you will demonstrate it for five by means of four by removing two middle terms, and for six by means of five by removing three; and so on for the rest.

### Proposition 24.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram consisting of several horizontal line segments. The first line is composed of segments labeled 'a' (with the number 9) and 'b' (with the number 6). Next to it is a segment 'g' (10) followed by 'd' (6), 'e' (4), and 'h'. Below these are two smaller, separate lines labeled 'c' (3) and 'f' (2). This visualizes the ratios being added together.</image-desc>

If the proportion of the first to the second is as the third to the fourth, and the proportion of the fifth to the second is as the sixth to the fourth: the proportion of the first and fifth added together to the second will be as the sixth and third added together to the fourth.

¶ Just as the second proposition <note>referring to Euclid V.2</note> dealt with multiples, this one proposes a rule universally for all proportions. Hence, this rule is as much more common as the general concept of proportion is to the specific concept of multiplicity—much like the relationship of Proposition 13 to the first. Let the proportion of the whole **a**-**b** to **c** be as **d**-**e** is to **f**; and likewise **b**-**g** to **c** as **e**-**h** is to **f**. I say that the proportion of the whole **a**-**g** to **c** is as **d**-**h** is to **f**. For by inverse proportionality <note>original: "conuersam proportionalitatem"</note>, **c** will be to **b**-**g** as **f** is to **e**-**h**. Therefore, by Proposition 22, it will be in equal proportionality that **a**-**b** is to **b**-**g** as **d**-**e** is to **e**-**h**. Therefore, by addition <note>term: "coniunctim" (by addition), referring to Proposition 18, which allows the addition of terms in a ratio</note>, **a**-**g** is to **b**-**g** as **d**-**h** is to **e**-**h**. Thus, by Proposition 22, it will be in equal proportionality that **a**-**g** is to **c** as **d**-**h** is to **f**, which is what was to be shown.

### Proposition 25.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram with line segments. The top line shows a long segment divided into 'a' (8) and 'g' (4), with another segment 'b' or 'e' (4) nearby. Below are lines 'c' (4), 'h' (2), and 'f' (2). The numbers illustrate the rule that 8+2 > 4+4.</image-desc>

<margin>
If equals are added to equals.
</margin>

If there are proportional quantities, and the first of them is the greatest while the last is the least, it is necessarily proven that the first and last taken together are greater than the other two taken together.

¶ This proposition only holds true when all four quantities are of the same kind <note>i.e., they must all be lengths, or all areas, so they can be added together</note>. Let there be four quantities of the same kind in the proportion **a**-**b** to **c**-**d** as **e** is to **f**. Let **a**-**b** be the greatest. It is not necessary to assume that **f** is the least, because it follows from the fact that **a**-**b** was set as the greatest (hence the author did not put this in the conclusion as an assumption, but rather as a result of the preceding setup). I say that when it is so, the sum of **a**-**b** and **f** will be greater than the sum of **c**-**d** and **e**. Since **a**-**b** is greater than **e**, I shall cut off from **b**-**a** a segment **g**-**b** equal to **e**. ¶ Similarly, because **c**-**d** is greater than **f**, I shall cut off from **c**-**d** a segment **h**-**d** equal to **f**. By the hypothesis <note>original: "ypothefim"</note>, **a**-**b** will be to **c**-**d** as **g**-**b** is to **h**-**d**. Therefore, by Proposition 19, the remainder **a**-**g** is to the remainder **c**-**h** as the whole **a**-**b** is to the whole **c**-**d**. Since **a**-**b** is greater than **c**-**d**, it follows that **a**-**g** is greater than **c**-**h**. Therefore, if the two quantities **g**-**b** and **h**-**d** are added to both, it will be by common knowledge <note>original: "communem scientiam," referring to a common notion or axiom in geometry</note> that the sum of **a**-**b** and **h**-**d** is greater than the sum of **c**-**d** and **g**-**b**. And because **d**-**h** was set equal to **f**, and **g**-**b** to **e**, the sum of **a**-**b** and **f** will be greater than the sum of **c**-**d** and **e**, which is what was to be shown.

### Proposition 26.

If there are four quantities where the proportion of the first to the second is greater than that of the third to the fourth, the inverse will be the opposite: the proportion of the second to the first will be less than the fourth to the third. Let the proportion of **a** to **b** be greater than **c** to **d**. I say that in the inverse way, the proportion of **b** to **a** will be less than **d** to **c**. For if **b** to **a** were the same as **d** to **c**, it would...

But indeed if **b** to **a** is greater than **d** to **c**, let **e** be to **a** as **d** is to **c**. Therefore, by Proposition 12, the proportion of **b** to **a** is less than **d** to **c**, which is what we wanted [to prove].

### Proposition 27.

If there are four quantities where the proportion of the first to the second is greater than the third to the fourth, then by permutation <note>original: "p̄mutatim," also known as alternating the terms of the ratio</note> the proportion of the first to the third will be greater than the second to the fourth.
¶ Let here also the proportion of **a** to **b** be greater than **c** to **d**. I say that by permutation the proportion of **a** to **c** will be greater than **b** to **d**. For it will not be equal, because then by permutation **a** to **b** would be as **c** to **d**; nor will it be less. For if this is posited: let **e** be to **c** as **b** is to **d**. Then from Proposition 12, the proportion of **e** to **c** is greater than **a** to **c**, wherefore from the first part of Proposition 10, **e** is greater than **a**. Therefore, by the first part of Proposition 8, the proportion of **e** to **b** is greater than **a** to **b**. And because it was posited that **e** be to **c** as **b** is to **d**, it will be by permutation **e** to **b** as **c** to **d** from Proposition 12. Therefore the proportion of **c** to **d** will be greater than **a** to **b**, but the opposite was proposed. Therefore the proposition is true. ¶ The same can also be shown directly as in the previous one: for if **e** is taken to **b** as **c** is to **d**, from the first part of Proposition 10, **e** will be less than **a**. Wherefore from the first part of Proposition 8, **a** to **c** will be greater than **e** to **c**. But from permuted proportionality, **e** to **c** is as **b** to **d**; therefore from Proposition 12, **a** to **c** is greater than **b** to **d**, which is what was proposed.
