### Proposition 28.

<margin>
**a**, **b**, **b**, **e**, **d**, **d**, **a**, **b**, **b**.
<image-desc>Diagram for Proposition 28 illustrating the composition of ratios. It features two intersecting lines labeled with segments a, b, c, d and numerical values 12, 6, 4, and 3.</image-desc>
**e**, **d**, **e**, **b**, **a**, **b**.
</margin>

If there are four quantities where the proportion of the first to the second is greater than the third to the fourth, then also by composition <note>original: "coniunctim," adding the antecedent and the consequent together</note> the proportion of the first and second [added] to the second will be greater than the third and fourth [added] to the fourth.
¶ Let the proportion of **a** to **b** be greater than **c** to **d**. I say that the proportion of the whole **a**+**b** to **b** will be greater than the whole **c**+**d** to **d**. For it will be neither equal nor less. If it were equal, then by separation <note>original: "disiunctim," the inverse of composition</note> **a** to **b** would be as **c** to **d**. If however it is less: let **e**+**b** be to **b** as **c**+**d** is to **d**. Then from Proposition 12, the proportion of **e**+**b** to **b** is greater than **a**+**b** to **b**. Thus from the first part of Proposition 10, **e**+**b** is greater than **a**+**b**, and by common conception **e** is greater than **a**. Wherefore from the first part of Proposition 8, the proportion of **e** to **b** is greater than **a** to **b**. But **e** to **b** is as **c** to **d** by separated proportionality (because **e**+**b** was to **b** as **c**+**d** was to **d**). Therefore by Proposition 12, **c** to **d** is greater than **a** to **b**; but this is against the hypothesis. ¶ The same can also be shown directly: for since it is proposed that the proportion **a** to **b** is greater than **c** to **d**, let the proportion **e** to **b** be as **c** to **d**, then from the first part of Proposition 10, **e** will be less than **a**.

## Proposition 29.

<margin>c. d. d. e. b. b. ab. b.</margin>
<image-desc>A geometric diagram consisting of two horizontal lines. The upper line contains points labeled a, e, and b. The lower line contains points labeled c and d.</image-desc>
If there are four quantities such that the ratio of the first and second together to the second is greater than the ratio of the third and fourth together to the fourth, then by separation <note>original: "disiunctis," referring to the operation of subtracting the denominator from the numerator in a ratio</note>, the ratio of the first to the second will also be greater than the ratio of the third to the fourth.
¶ Let the proportion of **a.b.** to **b.** be greater than **c.d.** to **d.** I say that by separation, the proportion of **a.** to **b.** will be greater than **c.** to **d.** Otherwise, it would be equal or less. If it were equal, then by joined proportionality, **a.b.** would be to **b.** as **c.d.** is to **d.** If, however, it were less, then **c.** to **d.** would be greater than **a.** to **b.**; therefore, by the previous proposition, **c.d.** to **d.** would be greater than **a.b.** to **b.**, which is inconsistent, because it was posited as less. Therefore, what is said is true. ¶ We shall also establish this through direct proof <note>original: "ostensiue," a demonstration showing how the result follows directly from known truths rather than proving a contradiction</note> in this manner: we shall set the proportion of **e.b.** to **b.** to be the same as the proportion of **c.d.** to **d.** From the first part of Proposition 10, **e.b.** will be less than **a.b.** Wherefore, from common knowledge, **e.** is less than **a.** Therefore, from the first part of Proposition 8, the proportion of **e.** to **b.** is less than **a.** to **b.** But the proportion of **e.** to **b.** is as **c.** to **d.** from separated proportionality; thus, from Proposition 12, the proportion of **a.** to **b.** is greater than **c.** to **d.**, which is what was proposed.

If there are four quantities such that the ratio of the first and second to the second is greater than the ratio of the third and fourth to the fourth, then by conversion <note>original: "euersim," an operation where the ratio (a+b):b > (c+d):d becomes (a+b):a < (c+d):c</note>, the ratio of the first and second to the first will be less than the ratio of the third and fourth to the third.
¶ Let the proportion of **a.b.** to **b.** be greater than **c.d.** to **d.** I say that by conversion, the proportion of **a.b.** to **a.** will be less than **c.d.** to **c.** For by the previous proposition, the separated proportion of **a.** to **b.** will be greater than **c.** to **d.** Thus, by Proposition 26, the converse will be less, namely **b.** to **a.** is less than **d.** to **c.** Wherefore, by the proposition before the last <note>referring to Proposition 28</note>, the joined ratio of **b.a.** to **a.** will be less than **c.d.** to **c.**, which is what was proposed.

If there are three quantities in one order, and likewise three in another, and if the ratio of the second of the first [set] to the third is greater than the first of the second [set] to the second; and likewise the first of the first [set] to the second is greater than the second of the second [set] to the third; then the ratio of the first of the first [set] to the third will be greater than the first of the second [set] to the third.
¶ For let there be three quantities in one order, **a, b, c**. Likewise, let there be three in another, **d, e, f**, just as in the previous [proposition]. And let the ratio of **b** to **c** be greater than **d** to **e**, and the ratio of **a** to **b** be greater than **e** to **f**. I say that the ratio of **a** to **c** will be greater than **d** to **f**.
¶ For let **g** be to **c** as **d** is to **e**. Then **g** will be less than **b** by the first part of Proposition 10 <note>Proposition 10 of Book V states that if two ratios have the same denominator, the one with the larger numerator is the greater ratio</note>; wherefore the ratio of **a** to **g** will be greater than the ratio to **b** by the second part of Proposition 8. Therefore, the ratio of **a** to **g** is much greater than **e** to **f**. Let it be then that **h** is to **g** as **e** is to **f**. Then **a** will be greater than **h** from the first part of Proposition 10. Wherefore the ratio of **a** to **c** is greater than **h** to **c** from the first part of Proposition 8. But indeed, from Proposition 23, the ratio of **h** to **c** is as **d** to **f**, because **g** is to **c** as **d** is to **e**, and **h** is to **g** as **e** is to **f**. Therefore, from Proposition 12, the ratio of **a** to **c** is greater than **d** to **f**, which is what was proposed.

If the ratio of the whole to the whole is greater than the ratio of the part removed to the part removed, then the ratio of the remainder to the remainder will be a greater ratio than the whole to the whole.
¶ Let there be two quantities **a** and **b**, from which are cut off <note>original: "abscindantur," meaning to subtract or separate a segment</note> **c** and **d**, and the remainders are **e** and **f**. And let the ratio of **a** to **b** be greater than **c** to **d**. I say that the ratio of **e** to **f** will be greater than **a** to **b**. For from Proposition 27, by permutation <note>original: "permutatim," the operation of swapping the inner terms of a proportion (if a:b > c:d, then a:c > b:d)</note>, the ratio of **a** to **c** will be greater than **b** to **d**. Wherefore from Proposition 30, by eversion <note>original: "euersim," the operation of comparing the whole to the remainder (if a:c > b:d, then a:(a-c) < b:(b-d))</note>, the ratio of **a** to **e** will be less than **b** to **f**. **Similar figures** are said to be those whose angles in one are equal to the angles in the other, and the sides containing the equal angles are proportional.
As if triangle **a.b.c.** were equiangular to triangle **d.e.f.**, and angle **a** were equal to angle **d**, and angle **b** equal to angle **e**, and the ratio of **a.b.** to **d.e.** were as **a.c.** to **d.f.** and **z.b.c.** to **e.f.**; they themselves will be similar.

**Figures of reciprocal sides** <note>original: "mutuorum laterum," referring to reciprocal proportion in geometry</note> are those between whose sides a continuous proportionality is maintained in a reciprocal manner.
As if for two quadrilaterals **a.b.c.d.** and **e.f.**, the ratio of side **a.b.** of the first to side **d.c.** of the second were as the ratio of side **e.f.** of the second to side **b.c.** of the first, those two quadrilaterals are said to be of reciprocal sides or **mutekesia** <note>original: "mutekesia," a Latinized form of the Greek term for reciprocal proportion</note>. A line is said to be **divided according to a ratio having a mean and two extremes** <note>This refers to the "Golden Ratio"</note> when the ratio of the whole to its greater segment is the same as the ratio of the greater segment to the lesser.

->Proposition 1<-

If two rectilinear surfaces of parallel sides <note>parallelograms</note> or triangles have one [and the same] height: each of them will be to the other as its base is to the base of the other.
Let there be two parallelograms **a.b.c.d.** and **e.f.** of equal height. I say that their ratio is as **b.c.** to **e.f.** I will place those two parallelograms upon one line, which is **g.m.**; and because they are of equal height, they will be between parallel lines, of which the other is **k.n.** Then, from line **g.m.** I will take **g.c.** as a multiple of **b.c.** according to whatever number I wish, and I will divide it into equal parts **b.c.** at points **h, z, b**. From these bases and point **g**, I will draw lines parallel to line **a.b.**, which are **g.k, z.l, b**, and I will complete the parallelograms **k.h, z.l, b**. Each of these will be equal to **a.c.** by the 36th [proposition] of the first [book]. Therefore, just as line **g.c.** is a multiple of line **b.c.**, so surface **c.k.** is a multiple of surface **a.c.** Similarly, for line **e.f.**, I will take from line **g.m.** line **f.m.** as a multiple of **e.f.** according to whatever number I wish, and I will complete the parallelograms by drawing line **m.n.** parallel to line **d.e.** Surface **n.f.** will be the same multiple of surface **d.f.** as line **m.f.** is of line **e.f.** Because by the 36th [proposition] of the first [book], if line **g.c.** is greater than line **f.m.**, surface **k.c.** is greater than surface **n.f.**; and if it is less, it will be less; and if equal, it will be equal, by the definition of proportionality.

### Proposition 2.

**If a straight line cutting two sides of a triangle is parallel to the remaining side: it cuts those two sides proportionally. Conversely, if it cuts them proportionally, it must be parallel to the remaining side.**

Let there be a triangle **a.b.c.** whose two sides **a.b.** and **a.c.** are cut by line **d.e.** parallel to the third side, which is **b.c.** I say that the ratio of **a.d.** to **d.b.** will be as **a.e.** to **e.c.**; and conversely, if the ratio of **a.d.** to **d.b.** is as **a.e.** to **e.c.**, line **d.e.** will be parallel to line **b.c.** I shall draw two lines, **e.b.** and **d.c.** By the 37th [proposition] of the first [book] <note>Book I, Prop 37: Triangles on the same base and in the same parallels are equal to one another</note>, triangle **e.d.b.** will be equal to triangle **d.e.c.**, because they are both on the line **d.e.** between parallel lines. Therefore, by the second part of the 7th [proposition] of the fifth [book], the ratio of triangle **a.d.e.** to each of them will be the same. But by the previously mentioned [proposition] <note>Referring to Proposition 1 on this page</note>, the ratio of [triangle **a.d.e.**] to triangle **e.d.b.** is as line **a.d.** to line **d.b.**, and to triangle **d.e.c.** as line **a.e.** to line **e.c.** For the former [triangle **a.d.e.**] is of equal height with each of the others. Therefore, the ratio of **a.d.** to **d.b.** will be as **a.e.** to **e.c.**, which is the first [part]. And if this is the case, by the previous [proposition] the ratio of **a.d.e.** to each of them will be one and the same; therefore, by the second part of the 9th [proposition] of the fifth [book], they are equal to each other. And because they are on the same base—namely line **d.e.**—and on the same side, then by the 39th [proposition] of the first [book], line **d.e.** is parallel to line **b.c.**, which is the second [part].

### Proposition 3.

**If a straight line drawn from any angle of a triangle to the base bisects that angle: the two parts of the base will be proportional to the remaining sides of the same triangle. Conversely, if the two parts of the base which the line drawn from the angle divides are proportional to the remaining sides of the triangle, it is necessarily proved that the line divides the angle into equal parts.**

Let there be a triangle <term>trigonus<gloss>triangle</gloss></term> **a.b.c.** whose angle **a** is divided by line **a.d.** into equal parts. I say that the ratio of **b.d.** to **d.c.** is as **b.a.** to **a.c.** and vice versa. For I shall draw **b.e.** parallel to **a.d.** and extend **c.a.** until it meets **b.e.** at point **e.** By the first part of the 29th [proposition] of the first [book] <note>Book I, Prop 29: A straight line falling on parallel straight lines makes the alternate angles equal</note>, angle **e.b.a.** will be equal to angle **b.a.d.**, and by the second part of the same, angle **e.** is equal to angle **d.a.c.** Therefore, angle **e.** is equal to angle **e.b.a.** Thus, by the 6th [proposition] of the first [book] <note>Book I, Prop 6: If in a triangle two angles are equal, the sides opposite them are also equal</note>, **c.a.** is equal to **a.b.** <note>The text likely meant side **a.e.** is equal to **a.b.** based on the logic of the isosceles triangle formed</note>. And for that reason, by the first part of the 7th [proposition] of the fifth [book], the ratio of **c.a.** to **a.e.** is as **b.a.** to **a.c.** But by the previous [proposition], **e.a.** to **a.c.** is as **b.d.** to **d.c.** Therefore, **b.a.** to **a.c.** is as **b.d.** to **d.c.**, which is the first [part]. The second part, which is the converse of the first part, will be proved in the opposite way. For with the same arrangement remaining, if the ratio of **b.a.** to **a.c.** is as **b.d.** to **d.c.**—since by the previous [proposition] **e.a.** to **a.c.** is as **b.d.** to **d.c.**—then the ratio of **e.a.** to **a.c.** is the same as **b.a.** to **a.c.** Therefore, by the first part of the 9th [proposition] of the fifth [book], **e.a.** and **a.b.** are equal. Hence, by the 5th [proposition] of the first [book], the two angles **e.** and **e.b.a.** are equal. Therefore, by the first and second parts of the 29th [proposition] of the first [book], angle **b.a.d.** is equal to angle **d.a.c.**, which is the second [part].

### Proposition 4.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram illustrating Proposition 4. It features two separate triangles labeled a-b-c and d-e-f on the left. To their right is a larger, composite diagram where triangle d-e-f is placed upon triangle a-b-c along a common base line, and additional lines are drawn to create a parallelogram g-a-c-f with vertex g at the top right.</image-desc>

**In all** pairs of triangles whose angles are equal to the angles of the other: the sides opposite the equal angles are proportional.
¶ There are two triangles, **a.b.c.** and **d.e.f.**, which are equiangular <note>Having equal angles</note>. Let angle **a.** be equal to angle **d.**, and angle **b.** to angle **e.**, and angle **c.** to angle **f.** I say that the ratio of **d.e.** to **a.b.** and **d.f.** to **a.c.** is the same as **e.f.** to **b.c.** For I shall place both triangles upon one line which is **e.c.**, so that the two angles of one which will be upon this line are equal to the two of the other which will be upon the same [line]; not indeed the middle to the middle or the extreme to the extreme, but the middle of one to the extreme of the other. And I shall place two of their middle angles to meet at the same point. And let **a.f.c.** be that same triangle which was **a.b.c.** <note>The author is effectively "moving" triangle a.b.c. to a new position labeled a.f.c. to facilitate the proof</note>. And since angle **a.f.c.** is equal to angle **c.**, and angle **d.f.e.** to angle **c.** by the hypothesis <note>original: "ypothefiz"</note>: by the first part of the 28th [proposition] of the first [book] <note>Euclid I.28 states that if a line falling on two lines makes the exterior angle equal to the interior and opposite angle, the lines are parallel</note>, line **a.f.** will be parallel <note>original: "equidistans"</note> to **d.e.**, and **d.f.** parallel to **a.c.** I shall therefore complete the parallelogram <note>original: "superficiem equidistantium laterum," literally a "surface of equidistant sides"</note> which is **g.f.** By the 34th [proposition] of the first [book], **g.a.** will be equal to **d.f.**, and **g.d.** equal to **a.f.** Therefore, because by the second [proposition] of this [book], **g.a.** is to **a.c.** as **e.f.** is to **f.c.**, and by the same [proposition] **e.f.** is to **f.c.** as **e.d.** is to **d.g.**; it will be, by the 7th [proposition] of the fifth [book], that **d.f.** is to **a.c.**, and by the same, **e.d.** is to **f.a.** as **e.f.** is to **f.c.**, which is what was proposed.

### Proposition 5.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram for Proposition 5. It shows two separate triangles, a-b-c and d-e-f. Below triangle d-e-f, a third triangle g-e-f is constructed sharing the same base e-f, creating an overall quadrilateral shape d-e-g-f.</image-desc>

**In all** pairs of triangles where the ratio of all corresponding sides is the same, the angles contained by the proportional sides are proven to be equal to one another.
¶ This is the converse of the previous [proposition], nor did he [Euclid] make one conclusion from this and the preceding one, as he did in the second and third of this [book]: because they are demonstrated neither by the same configuration nor by the same means as the preceding. Let there be, then, two triangles **a.b.c.** and **d.e.f.**, and let the ratio of **a.b.** to **d.e.** and **a.c.** to **d.f.** be as **b.c.** to **e.f.** I say that angle **a.** is equal to angle **d.**, and angle **b.** to angle **e.**, and angle **c.** to angle **f.** I shall construct upon line **e.f.**, on the side opposite triangle **d.e.f.**, angle **f.e.g.** equal to angle **b.**, and angle **e.f.g.** equal to angle **c.** By the 32nd [proposition] of the first [book] <note>The sum of angles in a triangle is 180 degrees</note>, angle **g.** will be equal to angle **a.** Therefore, by the preceding [proposition], the ratio of **a.b.** to **e.g.** and **a.c.** to **f.g.** is as **b.c.** to **e.f.** Wherefore, **a.b.** is to **d.e.** as it is to **e.g.**, and **a.c.** to **d.f.** as it is to **f.g.** Therefore, by the second part of the ninth [proposition] of the fifth [book], **d.e.** is equal to **e.g.**, and by the same, **d.f.** is equal to **f.g.** Wherefore, by the 8th [proposition] of the first [book], the two triangles **d.e.f.** and **g.e.f.** are equiangular <note>This uses the SSS (Side-Side-Side) congruence theorem</note>. Therefore, since triangle **g.e.f.** is also equiangular to triangle **a.b.c.**, the proposition is established.

### Proposition 6.

**All** pairs of triangles that have one angle of the one equal to one angle of the other, and the sides containing those two equal angles are proportional to each other, are equiangular.
¶ So that the previous arrangement remains, let only angle **b.** be equal to angle **d.e.f.**, and the ratio of **a.b.** to **d.e.** be as **b.c.** to **e.f.** I say further that the two triangles **a.b.c.** and **d.e.f.** are equiangular. For since, by the 4th [proposition] of this [book], because of the hypotheses of the premise...

### Proposition 7.

If there are two triangles in which one angle of the one is equal to one angle of the other, and the sides about two of their remaining angles are proportional; and if, of the two remaining angles, each is either less than a right angle or neither is less than a right angle <note>original: "vterqʒ aut neuter recto angulo minor"</note>, it is necessary that those two triangles be equiangular to one another in all their angles.

<image-desc>
Two geometric diagrams placed in the right margin.
Top diagram: Two triangles, labeled a-b-c and d-e-f. In triangle a-b-c, a point g is marked on side a-b, and a line segment is drawn from g to vertex c, dividing the larger triangle into two.
Bottom diagram: A right-angled triangle labeled a-b-c, with a perpendicular line segment a-d dropped from the right-angle vertex a to the hypotenuse b-c.
</image-desc>

<margin>
Nevertheless, the final angles of both [are considered].
</margin>

Let there be two triangles **a.b.c.** and **d.e.f.**, and let angle **a.** be equal to angle **d.**, and let the proportion of **a.c.** to **d.f.** be as **c.b.** is to **f.e.** And let each of the two angles **b.** and **e.** be less than a right angle, or let neither be less. I say that they are equiangular. For if angle **c.** of the one is equal to angle **f.** of the other, the proposition is clear by the preceding [proposition]. But if **c.** be greater, let angle **a.c.g.** be made equal to it; then, by the 32nd [proposition] of the first [book], triangle **a.g.c.** will be equiangular to triangle **d.e.f.** Wherefore, by the fourth [proposition] of this [book], the ratio of **a.c.** to **d.f.** is as **g.c.** to **e.f.** But so also was **b.c.** to **e.f.** Therefore, by the 9th [proposition] of the fifth [book], **g.c.** and **b.c.** are equal. Thus, by the fifth [proposition] of the first [book], angle **b.** is equal to angle **b.g.c.** If, then, neither of the two angles **b.** and **e.** were less than a right angle, it would happen that two angles of one triangle are not less than two right angles <note>This is a geometric impossibility; the sum of any two angles in a triangle must be less than 180 degrees</note>, which cannot be, by the 32nd [proposition] of the first [book]. But if each were less than a right angle, then angle **a.g.c.** would be greater than a right angle by the 13th [proposition] of the first [book] <note>Because it is supplementary to angle b.g.c.</note>; wherefore angle **e.**, being equal to it, is also greater than a right angle, which is contrary to the hypothesis. Therefore, the opposite having been destroyed, the proposition remains. It is necessary, however, that both of the remaining angles, or neither, be less than a right angle. For it is possible in the same triangle, as in triangle **a.b.c.**, for the line **g.c.** to be equal to **b.c.**, and thus there will be one proportion of **a.c.** to each of them by the 7th [proposition] of the fifth [book]. Yet triangles **a.g.c.** and **a.b.c.** will not be equiangular, even though one angle of the one is equal to one angle of the other—indeed, the same angle, such as angle **a.**—and the proportion of line **a.c.** (as it is the side of the large triangle) to **a.c.** (as it is the side of the small triangle) is as side **b.c.** of the large triangle to side **g.c.** of the small triangle, for both are equal. This is because angle **g.** of the smaller triangle is greater than a right angle, and angle **b.** of the larger triangle is less. For in every triangle with two equal sides, each of the angles at the base is less than a right angle.

### Proposition 8.

If a perpendicular line is drawn from the right angle of a right-angled triangle to its base, it creates two partial triangles similar to the whole triangle and to each other. From this it is also clear that in every right-angled triangle, if a perpendicular is drawn from its right angle to the base, that perpendicular will be a mean proportional between the two sections of the base. Likewise, each side [of the triangle] is a mean proportional between the whole base and the segment of the base adjacent to it.
Let there be a right-angled triangle **a.b.c.** whose angle **a.** is a right angle, from which is drawn **a.d.**

### Proposition 9.
**Given two lines, to place a third between them in continuous proportionality.**

<margin>
<image-desc>A geometric construction within a semicircle on diameter ad. From a point b on the diameter, a perpendicular line be is drawn to the arc at point e. Lines ae and ed are drawn. Below the diameter, a separate line segment c is shown, equal in length to segment bd.</image-desc>

Let the two proposed lines be **a.b.** and **c.**, between which I wish to place one line in continuous proportionality <note>This construction finds the "mean proportional" (the geometric mean) between two lengths.</note>. I say that line **b.e.** is the one we seek. For I draw the lines **e.a.** and **e.d.**, and by the 30th [proposition] of the third [book], the total angle **e.** will be a right angle. Therefore, by the first part of the corollary of the previous [proposition], the proportion of **a.b.** is to **b.e.** as **b.e.** is to **b.d.**, which is what was proposed.

### Proposition 10.
**Given two lines, to append a third to them in continuous proportionality.**

<margin>
<image-desc>A triangle afe with a transversal line bd drawn parallel to the base fe. Points are labeled a (vertex), b and d (on the sides), and e and f (at the base). Below the figure is a small line segment labeled c.</image-desc>
</margin>
Let the two proposed lines be **a.b.** and **c.**, to which I wish to append a third in continuous proportionality <note>Finding a "third proportional" x such that a:b = b:x.</note>. I join line **c.** at an angle as it happens to line **a.b.**, and let **a.d.** be equal to it. I extend line **a.b.** to **e.** until **b.e.** is equal to **a.d.** Then, having drawn line **b.d.**, I lead a line from point **e.** parallel to it, and I extend line **a.d.** until they meet at point **f.** I say, therefore, that line **d.f.** is the one we seek. For by the second [proposition] of this [book], the proportion of **a.b.** to **b.e.** is as **a.d.** is to **d.f.** But **a.b.** to **b.e.** is as **a.b.** to **a.d.** by the second part of the 7th [proposition] of the fifth [book]; therefore, **a.b.** is to **a.d.** as **a.d.** is to **d.f.**, which is what was proposed. If, however, we wish to find a fourth line for three proposed lines, such that the ratio of the third to the fourth is as the first is to the second: from the first and second let one line be made, and let the third be joined at an angle to the whole composite; and from the common endpoint of the first and second, let a line be drawn to the end of the third; and from the other endpoint of the second, let a line be drawn parallel to this line, until it meets the third extended in a straight line. By the second [proposition] of this [book], the line which this parallel cuts off will be what is sought; just as if in this figure the first were **a.b.**, the second **b.e.**, and the third **a.d.**, the fourth would be **d.f.**

## Proposition 12.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing two lines meeting at point 'a'. Parallel lines connect points 'f' and 'b' on the lower line to points 'd' and 'e' on the upper line.</image-desc>

**Given two lines, one undivided and the other divided into parts: to divide the undivided line in the same manner as the divided one.**
¶ Let there be two lines which I shall join at an angle as it happens, **a.b.** and **a.c.** Let **a.b.** be divided into three or however many parts by the marked points **d.** and **e.** I wish to divide the line **a.c.** according to those same portions. When I have joined them at an angle, I will draw the line **b.c.** and the parallels **e.i.**, **d.f.**, and **e.g.** <note>The letters in the text and diagram labels sometimes vary slightly due to early printing conventions.</note> I say that these parallels divide the line **a.c.** into parts proportional to the parts of **a.b.** For I will draw **f.b.** parallel to **a.b.** which cuts **e.g.** at point **k.** By the second [proposition] of this book, the proportion of **g.f.** to **f.a.** will be as **e.d.** to **d.a.**, and **e.g.** to **g.f.** as **b.k.** to **k.f.** Therefore, it is also as **b.e.** to **e.d.** by the 34th [proposition] of the first [book] and the second part of the 7th of the fifth [book], which is what was proposed. It is necessary to repeat the second [proposition] of this book as many times as there are parts of the line **a.b.** minus one. But truly, [repeat] the 34th of the first and the 7th of the fifth minus two.

## Proposition 13.

**If two parallelograms <note>original: "superficies equidistantium laterum" — literally "surfaces of equidistant sides."</note> which have one angle of the one equal to one angle of the other are equal in area, then the sides containing the equal angles are reciprocally proportional <term>mutekesia | reciprocally proportional</term>. If indeed the sides containing the two equal angles are reciprocally proportional, it is necessary that the two surfaces be equal.**
¶ Let there be two parallelograms **a.b.c.d.** and **c.e.f.g.** which are equal. Let angle **c.** of one be equal to angle **c.** of the other. I say the proportion of **b.c.** to **c.g.** is as **e.c.** to **c.d.** And if the proportion of **b.c.** to **c.g.** is as **e.c.** to **c.d.**, provided the aforementioned angles are equal, I say those two parallelograms are equal. For I will join them at an angle, specifically angle **c.** of one with angle **c.** of the other, so that their two sides **b.c.** and **c.g.** form one straight line. Likewise, the two remaining sides **d.c.** and **c.e.** will form one line. Otherwise, it would contradict the present hypothesis—which is that angle **c.** of one equals angle **c.** of the other—and by the 15th [proposition] of the first [book] <note>Vertical angles are equal.</note>, a part would be equal to the whole. I will then complete the parallelogram by extending lines **a.d.** and **f.g.** until they meet at **h.** By the first part of the 7th [proposition] of the fifth [book], there will be one proportion of each surface **a.c.** and **c.f.** to the surface **c.h.** And because, by the first [proposition] of this book, the proportion of surface **a.c.** to surface **c.h.** is as line **b.c.** to line **c.g.**, and the proportion of surface **c.f.** to the same surface **c.h.** is as **e.c.** to **c.d.**, the first part of the proposed conclusion is manifest. The second part is also clear; for the first [proposition] of this book shows **b.c.** is to **c.g.** as **a.c.** is to **c.h.**, and **e.c.** to **c.d.** as **c.f.** is to the same **c.h.** Since it is proposed that the proportion of **b.c.** to **c.g.** is as **e.c.** to **c.d.**, there will be one proportion of both surfaces **a.c.** and **e.g.** to surface **c.h.** Therefore, by the first part of the 9th [proposition] of the fifth [book], **a.c.** is equal to **c.f.**, and thus the second part is clear.

## Proposition 14.

**If two triangles which have one angle of the one equal to one angle of the other are equal in area, the sides containing the equal angles will be reciprocally proportional. If indeed the sides containing the equal angles are reciprocally proportional, the two triangles are equal.**

## Proposition 15.

<image-desc>A diagram in the left margin illustrating Proposition 15. At the top, four horizontal line segments are labeled a, b, c, and d, with numerical values 8, 4, 4, and 2 respectively. Below these, a vertical geometric figure shows two rectangles joined. The top rectangle is labeled d on its right side and a on its bottom side; the bottom rectangle is labeled b on its top side and c on its right side, demonstrating that the product of the extremes (a and d) equals the product of the means (b and c).</image-desc>

**If there be four proportional lines, the rectangle contained under the first and the last shall be equal to that which is contained under the two remaining. If, however, the rectangle contained under the first and the last be equal to the rectangle contained under the two remaining, it is necessary that the four lines be proportional.**
¶ Let there be four proportional lines, **a.**, **b.**, **c.**, and **d.** Let the proportion of **a.** to **b.** be as **c.** to **d.** I say that the surface <note>original: "superficies" — meaning the area.</note> contained under **a.** and **d.** is equal to the surface contained under **b.** and **c.** And if the surface contained under **a.** and **d.** is equal to the surface contained under **b.** and **c.**, I say the proportion of **a.** to **b.** is as **c.** to **d.** For let the surfaces be formed, one contained under **a.** and **d.** and the other contained under **b.** and **c.** If, therefore, the proportion of **a.** to **b.** is as **c.** to **d.**, the sides of those surfaces will be reciprocal <note>original: "mutekesia" — a Latinization of a Greek term meaning reciprocal or mutually related in proportion.</note>. Furthermore, the angles contained by them are equal, because each is composed of right angles. Therefore, by the second part of the 13th [proposition] of this book, they are equal, which is the first [point]. ¶ The second [point] is clear by the first part of the same [proposition]. For if they are equal, because all their angles are right angles, their sides will be reciprocal. Therefore, the proportion of **a.** to **b.** is as **c.** to **d.**, which is the second [point].

## Proposition 16.

<image-desc>A diagram in the left margin illustrating Proposition 16. It shows three horizontal line segments labeled a, b, and c with numerical values 8, 4, and 2 respectively. Below these, a figure shows a rectangle with sides a and c, and a square with sides b, illustrating that the product of the first and third lines (a and c) equals the square of the second line (b).</image-desc>

**If there be three proportional lines, the rectangle contained under the first and third shall be equal to the square described by the second. If, however, the rectangle contained under the first and third be equal to the square produced by the second, those three lines shall be proportional.**
¶ Let the proportion of line **a.** to line **b.** be as line **b.** to line **c.** I say that the surface contained under **a.** and **c.** is equal to the square of **b.** And if the surface contained under **a.** and **c.** is equal to the square of **b.**, I say that the proportion of **a.** to **b.** is as **b.** to **c.** This, moreover, is evident through the preceding [proposition], by positing another line which is equal to **b.**, so that **b.** stands in the ratio of both the second and third [terms].

### Proposition 17.

<margin>d</margin>
If there are two similar triangles, the proportion of one to the other is as the duplicate proportion <note>A "duplicate proportion" refers to the square of a ratio. For example, if the ratio of the sides is 2:1, the ratio of the areas is the duplicate of that, which is 4:1.</note> of any of its sides to the corresponding side of the other. It is also manifest from this that for any three continuously proportional lines, the proportion of the first to the third will be the same as the proportion of the surface built upon the first to the surface built upon the second, provided it is similar in shape and construction. 
¶ Let there be two triangles, **a.b.c.** and **d.e.f.**, which are similar; therefore, by definition, they will be equiangular <term>equiangular</term><note>Figures are equiangular when all their corresponding angles are equal.</note> and have proportional sides. Let angle **a.** be equal to angle **d.**, angle **b.** to angle **e.**, and angle **c.** to angle **f.** Thus, the proportion of **a.b.** to **d.e.** and **a.c.** to **d.f.** is as **b.c.** to **e.f.** I say that the proportion of triangle **a.b.c.** to triangle **d.e.f.** is as the duplicate proportion of **b.c.** to **e.f.** For, following the teaching of the 11th [proposition] of this book, let a third line **c.g.** be joined to the two lines **b.c.** and **e.f.** in continuous proportionality; let it be drawn out or cut from **c.b.** depending on whether **c.g.** is larger or smaller, and let line **g.a.** be produced. Then, by the second part of the 14th [proposition] of this book, triangle **a.g.c.** will be equal to triangle **d.e.f.**, because the proportion of **a.c.** to **d.f.** is as **e.f.** to **c.g.** and angle **c.** is equal to angle **f.** Therefore, by the second part of the 7th [proposition] of the fifth [book], there will be one proportion of triangle **a.b.c.** to both of them. But by the first [proposition] of this book, the proportion of triangle **a.b.c.** to triangle **a.g.c.** is as **b.c.** to **g.c.** Truly, the proportion of **b.c.** to **c.g.** is as the duplicate proportion of **b.c.** to **e.f.** by the 10th definition of the fifth [book]. Thus, the proportion of triangle **a.b.c.** to triangle **d.e.f.** is as the duplicate proportion of **b.c.** to **d.f.** <note>The text likely means e.f. here to match the earlier logic.</note>, which is what was proposed. If, however, **c.g.** were equal to **b.c.**, then by the second part of the 14th [proposition] of this book, triangle **a.b.c.** would be equal to triangle **d.e.f.**; an equal proportion is composed of equal parts whether doubled, tripled, or taken any number of times. We can demonstrate this same property in the same way and through the same means for similar surfaces of equidistant sides <note>Parallelograms.</note> by simply using the 13th [proposition] of the present book instead of the 14th. However, he does not demonstrate it here because it is demonstrated universally for all similar surfaces in the following [proposition]. Therefore, through this conclusion, what is proposed universally about all similar surfaces is not yet clear except for triangles; but once the following is demonstrated, it will be clear for all. He placed it here and not in the following because it is a conclusion of this [logic] and not the next; for its truth is made manifest by the method of this demonstration, not by the method of that one.

### Proposition 18.

All similar multi-angled surfaces <term>multi-angled surfaces</term><note>A polygon, or any flat shape with many angles and sides.</note> are divisible into similar triangles equal in number. And the proportion of one of them to the other is as the duplicate proportion of any of its sides to the corresponding side of the other.
¶ Let there be, for example, two similar pentagons **a.b.c.d.e.** and **f.g.h.k.l.** I say that they are divisible into triangles similar and equal in number, and that the proportion of one of them to the other is as the duplicate proportion of **a.b.** to **f.g.** For let the lines **a.c.** and **a.d.** be drawn, and likewise **f.h.** and **f.k.** By the present hypothesis and by the 6th [proposition] of this book, triangle **a.b.c.** will be equiangular to triangle **f.g.h.**, and triangle **a.e.d.** to triangle **f.l.k.** Similarly also, by this common knowledge: "If you take away equals from equals, the remainders are equal," triangle **a.c.d.** will be equiangular to triangle **f.h.k.** For the pentagons themselves were set as equiangular and having proportional sides; and since the triangles into which they are divided are mutually equiangular, as has been proved, they will also be similar by the 4th [proposition] of this book and the definition of similar surfaces. Since they are equal in number, the first part is clear. ¶ The second part [is proved] thus: let **b.d.** be drawn, which cuts **a.c.** at point...

**U**pon a given line, to describe a figure similar to a given figure. <note>In modern editions of Euclid’s Elements, this is Book VI, Proposition 18.</note>

I also make angle **h.b.k.** by drawing line **h.k.** equal to angle **g.d.f.**, and angle **k.h.b.** by drawing line **b.e.** equal to angle **f.c.d.**, and angle **b.h.k.** by drawing line **h.k.** equal to angle **d.g.f.**, and angle **b.k.l.** by drawing line **k.l.** equal to angle **d.f.e.** Thus, the completed pentagon is that which was to be constructed upon line **a.b.** For it is equiangular <term>equiangulus</term><note>A figure where all corresponding angles match those of another figure.</note> to the given pentagon because of the equality of the angles of the triangles into which each is divided, and also the sides are proportional because of the proportionality of the sides of those triangles, which is clearly evident from the 4th proposition of this book. Therefore, by the definition of similar figures, the pentagon constructed upon line **a.b.** is similar to the given pentagon, which is what was proposed.

If there are any number of proportional lines and similar figures are constructed on pairs of them: those figures will also be proportional. Conversely, if similar figures constructed on pairs of lines are proportional: it is necessary that the lines themselves are proportional.
¶ Let there be four proportional lines **a, b, c,** and **d**. Let the proportion of **a** to **b** be as **c** is to **d**. I say that if similar figures are constructed on **a** and **b**, for example two similar pentagons, and other similar figures are constructed on **c** and **d**, for example two similar triangles: the proportion of the pentagons will be as the proportion of the triangles. Furthermore, if there are similar pentagons and likewise similar triangles, and the proportion of pentagon to pentagon is as triangle to triangle: I say that the proportion of **a** to **b** will be as **c** to **d**. For let there be added to lines **a** and **b** [a third line] **e**, and to lines **c** and **d** [a third line] **f**, in continued proportion <note>A continued proportion is a sequence like a:b = b:e</note>, just as the 10th [proposition] of this book teaches. By the 22nd [proposition] of the Fifth Book and by equal proportionality, **a** will be to **e** as **c** is to **f**. Since, therefore, by the corollary of the 17th [proposition] of this book, the proportion of the pentagons is as **a** to **e**, and the proportion of the triangles is as **c** to **f**, the proportion of the pentagons will be as the proportion of the triangles; and this is the first part. ¶ The second part is shown thus: Let there be two similar pentagons and two similar triangles, and let the proportion of the pentagons be as the proportion of the triangles. I say that the proportion of **a** to **b** is as **c** to **d**. For let **c** be to **g** as **a** is to **b**; how this is done was said above in the 10th [proposition] of this book. And upon **g**, let there be made (as the 19th [proposition] of this book teaches) a figure similar to that which is constructed on line **c**. By the previous premise, it will be similar to the one constructed on line **d**. Also, by the first part of this 21st [proposition], the proportion of pentagon **a** to pentagon **b** is the same as triangle **c** to triangle **g**. But the proportion was also the same as triangle **c** to triangle **d**. Therefore, by the second part of the 9th [proposition] of the Fifth Book, triangle **d** is equal to triangle **g**. And because they are similar, line **d** will be equal to line **g** by the first part of the 17th [proposition] of this book, since triangles are on lines **c, d,** and **g**; or by the second part of the 18th [proposition] when they are any other multi-angled figures. For equality is not produced from any duplicate or triplicate proportion (or however many times taken) except from an equal ratio. Therefore, **c** will be to **d** as **a** is to **b**, which is what was proposed.

### Proposition 23.

**I**f a partial parallelogram is marked off within the space of a larger parallelogram, being similar to the whole and sharing a common angle with it: it lies about the same <term>diagonal<note>original: "diameter"; in medieval Latin geometry, "diameter" was frequently used to refer to the diagonal of a four-sided figure.</note></term>.

¶ Let there be a partial parallelogram **f.g.** within the parallelogram **b.d.**, which is similar to it and shares the angle **c**. I say that the parallelogram **f.g.** lies about the diagonal of parallelogram **b.d.**, and this is the <term>converse<note>A logical statement where the hypothesis and conclusion are swapped.</note></term> of the preceding proposition. Let the line **a.e.c.** be extended; if this is the diagonal of parallelogram **b.d.**, the proposition is established. But if **a.b.c.** were its diagonal, and the lines **h.k.** are drawn parallel to **f.c.**, then by the previous proposition, parallelogram **f.k.** would be similar to parallelogram **b.d.** Therefore, by the conversion of the definition of similar surfaces, the proportion of **b.c.** to **k.c.** is as **d.c.** is to **f.c.** But by that same conversion of said definition, the proportion of **b.c.** to **g.c.** is as **d.c.** to **f.e.** <note>The transcription likely contains a minor scribal error here, as f.e. and f.c. refer to the corresponding sides in the ratio.</note> because parallelogram **f.g.** was stated to be similar to parallelogram **b.d.** Therefore, by the 11th proposition of the fifth book, the proportion of **b.c.** to **g.c.** is as **b.c.** is to **k.c.**, for each is as **d.c.** to **f.c.** Consequently, by the second part of the ninth proposition of the fifth book, **g.c.** is equal to **k.c.**—namely, the part being equal to the whole, which is impossible. Therefore, **a.e.c.** must be the diagonal of parallelogram **b.d.**, which is what was proposed.

### Proposition 24.

**O**f any two parallelograms <note>original: "superficierum equidistantium laterum"; literally "surfaces of equidistant sides."</note> in which one angle of one is equal to one angle of the other, the ratio of one to the other is <term>compounded<note>original: "p̄ducitur"; literally "produced from." In geometry, this means the ratio is the product of two other ratios.</note></term> of the two ratios of their sides containing the two equal angles.

¶ Let there be two parallelograms **a.c.** and **c.d.**, and let angle **b** of one be equal to angle **b** of the other. I say that the ratio of one to the other is compounded of the ratio of **a.b.** to **b.d.** and **c.b.** to **b.e.** I shall arrange these two surfaces exactly as I arranged them in the 13th proposition of this book, with the parallelogram **c.d.** added to each, and I will set the proportion of line **f** to line **g** to be as **a.b.** to **b.d.**, and **g** to **h** as **c.b.** to **b.e.** How this is done was stated above in the 10th proposition of this book. By the first proposition of this book and the 11th of the fifth book, **a.c.** is to **c.d.** as **f** is to **g**, and **c.d.** is to **d.e.** as **g** is to **h**. Therefore, by the 22nd of the fifth book, there will be an equal proportionality of **a.c.** to **d.e.** as **f** is to **h**. And because the ratio of **f** to **h** is compounded of **f** to **g** and **g** to **h**, as was said at the end of the exposition of the 11th definition of the fifth book, it follows that **a.c.** to **d.e.** is compounded of the same. Thus the proposition is established.

### Proposition 25.

**T**o construct a figure similar to one given surface and equal to another given surface.

¶ Let two rectilineal surfaces be given: **A**, a pentagon, and **B**, a hexagon. I wish to make one surface similar to **a** and equal to **b**. I resolve each of the given surfaces into triangles: **A** into triangles **c, a, d**; and **B** into triangles **e, b, f, g**. Upon the base of surface **a**, which is **b.k.**, I construct—according to the teaching of the 44th proposition of the first book—a rectangular parallelogram equal to **c**, which shall be **b.l.**; and **l.m.** equal to **a**, and **m.n.** equal to **d**, so that the whole parallelogram **b.n.**, constructed upon the base **b.k.**, is equal to the pentagon **a**. In the same way, upon the line **k.n.**, which is the second side of this surface, I construct another rectangular surface equal to the hexagon **b**, by making **k.o.** equal to **e**, and **o.p.** equal to **h**, and **p.q.** equal to **f**, and **q.r.** equal to **g**, so that the whole rectangular surface **n.r.** is equal to the hexagon.

...and I set, through the 9th proposition of this book, the line **s.t.** as a <term>mean proportional<note>A value that mediates between two others in a geometric progression; here, the line s.t. is the geometric mean of b.k. and k.r.</note></term> between line **b.k.** and line **k.r.** Upon it, according to the teaching of the 19th proposition of this book, I construct the surface **v.** similar to surface **a.** I say that this is the figure we seek and that it is equal to surface **b.** For since the three lines **b.k.**, **s.t.**, and **k.r.** are in continuous proportion, and similar surfaces—namely **a.** and **v.**—are constructed upon the first and second lines, it will be (by the 17th conclusion of this book) that **a.** is to **v.** as **b.k.** is to **k.r.** Therefore, by the first proposition of this book, it is as **b.n.** is to **n.r.**, and thus by the first part of the 7th proposition of the fifth book, it is as **a.** is to **n.r.** Because of this, by the second part of that same proposition, it is as **a.** is to **b.** It follows by the second part of the 9th proposition of the fifth book that **v.** is equal to **b.**, which is what was proposed. 

We can also easily prove this from permuted proportionality. Since **a.** is to **v.** as **b.n.** is to **n.r.**, it will be (by permutation) that **a.** is to **b.n.** as **v.** is to **n.r.** And because **a.** is equal to **b.n.**, **v.** will be equal to **n.r.**; therefore **v.** is also equal to **b.** by this <term>common notion<note>original: "communem scientiam"; referring to the Euclidean axiom that things equal to the same thing are equal to each other.</note></term>: things which are equal to one and the same thing are equal to each other. Furthermore, it is not necessary that the parallelograms **b.l.**, **i.m.**, and **m.n.** (which are equal to the triangles **c.**, **a.**, **d.**) or the surfaces **k.o.**, **o.p.**, **p.q.**, **z.q.**, **r.** (equal to triangles **e.**, **b.**, **f.**, **g.**) be rectangular. Rather, it is required that the external angle of surface **l.m.** be equal to the internal angle of surface **i.b.**, and the external of **m.n.** to the internal of **m.l.** Similarly, the external of surface **k.o.** must be equal to the internal of surface **b.n.**, and the external of **o.p.** to the internal of **k.o.**, and so on for the rest. For when it is so, each of the lines **k.n.** and its opposite **b.m.**, as well as **b.r.** and its opposite **n.q.**, will be a single line by the last part of the 29th proposition of the first book and by the 14th of the same—repeated as many times as necessary. This is because all the surfaces **b.l.**, **i.m.**, and **m.n.**, as well as **k.o.**, **o.p.**, **p.q.**, **z.q.**, and **r.**, have parallel sides, and the external angle of each following figure is equal to the internal angle of the preceding one. Therefore, the two surfaces **b.l.i.m.** and **n.r.** will be <term>parallelograms<note>original: "equidistantium laterum"; literally "of equidistant sides," the standard medieval term for parallelograms.</note></term> situated between parallel lines and of equal height. Therefore, argue the rest as before.

### Proposition 26.

**A** parallelogram described on half of a given line is greater than any [other] parallelogram applied to the same line which falls short of completing the line and consists of a figure similar to and standing upon the same <term>diagonal<note>original: "diametruz"; in this context, the diagonal of the parallelogram.</note></term> as the one placed on the half-line.

Let the given line be **a.b.**, upon whose half **c.b.** is constructed the parallelogram **c.d.** with diagonal **b.e.** Let there be applied to line **a.b.** the parallelogram **a.f.**, one side of which cuts **c.e.** at point **g.**, such that for the completion of the whole line **a.b.**, there is lacking the surface **f.b.**, which is similar to surface **c.d.** and stands about its diagonal. I say then that parallelogram **c.d.** is greater than parallelogram **a.f.** For by the first [proposition] of this book, **a.g.** is equal to **g.b.**, and by the 43rd of the first book, **c.f.** is equal to **f.d.** Therefore, by this common notion—if you add equals to equals, etc.—the <term>gnomon<note>The L-shaped remainder of a parallelogram after a smaller similar parallelogram has been removed from one of its corners.</note></term> consisting of the three parallelograms **c.f.**, **f.b.**, and **f.d.** will be equal to parallelogram **a.f.** Thus, parallelogram **c.d.** is greater than parallelogram **a.f.** by the parallelogram **e.f.**, which is what was proposed. The same will also be true if the surface **a.f.** were made taller than surface **c.d.**, as you can see in the second figure, in which also (by the first of this book) **a.g.** is equal to **g.b.**; thus, when the two supplements of surface **f.b.** are taken away from both, parallelogram **c.d.** will exceed parallelogram **a.f.** by parallelogram **f.e.**

### Proposition 27.

**F**or a given three-sided surface, to describe an equal parallelogram upon any assigned line, which falls short of completing the line by a figure similar to another given surface, provided that the parallelogram so constructed is not greater than the parallelogram placed upon half of the given line.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram in the upper left. At the top are a triangle labeled 'c' and a rectangle labeled 'd'. Below them is a larger rectangular construction with vertices and intersection points labeled: g, k, l, f across the top horizontal; b, e, m, a across the bottom horizontal; and n, p, o, h labeling points within the figure or on the right side. ¶ Let line **a.b.** be assigned, let triangle **c.** be given, and let parallelogram **d.** also be given. I wish to describe upon line **a.b.** a parallelogram equal to triangle **c.**, such that it falls short of completing the line **a.b.** by a parallelogram similar to **d.** This is conditioned on the requirement that triangle **c.** must not be larger than the parallelogram similar to **d.** when placed upon half of line **a.b.**; otherwise, the task would be impossible according to the previous proposition <note>This refers to Proposition 27, which establishes the maximum area for such constructions.</note>. I therefore divide line **a.b.** into equal halves at point **e.**, and following the teaching of the 19th proposition of this book, I construct upon its half **e.b.** a parallelogram **e.f.** similar to **d.**, and I will complete the parallelogram **b.g.** over the whole line **a.b.** Since triangle **c.** is not larger than parallelogram **e.f.**, but is either equal to it or smaller (as was stated), if it were equal, then parallelogram **e.g.** would be what is intended according to the 36th proposition of the first book, supported by the first part of the 9th and the 1st definition of similar surfaces in the 7th and 20th propositions of this book. However, if it is smaller, let it be smaller by some surface area to which a similar and equal figure **d.** is made according to the 25th proposition of this book, which shall be **b.**; and **b.** will be similar to **e.f.** by the 20th proposition of this book. Therefore, by the conversion of the definition of <term>equiangular<note>Having all angles equal.</note></term> figures and proportional sides, I will draw the diagonal **b.k.** within parallelogram **e.f.**, and I will mark off the sides **k.f.** and **e.k.** of the surface **e.f.** to the measure of the sides of surface **b.** By drawing lines **l.m.** and **n.o.** parallel to the sides of surface **e.f.** and intersecting at point **p.**, the surface **k.p.** will be equal and similar to surface **b.** By the 23rd proposition of this book, point **p.** will lie on the diagonal **k.b.** Having extended **o.n.** all the way to **a.g.**, I declare that parallelogram **a.p.** is what was proposed. For it falls short of completing the line **a.b.** by the parallelogram **p.b.**, which (by the 22nd and 20th propositions of this book) is similar to parallelogram **d.** Furthermore, parallelogram **a.p.** is equal to triangle **c.** For by the first proposition of this book, **a.n.** is equal to **n.b.**; therefore, by the 43rd proposition of the first book and this <term>common notion<note>original: "communem scientiam"; referring to the Euclidean axiom: "If equals be added to equals, the wholes are equal."</note></term>—if you add equals to equals, etc.—the parallelogram **a.p.** is equal to the <term>gnomon<note>An L-shaped figure remaining after a smaller similar parallelogram is removed from a corner of a larger one.</note></term> **n.b.l.** And because this gnomon is equal to triangle **c.** (owing to the fact that parallelogram **e.f.** was set to be greater than triangle **c.** by the parallelogram **b.**, which is equal to parallelogram **k.p.**), the proposal is clearly demonstrated.

## Proposition 28
<note>Although labeled "Proposition 28" in the manuscript, the text following describes the construction for Proposition 29, which deals with an "excess" rather than a "deficiency."</note>

<image-desc>A geometric diagram associated with Proposition 28 (which contains the text of Proposition 29). Above are triangle 'c' and rectangle 'd'. The main figure is a complex arrangement of rectangles on a baseline with points g, e, a, f, l. Points n and m are located on vertical lines above e and f respectively, meeting internal intersection b. Points k and h mark the highest horizontal level.</image-desc>

> **To construct** a parallelogram equal to a given three-sided surface [a triangle] upon a given line, which adds onto the completion of the given line a parallelogram similar to a given parallelogram.

As before, let the given line be **a.b.**, the given triangle **c.**, and the given parallelogram **d.** I wish to construct upon line **a.b.** a parallelogram equal to triangle **c.**, which exceeds the total line **a.b.** by a parallelogram similar to **d.** I divide line **a.b.** into two equal parts at point **e.**, and upon its half **e.b.**, I make **e.f.** similar to **d.** as the 19th proposition of this book teaches. Then, according to the teaching of the 25th proposition, I create **k.l.** (with diagonal **g.b.**) similar to **d.** and equal to the two surfaces **e.f.** and **c.** combined. By the 20th proposition of this book, **k.l.** will be similar to **e.f.** Thus, if surface **k.l.** is placed upon surface **e.f.** so that they share angle **g.**, then by the 23rd proposition, surface **e.f.** will lie around the diagonal of surface **k.l.**; therefore point **b.** is on the diagonal **g.h.** I will then complete the parallelogram **a.b.**, and I say it is what was proposed. This is evident once the lines **f.b.** (extended to **m.**) and **e.b.** (extended to **n.**) are drawn. For by the first part of this work, **a.k.** is equal to **k.b.**, and therefore by the 43rd of the first book, it is also equal to **n.f.** When **e.b.** is added to both, it will be (by the common notion) that **a.b.** is equal to the gnomon **e.b.f.** But this gnomon is equal to triangle **c.**, because parallelogram **k.l.** was set equal to the two surfaces **c.** and **e.f.** combined. Therefore, parallelogram **a.b.** is equal to **c.**, and it adds to the completion of line **a.b.** the parallelogram **m.n.**, which by the 22nd and 20th propositions of this book is similar to parallelogram **d.** Thus, it is clear that what was sought has been accomplished.

...we wish. We are also able to attach to a given line a parallelogram equal not only to a given triangular surface, but also to any proposed rectilinear figure, whatever it may be, which falls short of completing the given line by a surface similar to a proposed parallelogram; just as the preceding proposition teaches, provided the observed condition is met so that one does not labor toward the impossible according to the proposition before that. How this may be done, if you wish to know, look to the 25th proposition of this book. To this triangle, therefore, if you attach an equal parallelogram to the given line—which either adds to the completion of the line or subtracts a parallelogram similar to the given parallelogram according to what this and the preceding proposition teach—you should not doubt that you have perfected what was proposed.

## Proposition .29.

<image-desc>Geometric diagram showing a triangle with its base resting upon the top edge of a rectangle.</image-desc>

To cut any proposed line according to the ratio having a mean and two extremes. <note>This is the classical definition of the Golden Ratio, where the whole line is to the larger segment as the larger segment is to the smaller.</note>

<image-desc>Geometric diagram of a large square divided into internal sections. A smaller square in the top left is labeled 'a d' and a rectangle in the bottom right is labeled 'e b'. Vertices and intersection points are labeled a, b, c, d, e, and f.</image-desc>

Let **a. b.** be the proposed line which I wish to divide according to the ratio having a mean and two extremes. From it, I describe a square **b. c.**, and to its side **a. c.**, I attach (following what the preceding proposition teaches) a parallelogram **c. d.** equal to square **b. c.**, such that it adds to the completion of line **a. c.** a parallelogram **a. d.** which is similar to **b. c.** Let the side of parallelogram **c. d.** that is equidistant to **a. c.** be **d. e.**, and let it cut line **a. b.** at point **f.** I say that line **a. b.** is divided at point **f.** just as is proposed. For **a. d.** is a square because it is similar to **b. c.**; therefore **a. f.** is equal to **f. d.** But also **f. e.** is equal to **a. b.** because it is equal to **a. c.** by the 34th proposition of the first book. And because **c. d.** is equal to **b. c.**, when **c. f.** is taken away from both, **a. d.** will be equal to **e. b.**, and the angle **f.** of one is equal to the angle **f.** of the other. Therefore, by the 13th proposition of this book, the sides are reciprocally proportional <note>original: "mutekefia", a medieval term derived from Arabic translations of Euclid meaning "reciprocally proportional".</note>; therefore **e. f.** is to **f. d.** as **a. f.** is to **f. b.** And since **e. f.** is equal to **a. b.** and **f. d.** is equal to **a. f.**, it will be that **a. b.** is to **a. f.** as **a. f.** is to **f. b.** Therefore, by the definition, it is divided as proposed. The same can also be demonstrated from the 11th proposition of the second book: for let **a. b.** be divided at point **f.** according to what the 11th of the second book teaches; and let **e. b.** be that which is contained under the whole **a. b.** and its part **f. b.**, so that **f. e.** is equal to **a. b.**, and **a. d.** is the square of **a. f.** Thus, by the aforesaid 11th of the second book, **e. b.** is equal to **a. d.**, which remains to be argued as before through the 13th proposition of this book. Or thus: since **a. b.** is divided at point **f.** according to the 11th of the second book, that which is produced from the first, **a. b.**, multiplied by the third, **f. b.**, is equal to the square of the second, **a. f.** Therefore, by the second part of the 16th proposition of this book, the proportion of the first, **a. b.**, to the second, **a. f.**, is as the second, **a. f.**, to the third, **f. b.** Therefore, by the definition, **a. b.** is divided as proposed.

### Proposition 31

In every right-angled triangle, the area of the figure described on the side subtending the right angle <note>The "side subtending the right angle" is the hypotenuse.</note> is equal to the areas of the figures described on the two sides containing the right angle, when they are similar to it in form and construction.

Where the penultimate proposition of the first book <note>Referring to Proposition 47 of Book I, commonly known as the Pythagorean Theorem.</note> proposed this concerning square areas, this penultimate proposition of the sixth book proposes it for all similar figures. Hence, this version is more universal, as it applies to any many-sided figure as well as a square. Therefore, let there be a right-angled triangle *abc*, in which angle *a* is the right angle. I say that the figure constructed upon the side *bc* is equal to the two figures constructed upon sides *ab* and *ac*, provided all three figures are similar in shape and orientation. I shall draw a perpendicular line *ad* to the line *bc*. By the second part of the corollary to the 8th proposition of this book, the ratio of *bc* to *ca* is as *ca* to *dc*; and the ratio of *cb* to *ba* is as *ba* to *db*. 

If, therefore, upon each of the three lines *bc*, *ca*, and *ab*, a figure is made that is similar to the others in shape and orientation, it will be (by the corollary to the 17th proposition of this book) that the ratio of the first figure (constructed on *bc*) to the second figure (constructed on *ca*) is as the first line *bc* is to the third line *dc*. Likewise, the ratio of the same first figure (constructed on *bc*) to the second figure (on *ab*) is as the first line *bc* is to the third line *db*, by the same corollary. Therefore, by inverse proportionality, the ratio of the figure on *ac* to the figure on *cb* is as *cd* to *cb*; and similarly, the ratio of the figure on *ab* to the figure on *bc* is as *bd* to the figure on *bc*. 

Let the figure on *ac* be the first, the figure on *cb* be the second and fourth, the figure on *cd* be the third, the figure on *ab* be the fifth, and the figure on *bd* be the sixth. Then, by the 24th proposition of the fifth book, let it be argued that the ratio of the figure constructed on *bc* to the two figures constructed on *ca* and *ab* together is as *bc* is to *cd* and *db* together. Since *bc* is equal to the two lines *cd* and *db* taken together, the figure constructed on *bc* must be equal to the two figures constructed on *ca* and *ab* taken together, which is what was proposed. 

We can also easily demonstrate the converse of this by the method used in the final proof of the first book. Let there be a triangle *abc*, and let the figure constructed on *bc* be equal to the two figures constructed on the two lines *ab* and *ac* which are similar to it. I say that angle *a* is a right angle. For I shall set angle *cad* as a right angle, and make line *ad* equal to *ab*, and close the figure by drawing line *dc*. By this 31st proposition, the figure constructed on *cd* will be equal to the two figures constructed on the two lines *ca* and *ad* which are similar to it. Since the figure on *bc* was also set as equal to the two figures constructed on *ab* and *ac*, line *bc* must be equal to line *cd*. Therefore, by the 8th proposition of the first book, angle *a* is a right angle, which is what was proposed.

If in equal circles angles stand upon the center or upon the circumference, the ratio of the angles will be as the ratio of the arcs that support those angles.

I say that the ratio of the angles, both those which are at the centers...

...of those which are upon the circumferences: it is as arc *b-c* is to arc *f-g*. For I will add to those two arcs other equal arcs, either according to the same number or according to different numbers; let arc *k-b* be equal to *b-c*, and let each of the two arcs *l-m* and *f-l* be equal to *f-g*. I will then draw lines *k-d*, *k-a*, *m-b*, *l-b*, *m-c*, and *l-c*. By the 26th proposition of the third book, the angles which are at *d* <note>The angles at the circumference.</note> will be equal to each other. Likewise, those at *b* <note>The angles at the center.</note> are also equal to each other. The same applies to those at *a* and those at *e*. Therefore, just as arc *k-c* is a multiple of arc *b-c*, so angle *k-d-c* is a multiple of angle *b-d-c*, and angle *k-a-c* is a multiple of angle *b-a-c*. But if arc *k-c* is equal to arc *m-g*, angle *k-d-c* is equal to angle *m-b-g*, and angle *k-a-c* is equal to angle *m-e-g*. If it is greater, they are greater; and if it is lesser, they are lesser, by the 26th proposition of the third book. Therefore, by the definition of <term>proportionality</term><note>The author refers to the definition of proportionality through multiples, famously established by Eudoxus in Book V.</note>, the ratio of arc *b-c* to arc *f-g* is as the ratio of angle *b-d-c* to angle *f-b-g*, and as the ratio of angle *b-a-c* to angle *f-e-g*; which is what was proposed. Understand the same to hold within a single circle.

<image-desc>A large decorative drop cap 'U' featuring elaborate foliate and floral patterns within a square frame. The letter itself is composed of stylized ribbons or leaves.</image-desc>

**Unit** <note>original: "Unitas"</note> is that by which each thing is said to be one.
**Number** is a multitude composed of units. A **Natural** series of numbers is said to be that in which their counting occurs according to the addition of a unit. The **Difference** of numbers is the name given to the number by which the greater exceeds the lesser. A **Prime** number <note>original: "Numerus primus"</note> is said to be that which is measured <note>meaning "divisible"</note> by unity alone. A **Composite** number is said to be that which another number measures. Numbers are said to be **prime to each other** when they are measured by no number except unity alone. Numbers are called **composite to each other** or **communicating** when a number other than unity measures them, and none of them is prime to the other.
A **Number** is said to be **multiplied** by another when it is added to itself as many times as there are units in the multiplier. The **Product** <note>original: "Productus"</note> is said to be that which grows from their multiplication. A **Number** is said to **measure** another when, being multiplied according to some number, it produces it. A **Part** is a number of a number, the lesser of the greater, when the lesser measures the greater. And that which is measured is called the **multiple** of the measuring number. The **Denominator** is the number according to which a part is taken in its whole. **Similar** parts are said to be those which are named by the same number. The **first** and simplest part of a number is unity. **When** two numbers have a common part, the lesser is said to be so many parts of the greater as that same part is contained in the lesser, and the greater as many as the part is in the greater. The **ratio** of a number to a number is said to be of the lesser to the greater in that it is a part or parts of the greater; and of the **greater** to the lesser according to how it contains it and its part or parts. **When** any number of numbers are in **continued proportion**, the ratio of the first to the third is said to be as the duplicate <note>the square</note> of the first, and to the fourth as the triplicate <note>the cube</note>. **When** the same or different ratios are continued, the ratio of the first to the last is said to be **composed** of all of them.

Therefore, it can be demonstrated that those wishing to save Aristotle <note>A common medieval practice of reconciling Euclidean geometry with Aristotelian physics.</note> <unclear>not [at the] weight [of] Christory</unclear> certain rules concerning the ratio of the force of local motion? <insert>The ratio of the first to the last is as the ratio of the first to the middle and the middle to the last. <note>original: "proportio p[ri]mi ad extrẽmū[m] est sicut p[ri]mi ad mediū et mediij ad extrẽmū[m]"</note></insert>

¶ The **denomination** <note>The "denomination" refers to the numerical value of a ratio, often expressed as a fraction or a whole number.</note> of a ratio of a smaller number to a larger is called the part or parts of the smaller which are contained within the larger. ¶ Of a larger number to a smaller, it is called the whole, or the whole and a part or parts, according to how much the larger exceeds the smaller. ¶ **Similar** or the same ratios are those which receive the same denomination. ¶ A **Greater** ratio is that which receives a greater denomination. ¶ A **Lesser** ratio is that which receives a lesser one. ¶ Numbers whose ratio is the same are called **proportional**. ¶ **Terms** (or "roots") are those numbers for which it is impossible to find smaller numbers in the same ratio. ¶ There are four **Postulates**: ¶ That for any number, as many equals as one wishes may be taken, or as many multiples. ¶ That for any number, one can take another as much larger as one wishes. ¶ That the series of numbers can proceed toward infinity. ¶ That no number can be diminished into infinity <note>Meaning there is a smallest unit, the "one," and you cannot divide whole numbers indefinitely as you can with geometric lines.</note>. ¶ There are ten **Common Notions**: ¶ Every part is smaller than its whole. ¶ Those which are equal multiples of the same or of equals are themselves equal. ¶ Numbers of which the same number is an equal multiple, or those whose equal multiples are equal, are also themselves equal. ¶ A part of every number is the unit <note>the number 1</note> named by that number. ¶ Every part is smaller when it has a larger denomination, and larger when it has a smaller one. <note>This is an early way of explaining that 1/10 is smaller than 1/2.</note> ¶ Every whole number is made of units, and the unit is a part of it. ¶ Any number multiplied by the unit produces itself; likewise, the unit multiplied by any number produces that same number. ¶ Any number that **measures** <term>measures</term><note>In Greek mathematics, a number "measures" another if it divides into it exactly with no remainder (e.g., 3 measures 9).</note> two numbers also measures the sum composed of them. ¶ Any number that measures another also measures every number measured by that one. ¶ Any number that measures the whole and a part taken away also measures the remainder.

## Proposition I

<margin>
<image-desc>Two geometric diagrams stacked vertically. The upper diagram depicts a horizontal arc divided into segments labeled 35, 39, and 4, with points marked a, b, c, d, e, and g. The lower diagram shows a line segment h with two tangent arcs labeled 4, 7, 3, and f.</image-desc>
</margin>

If, of two unequal numbers, the smaller is subtracted from the larger until a remainder less than itself is left, and then that remainder is subtracted from the smaller until a remainder less than it is left, and if this process of continual subtraction continues and no remainder is found that measures the previous one until the unit <note>the number 1</note> is reached, then those two numbers are **prime to one another**.

Let there be two numbers, *a-b* and *c-d*, and let *c-d* be the smaller. Let *c-d* be subtracted from *a-b* as many times as possible, leaving a remainder *e-b* which is smaller than *c-d* (otherwise it could be subtracted again). Then let *e-b* be subtracted from *c-d* as many times as possible, leaving a remainder *f-d*. Then let *f-d* be subtracted from *e-b* as many times as possible; and if the final remainder *g-b* is the unit, I say then that the two numbers *a-b* and *c-d* are prime to each other. For if they were composite <note>not prime</note>, some number other than the unit (let it be *h*) would measure them both. Since *h* measures *c-d*, it must measure *a-e* (by the second to last common notion); and since it measures the whole *a-b*, it must also measure the remainder *e-b* (by the last common notion). Therefore, it would also measure *c-f*, and consequently *f-d*, then *g-c*, and finally *g-b*. But since *g-b* is the unit, it would follow that a number measures the unit or is equal to it, which is impossible. Therefore, *a-b* and *c-d* are prime to each other, which is what was proposed. Conversely, if two numbers are prime to each other, this mutual subtraction will not stop until it reaches the unit.
