If there should be a stopping point in the subtraction before reaching unity: let number $g. b.$ be the number which is subtracted from $f. d.$ and let nothing remain. Therefore, $g. b.$ measures $f. d.$ <note>In Greek and Latin mathematics, one number "measures" another if it divides into it exactly with no remainder. Today we say $g. b.$ is a factor of $f. d.$</note> Therefore, by the penultimate common notion, <note>Euclid relies on "Common Notions" or axioms. The "penultimate" one referred to here likely means: "If a number measures two numbers, it will also measure their difference."</note> it measures $z. c. g.$ <note>original: "z. c. g."</note> and because it also measures itself, it will measure the whole $e. b.$ by the antepenultimate common notion. <note>The antepenultimate (third to last) common notion: "If a number measures two numbers, it will also measure their sum."</note> Therefore, by the penultimate notion, it measures $c. f.$ But it was shown before that it measures $f. d.$ Therefore, by the antepenultimate notion, it measures the whole $c. d.$ Wherefore, by the penultimate notion, it measures $a. e.$ and since it was shown before that it also measures $e. b.$, it follows by the antepenultimate notion that it measures numbers $a. b.$ and $c. d.$ The numbers $a. b.$ and $c. d.$ are therefore composite; <note>original: "compositi"</note> thus they are not prime to each other, which is against the hypothesis. ¶ By this path, therefore, given any two numbers, we investigate whether they are prime to each other. For if, by such a mutual subtraction being made, they arrive at unity, they are prime to each other. If, however, there is a stopping point before they arrive at unity, they are composite.

### ¶ Proposition 2

<image-desc>To the right of Proposition 2 are three horizontal line segments representing numbers. The top segment is marked with points 'a', 'e', and 'b'. The middle segment is marked 'c', 'f', and 'd'. The bottom, shortest segment is labeled 'g'. These represent the lengths of numbers being compared and subtracted.</image-desc>

**Given two numbers composite to each other, to find the greatest common number measuring them.** ¶ It is manifest that every number measuring two numbers also measures the greatest number measuring both of them. ¶ Let there be two composite numbers $a. b.$ and $c. d.$, where $c. d.$ is the smaller: since some number measures them commonly by definition, I wish to find the greatest number commonly measuring them. Following the manner and likeness of the previous [proposition]: I subtract the smaller from the larger as many times as I can, namely $c. d.$ from $a. b.$, and let the remainder be $e. b.$ Likewise, I subtract $e. b.$ from $c. d.$ as many times as I can, and let the remainder be $f. d.$ And because this lessening cannot be done infinitely by the final postulate, <note>This refers to the "Axiom of Archimedes" or the principle that whole numbers cannot be divided infinitely; you must eventually hit a remainder or zero.</note> nor can it arrive at unity in this case by the preceding [proposition] (because then the given numbers would be prime to each other, which is against the hypothesis), let it be that when I have subtracted $f. d.$ from $e. b.$ as many times as I can, nothing remains. I say then that $f. d.$ is the greatest number measuring $a. b.$ and $c. d.$ For that it measures them is clear through the penultimate and antepenultimate common notions, alternating as many times as it is necessary to repeat them, just as in the proof of the converse of the preceding [proposition]. For $f. d.$ measures $e. b.$ because when it is subtracted from it as many times as possible, nothing remains; therefore it also measures $c. f.$ by the penultimate notion, and thus $c. d.$ by the antepenultimate. Wherefore it also measures $a. e.$ by the penultimate notion, and therefore $a. b.$ by the antepenultimate. That no number greater than $f. d.$ measures $a. b.$ and $c. d.$ is shown thus: If it were possible, let there be a number $g$ greater than $f. d.$ measuring both of the two numbers $a. b.$ and $c. d.$ Since $g$ measures $c. d.$, it will measure $a. e.$ by the penultimate notion; and since it measures $a. b.$, it will measure $e. b.$ by the last [notion]. Therefore, it measures $c. f.$ by the penultimate notion, and because it also measures $c. d.$, it will measure $f. d.$ by the last—namely, a greater number measures a smaller, which is impossible. From this second process the conclusion is clear.

If $d$ measures $c$, then $a, b, c$ will be composite to each other by definition. If, however, it does not measure it, but $c$ and $d$ are themselves prime to each other, then $a, b, c$ will not be composite to each other. For whatever measured them would measure...

From the final step of this demonstration, we can also add this corollary to this third conclusion: whence it is manifest that every number measuring any number of mutually composite numbers also measures the greatest common divisor of them all, and also the greatest common divisors of them taken two by two.

### ¶ Proposition 4

<image-desc>A marginal diagram showing two horizontal line segments. The upper segment is longer and labeled 'a'; the lower segment is shorter and labeled 'b'.</image-desc>

**Of** any two unequal numbers, the smaller is either a part or parts of the larger.
¶ Let there be two numbers, $a$ and $b$, with $b$ being the smaller. I say that $b$ is either a part or parts of $a$. Either $b$ measures $a$ or it does not. If it measures it, it is a "part" of it by definition. <note>In Euclidean geometry, a "part" refers to a unit fraction like 1/3, whereas "parts" refers to a non-unit fraction like 2/3.</note> If it does not measure it, then they are either relatively prime to each other or they are not. If they are not relatively prime, they will have, by definition, a common part; however many times this part is contained in $b$, $b$ is said to be that many "parts" of $a$ by definition. If, however, they are relatively prime, since the unit <note>original: "unitas"; the number 1.</note> is a part of every number named by that number, the same is evident through the units.

# Proposition 6

**If** there be four numbers of which the first is the same parts of the second as the third is of the fourth: the first and third taken together will be the same parts of the second and fourth taken together as the first is of the second.

What he proposed in the preceding [proposition] concerning a "part" <note>In this context, a "part" refers to a unit fraction, like 1/3 or 1/10.</note>, he now proposes concerning "parts" <note>In this context, "parts" refers to proper fractions that are not unit fractions, such as 2/3 or 3/10.</note>. Let there be, therefore, as before, four numbers $a, b, c, d$. And let $b$ be as many parts of $a$ as $d$ is of $c$. I say that $b$ and $d$ taken together will be the same parts of $a$ and $c$ taken together as $b$ is of $a$. I say "as many parts": because a plurality [of parts] is defined by two numbers, of which one is called the numerator and the other the denominator; as when we say "three fifths," three numerates and five denominates. Because, therefore, $b$ is parts of $a$, let it be that those parts are numbered by $b$ and denominated by $k$ <note>The author is using these letters to represent the ratio; $k$ represents the size of the unit fraction and $b$ represents how many of them there are.</note>. Likewise, by the setup, $d$ will be parts of $c$ numbered by $b$ and denominated by $k$. Let one of the parts of $b$ be $e$, and one of the parts of $d$ be $f$. By the hypothesis, $e$ will be a part of $b$ denominated by $b$ and a part of $a$ denominated by $k$. Similarly, $f$ will be a part of $d$ according to $b$ and a part of $c$ according to $k$. Therefore, let the sum of $e$ and $f$ be $g$. By the preceding proposition, $g$ will be a part of $b$ and $d$ taken together according to $b$; likewise by the same proposition, it will be a part of $a$ and $c$ taken together according to $k$. Wherefore, by the 16th definition, $b$ and $d$ taken together will be parts of $a$ and $c$ taken together, numbered by $b$ and denominated by $k$, because their common part is $g$, which is the part of the smaller according to $b$ and of the larger according to $k$. And because $b$ was related to $a$ in this same way, the proposition stands.

<image-desc>A geometric/numerical diagram with horizontal lines. It shows line segments labeled a, b, c, d, e, f, g, h, and k arranged to represent proportional parts and magnitudes as discussed in Proposition 6.</image-desc>

¶ You can, however, through both this and the preceding [proposition], expand what is proposed concerning four numbers to any number of numbers: for if any number of smaller numbers are compared to as many larger numbers, and each is the same part or parts of each as the first is of the second, then all [the smaller ones] taken together will be the same part or parts of all [the larger ones] taken together as the first is of the second. This is easily proven through this and the preceding proposition, repeated as many times as necessary. And if we believed it were the intention of Euclid to assume from things previously demonstrated some things for the demonstration of those which he proposes here from the 13th [proposition] of the fifth book, I would have easily demonstrated this sixth [proposition]. Now, however, because the opposite seems to be the case—for otherwise he would have needlessly proposed many things concerning numbers which were already demonstrated in the fifth book concerning quantities in general—we have found it necessary to use specific demonstrations, as if taking nothing from the earlier books, being content only with the principles of this seventh book. For this reason, we have not inappropriately placed the postulates <note>original: "petitiones"</note> and common notions <note>original: "cōes animi cōceptiones"; these are basic axioms or logical truths.</note> proper to the subject at the beginning of this seventh book.

# Proposition 7

**If** there be two numbers of which one is a part of the other, and the same part be subtracted from both: the remainder will be the same part of the remainder as the whole was of the whole.

What Euclid proposes here concerning numbers, he proposed above in the fifth [proposition] of the fifth book concerning quantities in general. Let it be, therefore, that the whole $a$ is the same part of the whole $b$ as the part $c$ (subtracted from $a$) is of $d$ (subtracted from $b$). I say that the remainder of $a$ will be the same part of the remainder of $b$ as the whole $a$ is of the whole $b$. And this is, as it were, the converse of the fifth [proposition]. For let, by the postulate, $e$ be the same part of $g$ as $c$ is of $d$. By the 5th [proposition], the whole $a$ (composed of $g$ and $d$) <note>The text here seems to use $g$ and $d$ to reconstruct the whole.</note> will be the same part as $c$ is of $d$; wherefore it is the same as $a$ is of $b$. Therefore, by the second common notion, the sum of $g$ and $d$ is equal to $b$. Thus, by taking away $d$ from both numbers, $g$ will be equal to the remainder $f$. Wherefore it will be...

### Proposition 8

<image-desc>Geometric diagram showing several horizontal line segments of varying lengths. The segments are labeled with letters (a, b, c, d, e, f, g, h, k) and numerical values (18, 6, 12, 4, 8). The diagram illustrates relationships between wholes and parts, specifically relating to numerical proportions.</image-desc>

**If** from two numbers, one of which is the same parts of the other, these same parts are subtracted: the remainder will be the same parts of the remainder as the whole was of the whole.
¶ This is, as it were, the converse of the sixth [proposition]: as if the whole $a$ is as many and such parts of the whole $b$, and $c$ (subtracted from $a$) is as many and such parts of $d$ (subtracted from $b$); then $e$, the remainder of $a$, will be as many and such parts of $f$, the remainder of $b$, as $a$ is of $b$. For let $g$ be one of the parts of $a$, and [let another be] one of the parts of $c$. By the hypothesis <note>original: "ypoth."</note>, the whole $g$ will be the same part of $a$ as $b$ is of $c$ <note>The text here uses letters to track unit fractions that make up the larger "parts."</note>, and the whole $b$ is the same part as $b$ is of $d$. Therefore, let $b$ be subtracted from $g$, and let $k$ remain. By the preceding [proposition], $k$ will be the same part of $e$ as $g$ is of $a$, and $f$ [will be the same] by the same reasoning as $g$ is of $b$. Since, therefore, $e$ and $f$ have a common part which is $k$, it will be by the 16th definition <note>Euclid's definition of "parts" or fractions.</note> that $e$ is parts of $f$, precisely as many as $k$ is a part of $e$, and as many as $k$ is of $f$. And since $a$ was as many and such parts of $b$, the proposition is clear.

### Proposition 9

<image-desc>Geometric diagram consisting of four horizontal line segments labeled b, d (the longer upper lines) and a, c (the shorter lines below them), representing a proportional relationship between four numbers.</image-desc>

**If** there are four numbers of which the first is the same part <note>A unit fraction, like 1/3.</note> of the second as the third is of the fourth: then, alternately <note>original: "pmutatim"; this refers to switching the middle terms of a proportion (if a:b = c:d, then a:c = b:d).</note>, the first will be the same part or parts of the third as the second is of the fourth.
¶ Let $a$ be the first, being the same part of $b$ (the second) as $c$ (the third) is of $d$ (the fourth). Let $a$ and $b$ be smaller than $c$ and $d$, for otherwise the proposition would be the other way around. I say that whatever part or parts $a$ is of $c$, the same part or parts is $b$ of $d$. For let $b$ be divided according to the quantity of $a$, and $d$ according to $c$. By the present hypothesis, there will be as many parts in $b$ as there are in $d$. And because each of the parts of $b$ is equal to $a$, and each [part] of $d$ is equal to $c$; and $a$ is a part or parts of $c$ by the present hypothesis; then by the fourth [proposition], each of the parts of $b$ will be the same as its corresponding part from $d$, just as the first is to the first, and the second to the second. Thus, for all the rest, the whole part or parts will be the same as $a$ is of $c$. Therefore, by the 5th or 6th [proposition], repeated as many times as necessary under disjunction, $b$ will be the same part or parts of $d$ as $a$ is of $c$. Which is what was proposed.

### Proposition 10

<image-desc>Geometric diagram similar to the one for Proposition 9, with segments labeled b, a, d, c. This diagram additionally includes small tick marks on the lines for a and c, with numbers 5, 6, 7 next to them on the left, indicating divisions of the segments.</image-desc>

**If** there are four numbers of which the first is the same parts <note>A proper fraction, like 2/3.</note> of the second as the third is of the fourth: then, alternately, the first will be the same part or parts of the third as the second is of the fourth.
¶ Let there be four numbers as before, of which $a$ and $b$ are similarly the smaller. Let $a$ be the same parts of $b$ as $c$ is of $d$. I say that whatever part or parts $a$ is of $c$, the same part or parts is $b$ of $d$. For let the smaller numbers, which are $a$ and $c$, be divided into those [constituent] parts. By the present hypothesis, there will be as many parts in $a$ as in $c$. And because each of the parts of $a$ is the same part of $b$ as any of the parts of $c$ is of $d$—for we have this from our hypothesis—it will be, alternately by the preceding [proposition], that whatever part or parts $b$ is of $d$, the same part or parts is each of the parts of $a$ to its corresponding part from $c$. Therefore, by the 5th or 6th [proposition], repeated as many times as necessary under disjunction, $b$ will be the same part or parts of $d$ as $a$ is of $c$. Which is what was proposed.

### Proposition 11

**If** there are four proportional numbers of which the first is greater than the second and the third is greater than the fourth: then the second will be the same part or parts of the first as the fourth is of the third. Furthermore, if the second is the same part or parts of the first as the fourth is of the third, it follows that the four numbers are proportional.
¶ Let the proportion of $a$ to $b$ be as $c$ to $d$, and let $a$ and $c$ be the greater. I say that whatever part or...

<meta>This page continues the logical demonstration of Proposition 11 from Book VII of Euclid’s Elements. The previous page established the relationship between proportions and the concept of "parts" (fractions). This page concludes that proof and presents Proposition 12, which deals with the subtraction of proportional numbers, similar to a rule established for general magnitudes in Book V.</meta>

[The conclusion of the proof for Proposition 11]

...$b$ is a part of $a$. The whole $d$ is a part or parts of $c$, and vice versa: for it will be through the conversion of the definition of similar proportions that as many times as $b$ is in $a$, so many times is $d$ in $c$. And if any part or parts of $b$ remain <note>original: "superfluunt", meaning to be left over or exceed</note> in $a$, the same part or parts of $d$ remain in $c$. If, therefore, $b$ is contained in $a$ without a remainder of a part: because it is contained as many times without a remainder as $d$ is in $c$, it will be (by the definition of similar parts) that $b$ is the same part of $a$ as $d$ is of $c$. 

But if $b$ is contained in $a$ any number of times with the remainder of a part: because $d$ is contained as many times in $c$ with the remainder of a similar part, let $a$ be divided according to $b$ so that $e$ remains, and $c$ according to $d$ so that $f$ remains. Then $e$ will be the same part of $b$ as $f$ is of $d$. And since $b$ is contained in the whole of $a$ minus $e$ as many times as $d$ is in the whole of $c$ minus $f$, it will be (by common knowledge <note>original: "commuunem scientiam", referring to a "Common Notion" or mathematical axiom</note>) that $e$ is in $a$ as many times as $f$ is in $c$. Since, therefore, $a$ and $b$ have $e$ as a common part, and likewise $c$ and $d$ have $f$: let $e$ be in $b$ as many times as $f$ is in $d$, and likewise $e$ in $a$ as many times as $f$ in $c$. It will be, by the 16th definition, that $b$ is as many and such parts of $a$ as $d$ is of $c$. 

If, however, $b$ is contained in $a$ any number of times with the remainder of any parts: because $d$ is contained as many times in $c$ with the remainder of just as many and similar parts, let $a$ be divided according to $b$ so that $e$ remains, and similarly $c$ according to $d$ so that $f$ remains. Then $e$ will be as many and such parts of $b$ as $f$ is of $d$. Taking one from these, we must argue as before; and thus the first part is evident. 

The second part is as follows: let $b$ be the same part or parts of the whole $a$ as $d$ is of the whole $c$. I say that the proportion of $a$ to $b$ will be as $c$ to $d$. If it is a single part, the proposition is established. But if it is multiple parts, by dividing them according to those parts, it will be clear that $b$ is in $a$ as many times as $d$ is in $c$, and that the same part or parts of $b$ remain in $a$ as $d$ remain in $c$. Therefore, by the definition, the proportion of $a$ to $b$ is as $c$ to $d$, and thus the whole is clear.

### Proposition 12.

**If from two numbers two numbers are subtracted according to their proportions: the proportion of the remainder to the remainder will be as the proportion of the whole to the whole.**

<image-desc>A diagram in the middle right margin showing two sets of horizontal line segments. The upper set consists of segments 'f' and 'd' together forming 'b'. The lower set consists of segments 'e' and 'c' together forming 'a'.</image-desc>

What Euclid proposed in the 19th [proposition] of the fifth [book] concerning quantities in general, he proposes here concerning numbers. For example, if the proportion of the whole $a$ to the whole $b$ is as $c$ (subtracted from $a$) is to $d$ (subtracted from $b$), then the proportion of the remainder $e$ (of $a$) to the remainder $f$ (of $b$) will be as $a$ is to $b$. 

For if $a$ is less than $b$, it will be (by the preceding hypothesis and the conversion of the definition) that $c$ is the same part or parts of $d$ as $a$ is of $b$. By the 7th or 8th [propositions], therefore, $e$ will be the same part or parts of $f$ as $a$ is of $b$. Therefore, by the definition, there will be one proportion; which is what was proposed. 

But if $a$ is greater than $b$, it will be (by the first part of the premise) that $b$ is the same part or parts of $a$ as $d$ is of $c$. Wherefore, by the 7th or 8th, $f$ will be the same part or parts of $e$. Thus, by the second part of the premise, $c$ is to $f$ as $a$ is to $b$; wherefore the proposition stands. 

However, the 7th and 8th [propositions] apply here, for they alone contain both of those cases. Some wish to prove the second part of this by the 19th of the fifth book; but if Euclid had intended this—since he proposes these specifically while the others are universal—he would have proposed this here in the seventh book in vain after demonstrating it in the fifth. Furthermore, he does not demonstrate it simply through the 19th of the fifth. Indeed, they cannot even confirm the method of that demonstration for the demonstration of this one, since that is demonstrated in quantities in general through permuted proportionality, which is demonstrated below specifically for numbers. 

Moreover, I believe it is reasonable to conclude that Euclid assumes the persona of an arithmetic demonstrator for the sake of the tenth book <note>The tenth book of the Elements deals with irrational magnitudes and requires a firm grasp of rational number theory</note>, in which one cannot proceed without some prior knowledge of numbers. Therefore, he repeats many of those things here to be demonstrated for numbers which he demonstrated in the fifth book for quantities in general, because they are demonstrated through other principles specific to numbers, which are more known to the intellect than [general quantities].

**BOOK**

[the author] intends to demonstrate those things through which he proceeded in the fifth [book]: for the principles of the fifth book are difficult on account of the "malice" <note>original: "maliciam"; here referring to the inherent complexity or "stubbornness" of the subject matter</note> of incommensurable quantities <note>original: "quantitatum incommunicantium"; quantities that share no common measure, like the side and diagonal of a square. These are not found in whole numbers.</note>. The principles of numbers, however, apply themselves more of their own accord to the understanding, and are easier than the former. ### Proposition 13

**I**f there are any number of proportional numbers, as much as one antecedent <note>The first term in a ratio</note> is to its consequent <note>The second term in a ratio</note>, so will all the antecedents taken together be to all the consequents taken together.

<margin>
<image-desc>A diagram consisting of three sets of horizontal line segments of varying lengths. Each set consists of two lines: the first pair is labeled "a" and "b", the second "c" and "d", and the third "e" and "f".</image-desc>
</margin>

¶ That which Euclid proposes in Proposition 13 of the fifth [book] concerning quantities in general, he proposes through this [proposition] concerning numbers: as if $a, b, c, d, e, f$ are proportional, I say that whatever is the proportion of $a$ to $b$, the same is the proportion of $a, c, e$ taken together to $b, d, f$ taken together. For if $a, c, e$ are smaller than $b, d, f$, it will be by the conversion of the definition <note>Referencing the definition of proportional numbers found earlier in the book</note> that whatever part or parts $a$ is of $b$, so are the totals $c$ of $d$ and $e$ of $f$. By Proposition 9, and then by Proposition 6 repeated as many times as necessary, it will be that whatever part or parts $a$ is of $b$, the same is the whole of $a, c, e$ taken together of $b, d, f$ taken together; therefore, by the definition, there is one proportion. If, however, $a, c, e$ are larger than $b, d, f$, it will be through the first part of Proposition 11: whatever part or parts $b$ is of $a$, so are the totals $d$ of $c$ and $f$ of $e$. By Proposition 5, or 6, repeated as many times as necessary: whatever part or parts $b$ is of $a$, so will the whole of $b, d, f$ taken together be of $a, c, e$ taken together. Thus, by the second part of Proposition 11, the proportion of $a$ to $b$ is as $a, c, e$ taken together to $b, d, f$ taken together: which is what was proposed.

### Proposition 14

**I**f four numbers are proportional, they will also be proportional alternately <note>original: "permutatim"; if a:b = c:d, then a:c = b:d</note>.

<margin>
<image-desc>Three separate diagrams illustrating proportional relationships with line segments. The first set shows lines labeled "a", "b", "c", and "d". The second set shows similar lines in a different configuration. The third set shows lines labeled "a", "b", "e", and "c".</image-desc>
</margin>

¶ This mode of reasoning, which is called "permutated proportionality," which Euclid demonstrated through Proposition 16 of the fifth [book] in quantities in general, he proposes here to be demonstrated in numbers: as if the proportion of $a$ to $b$ is as $c$ to $d$, then alternately $a$ to $c$ will be as $b$ to $d$. For $a$ will be either greater or smaller than $b$; and similarly, $a$ will be either greater or smaller than $c$. Let it be first, therefore, that it is smaller than both: then by the present hypothesis and the conversion of the definition, $a$ is the same part or parts of $b$ as $c$ is of $d$. By Proposition 9, and thus by Proposition 10, it will be alternately that $a$ is the same part or parts of $c$ as $b$ is of $d$; therefore, by the definition, there is one proportion. Now, let $a$ be greater than both: and it will be by the first part of Proposition 11 that whatever part or parts $b$ is of $a$, the same part or parts $d$ is of $c$. Wherefore, by Proposition 9 or 10, $b$ will be the same part or parts of $d$ as $a$ is of $c$. Therefore, by the second part of Proposition 11, $a$ will be to $c$ as $b$ is to $d$. Thirdly, let $a$ be greater than $b$ and smaller than $c$. By the first part of Proposition 11, $b$ is some part or parts of $a$, as $d$ is of $c$. Wherefore, by Proposition 9 or 10, whatever [part or parts] $a$ is of $c$, the same will $b$ be of $d$; and so by the definition, there is one proportion. Finally, let $a$ be smaller than $b$ and greater than $c$. It will be that whatever part or parts $c$ is of $d$, the same is $a$ of $b$. By Proposition 9 or 10, the total $d$ will be to $b$ as $c$ is to $a$. Wherefore, by the second part of Proposition 11, $b$ is to $d$ as $a$ is to $c$. Thus the proposition is established. To this [proof], Propositions 9 or 10 are applied, because those two propose what this one alone proposes <note>This suggests that the properties of parts (fractions) are the foundation for the properties of ratios</note>.

### Proposition 15

**I**f there are any number of numbers, and others as many as they, and all pairs from the first set [are proportional] to all pairs from the second set in the same ratio, they will be proportional in the proportion of equality <note>original: "proportione equalitatis"; often called "ex aequali" proportionality. If a:b = d:e and b:c = e:f, then a:c = d:f</note>.

¶ This mode of reasoning, which is called "equal proportionality," which Euclid demonstrated through Proposition 22 of the fifth [book] concerning quantities in general, he proposes here to be demonstrated in numbers.

<header>VII</header>

...of direct proportionality: that same proportionality which he demonstrated through Proposition 23 of the fifth book. He does not propose to demonstrate the quantities of indirect proportionality <note>original: "indirecte proportionalitatis"; also known as inverse proportion</note> in numbers here, but they will be demonstrated below, under Proposition 19 of this book. Nor is it necessary for us to pre-demonstrate in numbers what was demonstrated through Proposition 11 of the fifth [book] concerning quantities in general: namely, that if any number of proportions in numbers are equal to or the same as one another, they are equal to or the same as themselves. For this is manifest through the definition; for example, if $a$ to $c$ and $c$ to $f$ are as $b$ to $d$, and $d$ [is the same], then both $a$ to $c$ and $c$ to $f$ will be the same "part or parts" <note>This is a standard Euclidean phrase. A "part" is a unit fraction (like 1/3), while "parts" refers to a non-unit fraction (like 2/3).</note> as $b$ to $d$. Or, $a$ and $c$, and $c$ and $e$ and $f$, will contain their counterparts as many times as $b$ and $d$ do, and the whole part or parts remain as $e$ in $a$ and $f$ in $e$, just as $d$ in $b$. Therefore, whatever part or parts $a$ is of $c$, the whole $e$ is of $f$; or as many times as $a$ contains $c$, so many times $c$ contains $f$. And whatever part or parts $c$ exceeds in $a$, the whole $f$ will exceed in $e$. By definition, therefore, $a$ is to $c$ as $e$ is to $f$. Let there be, therefore, as proposed, the numbers $a, b, e$ and as many others $c, d, f$; and let $a$ be to $b$ as $c$ is to $d$, and $b$ to $e$ as $d$ to $f$. I say that in equality of proportionality <note>original: "equa proportionalitate"; often called 'ex aequali' in geometry, where the middle terms are skipped to compare the first and last.</note>, $a$ will be to $e$ as $c$ is to $f$. For by the previous [proposition], $a$ will be to $c$ as $b$ is to $d$; but $b$ is to $d$ as $e$ is to $f$; wherefore $a$ is to $c$ as $e$ is to $f$. Therefore, by the same [reasoning], $a$ is to $e$ as $c$ is to $f$. The same will be true if more numbers are taken, and thus the proposition stands.

Since Euclid does not propose the other four species of proportionality to be demonstrated in numbers—which are converse, conjoined, disjointed, and everted—we think it appropriate to demonstrate those which the author passed over as being easily demonstrable. First, therefore, we will demonstrate the **converse**: as if $a$ is to $b$ as $c$ is to $d$, I say that conversely $b$ is to $a$ as $d$ is to $c$. For if $a$ is less than $b$, then $c$ will also be less than $d$, and $a$ is the same part or parts of $b$ as $c$ is of $d$. Wherefore, through the second part of Proposition 11, $b$ will be to $a$ as $d$ is to $c$. But if $a$ is greater than $b$, $c$ will also be greater than $d$, and through the first part of Proposition 11, $b$ is the same part or parts of $a$ as $d$ is of $c$. By definition, therefore, $b$ is to $a$ as $d$ is to $c$.

->¶ To show disjointed proportionality.<-

¶ As if $a$ to $b$ is as $c$ to $d$, then $ab$ <note>Here "ab" refers to the sum or combination of two segments.</note> will be to $b$ as $cd$ is to $d$. For it will be, alternately <note>original: "permutatim"; switching the means of the proportion.</note>, $ab$ to $cd$ as $b$ is to $d$, and through Proposition 12, as $a$ is to $c$. Because $a$ is to $c$ as $b$ is to $d$, it will be alternately $a$ to $b$ as $c$ to $d$.

->¶ To bring forth the demonstration for conjoined proportionality<-

¶ As if $a$ to $b$ is as $c$ to $d$, then $ab$ will be to $b$ as $cd$ is to $d$. For it will be alternately $a$ to $c$ as $b$ to $d$; wherefore through Proposition 13, $ab$ to $cd$ is as $b$ to $d$. Alternately, therefore, $ab$ will be to $b$ as $cd$ to $d$.

->¶ It remains to establish everted proportionality in numbers.<-

¶ As if $ab$ to $b$ is as $cd$ to $d$, then $ab$ will be to $a$ as $cd$ to $c$. For it will be alternately $ab$ to $cd$ as $b$ to $d$, wherefore through Proposition 12, it is as $a$ to $c$. Alternately, therefore, $ab$ will be to $a$ as $cd$ is to $c$. Thus the whole is clear. From these things it is also easy to demonstrate in numbers what Euclid proposes in the penultimate [proposition] of the fifth [book] concerning quantities in general, namely that:

¶ If the proportion of the first to the second is as the third to the fourth, and the fifth to the second is as the sixth to the fourth: then the proportion of the first and fifth taken together to the second will be as the third and sixth taken together to the fourth.

¶ For example, if $a$ is to $b$ as $c$ is to $d$, and likewise $e$ is to $b$ as $f$ is to $d$, then $a$ and $e$ taken together will be to $b$ as $c$ and $f$ taken together are to $d$. For by converse proportionality, $b$ is to $e$ as $d$ is to $f$; wherefore by equality of proportionality, $a$ is to $e$ as $c$ is to $f$. Therefore, conjoined, $a$ and $e$ are to $e$ as $c$ and $f$ are to $f$. Thus, by equality of proportionality, $a$ and $e$ are to $b$ as $c$ and $f$ are to $d$, which is what was proposed. And in the same way you will prove it conversely: if $b$ is to $a$ as $d$ is to $c$, and likewise $b$ is to $e$ as $d$ is to $f$, then $b$ will be to $a$ and $e$ as $d$ is to $c$ and $f$. For by converse proportionality, $a$ is to $b$ as $c$ is to $d$; wherefore by equality, $a$ is to $e$ as $c$ is to $f$, and conjoined, $a$ and $e$ are to $e$ as $c$ and $f$.

...to $f$. Therefore, conversely <note>original: "ecōuerſo"</note>, $e$ is to $a$, and $e$ is to $a$ as $f$ is to $c$ and $f$. Thus, by equal proportionality, $b$ will be to $a$ and $c$ as $d$ is to $c$ and $f$, which was proposed. From this, it is also clear that if there is a ratio of any number of antecedent terms to a first term, just as there are as many others to a second term, the sum of all the antecedents compared to the first will be the same as the sum of all the antecedents compared to the second. Likewise, conversely, if there is a ratio of a first term to any number of consequent terms, as there is a ratio of a second term to just as many others, the ratio of the first to the sum of all its consequents will be the same as the ratio of the second to the sum of all its consequents.

## Proposition 16

<image-desc>A line diagram in the left margin. A horizontal segment 'a' has the Roman numeral 'I' placed above it. To the right of segment 'a' are two separate horizontal segments labeled 'b' and 'c'.</image-desc>

If a unit <term>vnitas (unit)</term> measures <note>In Euclidean geometry, "to measure" means to divide exactly into a larger quantity without a remainder.</note> any number as many times as any third [number] measures any fourth, then it will also be true by permutation <term>permutatim (alternatingly)</term> that however many times the unit measures the third, the second measures the fourth.

For example, if the unit is to $a$ as $b$ is to $c$, then by permutation the unit will be to $b$ as $a$ is to $c$. However, this property was not derived from the [previously] demonstrated permuted proportion <note>Reference to Book V, Proposition 16, which deals with general magnitudes.</note>; for what is proposed here cannot be concluded from that one. For that previous demonstration concerned four proportional numbers, but the unit is not a "number" by definition <note>In ancient Greek and Medieval mathematics, a "number" was defined as a "multitude of units." Consequently, the unit (1) was considered the source or essence of number, but not a number itself.</note>. Therefore, let the proposition be shown in this way: let $a$ be divided into units and $c$ be divided according to the quantity $b$. By the current hypothesis, there will be as many parts in $a$ as there are in $c$. And because each of the parts of $a$ is a unit, and each of the parts of $c$ is equal to $b$, it follows that as many times as the unit is in $b$, so many times is each part of $a$ in its corresponding part <note>original: "cópari"</note> of $c$. Thus, following the method of demonstration in Proposition 5, it follows that $a$ is in $c$ as many times as the unit is in $b$, which is what was proposed.

## Proposition 17

<image-desc>A line diagram in the left margin. At the top, segment 'a' is marked with the number '3' and segment 'b' with the number '4'. Below them, two segments of equal length, 'c' and 'd', are both marked with the number '12'.</image-desc>

If each of two numbers is multiplied by the other, the resulting products will be equal.

Just as if from $a$ times $b$ comes $c$, and from $b$ times $a$ comes $d$, then $c$ and $d$ will be equal. For when $b$ is multiplied by $a$ to produce $c$, then by the converse of the definition <note>The definition of multiplication: $a \times b$ means $b$ is added to itself as many times as there are units in $a$.</note>, $b$ is in $c$ as many times as the unit is in $a$. Therefore, by the previous proposition, $a$ is in $c$ as many times as the unit is in $b$. And since $a$ is also in $d$ as many times [as the unit is in $b$]—because $d$ is produced from $b$ times $a$—it follows that $a$ is in $c$ just as many times as it is in $d$. Therefore, by common notion <note>original: "p concept." (per conceptionem), referring to common axioms like "things equal to the same thing are equal to each other."</note>, $c$ and $d$ are identical. We can also propose this conclusion in another way: if each of two numbers is multiplied by the other, the same number will result in both cases. For if from $a$ times $b$ comes $c$, then as before, by the converse of the definition, $b$ is in $c$ as many times as the unit is in $a$. And by permutation through the previous proposition, $a$ is in $c$ as many times as the unit is in $b$. Because, therefore, $a$ is added to itself as many times in $c$ as there are units in $b$, it follows by definition that $c$ is also produced from $b$ times $a$.

## Proposition 18

<image-desc>A line diagram in the left margin. Two top segments, 'd' and 'e', are marked with numbers '20' and '30' respectively. Below them, segments 'c' and 'b' are marked with '4' and '6'. At the bottom, segment 'a' is marked with '5' and the Roman numeral 'I' is centered below it.</image-desc>

If one number is multiplied by two [others], the ratio of the two resulting products will be the same as the ratio of the two [numbers] that were multiplied.

Let $a$ multiply both of the two numbers $b$ and $c$, and let $d$ and $e$ be produced. I say that the ratio <term>proportio</term> of $d$ to $e$ will be as the ratio of $b$ to $c$. It follows from the converse of the definition of multiplication that $b$ is in $d$ and $c$ is in $e$ as many times as the unit is in $a$. Therefore, by definition, the ratio of $d$ to $b$ is the same as the ratio of $e$ to $c$, for they contain them equally—namely, as many times as $a$ contains the unit. Therefore, by permutation, $d$ is to $e$ as $b$ is to $c$, which is what was proposed.

## Proposition 19

If two numbers multiply one [same number], the ratio of the two resulting products will be the same as the ratio of the two multipliers.

From the converse of the preceding premise, this same property <note>original: "paſſio" (passion/attribute)</note> is concluded as in the premise: for example, if each of the two numbers $b$ and $c$ multiplies $a$, and...

...come forth $d$ and $e$, then $d$ will be to $e$ as $b$ is to $c$. For by the previous proposition, as $a$ times $b$ and $r$ <note>The letter 'r' likely refers to a remaining value or a specific variable defined on the previous page.</note> make $d$ and $e$, then by the previous [proposition] $d$ is to $e$ as $b$ is to $c$, which was proposed.

One can also expand what is proposed by this and the previous proposition from two numbers to any number of them: for if one number multiplies any number of others, there will be one <note>Meaning the "same"</note> proportion of the products and the things multiplied. Similarly, if any number of things multiply one, there will be one proportion of the products and the multipliers, which you will easily prove by repeating this and the previous proposition as many times as necessary.

Here, however, as we have refined <note>original: "pollitici"</note> above, we wish to demonstrate equal proportionality in any number of terms of two sequences of indirect proportionality <term>indirecte proportionalitatis (perturbed proportion)</term>, which Euclid demonstrates in the 23rd [proposition] of the Fifth [Book] regarding quantities in general. We say, therefore, that:

If any number of terms are indirectly proportional to as many others, the extremes <term>extremi (the first and last terms)</term> will also be proportional in the same ratio.

For example, if $a$ is to $b$ as $d$ is to $f$, and $b$ is to $c$ as $c$ is to $d$, then $a$ will be to $c$ as $c$ is to $f$. <note>This explains "perturbed" or "indirect" proportions where the ratios are crossed between two sets.</note> For let $c$ be multiplied by $d$ and $f$, and let $g$ and $h$ be produced. Then, by the previous proposition, $g$ is to $h$ as $d$ is to $f$, and therefore as $a$ is to $b$. Likewise, let $f$ be multiplied by $d$, and let $k$ be produced. Then, by this 19th proposition, $g$ is to $k$ as $c$ is to $f$. And because $f$ times $d$ makes $k$, the same is made conversely <note>original: "e converso"</note> by the 10th [proposition] from $d$ times $f$. Because, therefore, from $c$ and $d$ [multiplied] into $f$ come $h$ and $k$, it will be by this 19th proposition that $h$ is to $k$ as $c$ is to $d$, and thus as $b$ is to $c$. Since it has already been shown that $g$ is to $h$ as $a$ is to $b$, it will be by the 15th [proposition] that $a$ is to $c$ as $g$ is to $k$. But it was also that $c$ is to $f$ [in that ratio]. Therefore, $a$ is to $c$ as $c$ is to $f$, which is what was proposed. You will prove the same if there are more than three numbers in either sequence, just as it is proven in the 23rd [proposition] of the Fifth [Book] concerning more than three quantities.

### Proposition 20

**I**f there are four numbers, that which is produced from the multiplication of the first and the last will be equal to that produced from the multiplication of the second and the third. Conversely, if that which is produced from the first and the last is equal to that from the second and third, those four numbers are proportional.

What Euclid proposed through the 15th [proposition] of the Sixth [Book] concerning four proportional lines, he proposes here concerning four proportional numbers. For example: Let the proportion of $a$ to $b$ be as $c$ to $d$. Let $e$ be produced from $a$ times $d$, and $f$ from $b$ times $c$. I say that $e$ and $f$ are equal. Conversely: let $a$ be multiplied by $b$ to make $g$. Then, by the 18th [proposition], $g$ is to $e$ as $b$ is to $d$. And because by the 17th [proposition] $b$ times $a$ makes $g$, and from the same $b$ times $c$ makes $f$, then by the 18th [proposition] $g$ is to $f$ as $a$ is to $c$. But by the 14th [proposition], $a$ is to $c$ as $b$ is to $d$. Therefore $g$ is to $f$ as $g$ is to $e$. Thus, $f$ and $e$ are equal, which is the first part.

Nor is it necessary to demonstrate further that if one number has one proportion to two others, then those two are equal; or if they are equal, that the proportion of one to them is the same. For if there is one proportion of $g$ to $e$ and to $f$, either $g$ will be the same part or parts <note>This refers to fractions, where a "part" is a unit fraction like 1/3, and "parts" are non-unit fractions like 2/3.</note> of $e$ as it is of $f$, and then by common conception it is clear that $e$ and $f$ are equal; or $g$ will contain $e$ as many times as it contains $f$, with the same part or parts of $e$ remaining as the part or parts of $f$ that remain, and then also by common conception it is clear they are equal. Likewise, if they are equal, it is clear by common conception that either $g$ will be the same part or parts of $e$ as of $f$, and then by definition the proportion of $g$ to both of them will be one; or it will contain both equally with a remainder of similar and equal parts, and then also by definition the proportion to both will be one.

The second part is clear as follows: let $e$ produced from $a$ times $d$ be equal to $f$ produced from $b$ times $c$. I say that the proportion of $a$ to $b$ is as $c$ to $d$, and this is the converse of the first part. For let it be as before...

### ->Proposition 21<-

<margin>
<image-desc>Geometric diagram for Proposition 21. Two columns of horizontal lines. The right column contains lines labeled 'c' (top), 'a' (middle), and 'e' (bottom). The left column contains lines labeled 'd' (top), 'b' (middle), and 'f' (bottom).</image-desc>

The smallest numbers in any given proportion measure <note>original: "numerant"; meaning they divide into them exactly</note> any other numbers in the same proportion an equal number of times—the smaller measuring the smaller and the larger measuring the larger.

Let $a$ and $b$ be the smallest numbers in their proportion, and let $c$ be to $d$ as $a$ is to $b$. I say that $a$ measures $c$, and $b$ measures $d$, an equal number of times. Since $a$ is to $b$ as $c$ is to $d$, then by permutation $a$ is to $c$ as $b$ is to $d$. Therefore, $a$ is either the same part or parts of $c$ as $b$ is of $d$. If it is a part, the proposition is proven. But if it is parts, let $e$ be one of the parts of $a$, and $f$ be one of the parts of $b$. Since by the hypothesis $e$ is the same part of $c$ as $f$ is of $d$, it follows by the definition that the proportion of $e$ to $c$ is as $f$ to $d$. Therefore, by permutation, $e$ is to $f$ as $c$ is to $d$, and thus also as $a$ is to $b$. Consequently, $a$ and $b$ are not the smallest in their proportion, which contradicts the initial assumption. Similarly also:

¶ Any number of terms, whether in the same or different proportions, if they are the smallest, measure all those in the same proportion, each its own corresponding term, an equal number of times.

¶ As if $a, b, c$ are the smallest in the same or different proportions, and $d, e, f$ are in the same proportion(s) as them, such that $d$ is to $e$ as $a$ is to $b$, and $e$ is to $f$ as $b$ is to $c$. I say that $a$ measures $d$, $b$ measures $e$, and $c$ measures $f$ an equal number of times. Because $a$ is to $b$ as $d$ is to $e$, by permutation $a$ is to $d$ as $b$ is to $e$. And because $b$ is to $c$ as $e$ is to $f$, by permutation $b$ is to $e$ as $c$ is to $f$. Thus $b$ to $e$ and $c$ to $f$ are equal. And because $a, b, c$ are smaller than $d, e, f$, then $b$ relative to $e$ and $c$ relative to $f$ will be the same part or parts as $a$ relative to $d$. If it is a part, the proposition is proven. But if it is parts, let $g$ be one of the parts of $a$, $h$ one of the parts of $b$, and $k$ one of the parts of $c$. By the current hypothesis, $b$ relative to $e$ and $c$ relative to $f$ <note>The text likely means $h$ and $k$</note> are the same part as $g$ relative to $d$. Therefore by definition $b$ to $e$ and $k$ to $f$ are as $g$ to $d$. By permutation, therefore, $g$ is to $b$ as $d$ is to $e$, and $h$ is to $e$ and $k$ as $e$ is to $f$. Thus $g$ is to $b$ as $a$ is to $b$, and $h$ is to $k$ as $b$ is to $c$. Since $g, h, k$ are smaller than $a, b, c$ and in the same proportion, the opposite of the assumption follows.

If two numbers are the smallest according to their proportion, they will be prime to one another <term>adinuicem primi (numbers that share no common divisor other than 1)</term>.

And because $d$ and $e$ are smaller than $a$ and $b$, it follows that $a$ and $b$ are not the smallest in their proportion, which contradicts the position. Similarly also:

¶ For instance, if $a$, $b$, and $c$ are the smallest in the continuation of their proportions: I say that no number will measure all of them. For if some number $d$ were to measure them—measuring $a$ according to $e$, $b$ according to $f$, and $c$ according to $g$—then by [Proposition] 18, $e$ is to $f$ as $a$ is to $b$, and $f$ is to $g$ as $b$ is to $c$. ¶ Although no number measures $a$, $b$, and $c$ if they are the smallest, it can nevertheless happen that one number measures any two of them. Indeed, if any number is multiplied by another number that is prime to it, and both of those are multiplied by a third number that is prime to each, three numbers will be produced of which any two will be composite <term>compositi (numbers that share a common factor other than 1)</term>. That no number measures all three will be clear from the previous demonstration, since $a$ is the greatest number measuring $d$ and $e$; $b$ is the greatest measuring $d$ and $f$; and $c$ is the greatest measuring $e$ and $f$. 

This is established as follows: if $a$ were not the greatest number measuring $d$ and $e$, let it be $g$. Let it measure $d$ according to $h$ and $e$ according to $k$. Because $b$ is to $h$ as $k$ is to $c$, each being as $a$ is to $c$ (as assumed twice by [Proposition] 18), and since $b$ and $k$ are smaller than $b$ and $c$, it follows by the immediate consequence and this hypothesis that we would find numbers smaller than the smallest where $b$ and $c$ are prime to each other—which is impossible. Therefore, $a$ must be the greatest number measuring $d$ and $e$. In the same way, it will be proven that $b$ is the greatest number measuring $d$ and $f$, and $c$ the greatest measuring $e$ and $f$. ¶ **Any numbers which one [common] number does not measure are the smallest according to the continuation of their proportions.**

¶ For instance, if $a$, $b$, and $c$ are any numbers which no single number measures all together, I say that they are the smallest in the continuation of their proportions. Otherwise, let $d$, $e$, and $f$ be the smallest, which by [Proposition] 21 will measure $a$, $b$, and $c$—each measuring its relative part equally. Let this be according to $g$. Then by [Proposition] 17, conversely, $g$ would measure $a$, $b$, and $c$ according to $d$, $e$, and $f$. Thus, the opposite of the [original] position occurs.

### Proposition 23.
->**Any numbers that are prime to each other are the smallest in their proportion.**<-

This is the converse of the previous proposition. For if two numbers $a$ and $b$ are prime to each other <term>contra se primi (relatively prime, meaning they share no common factor but 1)</term>, they will be the smallest in their proportion. If, however, there were smaller numbers in the same proportion—if possible, $c$ and $d$—it follows by [Proposition] 21 that $c$ measures $a$ and $d$ measures $b$ equally. Let this be according to $e$. By [Proposition] 17, conversely, $e$ measures $a$ and $b$ according to $c$ and $d$. Therefore $a$ and $b$ are not prime to each other, which is contrary to the hypothesis.

### Proposition 24.
->**If there are two numbers prime to each other, and if some number measures one of them, it is necessarily proven to be prime to the other.**<-

Let $a$ and $b$ be prime to each other, and let $c$ measure $a$. I say that $c$ and $b$ are prime to each other. If they were not, some number $d$ would measure them. Then, by the previous rule, $d$ would also measure $a$. Therefore $a$ and $b$ would not be prime to each other, because $d$ measures both.

### Proposition 25.
->**If two numbers are each prime to another number, the product that results from multiplying one by the other will also be prime to that same number.**<-

Let each of the two numbers $a$ and $b$ be prime to $c$, and let $d$ be produced from $a$ multiplied by $b$. I say that $d$ is prime to $c$. Otherwise, some number $e$ would measure them...

->Proposition .26.<-

**If there are two numbers prime to each other, the product of one of them multiplied by itself is prime to the remaining number.**
Let *a* and *b* be prime to each other, and from *a* multiplied by itself let *c* be produced. I say that *c* is prime to *b*. For let *d* be equal to *a*; then *d* will be prime to *b*. And since *c* is produced from *a* multiplied by *d*, it is evident by the previous proposition that *c* is prime to *b*, which is what we proposed.

<image-desc>Geometric diagram for Proposition 27, consisting of six horizontal line segments arranged in three vertical levels, labeled with the letters a, b, c, d, e, and f.</image-desc>

->Proposition .27.<-

**If, when two numbers are compared to two others, each of the first two is prime to each of the second two, then the product of the first two will be prime to the product of the second two.**
Let *a* and *b* be the first two numbers, and *c* and *d* the second two. Let each of the two, *a* and *b*, be prime to each of the two, *c* and *d*. Let *e* be the product of *a* times *b*, and let *f* be the product of *c* times *d*. I say that *e* is prime to *f*. This is clearly concluded by applying [Proposition] 25 three times. For since *e* is produced from *a* and *b*, each of which is prime to *c* and to *d*, then by that proposition, *e* is prime to *c*, and likewise prime to *d*. Furthermore, because *f* is produced from *c* and *d*, each of which is prime to *e*, then by that same proposition, *f* will be prime to *e*, which is the proposal.

<image-desc>Geometric diagram for Proposition 28, consisting of six horizontal line segments stacked vertically, labeled f, e, d, c, b, and a from top to bottom.</image-desc>

->Proposition .28.<-

**If there are two numbers prime to each other, and each is multiplied by itself, the resulting products will be prime to each other. Likewise, if each of those products is multiplied by its original root, the resulting products will also be prime to each other.**
Let *a* and *b* be prime to each other. Let each be multiplied by itself: let *c* come from *a*, and *d* from *b*. Likewise, let *a* be multiplied by *c* to produce *e*, and *b* by *d* to produce *f*. I say that *c* and *d* are prime to each other, and likewise *e* and *f* are prime to each other. For by [Proposition] 26, *c* is prime to *b*; therefore, by the same logic, *d* is prime to *a* and to *c*. Thus it is established that the first pair, *c* and *d*, are prime to each other. The rest follows thus: each of the two numbers *a* and *c* is prime to each of the two *b* and *d*; therefore, by [Proposition] 27, *e* will be prime to *f*, which is the remainder of the proof. Not only will *c* be prime to *f*, but also by [Proposition] 25 it is prime to *b* and *d*; and likewise *f* is prime to *a* and *c*. Thus, if each product were multiplied by its root infinitely many times, all the resulting products would be prime to each other—and not only those, but any number derived from *a* would be prime to any number derived from *b*.

->Proposition .29.<-

**If there are two numbers prime to each other, their sum <term>coaceruatur (collected together or summed)</term> will be prime to each of the original numbers. Conversely, if the sum of two numbers is prime to each of them, those two numbers will be prime to each other.**
Let *a* and *b* be prime to each other. I say that the sum composed of them, *a*+*b*, will be prime to each of them, and vice versa. For if some number *d* measures the whole *a*+*b*, and [measures] one of the parts, it will also measure the other part by common knowledge <note>original: "commuunem scientiam"; referring to a mathematical axiom or common notion</note>. Wherefore they would not be prime to each other, but this was already posited. Thus the first part is evident. The second part is as follows: let *a*+*b* be prime to each of its components, which are *a* and *b*. I say that *a* and *b* [are prime to each other]...

### Proposition .30.

**Every composite number is measured by some prime number.**

Let *a* be any composite number <note>A composite number is a positive integer greater than 1 that is not prime</note>. I say that some prime number measures it. For since it is composite, it will be measured by some number, let it be *b*. If *b* is prime, then what is said is true. But if it is composite, let it be measured by *c*, which also, by common knowledge, will measure *a*. If therefore *c* itself is prime, what is said is established. But if it is composite, it must be measured by another, let it be *d*, which also by common knowledge will measure *a*. Reasoning in this way as before: since every time a composite number occurs it is necessary to take a smaller one that measures it, it follows that one finally arrives at some prime number. Otherwise, an impossibility occurs, and it would be contrary to the postulate that numbers decrease infinitely <note>In Greek mathematics, a set of whole numbers cannot decrease forever; it must hit a "floor" (the number 1 or a prime)</note>.

### Proposition .31.

**Every number is either prime or is measured by a prime.**

Let *a* be any number. I say that it is either prime or measured by a prime. Because if it is not prime, it will be composite. Every such composite number is measured by some prime by the preceding proposition. Therefore *a* is either prime or is measured by a prime, which is what is proposed.

### Proposition .32.

**Every prime number is prime to every number it does not measure.**

Let *a* be a prime number not measuring *b*. I say that *a* and *b* are prime to each other. For if some number *c* were to measure both, then it would not be true that *a* is prime <note>Because a prime number can only be measured by 1 and itself</note>.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram for Proposition 32 showing three horizontal line segments. Segments 'a' and 'b' are on the top level, and a shorter segment 'c' is positioned below them.</image-desc>

### Proposition .33.

**If a number produced from two numbers is measured by any prime, it is necessary that the same prime measure one of those two numbers.**

Let *c* be the product of *a* multiplied by *b*, and let *d* be a prime number which is posited to measure *c*. I say that *d* measures *a* or *b*. For let it measure *c*. If therefore it does not measure *a*, it will be prime to it by the preceding proposition. And therefore it will be among the least according to its proportion <note>meaning the ratio is in its simplest form</note> by Proposition 23 of Book 7. Since *a* is to *d* as *c* is to *b* by the second part of Proposition 20, it follows that *d* measures *b* by Proposition 21, which is what was proposed. From this, it is manifest that if any number measures the product of two numbers, or if it is commensurable <note>original: "commensurabilis"; having a common measure or divisor</note> with it, it will also be commensurable with one of them.

<image-desc>Geometric diagram for Proposition 33 showing five horizontal segments. The top row contains segments 'a' and 'b'; below them is 'c'; and beneath 'c' are two segments labeled 'd' and 'e'.</image-desc>

# Proposition .35.

Any two numbers, by multiplying the least numbers of their ratio—the greater by the smaller and the smaller by the greater—produce the least number measured by them <note>This identifies the Least Common Multiple (LCM). For example, if the ratio of 6 and 8 is reduced to 3 and 4, then 6 × 4 = 24 and 8 × 3 = 24. 24 is the LCM</note>. From which it is manifest that the least number which two numbers measure also measures any other number measured by them.

¶ Let there be two numbers *a* and *b*, and the least numbers in their ratio be *c* and *d*. By the first part of the 20th proposition, from *a* times *d* and *b* times *c*, the same number is produced, which let be *e*. I say that *e* is the least number measured by *a* and *b*. Otherwise, let it be *f*, which *a* and *b* measure according to *g* and *h*. By the second part of the 20th proposition, *b* is to *g* as *a* is to *b*, and as *c* is to *d*. And by the 18th proposition, *c* is to *b* as *e* is to *f*. Since therefore by the 21st proposition *c* measures *b*, *e* will measure *f*—the greater measuring the smaller—which is impossible. Therefore, what was said stands.

# Proposition .36.

**Given any number of numbers, to find the least number measured by them.**

¶ It is also manifest from this that the least number which any number of numbers measure also measures any other number measured by them.

¶ Let the given numbers be *a, b, c, d*. I wish to find the least number measured by them. I find first the least number measured by *a* and *b*. If *a* measures *b*, there will be no other than *b*. But if it does not measure it, nor vice versa: if they are prime to each other <note>original: "contra se primi"; relatively prime</note>, the product of one multiplied by the other will be the least by the 23rd proposition and the preceding one. But if they share a common divisor <note>original: "communicantes"</note>, let the least numbers in their ratio be taken as the 34th proposition teaches, and let the greater multiplied by the smaller result in *e*, which will be the least number measured by them by the preceding proposition. In the same way, let the least number measured by *e* and *c* be found, which let be *f*. Then *f* will be the least number measured by *a, b, c*. And let the least number which *f* and *d* measure be *g*. Then *g* will be the least number which the given numbers measure. That all of them measure it is clear by the concept; but if it is not the least, let it be *h*. Since *a* and *b* measure *h*, they will also measure it by the corollary of the preceding proposition. By the same corollary, *c* will measure *f*, and also *g*. Thus, a greater number measures a smaller, which is impossible. This and the preceding proposition are proposed in another place under three conclusions, of which the first is equivalent to the preceding, the second is composed of both corollaries, and the third proposes for three numbers what this one does for any number of numbers. ## ¶ Given three numbers: to find the smallest of the numbers measured by them.

¶ Let the three proposed numbers be *a, b, c*, and the smallest number that *a* and *b* measure be *d*, which is found as the first of the three conclusions teaches. ### Proposition 37.

**If any number measures another number: there will be in the measured number a part named by the measurer.**

¶ The sense of this is that every number measured by a three <note>original: "ternario"</note> has a third, and every number measured by a five <note>original: "quinario"</note> has a fifth, and so on for the others. As if *b* measures *a*, there will be in *a* a part named by *b*. For let it measure it as many times as unity <note>term: unity/vnitas | The number one, considered the building block of all numbers.</note> is in *c*. Then by Proposition 16, *c* will also measure *a* as many times as unity is in *b*. Therefore the whole part is *c*, of which *b* is the number of units. And because unity is a part of every number named by it through common knowledge, *c* will be the part of *a* named by *b*, which is what was proposed.

# Proposition 39.

To find the smallest number having parts of the proposed denominations <note>term: denominations | In this context, the "name" of a fraction's divisor. For example, the denomination of a "third" is 3.</note>. From which it is manifest that the smallest number measured by any given numbers is the smallest having parts denominated by them.
¶ Let *a, b, c, d* be the numbers denominating the proposed parts, and *e* be the smallest number measured by them, taken according to Proposition 36 <note>original: "sumptum secundum 36"; Prop. 36 describes finding the Least Common Multiple (LCM) of three numbers.</note>: I say that *e* is the one we seek. For let the individual numbers measure it as *f, g, h, k*. It will be by Proposition 16 and this common science: unity is a part of every number named by it: so that conversely *f, g, h, k* measure *e* according to *a, b, c, d*; wherefore they are parts of it named by those denominations. Therefore, *e* has parts of the proposed denominations. ¶ It is also the smallest, because if there were another, such as *l*, and let the parts of *l* named by them be *m, n, p, q*, then by Proposition 16 and the aforesaid common science, *a, b, c, d* would conversely be parts of *l* named by *m, n, p, q*; wherefore *e* would not be the smallest number which *a, b, c, d* measure, which is inconvenient <note>original: "inconveniens"; in a logical proof, this means a contradiction or absurdity.</note>. ¶ Having found the minimum: if there is a desire to find the second, or whichever one you please: if the second, take double the minimum; if the third, triple; and in this manner for the others. For since every multiple of *e* is measured by *a, b, c, d* by this common science: every number measuring another necessarily measures everything measured by that one, by Proposition 37, so that every multiple of *e* has parts denominated by *a, b, c, d*. If, therefore, double *e* were not the second number having parts of the proposed denominations, there would be another second number greater than *e* and less than double *e*; and because *a, b, c, d* measure it, by Proposition 38, it follows by the corollary of Proposition 36 that *e* measures it, which is impossible. For since it measures itself, it would measure by this common science [that] every number measuring the whole and a part taken away measures the remainder: specifically, the difference between that number and itself. Which, since it is smaller than itself, a larger number would measure a smaller, which cannot be. It follows, therefore, that double *e* is the second number having parts of the proposed denominations. ¶ Similarly, you may also argue that triple *e* is the third, once the double has been proved to be the second; otherwise, because it would be less than triple and greater than double, it would follow that *e* measures something between its own double and triple, which as before is seen to be impossible. Having proved the triple is the third, by similar reasoning you will prove the quadruple is the fourth, and so on for the others.

## ¶ To find the smallest number having parts of the proposed denominations taken continuously.

¶ As in finding the smallest number having a third, which third has a fourth, which fourth also has a fifth, or a seventh, or however it may happen that they are denominated by the same or different numbers. ¶ It is necessary to multiply the denominator <note>term: denominator | The Latin "denominator" refers to the integer that names the fractional part.</note> of the first part by the denominator of the second, and the product of those by the denominator of the third, and the product of that by the denominator of the fourth, and so on for the others until the last. Whether from the first to the last or from the last to the first, whatever number results will be the one sought, as in the proposed examples 60 or 84 <note>note: 60 is the product of 3, 4, and 5 (a third of a fourth of a fifth); 84 is the product of 3, 4, and 7.</note>. ¶ Now, to have this shown demonstratively, let it be thus. Let the numbers denominating the proposed parts be *a, b, c, d*. We wish to find the smallest number which has a part denominated by *a*, such that that part has a part denominated by *b*, and that part has another denominated by *c*, and also this one has another named by *d*.

Therefore, let **d** be multiplied by **c** and let **e** be produced; and **e** multiplied by **b** and let **f** be produced; also let **f** be multiplied by **a** and let **g** be produced, which I say is the number we are seeking. Since **g** results from **a** multiplied by **f**, then by Proposition 17, **f** will be a part of **g** denominated by **a**. <note>The text is using a chain of multiplication: $d \times c = e$, then $e \times b = f$, then $f \times a = g$. By the rules of multiplication, this means $g$ can be divided by $a$ to get $f$, making $f$ the "a-th" part of $g$.</note> And because **f** was produced by the same logic from **b** multiplied by **e**, **e** will be the part of **f** denominated by **b**. But also because of this, **d** will be the part of **e** denominated by **c**. If, therefore, **g** is not the smallest such number, let there be a smaller one, **h**. Furthermore, **d** is to unity as **m** is to **n**. Therefore, by Proposition 15 <note>This refers to the "proportion of equality," a rule for comparing ratios across a series.</note>, in a proportion of equality, **g** is to unity as **h** is to **n**. Therefore, by permutation, **g** is to **h** as unity is to **n**. Since **h** is smaller than **g**, it follows that **n** must be smaller than unity. But it is impossible for a part of a number to be smaller than unity. <note>In ancient Greek and medieval mathematics, the number 1 was the smallest possible unit; there were no "fractions" smaller than 1, only "parts" of a whole.</note> Therefore, **g** is the smallest number having the parts as proposed. Having found this, if one desires to have a second or any number of such values, they must be taken from the multiples of the minimum, as was said before. ### ¶ Given any number of parts: to find the minimum number containing them.

¶ As if the proposed parts are **a, b, c**, and their denominators <note>term: denominator | The number that names the part; for example, 3 is the denominator of a "third."</note> are **d, e, f**. Let the smallest number that **d, e, f** measure be **g**. I say this is the one we seek. For the proposed parts will be in it by Proposition 37. If **g** is not the minimum number containing them, let there be a smaller one, **h**, which **d, e, f** will measure by Proposition 38. Therefore, **g** would not be the smallest number measured by them, which is a contradiction. 

I understand "parts **a, b, c**" to be placed indeterminately and not as a fixed quantity; otherwise, it would not necessarily follow that the smallest number measured by denominators **d, e, f** would be the smallest number containing the proposed parts. For it happens that one can find many parts which a number measured by their denominators does not contain. For example: Three numbers which are 120, 90, and 72 are parts of the same number. The first is a third, the second a fourth, and the third a fifth. Yet the smallest number measured by the denominators <note>The denominators are 3, 4, and 5.</note>, which is 60, does not contain these parts <note>60 is too small to contain the actual values 120, 90, and 72, even though it is the Least Common Multiple of the fractions' names.</note>. 

One must insist, therefore, that if parts are set as certain quantities, the first consequences of this demonstration follow: for it does not follow (as argued in Prop. 37) that if three measures this number, then this number is its third; rather, it *has* a third. Because of this, the proposition is the same in both ways; but the first way seems more suitable for what is intended to be proposed. One must observe that every part has a quantity; in a number, one can place any number of parts of any quantity, and inquire what is the smallest number containing them and under which denominations. It is established that the minimum number containing them is the smallest number measured by them <note>In modern terms, the Least Common Multiple of the values themselves.</note>. 

Conversely, one can set any number of denominations and inquire in what minimum number these denominations are found, and according to what quantities. It is established that the minimum is the smallest number measured by those denominations. In both cases, the minimum is sought because there are infinite numbers that contain these parts or in which these denominations are found. Again, one can set any number of parts and the same number of denominations, or vice versa—but not just any part with any denomination. If I were to set the parts three, four, and five, and their denominations as 6, 7, and 8, and ask what number contains these parts under those denominations, I would be like a vain inquirer seeking the impossible. <note>It is impossible because a "6th part" of a number cannot be 3 if an "8th part" of the same number is 5; the ratios do not match.</note> It is therefore appropriate to set specific parts with specific denominations and inquire which number contains those parts under those denominations. There is only one such minimum; whether one part and one denomination are proposed, or many of each.

it will not be possible to take more numbers than those that contain what was proposed. For it is only the **three** <note>original: "ternarius"</note> which is a fifth <note>This refers to the specific numerical relationship discussed in the preceding proof.</note>: no more. Likewise, it is only that whose **three** is an eighth and whose **six** is a fourth: no more. Therefore, when proposing parts and their denominations within a whole, one should not ask which smallest number contains these parts under those denominations, but rather which single number contains them. However, when proposing parts alone, it is appropriate to ask which smallest number contains them and by which numbers they are denominated within it. When proposing denominations alone, it is suitable to ask which parts are designated by them and in what smallest number they are found. It seems more convenient, however, to investigate parts through denominations than denominations through parts; for indeed, the diversity of proportions accompanies the diversity of denominations, not of the parts.

**Here ends the seventh book; here begins the Eighth book.**

The **sides** of numbers are said to be those whose multiplication produces the numbers. ¶ A **surface** <note>term: surface | Also called a "plane number," this is a number representing the area of a rectangle, formed by multiplying two "side" numbers.</note> is the name given to a number which is contained by two sides. ¶ A **solid** is a number contained by three sides, which is produced by their continuous multiplication. ¶ A **square** is a surface number consisting of equal sides. ¶ A **cube** is a solid consisting of equal sides. ¶ Surface or solid numbers are called **similar** if their sides are proportional.

### Proposition 1

**If there are any number of numbers in continued proportion, and the two extremes are prime to each other, it is necessary that all of them be the smallest in their proportion.**
¶ Let **a**, **b**, and **c** be in continued proportion <note>term: continued proportion | A sequence where the ratio of each number to the next is constant, such as 4:6:9 (both are 2:3).</note>, and let the extremes **a** and **c** be prime to each other <note>term: prime to each other | Often called "coprime," meaning they share no common factor other than 1.</note>. I say that there cannot be as many smaller numbers found in that same proportion. For if it were possible, let them be **d**, **e**, and **f**. By Proposition 15 of the seventh book, **a** is to **c** as **d** is to **f**. And because **a** and **c** are the smallest in their proportion according to Proposition 23 of the same book, it follows by Proposition 21 that **a** would measure <note>In this context, "measure" means "to divide evenly into."</note> **d**, and **c** would measure **f**. Thus, the larger numbers would measure the smaller ones, which is impossible.

### Proposition 2

**To find as many numbers as one wishes in continued proportion according to a given ratio, which are the smallest [in that ratio]. From which it will be manifest: that if there are three numbers in continued proportion that are the smallest, the two extremes will be squares; and if there are four, the extremes will be cubes.**
¶ Let **a** and **b** be the smallest numbers of the given ratio. Let **a** be multiplied by itself to produce **c**, and by **b** to produce **d**. Also let **b** be multiplied by itself to produce **e**. Then **c**, **d**, and **e** will be in continued proportion in the ratio of **a** to **b** by Propositions 18 and 19 of the seventh book. And because **c** and **e** are prime to each other by Proposition 28 of the same book, **c**, **d**, and **e** will be the smallest in the given ratio by the previous proposition. Now multiply **a** by all of those to produce **f**, **g**, and **h**; and multiply **b** by **e** to produce **k**. Then **f**, **g**, **h**, and **k** will also be in continued proportion in the ratio of **a** to **b** by Propositions 18 and 19 of the seventh book. They are also the smallest by Proposition 28 and the previous one. In this way and by this logic, one may find...

### Proposition 4.

<margin>
<image-desc>A set of horizontal line segments arranged in rows to illustrate proportional relationships between numbers.
