**Given as many proportions as one wishes in their smallest numbers, to find the smallest numbers in those same proportions continually proportional.**

Let the assigned proportions in their smallest terms be found as the 34th Proposition of the Seventh Book <note>Book VII, Prop 34 explains how to find the least common multiple of two numbers.</note> teaches. Let the first be between **a** and **b**, the second between **c** and **d**, the third between **e** and **f**, and let there be more if more were given. I wish to continue these proportions in four smallest numbers. I therefore take **g**, the smallest number which **b** and **c** both measure <note>i.e., the least common multiple of b and c</note>. As many times as **b** measures **g**, so many times let **a** measure **h**. Likewise, let **d** measure **k** as many times as **c** measures **g**. Therefore, if **e** measures **k**, let it be that **f** measures **l** just as many times. Then **h**, **g**, **k**, **l** will be the numbers we seek. For it is established by Proposition 18 of the Seventh Book that **h** is to **g** as **a** is to **b**, and **g** is to **k** as **c** is to **d**, and **k** is to **l** as **e** is to **f**. 

They are also the smallest; for if there were other smallest numbers like **m**, **n**, **p**, **q**, it would be necessary by Proposition 21 of the Seventh Book (taken twice) that both **b** and **c** measure **p**, whereby **g** would also measure it; and by the corollary of Prop 35 of the Seventh Book, this is inconsistent. Therefore, **h**, **g**, **k**, **l** are the smallest. But if **e** does not measure **k**, let **m** be the smallest number measured by them (namely **e** and **k**). As many times as **m** measures **k**, so many times let **h** measure **n** and **g** measure **p**. By Proposition 18 of the Seventh Book, **n**, **p**, **m** will be in the proportion of **h**, **g**, **k**. Wherefore **n** is to **p** as **a** is to **b**, and **p** is to **m** as **c** is to **d**. But as many times as **e** measures **m**, so many times let **f** measure **q**. By the same rule, **m** will be to **q** as **e** is to **f**. It is manifest, therefore, that the assigned proportions are continued in the four numbers **n**, **p**, **m**, **q**. If these were not the smallest, let there be others if possible, **r**, **s**, **t**, **x**. Since by Prop 21 of the Seventh Book (taken twice) both numbers **b** and **c** measure **s**, it follows by the corollary of Prop 35 of the Seventh Book that **g** measures it, whereby **k** will also measure **t**. And since by Prop 21 of the Seventh Book **e** measures that same **t**, then **m** would not be the smallest number measured by **k** and **e**. By this reasoning, you will be able to continue a fourth and any number of others without any hindrance.

### Proposition 5.

**For any two composite numbers, the ratio of one to the other is produced from the ratios of their sides.**

<note>In ancient Greek and medieval mathematics, a "composite number" is often visualized as a "plane number"—the product of two numbers (its "sides"). For example, 12 is a composite number with sides 3 and 4.</note>

What Proposition 24 of the Sixth Book proposes regarding parallelograms with equal angles, this proposes here regarding composite numbers. Let there be two composite numbers **a** and **b**. Let the sides of **a** be **c** and **d**, and the sides of **b** be **e** and **f**. I say that the ratio of **a** to **b** consists of the ratio of **c** to **e** and the ratio of **d** to **f**. For let **g** be produced by multiplying **d** and **e**. Since **a** is produced from **d** and **c**, and **g** is produced from **d** and **e**, by Proposition 18 of the Seventh Book, **a** is to **g** as **c** is to **e**. And by Proposition 19 of the same book, **g** is to **b** as **d** is to **f**. Therefore, by the definition of proportion, the ratio of **a** to **b** is composed of the ratio of **c** to **e** and the ratio of **d** to **f**, which is what was proposed. Nor is it necessary that we continue the ratios of the sides (namely **c** to **e** and **d** to **f**) in the smallest found numbers according to the teaching of the preceding propositions, as some teach; for this is beyond what is necessary for the proposal. For it is argued that if those smallest were **h**, **k**, **l**, so that **h** is to **k** as **c** is to **e**, and **k** is to **l** as **d** is to **f**, the ratio of **a** to **l** would be composed of the ratios of the proposed sides. And by taking **g** to be formed from **d** and **c**, **a** to **g** is argued...

### Proposition 6.

**If** the first of any number of continued proportionals <note>A sequence of numbers where the ratio between any two consecutive terms is the same, such as 2, 4, 8, 16.</note> does not measure <note>In Euclidean mathematics, one number "measures" another if it divides into it perfectly with no remainder.</note> the second, then none of them will measure the last.

Let **a**, **b**, **c**, **d**, **e** be in continued proportion. I say that if **a** does not measure **b**, then none of them will measure **e**. It is manifest, however, that if it did measure it, all would measure **e**; quite simply, any preceding number would measure any following number. If, however, it does not measure it, it is clear that **d** will not measure **e**, nor will any of them measure the one immediately following, because they are placed in continued proportion. But that no other, such as **c**, measures it is established thus: let as many smallest continued proportionals be taken, according to the teaching of the second [proposition] of this book, in the same proportion as there are from **c** to **e**, and let these all be the following: **f**, **g**, **h**. By the third [proposition] of this book, **f** and **h** will be prime to each other <note>Numbers are "prime to each other" if they share no common divisor other than 1.</note>. And because by equal proportion **c** is to **e** as **f** is to **h**, and since **f** does not measure **h**, neither will **c** measure **e**. In the same way, no other will measure it; therefore, what was proposed is clear.

### Proposition 7.

**If** the first of several continued proportionals measures the last, that same number will also measure the second.

Let the numbers be as before in continued proportion. I say that if **a** measures **e**, it will also measure **b**. Otherwise, by the preceding [proposition], it would not measure **e**, which is contrary to the premise and impossible. Not only will it measure **b**, but also all the others, and each of them will measure any number following it.

### Proposition 8.

**If** any number of continued proportionals fall between two numbers, it is necessary that just as many fall between any other two numbers related in the same proportion.

Let there be **a** and **b**, between which fall **c** and **d** in continued proportion, having the same proportion as **e** to **f**. I say that just as many fall between **e** and **f** in the same proportion as those between **a** and **b**. For let **g**, **h**, **k**, **l** be as many smallest numbers as there are **a** and **b** [and the numbers] that fall between them, taken in continued proportion in the same ratio as the second [proposition] of this book teaches. By the third [proposition], **g** and **l** will be prime to each other; and by equal proportion, **g** is to **l** as **a** is to **b**, and therefore as **e** is to **f**. And because they are the smallest in their proportion by the 23rd [proposition] of the Seventh Book, it follows by the 21st [proposition] of the same that **g** measures **e**, and **l** measures **f** equally <note>Meaning they share the same multiplier.</note>. Let it measure them as many times as **b** measures **m** and **k** measures **n**. By placing **m** and **n** between **e** and **f**, it is established by the 18th [proposition] of the Seventh Book that **e**, **m**, **n**, **f** are in continued proportion, just as **g**, **h**, **k**, **l** are, and therefore just as **a**, **c**, **d**, **b** are. Wherefore what was said is clear. 

From this, it is established that no superparticular <note>original: "supricularē." A superparticular ratio is one where the numerator is one greater than the denominator (e.g., 3:2, 4:3, 9:8).</note> ratio can be divided into equal [rational] parts; for if this were so, it would be necessary for a middle number to fall between two numbers differing by only a single unit, which cannot be. Therefore, the whole tone in music, which the sesquioctave <note>original: "sexquioctā." The ratio 9:8.</note> proportion contains, cannot be divided into two true [equal] semitones; it is necessarily divided into a minor semitone and a major semitone.

### Proposition 9.

**If** any number of continued proportionals fall between two numbers prime to each other, it is necessary that just as many continued proportionals fall between each of those numbers and unity <note>The number 1.</note>.

Let **a** and **b** be prime to each other, between which fall in continued proportion **c** and **d**. I say that there will be just as many in continued proportion between **a** and unity, and likewise just as many between **b** and unity. For let **e** and **f** be the smallest in that proportion, taken as the 34th [proposition] of the Seventh Book teaches; from these, let three continued proportionals and smallest be taken...

->Proposition 10.<-

**If** between each of two numbers and the unit any number of numbers fall in continued proportion, then it is necessary that between both numbers there fall just as many numbers in continued proportion. <note>original: "continua proportionalitate" — this refers to a geometric progression like 1, 2, 4, 8.</note>
Let there be two numbers **a** and **b**, and let **c** and **d** be between **a** and the unit, and likewise **e** and **f** between **b** and the unit, in continued proportion. I say that there are just as many between **a** and **b** in continued proportion. This is the converse of the previous proposition, except that in the previous one it was specified that **a** and **b** were prime to each other, which is not required here for this property; therefore, this property is more general than the previous subject. Because, therefore, as many times as the unit is in **d**, so many times is **d** in **c**, and so many times is **c** in **a**, it is clear that from **d** into itself comes **c**, and from the same **d** into **c** comes **a**. Similarly, from **f** into itself and into **e** will come **e** and **b**. Let **d** be multiplied by **f** and let the product be **g**. Furthermore, let the same **d** be multiplied by **g** and **e**, and let the products be **h** and **k**. It is clear from the 18th proposition of the seventh book <note>Euclid VII.18: If two numbers multiplied by another make certain numbers, the products will have the same ratio as the multipliers.</note> that **d** is to **g** as **d** is to **f**. And from the 19th that **a** is to **e** as **d** is to **f**. Wherefore **c, g, e** are in continued proportion in the ratio of **d** to **f**. Again, by the 18th, **a, h, d, b** are as **d** to **g**, and **b** to **k** as **g** to **e**, and by the 19th, **k** to **b** as **d** to **f**. Therefore **a, h, k, b** are in continued proportion; wherefore the proposition is established.

<image-desc>A diagram for Proposition 10 showing three horizontal lines of different lengths. The top line is the longest and is marked with points a, h, k, b. The middle line is of medium length and marked c, g, e. The bottom line is the shortest and marked d, f.</image-desc>

->Proposition 11.<-

**If** both numbers are squares, the proportion of one to the other will be as the <term>duplicate proportion</term> <note>A "duplicate proportion" is the ratio of the squares of the sides. If the sides are x and y, the duplicate proportion is x²:y².</note> of its side to the side of the other. If indeed both are cubes, the proportion of one to the other will be as the <term>triplicate proportion</term> <note>A "triplicate proportion" is the ratio of the cubes, i.e., x³:y³.</note> of its side to the side of the other.
Let there be two squares **a** and **b**, and two cubes **c** and **d**. Let the sides of the squares and the cubes be **e** for **a** and **c**, and **f** for **b** and **d**. I say that the proportion of **a** to **b** will be as **e** to **f** duplicated, and **c** to **d** as the same tripled. For it is manifest that from **e** into itself comes **a**, and from the same **e** into **a** comes **c**. So also from **f** into itself comes **b**, and from it into **b** comes **d**. Therefore, let **e** be multiplied by **f** and let the result be **g**, and [multiplied] into **g** and **b**, and let the results be **h** and **k**. By the 18th proposition of the seventh book, **a** will be to **g** as **e** to **f**, and by the 19th, **g** to **b** as **e** to **f**. Therefore, by definition, **a** is to **b** as **e** to **f** duplicated, which is the first part. The second part is established in the same way: for by the 18th, **a** is to **h** as **a** is to **g**, and **b** is to **k** as **g** is to **b**, and by the 19th, **k** to **d** as **e** to **f**. Wherefore **c, h, k, d** are in continued proportion in the ratio of **e** to **f**. By definition, therefore, **c** will be to **d** as **e** to **f** tripled; which is the second part.

<image-desc>A diagram for Proposition 11 showing three horizontal lines. The top line is the longest and marked c, h, k, d. The middle line is marked a, g, b. The bottom line is the shortest and marked e, f.</image-desc>

->Proposition 12.<-

**If** each of a series of numbers in continued proportion is multiplied by itself, the resulting products will be in continued proportion. And if again these products are multiplied by their original numbers, those products must also be in continued proportion, and the same for all numbers produced in this way from the extremes.

¶ Let **a, b, c** be in continued proportion. <note>original: "continue proportionales"</note> Let each be multiplied by itself so that from **a** comes **d**, from **b** comes **e**, and from **c** comes **f**. I say that **d, e, f** are in continued proportion. Furthermore, if **a** is multiplied by **d** to produce **g**, **b** by **e** to produce **h**, and **c** by **f** to produce **k**, I say also that **g, h, k** will be in continued proportion. Let **l** be the result of **a** multiplied by **b**, and **m** be the result of **c** multiplied by the same [**b**]. Then, by Propositions 18 and 19 of the seventh book, **d, l, e, m, f** are in continued proportion in the same ratio as **a, b, c**. Therefore, by the rule of equal proportionality, <note>Euclid's "ex aequali" rule for proportions.</note> argue that **d** is to **e** as **e** is to **f**, which is the first part. For the remainder: let **a** be multiplied by **l** and **e** to produce **n** and **p**, and let **c** be multiplied by **e** and **m** to produce **q** and **r**. By the same propositions, **g, n, p, h, q, r, k** will also be in continued proportion in the same ratio as the first numbers. Therefore, by equal proportionality, conclude that **g** is to **h** as **h** is to **k**, which is the remainder. The same reasoning will hold as many times as the first numbers are multiplied into the products. <note>This proves that if numbers are in a geometric progression, their squares, cubes, and higher powers will also be in a geometric progression.</note>

->Proposition 13<-

<image-desc>A diagram with horizontal segments. The main column has three segments labeled a, e, and b. To the right are two smaller segments labeled c and d.</image-desc>

If a square <term>number measures</term> <note>In Euclidean geometry, "to measure" (numerare) means one number is a factor of another; for example, 2 measures 6.</note> another square number, the side of the first is proven to measure the side of the second. Conversely, if the side of one measures the side of another, the square of the first measures the square of the second.
¶ Let two numbers **a** and **b** be squares, and their sides be **c** and **d**. I say that if **a** measures **b**, then **c** will also measure **d**, and vice versa. It is established that from **c** multiplied by itself comes **a**, and from **d** multiplied by itself comes **b**. Let **e** be produced from **c** multiplied by **d**. Then, by Propositions 18 and 19 of the seventh book, **a, e, b** are in continued proportion in the ratio of **c** to **d**. If, therefore, **a** measures **b**, then by the 7th proposition of this book, it will also measure **e**; therefore **c** measures **d**, which is the first part. The converse is clear as follows: if **c** measures **d**, **a** will measure **e**, because the ratio of **a** to **e** is the same as **c** to **d**. And if it measures **e**, it will itself measure **b**, because they are in continued proportion.

->Proposition 14<-

<image-desc>A diagram with three columns of horizontal segments. The left column contains segments a, h, k, and b. The middle column has segments e, g, and f. The right column has two small segments labeled c and d.</image-desc>

If a <term>cube</term> <note>A number multiplied by itself twice, like 2 x 2 x 2 = 8.</note> measures another cube, the side of the first will measure the side of the other. Conversely, if the side measures the side of the other, the cube will measure the cube.
¶ Let two numbers **a** and **b** be cubes and their sides be **c** and **d**. I say that if **a** measures **b**, **c** will also measure **d**, and vice versa. Let **c** be multiplied by itself to produce **e**, and **d** by itself to produce **f**. It is established then that from **c** into **e** comes **a**, and from **d** into **f** comes **b**. Let **g** be produced from **c** multiplied by **d**. By Propositions 12 and 19 of the seventh book, **e, g, f** are in continued proportion in the ratio of **c** to **d**. Furthermore, let **h** and **k** be produced from **c** multiplied by **g** and **f**. By the same reasoning, **a, h, k, b** will also be in continued proportion in the same ratio. Therefore, if **a** measures **b**, then by the 7th proposition of this book, it will measure **h**; therefore **c** measures **d**, for **c** is to **d** as **a** is to **h**. Thus the first part is established. The converse is clear, just like the converse of the previous one. For if **c** measures **d**, **a** will also measure **h**; and if it measures that, it is necessary that it measures **b**.

->Proposition 15<-

<image-desc>A diagram with two columns of horizontal segments. The left column has segments labeled a and b. The right column has smaller segments labeled c and d.</image-desc>

If a square number does not measure another square number, neither will its side measure the other's side. Conversely, if the side does not measure the other's side, it is proven by necessity that the square does not measure that square.
¶ This 15th proposition proposes that the negations are converted—which are the opposites of the affirmations that the 13th proposition of this book proposed to be converted. For example, if there are two square numbers **a** and **b**, whose sides are **c** and **d**, if **a** does not measure **b**, **c** will also not measure **d**. And conversely: even if **c** does not measure **d**, neither does **a** measure **b**. First, let it be that **a** does not measure **b**. If, then, **c** measures **d**, by the second part of the 13th proposition of this book, **a** would also measure **b**, which is contrary to the position; thus the first part is clear. The second is also clear: let it be that **c** does not measure **d**. If, then, **a** measures **b**...

by the first part of [Proposition] 13. It is necessary that **c** measures **d**. <note>original: "numeret." In this context, to "measure" means to divide without a remainder.</note> It is therefore necessary that it measures it when it does not measure it: which is impossible. Moreover, just as it is necessary for the opposite negations to be converted into the affirmations which [Proposition] 13 demonstrated to be convertible; so also it is necessary that those negations which are opposed to those affirmations which the premise demonstrated to be convertible are themselves converted. From which, if a cube does not measure a cube, neither will its side measure the side of that other cube; and conversely, if the side of one does not measure the side of the other, neither will the cube itself measure the other cube. This is demonstrated by the premise through the "destruction of the consequent" <note>A logical proof method known as *modus tollens*: if the result is false, the cause must be false.</note>; just as that which was proposed through [Proposition] 13. Therefore, the author did not propose this [explicitly], but through that which was proposed, he allowed it to be understood.

### Proposition 16.

<image-desc>Diagram for Proposition 16: Three horizontal lines on the left labeled 'a', 'g', and 'b'. To their right is a vertical stack of four smaller lines labeled 'c', 'd', 'e', and 'f'.</image-desc>

**If** two plane numbers <term>superficial: geometric numbers representing area, i.e., the product of two factors</term> are similar, it is necessary that a third number exists between them in a continued proportion; and the ratio of one number to the other similar one will be as the duplicate ratio <note>A duplicate ratio is the square of the ratio of the sides (e.g., if the sides are 2:3, the duplicate ratio is 4:9).</note> of its side to the corresponding side of the other.

Let there be two plane and similar numbers **a** and **b**: I say that between them one number will fall in continued proportion. For let the sides of **a** be **c** and **d**, and let the sides of **b** be **e** and **f**. By the conversion of the definition of similar numbers, **c** is to **e** as **d** is to **f**. It is established that from **c** times **d** comes **a**, and from **e** times **f** comes **b**. Therefore, let **g** be produced from **c** times **f**. By Proposition 19 of the seventh book, **a** is to **g** as **d** is to **f**; and by Proposition 18 of the same book, **g** is to **b** as **c** is to **e**. Therefore, **a** is to **g** as **g** is to **b**. Thus, **g** is the mean in continued proportion between **a** and **b**, which is what was proposed. The conclusion is evident, since **a** is to **b**, by definition, as **a** is to **g** duplicated, which is the same ratio as **c** to **e**.

### Proposition 17.

<image-desc>Diagram for Proposition 17: Three horizontal lines on the left labeled 'a', 'c', and 'b'. To their right is a vertical stack of four smaller lines labeled 'd', 'f', 'e', and 'g'.</image-desc>

**If** a third number exists between two numbers in a continued proportion, those two numbers are plane and similar.

This is the converse of the preceding: so that if between **a** and **b** there is **c** established in a continued proportion, **a** and **b** will be plane and similar. For let **d** and **e** be the least numbers in the ratio by which **a, c, b** are continued. By Proposition 21 of the seventh book, these will measure **a** and **c** equally: let it be according to [the factor] **f**. By the same [proposition], they will measure **c** and **b** equally: let it be according to **g**. Therefore, by definition, **a** and **b** are plane numbers; and also by definition, **d** and **f** are the sides of number **a**, and **e** and **g** are the sides of number **b**. How they are similar is held thus: since from **d** times **g** comes **c**, and from **e** times **f** comes the same **c**, then by the second part of Proposition 20 of the seventh book, **d** is to **e** as **f** is to **g**. Therefore, by definition, **a** and **b** are similar, which is what was proposed. This last point—that **a** and **b** are similar—can also be obtained through Propositions 19 and 18 of the seventh book and through these hypotheses, because **a, c, b** are in continued proportion in the ratio of **d** to **e** (the least numbers measuring **a** and **c** according to **f**, and **c** and **b** according to **g**).

### Proposition 18.

<image-desc>Diagram for Proposition 18: Partially visible lines at the bottom right indicating the start of a geometric demonstration for three-dimensional numbers.</image-desc>

**If** there are two similar solid numbers <term>solid: geometric numbers representing volume, i.e., the product of three factors</term>, it is necessary that two numbers exist between them in a continued proportion. And the ratio of one solid to the other similar one is as the triplicate ratio <note>A triplicate ratio is the cube of the ratio of the sides (e.g., if the ratio of the sides is 2:3, the triplicate ratio is 8:27).</note> of any of its sides to the corresponding side of the other.

Let there be two similar solid numbers **a** and **b**: I say that between them two numbers will fall in continued proportion. For the sides of number **a** are **c, d, e**, and the sides of **b** are **f, g, h**. By the conversion of the definition of similar numbers, **c** is to **f** and **d** is to **g** just as **e** is to **h**. Thus, let **k** be produced from **c** times **d**, and **l** from **f** times **g**. By the definition, **k** and **l** will be plane and similar numbers.

Therefore, by [Proposition] 18 of this book, one number will fall between them as a mean proportional according to the proportion of **c** to **f**, which let be **m**. It is manifest, moreover, that from **e** times **k** results **a**, and from **h** times **l** results **b**. If, therefore, from **e** times **m** and **c** result **n** and **p**, they will be, by [Proposition] 18 of the seventh book, as **a** is to **n**, so **k** is to **m**, and as **n** is to **p**, so **m** is to **l**. Therefore **a**, **n**, and **p** are continually proportional in the proportion of **c** to **f**. And because by [Proposition] 19 of the same book, **p** is to **b** as **e** is to **b**, and therefore as **c** is to **f**, it follows that the four numbers **a**, **n**, **p**, and **b** are continually proportional according to the proportion of **c** to **f**. Thus, between **a** and **b** there are two mean numbers, **n** and **p**, interposed by the continued proportionality of their sides; which is what was proposed. Furthermore, it is clear that since the proportion of **a** to **b** is, by definition, as **a** to **n** tripled <note>original: "triplicata." In Euclidean mathematics, a "triplicate ratio" is the ratio of two volumes (cubes), which is the ratio of their sides raised to the third power ($a^3:b^3$).</note>, it is the same as that which is **c** to **f**.

### Proposition 19.

**If two mean numbers lie between any two numbers according to a continued proportionality, then those two numbers are solid and similar.**

This is the converse of the preceding [proposition]: that if between **a** and **b** there are two mean numbers **c** and **d** in a continued proportion, then **a** and **b** will be solid <term>solid: a number formed by the multiplication of three factors, representing volume</term> and similar. For let the three least numbers in that same proportion be taken, which are **e**, **f**, and **g**. By [Proposition] 17, **e** and **g** will be plane numbers <term>superficiales: numbers representing area, formed by the multiplication of two factors</term> and similar. Therefore, let **h** and **k** be the sides of **e**, and **l** and **m** be the sides of **g**. By the sixteenth conclusion of this book, **e** will be to **f** as **h** is to **l**, or as **k** is to **m**. It is manifest, moreover, from the third [proposition], that **e** and **g** are prime to each other <note>original: "contra se primi." This means they share no common factors other than 1.</note>; and therefore, by [Proposition] 23 of the seventh book, they are the least in their proportion. And because by equal proportionality **a** is to **d** and **c** is to **b** as **e** is to **g**, it follows by [Proposition] 21 of the seventh book that they measure **a** and **d** equally, which let be according to **n**, and likewise **c** and **b** equally, which let be according to **p**. Because, therefore, from **h** times **k** results **e**, and from **h** times **n** results **a**, it follows by definition that **a** is a solid number and its sides are **h**, **k**, and **n**. Similarly, because from **l** times **m** results **g**, and from **g** times **p** results **b**, it also follows that **b** is a solid number and its sides are **l**, **m**, and **p**. That these are similar will be established since from **g** times **n** results **d**, and from the same [g] times **p** results **b**, there will be by [Proposition] 18 of the seventh book a ratio of **n** to **p** as **d** is to **b**. And because the ratios were thus from **d** to **b** and **k** to **m**, it is manifest by definition that **a** and **b** are similar; which is what was proposed.

### Proposition 20.

**If, of three numbers in a continued proportion, the first is a square, the third must also be a square.**

Let there be three continually proportional numbers **a**, **b**, and **c**, and let **a** be a square. I say that **c** is also a square. For by [Proposition] 17, **a** and **c** are plane numbers and similar; since therefore **a** is a square by the hypothesis, **c** will also be a square <note>A square is simply a plane number where both sides/factors are equal. If they are similar and one is square, the other must be as well.</note>.

### Proposition 21.

**If, of four numbers in a continued proportion, the first is a cube, it is necessary that the fourth be a cube.**

Let there be four continually proportional numbers **a**, **b**, **c**, and **d**, and let **a** be a cube. I say that **d** is also a cube. For it is established by [Proposition] 19 that **a** and **d** are similar solid numbers; and since **a** is a cube by the hypothesis, **d** will also be a cube.

### Proposition 22.

**If there are two numbers whose ratio is as a square to a square, and one of them is a square, then the other must also be a square.**

Let there be two numbers **a** and **b** in the proportion of two squares, which are **c** and **d**. Let either **a** or **b** be a square. I say the remaining one is a square. For since **c** and **d** are squares, it follows that they are similar plane numbers. Therefore, by [Proposition] 16, one mean proportional falls between them in continued proportion; and therefore, by [Proposition] 8, one also falls between **a** and **b**, and by [Proposition] 20, the proposition is established.

### Proposition 23.

### Proposition 23

<image-desc>To the right of the text, four horizontal line segments are arranged in two columns. The left column shows a line labeled "a" above a line labeled "b". The right column shows a line labeled "c" above a line labeled "d".</image-desc>

If there are two numbers whose ratio to one another is as a cube is to another cube, and one of them is a cube, then the other must also be a cube.
¶ Let there be two numbers **a** and **b** in the proportion of two cubes **c** and **d**, and let **a** (or **b**) be a cube. I say that the remaining number is also a cube. For it is necessary by [Proposition] 18 <note>This refers to the previous book's property regarding similar solids</note> that **c** and **d** are <term>similar solids</term> <note>Similar solids are numbers whose sides are proportional; all cubes are inherently similar to one another.</note>. Since all cubes are similar and solid, according to [Proposition] 18, two <term>mean proportionals</term> fall between them in continued proportion. Therefore, by [Proposition] 8, the same number of means will fall between **a** and **b**. Thus, by [Proposition] 21, the statement is manifest.

### Proposition 24

<image-desc>To the right of the text, six horizontal line segments are arranged in two columns. The left column contains lines labeled "a", "c", and "b" from top to bottom. The right column contains lines labeled "d", "e", and "f" from top to bottom.</image-desc>

For <term>similar plane numbers</term> <note>Latin: "superficialium similiū." These are numbers that can be represented as rectangles with proportional sides.</note>, the ratio of one to the other is as the ratio of a square to a square.
¶ Let **a** and **b** be similar plane numbers. I say that the ratio of one to the other is as the ratio of a square to a square. For by [Proposition] 16, there will be one mean proportional number between them, which let be **c**. If we take the three smallest numbers in that same proportion, which are **d**, **e**, and **f**, then by the second corollary, **d** and **f** will be squares. And because by <term>equal proportionality</term> <note>A method of comparing ratios across different sets of numbers.</note> **a** is to **b** as **d** is to **f**, it is established that the proposition is true.

### Proposition 25

<image-desc>To the right of the text, eight horizontal line segments are arranged in two columns. The left column contains lines labeled "a", "c", "b", and "d" from top to bottom. The right column contains lines labeled "e", "f", "g", and "h" from top to bottom.</image-desc>

For any two similar solid numbers, the ratio of one to the other is as the ratio of some cube to another cube.
¶ Let **a** and **b** be similar solids. I say that the ratio of one to the other is as some cube to another cube. Indeed, by [Proposition] 18, there are two mean proportional numbers between them, which let be **c** and **d**. In their same proportion, let there be the four smallest numbers: **e**, **f**, **g**, and **h**. Of these, **e** and **h** will be cubes by the second corollary. Therefore, since by equal proportionality **a** is to **b** as **e** is to **h**, the proposition is clear.

Here ends the Eighth Book. Here begins the Ninth Book.

### [Definitions]

An **even number** is one that can be divided into two equal parts. ¶ An **odd number** is one that cannot be divided into two equal parts; it exceeds an even number by one unit. ¶ An **evenly even** number is one which all even numbers measuring it do so by even times. ¶ An **evenly odd** number is one which all even numbers measuring it do so by odd times. ¶ An **evenly even and odd** number is one which even numbers measuring it do so sometimes by even times and sometimes by odd times. ¶ An **oddly odd** number is one which all odd numbers measuring it do so by odd times. ¶ A **perfect number** is so called when it is equal to the sum of all its parts <note>The "parts" are the proper divisors of the number. For example, 6 is perfect because 1+2+3=6.</note> which measure it. ¶ An **abundant** number is one which is less than the sum of its parts. ¶ A **deficient** <note>original: "diminutus"</note> number is one which is greater than the sum of its parts.

### Proposition 1

<image-desc>To the right of the text, there are two sets of horizontal line segments. On the left, two short vertical lines connect three horizontal segments, the top labeled "a" and the bottom labeled "d". In the center is a single horizontal segment. On the right, another set of three horizontal segments are connected by vertical bars, the top labeled "b" and the bottom "c".</image-desc>

If there are two similar plane numbers, the number produced from the multiplication of one by the other must be a square.
¶ Let **a** and **b** be similar plane numbers, and from their multiplication let **c** be produced. I say that **c** is a square. For let **d** be produced from **a** multiplied by itself. By [Proposition] 18 of the seventh book, **d** is to **c** as **a** is to **b**. And because one mean proportional falls between **a** and **b** in continued proportionality by [Proposition] 17 of the eighth book, it follows by [Proposition] 8 of the same book that one mean also falls between **d** and **c**. Thus, since **d** is a square, by [Proposition] 20 of the same book, **c** will also be a square, which is what was to be shown.

<image-desc>A diagram showing four horizontal lines. The top pair is labeled 'b' and 'a'. The bottom pair is labeled 'c' and 'd'. These represent the numbers being multiplied and their products.</image-desc>

### Proposition 2

If the product of two numbers is a <term>square number</term> <note>original: "tetragonus"; a number formed by multiplying a number by itself, such as 4 or 9</note>, then those two numbers are <term>similar plane numbers</term> <note>original: "superficiales similes"; numbers whose sides are in the same ratio to one another</note>. From this it is evident:
1. That if a square is multiplied by a square, the product will be a square.
2. If the product of a square and some other number is a square, then that other number must be a square.
3. If the product of a square and some other number is not a square, then that other number is not a square.
4. If a square is multiplied by a number that is not a square, the resulting product must not be a square.

¶ This is the converse of the previous proposition. Suppose that from **a** multiplied by **b**, the product **c** is produced, and **c** is a square. Then **a** and **b** will be similar plane numbers. For let **d** be the product of **a** multiplied by itself; then, by [Book] VII, Proposition 18, the ratio of **d** to **c** is as **a** to **b**. Since both **d** and **c** are squares, they are similar plane numbers. By [Book] VIII, Proposition 8, there is one mean proportional number between them. Therefore, there is also one mean between **a** and **b**. Thus, by [Book] VIII, Proposition 17, **a** and **b** are similar plane numbers, which is what was to be proven. The first part of the <term>corollary</term> <note>original: "conetarius" or "consectarium"; a logical consequence following a proof</note> is clear from the premise, for all squares are similar plane numbers. The second part is clear from this proposition, as only a square is similar to another square. The third and fourth parts follow by the logic of contradiction from the preceding parts.

<image-desc>A vertical diagram consisting of five horizontal line segments. To the left, they are labeled 'b', 'a', 'd', 'c', and the Roman numeral 'I' (representing unity or the number 1).</image-desc>

### Proposition 3

If a <term>cube number</term> <note>a number formed by multiplying a number by itself twice, like 2 × 2 × 2 = 8</note> is multiplied by itself, the product will be a cube.
¶ Let **a** be a cube, which when multiplied by itself produces **b**. I say that **b** is a cube. Let **c** be the <term>side</term> <note>original: "latus"; what we now call the cube root</note> of cube **a**. Let **d** be the product of **c** multiplied by itself. It is clear that **c** times **d** results in **a**. Therefore, the <term>unit</term> <note>original: "unitas"; the number 1</note>, **c**, **d**, and **a** are in <term>continued proportion</term> <note>a sequence where the ratio of each number to the next is constant</note>, as is manifest from [Book] VII, Proposition 18 and the current hypotheses. Because the ratio of **a** to **b** is as the unit is to **a** (since the unit is in **a** as many times as **a** is in **b**), there will be two mean numbers between **a** and **b** in continued proportion by [Book] VIII, Proposition 8. Since **a** is a cube by hypothesis, **b** must also be a cube by [Book] VIII, Proposition 21, which was to be demonstrated.

<image-desc>Four horizontal line segments arranged in two rows. The top row is labeled 'a' and 'b'. The bottom row is labeled 'd' and 'c'.</image-desc>

### Proposition 4

If a cube number is multiplied by another cube, the product will be a cube.
¶ Let **a** and **b** be cubes, and let **c** be the product of **a** multiplied by **b**. I say that **c** is a cube. Let **d** be the product of **a** multiplied by itself. By the previous proposition, **d** is a cube. Since, by [Book] VII, Proposition 18, the ratio of **a** to **b** is as **d** to **c**, it is established by [Book] VIII, Proposition 23 that **c** is a cube, which is what was to be proven.

<image-desc>Four horizontal line segments arranged in two rows. The top row is labeled 'b' and 'a'. The bottom row is labeled 'c' and 'd'.</image-desc>

### Proposition 5

If a cube number is multiplied by another number and the product is a cube, then the number it was multiplied by must also be a cube. From this it is also manifest: that if a cube is multiplied by a non-cube, the product is a non-cube; and if a cube is multiplied by some number and the product is not a cube, the number it was multiplied by must be a non-cube.
¶ Let the product of cube **a** and number **b** be cube **c**. I say that **b** is a cube. Let **d** be the product of **a** multiplied by itself, which by the proposition before last [Proposition 3] is a cube. Therefore, since by [Book] VII, Proposition 18, the ratio of **a** to **b** is as **d** to **c**, and **a**, **d**, and **c** are all cubes, then by [Book] VIII, Proposition 23, **b** must be a cube, which is what was to be proven. The first part of the corollary is clear from the negation of this fifth proposition, and the second follows similarly by the negation of the previous proposition [Proposition 4].

### Proposition 6

If a <term>cube</term> <note>original: "cubus"; a number formed by multiplying a number by itself twice, such as 2 × 2 × 2 = 8</note> is produced by multiplying a certain number by itself, then that original number is necessarily proven to be a cube.
¶ Let it be that from **a** multiplied by itself, **b** is produced, and let **b** be a cube. I say, therefore, that **a** is a cube. For let **c** be produced from **a** multiplied by **b**; by definition, **c** will be a cube. And since it is established from [Book] VII, Proposition 18 that **a** is to **b** as **b** is to **c**, and since **b** and **c** are cubes, it follows from [Book] VIII, Proposition 23 that **a** is a cube, which is what was to be proposed.

### Proposition 7

If a <term>composite number</term> <note>original: "numerus compositus"; a number that can be divided evenly by numbers other than one and itself</note> is multiplied by any number, the product that is produced will be a <term>solid number</term> <note>original: "solidus"; a number representing the product of three factors, viewed as the three dimensions of a solid shape</note>.
¶ Let **a** be a composite number, let it be multiplied by **b**, and let **c** result. I say that **c** is a solid number. Since **a** is composite, it is measured by some number, let it be **d**, which contains it according to [the units in] **e**. Therefore, because **a** is produced from **e** multiplied by **d**, and **c** is produced from **a** multiplied by **b**, it follows from the definition of solid numbers that **c** is solid, and its sides are **e**, **d**, and **b**, which is what was to be proposed.

### Proposition 8

If there are numbers in <term>continuous proportion</term> <note>original: "continue proporzionales"; a geometric progression where the ratio between any two consecutive numbers is constant, e.g., 1, 2, 4, 8...</note> starting from <term>unity</term> <note>original: "vnitate"; the number one</note>: the third from unity will be a square, and every other one thereafter <note>the 3rd, 5th, 7th, etc.</note>. The fourth from unity will be a cube, and every third thereafter <note>the 4th, 7th, 10th, etc.</note>. Furthermore, the seventh from unity is a <term>square-cube</term> <note>original: "quadratus cubicus"; a number that is both a perfect square and a perfect cube, such as 64</note>, and every sixth thereafter in the sequence is also a square-cube.
¶ Let the numbers in continuous proportion be unity, **a**, **b**, **c**, **d**, **e**, **f**, **g**, **h**, **k**, **l**, **m**, and **n**. I say that **b** is a square, and **d** (skipping **c**), and so on, always skipping one. Thus, simply put, all those in odd positions are squares, such as the third, fifth, and seventh. I also say that **c** is a cube, and **f** (skipping two), and so on for the others. Simply put, every number whose position from unity is one more than a multiple of three is a cube: such as the fourth, seventh, tenth, thirteenth, and sixteenth; for in these positions fall all those that skip two. Furthermore, I say that **f**, the seventh from unity, is a square-cube; and similarly **n**, with five numbers skipped between them; and the same for the others. Simply put, I say that whatever position from unity is one more than six or any multiple of six—such as the seventh, thirteenth, nineteenth, and twenty-fifth—that number is a square-cube. It is a square because its position is odd, and it is a cube because its position is one more than a multiple of three; for it is necessary that all multiples of six are also multiples of three. These propositions are established as follows: From the hypothesis, **a** is in **b** as many times as unity is in **a** <note>meaning 1:a = a:b</note>; therefore, by definition, **b** is a square. Because **b**, **c**, and **d** are in continuous proportion and **b** is a square, it follows from [Book] VIII, Proposition 17 or 20 that **d** is a square. By the same reasoning, **f** is a square because **d**, **e**, and **f** are in continuous proportion and **d** is a square; the same follows for the others, skipping one. Thus the first part is clear.
Second: Since **b** is in **c** as many times as **a** is in **b**, it follows from the definition that **c** is produced from **a** multiplied by its own square, **b**. Therefore, by the definition of a cube, **c** is a cube. And because **c**, **d**, **e**, **f** are in continuous proportion, and likewise **f**, **g**, **h**, **k**, and since **c** is a cube, it is necessary by [Book] VIII, Proposition 19 or 21 that **f** also be a cube, and likewise **k**, and the same for the others skipping two; which makes the second part clear.
Furthermore, since in **f** (the seventh) and in **n** (the thirteenth) and others skipping five means—simply put, in all those whose position is always one more than any multiple of six—the computations of squares and cubes coincide. In these, by skipping one, it follows they are squares (from the first part), and by skipping two, it follows they are cubes (from the second part). Therefore, they are square-cubes. Thus the whole of what was said is established.

# Proposition 9

**If any number of numbers are arranged in <term>continuous proportion</term> <note>original: "continua pportionalitate"; a sequence where each number is multiplied by the same factor to get the next, such as 1, 2, 4, 8</note> starting from unity, and the number following unity is a <term>square</term>, then all the others will also be squares. If, however, the one following unity is a <term>cube</term>, then all the others will also be cubes.**

¶ Let there be a sequence in continuous proportion starting from unity as before. Let **a** <note>the first number after 1</note> be a square; I say that all the following numbers are squares. Or let that same **a** be a cube; then I also say all the following are cubes. It is established that **b** is a square by the previous proposition <note>Proposition 8</note>. Since the ratio of **a** to **b** is the same as **b** to **c**, it follows from [Book] VIII, Proposition 27 that **c** is a square. You can also argue this from Propositions 17 or 20 of the same book. You shall prove the same for the following numbers in the same manner; thus the first part is clear. The second part is shown thus: since **b** is produced by **a** multiplied by itself, if **a** is a cube, then by Proposition 3, **b** will also be a cube. It is established that **c** is a cube by the previous proposition. Therefore, by [Book] VIII, Proposition 23, you will prove that **d** and all following numbers are cubes. For the ratio of **a** to **b** is the same as **c** to **d**. You can also argue this from Propositions 19 or 21 of the same book, for **a**, **b**, **c**, **d**, and also **b**, **c**, **d**, **e**, and any four taken in sequence, are in continuous proportion.

# Proposition 10

**If any number of numbers are arranged in continuous proportion starting from unity, and the number following unity is not a square, then none of the others will be a square—except for unity and the third number, and those found thereafter by always skipping one. If, however, the second number from unity <note>the number "a"</note> is not a cube, none of the others will be a cube—except for unity and the fourth number, and those formed thereafter by always skipping two.**

This proposition infers the opposite of the previous one. I say "part of the opposite" because it is known from Proposition 8 that all numbers in odd positions <note>the 1st, 3rd, 5th, etc.</note> are squares. Likewise, all those whose position is the third, or adds one to any multiple of three <note>the 1st, 4th, 7th, etc.</note>, are cubes. Let there be a sequence from unity in continuous proportion, but let **a** be neither a square nor a cube. I say that none of the numbers are squares or cubes except those identified by Proposition 8. For if any other were assumed to be a square, it follows from [Book] VIII, Proposition 22 that **a** must be a square. And if any other were a cube, it follows from Proposition 23 of the same book that **a** must be a cube. Both of these contradict our <term>hypothesis</term> <note>original: "ypothe"; the starting assumption</note>. Therefore, the proposition stands.

# Proposition 11

**If any number of numbers are arranged in continuous proportion starting from unity, and some <term>prime number</term> <note>a number only divisible by 1 and itself</note> measures <note>original: "numeret"; divides evenly into</note> the last number, it is necessary that it also measures the number following unity.**

¶ Let the numbers up to **d** be in continuous proportion from unity; and let **e** be a prime number which we assume measures **d**. I say that the same number will measure **a**. For if it does not, it will be prime to it according to [Book] VII, Proposition 32. Since **b** is produced from **a** multiplied by itself, it follows from Proposition 26 of the same book that **e** would also be prime to **b**, and likewise prime to **c** and to **d**. It follows that it would be prime to it by Proposition 25 of the same book, because **c** is produced from **a** times **b**, and **d** from **a** times **c**. Therefore, it would not measure **d** if it were prime to it, which contradicts our hypothesis.
The same can be shown another way: since **e** is prime, if it does not measure **a**, it will be prime to it by [Book] VII, Proposition 32. Thus, by Proposition 32 of that book, they will be the least in their ratio. Since by hypothesis **e** measures **d**, let it be according to the number **f**. It is known that **d** is produced from **a** times **c**; therefore, by the second part of [Book] VII, Proposition 20, **a** is to **e** as **f** is to **c**. Thus by Proposition 21 of the same book, **e** will measure **c**. Let this be according to **g**. Since **c** is produced from **a** times **b**, it also follows by the same reasoning and in the same way that **e** will measure **b**. Let this be according to **h**. And since **b** is produced from **a** multiplied by itself, it is again necessary by the same reasoning that **e** measures **a**. But it was assumed that it did not measure it; thus an impossibility occurs.

# IX

**In a sequence of numbers in <term>continuous proportion</term> <note>a geometric progression, e.g., 1, 2, 4, 8, 16</note> starting from unity, a smaller number <term>measures</term> <note>divides exactly without a remainder</note> a larger one according to some other number found within that same sequence.**

¶ Let there be a sequence from unity up to **f** in continuous proportion. I say that none of them measures **f** except according to one of the others in the sequence: for it is clear that **e** measures **f** according to **a**. This is because **e** is to **f** as unity is to **a**. Furthermore, **d** measures the same **f** according to **b**, because by equal proportionality, **d** is to **f** as unity is to **b**. Concerning **c**, it is also clear in the same way that it measures **f** according to itself <note>meaning c multiplied by itself equals f, if c is the middle term</note>. Conversely, **a** measures **f** according to **e**, because just as unity is to **c**, so **a** is to **f**. Likewise, **b** measures it according to **d**, for as unity is to **b**, so **b** is to **f**. Therefore, the proposition is true. Indeed, whichever number is proposed to measure the last number will be found at the same distance from unity as the last is from the measuring number; it is proven to measure it by the definition of equal proportionality.

### Proposition 13

**If any number of numbers are in continuous proportion starting from unity, and the number following unity is a <term>prime number</term> <note>a number only divisible by 1 and itself</note>, then the greatest of them will be measured by no number except those already arranged in that sequence.**

¶ Let there be, as before, numbers in continuous proportion from unity up to **d**. Let **a** be a prime number: I say that no number will measure the last one—nor indeed any of them—unless it is one of those numbers that precedes the last one in the sequence. For if it were possible, let there be some number **e** that is different from those in the sequence and measures **d**. If **e** were prime, by Proposition 11 <note>of this same Book IX</note>, it would measure **a**. Therefore **a** would not be prime, which <term>contradicts the hypothesis</term> <note>original: "ↄ̄ ypoth."; goes against the initial assumption that 'a' is prime</note>. 

If, however, **e** is a <term>composite number</term> <note>a number with factors other than 1 and itself</note>, it is necessary by Proposition 30 of the Seventh Book <note>of Euclid's Elements</note> that some prime number measures it. This prime could only be **a**. For if it were another number besides **a**, such as **f**, since it must measure **d**, it would follow that it also measures **a** by Proposition 11; thus **a** would not be prime. Therefore, it is the prime **a** that measures **e**. 

Since **e** measures **d**, let it be according to **g**. By the second part of Proposition 20 of the Seventh Book, **a** is to **e** as **g** is to **c**. Since **d** is produced from **a** times **c**, and **a** measures **e**, then **g** will measure **c**. Let it be according to **h**. It follows that **a** measures **g**, just as it followed that it measured **c**. Otherwise, if **g** were prime while measuring **c**, it would follow from Proposition 11 that it measures **a**. If it were composite, by the same reasoning, it would follow that a prime number measuring **g** also measures **a**, which is <term>inconsistent</term> <note>original: "incōueniēs"; a logical absurdity</note>. 

Thus **a** measures **g**. It follows then, by the second part of Proposition 20 of the Seventh Book, that **c** also measures **b**, because it is established that it can be produced both from **a** times **b** and from **g** times **b**. Let **c** measure **b** according to **k**. It is clear, as before with **g**, that **a** measures **b**. For if not, **a** would not be prime. Thus, by the second part of Proposition 20 of the Seventh Book, it follows that **k** measures **a**. Let it be produced from **a** times itself as well as from **b** times **k**.

¶ It is manifest, however, that **k** is not **a**. None of the numbers **g, h, k** is among the numbers **a, b, c, d**. For if **g** were one of them, since it measures **d** according to **e**, it would be established by the previous proposition <note>Proposition 12</note> that **e** is also one of them. But it was not. Therefore **g** is not one of them. Similarly, since **b** measures **c** according to **g**, **b** would not be one of **a, b, c**. For it would be shown to be so by the previous proposition, and it was shown that it is not. Therefore, neither is **b**, nor by the same reasoning is **k**. For since **k** measures **b** according to **b**, if **k** were **a**, it would be proven by the previous proposition that **b** is also **a**. But it was not. Therefore **k** will not be **a**, yet it measures it. Thus **a** is not prime, which is impossible.

¶ Alternatively, the same thing: if **e**, being different from **a, b, c, d**, measures **d**, let it be according to **f**. And because the prime number **a** measures **d** (the product of **c** and **f**), it follows from Proposition 33 of the Seventh Book that it measures **e** or **f**. Let it measure **e**. Therefore, since **d** is produced from **a** times **c** and also from **e** times **f**, it will be, by the second part of Proposition 20 of the Seventh Book, that **a** is to **e** as **f** is to **c**. Therefore **f** measures **c**. Let it be according to **g**. It will be, by Proposition 33 of the Seventh Book, that **a** also measures **f** or **g**. Let it be **f**. It follows by the second part of Proposition 20 of the same book that **g** measures **b**. Let it be according to **b**, as before. Therefore **a** will measure **g** or **b**. Let it measure **g**. Therefore, by the second part of Proposition 20, it will measure **a**. If, therefore, **b** is not equal to **a**, **a** will not be prime, which is contrary to the hypothesis. If they were equal, each of the numbers **g, f, e** would be one of the numbers **a, b, c, d** by the previous proposition...

...it must be assumed. Therefore, **e** is not different from them: which is also contrary to the hypothesis. Thus it is clear that what is proposed is true.

## Proposition 14

**If a number is the smallest that is <term>measured</term> <note>divided exactly</note> by specific <term>prime numbers</term> <note>numbers divisible only by 1 and themselves</note>, no other prime number will measure it except for those originally assigned.**

Let **a** be the smallest number measured by the prime numbers **b**, **c**, and **d**. I say that no other prime besides them will measure **a**. If, however, there is another prime **e** that measures it according to **f** <note>meaning e × f = a</note>; since each of the numbers **b**, **c**, and **d** measures **a** (the product of **e** times **f**), and each of them is prime, it follows from <note>original: "33. septimi"</note> the 33rd proposition of the seventh book that each of them must measure either **e** or **f**. But none of them measures **e**, since **e** is prime. Therefore, each of them measures **f**. Since **f** is smaller than **a** (as it measures it according to **e**), **a** would not be the smallest number measured by those primes, which is a contradiction.

## Proposition 15

**If any number of numbers in <term>continuous proportion</term> <note>a geometric progression</note> are the <term>least in their ratio</term> <note>the simplest form of the ratio, such as 2:3 instead of 4:6</note>: whichever of them measures another, it will be <term>commensurable</term> <note>sharing a common factor</note> to the other terms of that ratio.**

¶ Let **a**, **b**, **c**, **d**, **e** be in continuous proportion and the least in the ratio of **f** to **g**, which themselves are the least in their ratio. Suppose **b** measures **c**. I say that **b** is commensurable to **f** or **g**. Let there be taken the four least in that same ratio, which are **k**, **l**, **m**, **n**. It is clear from the second proposition of the eighth book that from **f** times **m** comes **c**; otherwise, it would happen that something is less than the minimum, which cannot be. Therefore, by the 33rd conclusion of the seventh book, **b** will be commensurable to **f** or **m**. If it is commensurable to **f**, the proposition is established. If it is commensurable to **m**, let there be taken in the same ratio the three least, which are **p**, **q**, **r**. From the second of the eighth book, **m** is produced from **f** times **r**, and we would be forced to concede something is less than the minimum. Wherefore, by the aforesaid conclusion, **b** is commensurable to **f** or **r**. But it was not **f**, for then the proposition would already be established. Therefore, it is commensurable to **r**. Since **r**, by the second of the eighth book, is produced from **g** multiplied by itself, it follows from the stated conclusion that **b** is commensurable to **g**, which is what was proposed.

## Proposition 16

**If any number of numbers are in continuous proportion and are the least in their ratio, any one of them is necessarily proved to be prime to the sum of the remaining ones.**

¶ Let **a**, **b**, **c**, **d** be in continuous proportion and the least in their ratio. I say the sum of **a**, **b**, and **c** is prime to **d**. For if not, some number **e** will measure the sum of **a**, **b**, **c** and also **d**. By the previous proposition, therefore, **e** will share a factor with one of the terms of that ratio, which are **f** and **g**. There will thus be some number measuring **e** and one of the two, **f** or **g**, let it be **h** <note>OCR reads 'b' here, but 'h' is used for the common divisor in geometric proofs</note>. Because **h** measures **e**, it will measure **d** and the sum of **a**, **b**, and **c**. And because it measures **f** or **g**, both of which measure each of the middle terms—and simply all of them if there are more than two—it follows from the second of the eighth book that it measures **b** and **c**. Therefore it also measures **a**, because it measures the whole sum **a**, **b**, and **c**. Thus **a** and **d** are not prime to each other, which is impossible by the third proposition of the eighth book. Similarly, the proposition will be established that the sum of **a**, **b**, and **d** is prime to **c**. For if, as before, **e** measures both, it follows by the previous proposition that some number, which may also be **h**, measures **e** and one of the two, **f** or **g**. Thus **h** measures **c** and the whole sum **a**, **b**, **d**. But since **h** measures all the middle terms along with both roots <note>f and g</note>, it therefore also measures the sum of **a** and **d**. And since it necessarily measures one of the two, **a** or **d**, while measuring one of the two, **f** or **g**, it will also measure the other. Therefore **a** and **d** are not prime to each other; and so the result is the same as before. ¶ The same is demonstrated otherwise concerning three numbers in continuous proportion and the least in their ratio, without the help of the previous proposition; they prove that the sum of any two is prime to the remaining one. Let there be three in continuous proportion and the least, **a**, **b**, **c**, whose terms are **d** and **e**. I say now the sum of **a** and **b** is prime...

<meta>This page continues the arithmetical demonstrations of Euclid’s Book IX. It concludes a proof regarding the relationship between sums of numbers and their primality relative to one another, then transitions into a series of fundamental rules for multiplication that mirror the geometric theorems found in Book II of the Elements.</meta>

...to be relatively prime to **c**; and the sum of **b** and **c** to be prime to **a**; likewise the sum of **a** and **c** to be prime to **b**. For it is manifest from the <note>original: "secunda octaui"</note> second proposition of the eighth book that from **d** multiplied by itself comes **a**; from **d** multiplied by **e** comes **b**; and from **e** multiplied by itself comes **c**. From the <note>original: "22. septimi"</note> 22nd proposition of the seventh book, **d** and **e** are <term>prime to one another</term> <note>coprime; they share no common factors other than 1</note>. Therefore, from the first part of the 29th proposition of the same book, the whole **d** + **e** will be prime to each of them. Since, therefore, each of the two numbers **d** and **d + e** is prime to **e**, it follows by the 25th proposition of the same book that the product of **d** and **d + e**—which is the sum of **a** and **b**—is prime to **e**. It follows then by the 26th proposition of the same book that the sum of **a** and **b** is also prime to **c** (for **c** is produced by **e** multiplied by itself). By a similar demonstration, you will prove that the sum of **b** and **c** is prime to **a**. 

But to show that the sum of **a** and **c** is prime to **b**, proceed as follows: since each of the two, **d** and **e**, is prime to the whole **d + e**, then by the 25th proposition of the seventh book, their product—which is **b**—is prime to **d + e**. Therefore, by the 26th proposition of the same book, the square of **d + e**—which is the sum of **a**, **c**, and twice **b**—will be prime to **b**. It follows then that the sum of **a** and **c** is prime to **b**. For it is necessary that when a sum of two numbers is prime to one of the numbers that compose it, it must also be prime to the remaining one; this was demonstrated above in the 29th proposition of the seventh book. To strengthen this demonstration, it must be established that the sum of **a** and **b** is produced from **d** multiplied by the sum of **d** and **e**, assuming that **d** squared is **a** and **d** times **e** is **b**. Likewise, the square of **d + e** produces the sum of **a** and **c** and double **b**, assuming as before that **e** squared is **c**. For the sake of this, the following demonstrations are proposed.

**The product of one number multiplied by any number of others is equal to the product of that same number multiplied by the sum of those others.** 
<note>This is the distributive law: a(b+c+d) = ab + ac + ad.</note> 
The same is proposed in the first proposition of the second book regarding lines. For let it be that from **a** multiplied into **b**, **c**, and **d**, there come **e**, **f**, and **g**. I say that from **a** multiplied into the sum of **b**, **c**, and **d**, there comes the sum of **e**, **f**, and **g**. It follows from the conversion of the definition of multiplication that the part **b** is to **e**, and the part **c** is to **f**, and the part **d** is to **g**, as the unit is to **a**. Therefore, by the fifth proposition of the seventh book, the whole sum of **b**, **c**, and **d** will be the same part of the sum of **e**, **f**, and **g** as the unit is to **a**. Therefore, by definition, from **a** multiplied into the sum of **b**, **c**, and **d** comes the sum of **e**, **f**, and **g**, which is what was proposed. 

**The product of any number of numbers multiplied into one is equal to the product of their sum multiplied into that same one.**
This is the converse of what was just demonstrated. As if from **b**, **c**, and **d** multiplied into **a**, there come **e**, **f**, and **g**; the same sum will result from their sum multiplied into the same number. This is easily concluded from the 17th proposition of the seventh book and the previous demonstration. 

**The product of any number of numbers multiplied into any number of other numbers is equal to the product of the sum of the first group multiplied into the sum of the second group.** 
For example, if **a**, **b**, and **c** multiply **d**, **e**, and **f**, each multiplying each, and the products are joined together: I say the total of the products is equal to the product of the sum of **a**, **b**, and **c** multiplied into the sum of **d**, **e**, and **f**. This is clear from the preceding rules. 

**When a number is divided into any number of parts, the square of the whole is equal to the products of the whole multiplied by all its parts.** 
<note>a² = a(b + c + d) where a = b + c + d.</note> 
The same is proposed in the second proposition of the second book regarding lines. For instance, if **a** is divided into **b**, **c**, and **d**, I say that the square of **a** is equal to **a** multiplied by **b**, **c**, and **d**. For if **e** is set equal to **a**, it is clear from the first of these incidental rules that **e** times **a** is equal to **e** times all the parts of **a**. But by definition, **e** times **a** is the square of **a**, and **e** times the parts of **a** is the same as **a** times those same parts. It is manifest, therefore, that what is said is true. 

**When a number is divided into two parts, the product of the whole and one of the parts is equal to the square of that part plus the product of the two parts.** 
<note>a × c = c² + (b × c) where a = b + c.</note> 
The same is proposed in the third proposition of the second book regarding lines. Let **a** be divided into **b** and **c**. I say that **a** times **c** is equal to **c** squared plus **c** times **b**. For **a** times **c** is the same as **c** times **a** by the 17th proposition of the seventh book. Taking **d** equal to **c**, then **a** times **c** is the same as **d** times **a**. But by the first of these rules, **d** times **a** is equal to **d** times **b** and **d** times **c**. Since **d** is equal to **c**, then **d** times **a**, **b**, and **c** is the same as **c** times **a**, **b**, and itself. Thus the proposition is established.

¶ If a number is divided into two parts, the square produced from the whole multiplied by itself is equal to the squares of each of the parts multiplied by themselves, plus twice the product of one part multiplied by the other. <note>This is the arithmetical version of the algebraic identity (a + b)² = a² + b² + 2ab.</note>

<image-desc>A horizontal line segment representing a number. The letters "b" and "c" are at the ends of the segment, representing the two parts, and the letter "a" is centered above the whole line.</image-desc>

¶ The fourth proposition of the second book <note>original: "quarta secundi"</note> proposes the same regarding lines: as if **a.b.** were divided into **b.** and **c.**, I say that as much is produced from **a.** multiplied by itself as from **b.** by itself, **c.** by itself, and **b.** twice into **c.** For, by the fourth of these <note>referring to the propositions of this book</note>, the square of **a.** is as much as the product of itself into **b.** and into **c.** Moreover, by the preceding proposition, the product of **a.** into **b.** is as much as **b.** into itself and into **c.** And the product of **a.** into **c.**, by the same rule, is as much as **c.** into itself and into **b.** And because the product of **c.** into **b.** is the same as **b.** into **c.** (by the 17th proposition of the seventh book), it is clear that what is proposed is true.

¶ If a number is divided into two equal parts and also into two unequal parts, the product of the larger unequal part multiplied by the smaller, together with the square of the distance between the points of division <note>original: "quadrato intermedij," the square of the difference between the midpoint and the unequal cut</note>, is equal to the square of half the whole.

¶ The fifth proposition of the second book proposes the same regarding lines: as if **a.b.** were divided into two equal numbers, which are **a.c.** and **c.b.**, and also into two unequal parts where the larger is **a.d.** and the smaller is **d.b.** I say that the product of the whole **a.d.** into **d.b.**, with the square of **c.d.**, is equal to the square of **c.b.** For by the preceding proposition, the square of **c.b.** is equal to the square of **c.d.** and the square of **d.b.** and twice the product of **b.d.** into **c.d.** But the product of **b.d.** into itself and into **c.d.** is as much as its product into **c.b.** (by the first of these), and therefore as much as into **a.c.** Thus, the product of **b.d.** into itself and twice into **c.d.** is as much as the product of **b.d.** into **a.d.** Therefore, by the same logic, the square of **c.b.** exceeds the product of **b.d.** into **a.d.** by the square of **c.d.**, which confirms the proposition.

¶ When a number has been divided into two equal parts and another number is added to it: the product of the whole composite <note>the original number plus the addition</note> multiplied by the added part, together with the square of the half, is equal to the square of the composite made of the half and the added part.

¶ The sixth proposition of the second book proposes the same regarding lines: Let **a.b.** be divided into two equal numbers, **a.c.** and **c.b.**, and let the number **b.d.** be added to it. I say that the product of the whole **a.d.** into **d.b.**, with the square of **b.c.**, is equal to the square of **c.d.** For by the sixth of these, the square of **c.d.** is equal to the square of **d.b.** and the square of **b.c.** and twice the product of **d.b.** into **b.c.** But by the first of these, the product of **b.d.** into itself and twice into **b.c.** is the same as the product of **b.d.** into **d.a.** (since **a.c.** and **c.b.** are equal). Thus, the square of **c.d.** exceeds the product of **b.d.** into **d.a.** by the square of **b.c.**, which is what was proposed.

¶ When a number is divided into two, the square of the whole multiplied by itself, along with the square of one of the parts, is equal to twice the product of the whole multiplied by that same part, plus the square of the other part.

¶ The seventh proposition of the second book proposes the same regarding lines. Let the number **a.** be divided into **b.** and **d.** I say the square of **a.** with the square of **d.** is as much as twice the product of **a.** into **d.** with the square of **b.** It is established by the sixth of these that the square of **a.** is as much as the square of **d.** and the square of **b.** and twice the product of **d.** into **b.** Therefore, the square of **a.** with the square of **d.** is as much as twice the square of **d.** and twice the product of **d.** into **b.** with the square of **b.** But twice the square of **d.** and twice the product of **d.** into **b.** is the same as twice the product of **d.** into **a.** (by the first of these). Therefore, twice the product of **d.** into **a.** with the square of **b.** is equal to the square of **a.** with the square of **d.**, whereby the proposition is clear.

->To divide any number such that the product of the whole and one of its portions is equal to the square of the other is impossible.<-

<margin>
<image-desc>A horizontal line segment with five distinct points labeled 'a', 'c', 'd', 'e', and 'b'.</image-desc>

The 11th of the second book proposes this to be done with lines <note>This refers to the "Golden Ratio" construction, dividing a line in extreme and mean ratio.</note>. It demonstrates that this is impossible to do with whole numbers. For let there be any number **a.b.**; I say it is impossible for it to be divided as proposed. For if it were so divided, it would be according to a proportion having a mean and two extremes <note>The Golden Ratio</note>, as is clear from the definition and the 20th of the seventh book. But if it can be so divided, let it be divided at **c.**, and let **a.b.** be to **b.c.** as **b.c.** is to **a.c.** Thus, **a.c.** will be smaller than **c.b.** Let a part equal to it, **c.d.**, be subtracted from it. Because the proportion of the whole **a.b.** to the whole **b.c.** is the same as **b.c.** (subtracted from **a.b.**) to **c.d.** (subtracted from **b.c.**), it will be the same proportion from **a.c.** (the remainder of **a.b.**) to **b.d.** (the remainder of **b.c.**). Therefore, **b.c.** is to **c.d.** as **c.d.** is to **d.b.** Thus **c.d.** will be greater than **d.b.** Then, by subtracting **d.e.** from **c.d.** so that **d.e.** is equal to **d.b.**, the proportion of **b.c.** to **c.d.** will be as **c.d.** to **d.e.**, and as **d.b.** (the remainder of **c.b.**) is to **c.e.** (the remainder of **c.d.**). Therefore, **c.e.** can be subtracted from **e.d.**, and thus there will be no end to this subtraction <note>This is a proof by "infinite descent," showing that you can never reach a final unit, which contradicts the nature of whole numbers.</note>, which is impossible. Now let us return to the proposition.
