## Proposition 18.

<image-desc>A horizontal line segment divided by three marks, labeled a, b, and c.</image-desc>

**If, among any number of continued proportionals, the two extremes are prime to each other, it is impossible for the ratio of the first to the second to be the same as the ratio of the last to some other number.**
¶ Let **a., b.,** and **c.** be in <term>continued proportion</term> <note>A sequence where the ratio between successive terms is constant, like 4, 6, 9 (ratio 2:3).</note>. Let **a.** and **c.** be prime to each other. I say that another number cannot be added to them in that same proportion. For if it were possible, let it be **d.** Because, therefore, **a.** is to **b.** as **c.** is to **d.**, then by permutation **a.** is to **c.** as **b.** is to **d.** However, **a.** and **c.** are the least in their proportion by Proposition 23 of the seventh book; thus by Proposition 21 of the same, **a.** measures **b.** Consequently, **a.** also measures **c.**; for among numbers in continued proportion, if the first measures the second, it measures all of them, and simply any preceding number measures any following one. And since **a.** also measures itself, **a.** and **c.** would not be prime to each other, which is an inconsistency.

## Proposition 19.

<image-desc>Two sets of horizontal line segments. The top set consists of a single line divided into four segments labeled a, b, c, d. The bottom set is a single segment labeled e, aligned under segment c.</image-desc>

**To investigate, given two numbers, whether there is a third number in continued proportion with them.**
¶ Let **a.** and **b.** be the two proposed numbers; I wish to inquire whether a third can be added to them under continued proportionality. Therefore, if they are prime to each other, it is impossible by Proposition 17. If, however, they are composite, let **b.** be multiplied by itself and let **c.** be the result. If **a.** measures **c.**, the third number will exist; but if it does not measure it, it will not exist. Suppose it does measure it according to **d.**, which will be the number we seek by the second part of Proposition 20 of the seventh book. Now suppose that it does not measure it; yet let it be that **a.** is to **b.** as **b.** is to **d.** Thus, because **c.** is produced from **b.** times itself, it follows by the first part of Proposition 20 of the seventh book that the same is produced from **a.** times **d.** Therefore, **a.** measures **c.** according to **d.**, but it was posited that it did not; thus an impossibility follows.

## Proposition 20.

<image-desc>Two horizontal line segments. The upper line is divided into five parts labeled a, b, c, d, e. Below it are two separate segments labeled f and g, aligned under sections d and e.</image-desc>

**To investigate, given three numbers in continued proportion, whether there is some fourth number in continued proportion with them.**
¶ Let **a., b.,** and **c.** be in continued proportion; I wish to inquire whether another can be added to them under continued proportionality. Therefore, if **a.** and **c.** are prime to each other, it is impossible by Proposition 18. If, however, they are composite, let **d.** be the result of **b.** times **c.** If **a.** measures **d.**, the fourth number will exist; if it does not measure it, it will not. Suppose it measures it according to **e.**, which will be the number we seek by the second part of Proposition 20 of the seventh book. Now suppose that it does not measure it; yet let it be that **a.** is to **b.** as **c.** is to **e.** Thus, because **d.** is produced from **b.** times **c.**, it follows by the first part of Proposition 20 of the seventh book that the same is produced from **a.** times **e.** Therefore, **a.** measures **d.** according to **e.**, but it was posited that it did not. You can investigate the same for any number of proposed continued proportionals. For if the two extremes are prime to each other, the inquiry ends by Proposition 18. If, however, they are composite: multiply the second by the last; if the first measures the product, the factor by which it measures it is the number we seek by the second part of Proposition 20 of the seventh book. If the first does not measure the product, there will be no such number; for whatever number were posited, by the first part of the same proposition, the first would measure the product according to that posited number, which was posited not to be measured.

## Proposition 21.

**Given any number of prime numbers, it is necessary that there is some prime number different from them.**
¶ This intends nothing other than to demonstrate that prime numbers are infinite. For let **a., b.,** and **c.** be prime numbers. I say there is some prime different from them. Let **d., e., f.** be the least number which they measure <note>The least common multiple.</note>, to which, with a unit added, let **d. g.** be made, which...

...is either prime or composite. If it is prime, the proposition is established. If it is composite, it must be measured <note>In this context, "measures" means that a smaller number divides a larger number exactly, with no remainder.</note> by some prime number, let us call it **b.** It is not possible for **b.** to be any of the prime numbers originally proposed. For if it were one of them—since each of those measures the product **d. f.**—then **b.** would also measure that same product. And since **b.** also measures the total **d. g.** <note>The number constructed by adding 1 to the product of the primes.</note>, it would necessarily follow that it measures the difference **f. g.**, which is unity <note>The number 1.</note>. This is impossible <note>Because no prime number can divide 1.</note>. The same result follows if we set **d. f.** as any number which **a., b.,** and **c.** measure. Wherefore, the proposition stands.

### Proposition 22.

**If any number of even numbers are added together, the total sum produced from them will also be even.**
Let each of the numbers **a., b.,** and **c.** be even: I say that the sum composed of them is even. For, by the converse of the definition <note>The definition of an even number is one that can be divided into two equal halves.</note>, each of them has a half-part. Let their halves, therefore, be **d., e.,** and **f.** Because, then, as **a.** is to **d.**, so **b.** is to **e.** and **c.** is to **f.**, it will follow from Proposition 13 of the seventh book that the whole **a. b. c.** is to the whole **d. e. f.** in that same ratio. Thus, **d. e. f.** is the half of **a. b. c.** Therefore, by the definition, **a. b. c.** is even: which is what was proposed.

### Proposition 23.

**If an even number of odd numbers are added together, the total sum produced from them will also be even.**
Let any number of numbers, such as **a., b., c.,** and **d.,** be odd <note>The quantity of numbers added must be an even amount (e.g., four odd numbers).</note>: I say the sum composed of them is even. For if a unit is taken away from each, it is certain that the remainders are even. And because those subtracted units, when added together, form an even number (since they themselves are even in number), the proposition is established by the preceding proof.

### Proposition 24.

**If an odd number of odd numbers are added together, the total sum produced will also be odd.**
Let any number of numbers, **a., b.,** and **c.**, be odd: I say the total sum composed of them is odd. For by the preceding proposition, the sum of **a.** and **b.** will be even. And because **c.**, with a unit removed, is even, it follows from the proposition before that one <note>Proposition 22.</note> that the whole sum **a. b. c.**, with a unit removed, is even. Therefore, by the definition, it is clear that the total is odd.

### Proposition 25.

<warning>Red wax or ink stain obscures several words in Proposition 25 and 26.</warning>

**If an even number is subtracted from an even number, the remainder will be even.**
Let the whole **a.** be even, from which **b.** (which is also even) is subtracted, and let the remainder be **c.** I say that **c.** is even. For let **d.** be the half of **a.**, and let **e.** be the half of **b.** When **e.** is subtracted from **d.**, let the remainder be **f.** By Proposition 13 of the seventh book, **c.** is to **f.** as **a.** is to **d.** Wherefore **f.** is the half [of **c.**]. Thus **c.** is even: which is what was proposed.

### Proposition 26.

**If an odd number is subtracted from an odd number, the remainder will be even.**
Let the number **a. b.** be odd, from which **b. c.** (which is also odd) is subtracted. I say the remainder, which is **a. c.**, is even. For let a unit be subtracted from each of the two numbers **a. b.** and **b. c.**, which let be **b. d.** <note>Subtracting 1 from an odd number makes it even.</note>. It will then be that each of the two remainders, which are **a. d.** and **d. c.**, is even. By the preceding logic, it is therefore clear that **a. c.** is even: which is what was proposed.

### Proposition 27.

**If you subtract an even number from an odd number, the remainder is odd.**
Let **a. b.** be odd, from which **a. c.** (which is even) is subtracted. I say the remainder **c. b.** is odd. For let **b. d.** be a unit; thus **a. d.** will be even. And because **a. c.** is even, it follows from Proposition 25 that **c. d.** is even. Since **d. b.** is a unit, it follows that **c. b.** is odd: which is what was proposed.

### Proposition 28.

If from an even number you take away an odd number, the remainder is odd.
¶ Let **a. b.** be an even number from which is taken **a. c.**, which is odd: I say that the remainder **c. b.** is odd. For let a unit <note>original: "unitatem"; the number 1</note> **c. d.** be subtracted from **a. c.**; then **a. d.** will be even. Therefore, by Proposition 25, **d. b.** will also be even. Because, therefore, **d. c.** is a unit, it follows that **c. b.** is odd, which is what was proposed.

### Proposition 29.

If an odd number is multiplied into <note>In historical geometry, to "lead" or "multiply" one number into another is to find their product.</note> an even number, the product will be even.
¶ This is manifest from Proposition 23.

### Proposition 30.

If an odd number is multiplied into an odd number, the product will be odd.
¶ This is also manifest from Proposition 24.

### Proposition 31.

If an odd number measures <term>measures: divides exactly with no remainder</term> an even number, it will measure it by an even number.
¶ For if it measured it by an odd number, then from an odd multiplied by an odd, an even would be produced; which is impossible by Proposition 29. <note>The text likely meant Proposition 30 here, as odd times odd is odd.</note>

### Proposition 32.

If an odd number measures an odd number, it measures it by an odd number.
¶ For if it measured it by an even number, then from an odd number multiplied by an even number, an odd would be produced; which is impossible by Proposition 29.

### Proposition 33.

<margin>
<image-desc>Two sets of geometric line diagrams. The upper set consists of three horizontal lines: line 'a' (with points f and b marked), line 'c' (with point d marked), and line 'e'. The lower set consists of two horizontal lines: line 'c' (with point b marked) and line 'a' (with point d marked).</image-desc>

If an odd number measures an even number, it is necessary that it also measures the half of that same number.
¶ Let **a.** be an even number whose half is **b.**, and let **c.** be an odd number which measures **a.**: I say that **c.** will measure **b.** For let it measure **a.** according to **d.** <note>Meaning c times d equals a.</note>. Then by Proposition 31, **d.** is an even number. Let its half, therefore, be **e.**, and let **c.** be multiplied by **e.** to produce **f.** By Proposition 18 of the seventh book, as **a.** is to **f.**, so **d.** is to **e.** And because **a.** is to **b.** as **d.** is to **e.** <note>Since both are in a 2:1 ratio</note>, it follows that **b.** and **f.** are equal. Since, therefore, **c.** measures **f.**, it will measure **b.**, which is what was proposed.

### Proposition 34.

If an odd number is prime to <term>prime to: "relatively prime," meaning they share no common divisors other than 1</term> any number, it will also be prime to the double of that same number.
¶ Let **a.** be an odd number prime to **b.**, whose double is **c.**: I say that **a.** is prime to **c.** If it were not, let **d.** measure them. Since **a.** is odd, it follows that **d.** must be odd; for whoever measures an odd number is odd, according to the previous proposition. Therefore, **d.** will measure **b.** <note>Because d measures c (the double) and is odd, it must divide the half.</note>. Thus **a.** and **b.** are not prime to each other, which is against the hypothesis.

### Proposition 35.

<margin>
<image-desc>A diagram showing five horizontal lines of increasing length stacked vertically. They are labeled from top to bottom as: 16 (D), 8 (c), 4 (b), 2 (a). The shortest line at the bottom is labeled with the Roman numeral I (Unity). A bracket is centered below.</image-desc>
</margin>

Numbers doubled from two are "even-times-even" <term>even-times-even: numbers that are powers of 2 (2, 4, 8, 16...), having no odd factors</term> only.
¶ Let unity, **a., b., c., d.** be continuously proportional <note>A sequence where each term is multiplied by the same factor (here, 2).</note>, and let **a.** be the number two: I say all of these are even-times-even, and as they are increased infinitely according to this proportion, no others are even-times-even. Regarding these, it is clear by the definition, since by Proposition 12, any preceding number measures any following number an even number of times—all of which must be even. And no other number <note>meaning no odd number</note> measures any of them, by Proposition 13, because **a.**, which is two following unity, is prime <note>Two is the only even prime number.</note>. That no other number aside from these is even-times-even is established thus: if some other number is proposed, let it be divided into two halves, and its half into two; let this be done until either an [odd] number or unity stops the division, which must happen by the last postulate. If an [odd] number stops it, then that number measures the proposed number, so it was not even-times-even. If it ends in unity, it must be one of the numbers in the double proportion starting from unity.

## Proposition 36.

**A number whose half is odd is even-times-odd.**
Let **a.** be a number whose half, let it be **b.**, is odd; I say that **a.** is even-times-odd <note>original: "pariter impar"; this refers to an even number that, when divided by 2, yields an odd number, such as 6, 10, or 14.</note>. For let **c.** be the number two <note>original: "binarius"</note>; it is therefore manifest that from **c.** multiplied by **b.**, **a.** is produced. Now let **d.** be any even number measuring <term>measuring: dividing exactly without a remainder</term> **a.**, which measures it according to **e.** By the second part of Proposition 20 of the Seventh Book, it will be that **c.** is to **b.** as **c.** is to **d.** <note>This refers to the proportionality of factors.</note>. Therefore **e.** measures **b.** Since **c.** measures **d.**, **e.** will be an odd number. For **b.** was odd by definition; therefore **a.** is even-times-odd.

## Proposition 37.

**Every number not a power of two, whose half is even, is both even-times-even and odd-times-even.**
Let **a.** be a number that is not a power of two <note>original: "non duplus a duobus"; literally "not doubled from two," referring to numbers in the geometric sequence 2, 4, 8, 16...</note> whose half, let it be **b.**, is set as even. I say that this number is even-times-even and odd-times-even <note>original: "pariter pariterque impariter"; a number having both even and odd factors, such as 12 or 20.</note>. Let **c.** be the number two, from which it is manifest that it measures **a.** according to **b.** But because **a.** is not a power of two, it is necessary that if its half **b.** is divided into two other halves, and the half of that half into two others, eventually a number will be encountered that prevents further division; this number, because it does not accept division, will be odd. Let this number where the division stops be **d.** It is necessary to stop at a number, because if the division reached unity, **a.** would be one of the numbers doubled from two, which it is not. Regarding **d.**, it is manifest that it measures **a.** by this common principle: every number measuring another measures everything measured by that one. Therefore, let it measure it according to **e.**, and **e.** will be even. Otherwise, since **d.** is a larger odd number, it would follow by Proposition 30 that **a.** is odd. Therefore, since the even number **b.** measures **a.** according to **c.**, which is also even (for it is the number two), and yet the even number **e.** measures the same according to **d.**, which is odd, it stands by definition that the number **a.** is even-times-even and odd-times-even; which is what was proposed.

## Proposition 38.

**If from the second and the last of a series of numbers in continuous proportion a quantity equal to the first is taken away, it is necessarily proved that the ratio of the remainder of the second to the first is the same as the ratio of the remainder of the last to the sum of all those preceding it.**
Let **a. b., c. d., e. f., g. h.** be in continuous proportion. From **c. d.** let a part equal to **a. b.** be taken, which is **c. k.**, and from **g. h.** a part which is **g. l.** I say then that the proportion of the remainder **k. d.** to **a. b.** is as the remainder **l. h.** is to the sum composed of **e. f., c. d.** and **a. b.** Let there be taken from **g. h.** a part equal to **e. f.**, which is **g. m.**, and one equal to **c. d.**, which is **g. n.** Then the remainder **l. n.** will be equal to **k. d.** It is manifest through Proposition 12 of the Seventh Book that since **g. h.** is to **g. m.** as **g. n.** is to **g. l.**, the remainder **m. h.** to the remainder **m. n.** will be as **g. h.** is to **g. m.**, and therefore as **e. f.** is to **c. d.** In a similar way, **m. n.** will be to **l. n.** as **c. d.** is to **a. b.** By permutation, therefore, **m. h.** will be to **e. f.**, and **m. n.** to **c. d.**, as **l. n.** is to **a. b.** Therefore, joined by Proposition 13 of the Seventh Book, the sum **l. h.**—composed of **m. h.**, **m. n.**, and **l. n.**—to the sum composed of **e. f.**, **c. d.**, and **a. b.**, will be as **l. n.** is to **a. b.**, and therefore as **k. d.** is to **a. b.**, which is what was proposed.

## Proposition 39.

**When numbers starting from unity have been arranged in a continuous double proportion, which when joined together make a prime number, the last of them multiplied into their sum produces a perfect number.**
Let **a., b., c., d.** be continuously doubled from unity <note>The sequence 1, 2, 4, 8...</note>. Let the sum of these and the unit be **e.**, which is posited to be a prime number. Let **d.** be multiplied by **e.** and let the product be **f. g.** I say that **f. g.** is a perfect number <note>A perfect number is a positive integer that is equal to the sum of its proper divisors. Examples include 6 and 28.</note>. Let there be taken **b., k., l.** in continuous double proportion to **e.**, so that there are as many numbers in the sequence **e., b., k., l.** as there are in the continuous doubles from unity. By equal proportionality, **l.** will be to **e.** as **d.** is to **a.** Wherefore, by the first part of Proposition 20 of the Seventh Book, from **a.** multiplied into **l.** comes **f. g.** Since **f. g.** itself comes from **d.** multiplied into **e.**, and because **a.** is the number two, **f. g.** is the double of **l.** Therefore the numbers are **e., b., k., l.** and **f. g.**

# BOOK IX

...continued proportionals <note>original: "continue proportionales"; a geometric sequence where the ratio between successive terms is constant.</note>. Therefore, let there be taken from **b.** a length equal to **e.**, which shall be **m.b.**, and the remainder of **b.** shall be **n.**, which will also be equal to **e.** Likewise, from **f.g.** let there be taken a length equal to the same, which shall be **f.n.**; then, by the previous premise, **n.g.** will be as much as the sum of **c.**, **b.**, **k.**, and **l.** But since **f.n.** is equal to **e.**, it is as much as the sum of **a.**, **b.**, **c.**, **d.**, and a unit. Similarly, the whole **f.g.** is as much as the sum of all these doubled—namely **a.**, **b.**, **c.**, **d.**, and the unit—and those segments **e.**, **b.**, **k.**, and **l.** From all this, it is manifest that **c.** measures <term>measures: divides exactly without a remainder</term> **f.g.** according to **b.**, and **b.** measures it according to **k.**, which is proven from the first part of Proposition 20 of the Seventh Book, with the help of equal proportionality where necessary. For as **d.** is to **c.**, so **b.** is to **e.**; and as **d.** is to **b.**, so **k.** is to **e.** by equal proportionality. Therefore, from **c.** multiplied by **b.** and from **b.** multiplied by **k.**, it is necessary to arrive at **f.g.**, in the same way that **d.** produced **e.** If, therefore, no other number measures **f.g.**, it will be by definition a perfect number <note>original: "numerus pfectus"; a number that equals the sum of its proper divisors, like 6 or 28.</note>. That no other number measures it is clear: for if it were possible, let it be **p.** which measures it according to **q.** By Proposition 33 of the Seventh Book, **e.** would measure one of them. Let it be assumed that it measures **p.**, and by the second part of Proposition 20 of the Seventh Book, as **q.** is to **d.**, so is **e.** to **p.** It follows that **q.** measures **d.** Since **a.**, which follows the unit, is prime <note>original: "primus"; in this context, the number two, which is the first prime.</note>—for it is the number two—then by Proposition 13 of this book, **q.p.** must be **a.**, **b.**, or **c.** Whichever of these it may be, **p.** will be **l.**, **k.**, or **b.** For if **q.** were **a.**, it is established that **p.** will be **l.**; if it were **b.**, **p.** will be **k.**; and if **c.**, **p.** will also be **b.** Thus, **p.** is not different from those already established. It remains, therefore, that **f.g.** is a perfect number, which was to be demonstrated.

# BOOK X

Quantities that have a single common quantity measuring them are called commensurable <note>original: "communicantes"; sharing a common measure.</note>. Those that do not have a single common quantity measuring them are called incommensurable. Lines are said to be commensurable in power <note>original: "in potentia"; referring to the areas of the squares built upon those lines.</note> when a single common surface measures their square surfaces. Lines are said to be incommensurable in power when no single common surface measures their square surfaces. This being so, it is manifest that given any line, many others are incommensurable to it: some in length only, and others in both length and power. Now, let every line with which we reason be called rational <note>original: "rationalis."</note>. Lines commensurable with it are also called rational; those incommensurable with it are called irrational or surds <note>original: "surde"; literally "deaf" or "mute," an old term for roots that cannot be expressed as a ratio.</note>. To these, the square of the surface from which we reason by hypothesis is called rational. Surfaces commensurable with it are called rational. Surfaces incommensurable with it are called irrational or surds. The sides that have power over those squares are called rational.
**Any quantity can be multiplied so many times that it exceeds any other given quantity of the same kind.** <note>This is known as the Archimedean Property.</note>

### Proposition 1.

**If, from two unequal quantities, more than half is subtracted from the greater, and from the remainder more than half is subtracted, and this is done repeatedly in the same manner, eventually a quantity will remain that is less than the smaller of the original quantities.**
Let there be two unequal quantities, **a.** and **b.c.**, with **b.c.** being the greater. I say that more than half can be subtracted from **b.c.** or its remainder so many times that it will be necessary for a quantity smaller than **a.** to remain. For let **a.** be multiplied until it exceeds **b.c.**, and let its multiple be **d.e.f.**, which is greater than **b.c.** Now, let there be subtracted from **b.c.** more than its half, which shall be **b.g.**, and from the remainder, which is **g.c.**, let more than its half be subtracted, which shall be **g.h.** Let this be done as many times as **a.** is contained in **d.e.f.** I say then that the last remainder, as here **h.c.**, is less than **a.** Let it be multiplied...

<meta>This page transitions from the final proofs of Book IX into the foundational definitions and propositions of Book X of Euclid's Elements. Book X focuses on "incommensurable" magnitudes—what we now call irrational numbers—and begins with the "Method of Exhaustion."</meta>

For as many times as **b.c.** is multiplied to produce **a.** into **d.e.f.**, let **k.l.m.** be its multiple. Since each of the quantities **k.l.m.** is equal to **b.c.**, it follows that **r.k.** is less than **b.g.**, but **r.l.** is less than **g.h.** And since **r.m.** is equal to **b.c.**, it will be, by common notion <note>original: "p cōceptionē"; refers to the "Common Notions" or axioms at the start of Euclid's Elements.</note>, that **k.l.m.** is less than **b.c.**, and therefore less than **d.e.f.** Since, then, **d.e.f.** is to **a.** as **k.l.m.** is to **b.c.**, and **d.e.f.** is greater than **k.l.m.**, it follows by Proposition 14 of the Fifth Book that **a.** is greater than **b.e.**, which is what was proposed. The same follows if a half is taken from the greater **a.**, and then a half from the remainder, and so on until the greater is divided into as many parts as the smaller is contained in its multiple, exceeding the greater by however much. <gloss>¶</gloss> However, one ought to note that this appears to contradict Proposition 15 of the Third Book, which proposes that the angle of contingency <term>angle of contingency: the "horn-like" angle between the circumference of a circle and its tangent line</term> is smaller than any angle contained by two straight lines. For if any rectilinear angle is given, and if more than half is taken from it, and more than half from the remainder, it would seem necessary that this could be done until a rectilinear angle is left that is smaller than the angle of contingency. Proposition 15 of the Third Book argues the opposite; but these are not univocal <note>original: "vni/uoce"; meaning they are not of the same kind or species and thus cannot be compared in this way.</note> angles, for they are simply not of the same genus, being curved and straight. Indeed, it is not possible to take the angle of contingency so many times that it exceeds any rectilinear angle, which would be necessary for the present conclusion to follow from the antecedent, as is clear from the previous demonstration. It is also plain that any rectilinear angle is greater than an infinite number of angles of contingency.

### Proposition .2.

If there are two unequal quantities, and if from the greater there is subtracted a part equal to the smaller until what remains is less than the smaller; and then from the smaller there is subtracted a part equal to that remainder until less than it remains; and again from the first remainder there is subtracted a part equal to the second remainder until less than it remains; and if in this continuous subtraction no remainder is ever found to measure <term>measure: to divide exactly without leaving a remainder, like a ruler fitting perfectly into a length</term> the one that preceded it: those two quantities must be incommensurable <term>incommensurable: quantities that have no common "unit" or measure that can divide both perfectly, such as the side and diagonal of a square.</term>. <gloss>¶</gloss> A similar thing was proposed in Proposition 1 of the Seventh Book regarding numbers. Let there be two unequal quantities **a.** and **b.**, where **a.** is the greater. If a reciprocal subtraction is made as much as possible, and even if it is done infinitely many times, no quantity is found that measures the one before it, I say they are incommensurable. For if there were a common measure **c.** for them, let **b.** be subtracted from **a.** as many times as possible, and let the remainder be **d.** Let that remainder **d.** be subtracted from **b.** as many times as possible, and let the remainder be **e.** Let this subtraction be done until from either of the two quantities **a.** or **b.** there remains something less than **c.**, for this must be possible by the preceding proposition. If this **e.** is less than **c.**, then since **c.** measures **b.** (which was subtracted from **a.**), it will also measure the remainder **d.** by common notion. Therefore, since it measures **d.** (subtracted from **b.**), it will also measure the remainder **e.** But **e.** was less than the measure **c.**; therefore, a quantity measures one smaller than itself, which is impossible.

### Proposition .3.

Given two unequal commensurable quantities, to find the greatest common quantity that measures them both. <gloss>¶</gloss> From this it is manifest that whatever measures two quantities also measures the greatest quantity that measures them both. <gloss>¶</gloss> If you are not ignorant of the second proposition of the Seventh Book, you cannot be ignorant of the demonstration of this one, for the process is the same in both.

### Proposition .4.

Given three commensurable quantities, to find the greatest common quantity that measures them all. <gloss>¶</gloss> This is clear from the third proposition of the Seventh Book, just as the previous was from the second of the Seventh.

### Proposition .5.

<meta>This page continues the transition into Book X of Euclid's Elements, focusing on the relationship between magnitudes (lengths or areas) and numbers. It establishes the fundamental definitions of commensurability—whether two quantities can be measured by the same "ruler"—and how those relationships correspond to the ratios of whole numbers.</meta>

->BOOK<-

The ratio of any two commensurable <term>commensurable: quantities that can both be measured exactly by the same smaller unit</term> quantities is as that of one whole number to another.
Let there be two commensurable quantities, **a.** and **b.**; I say that their ratio is as that of some number to another number. For let **c.** be the greatest common measure <note>original: "maxima quantitas cōmuniter mensurans"; refers to the Greatest Common Divisor</note> measuring both **a.** and **b.**, found as the second proposition of this book teaches. Let **c.** measure **a.** according to the number **d.**, and let it measure **b.** according to the number **e.** The ratio of **a.** to **c.** will be as the ratio of **d.** to the unit, because just as **a.** is a multiple of **c.**, so **d.** is a multiple of the unit. Furthermore, the ratio of **c.** to **b.** is as the unit to **e.**, since just as **c.** is a submultiple of **b.**, so the unit is a submultiple of **e.** Therefore, by equal proportionality, the ratio of **a.** to **b.** is as **d.** to **e.**, which is what was proposed.

---

### Proposition .6.

If there are two quantities whose ratio to one another is as that of one whole number to another, those two quantities must be commensurable.
This is the converse of the previous proposition: if the ratio of **a.** to **b.** is as the number **c.** to the number **d.**, then the two quantities **a.** and **b.** will be commensurable. For let **e.** measure **b.** as many times as there is a unit in **d.**, and let it measure **f.** as many times as there is a unit in **c.** Since, therefore, the ratio of **f.** to **e.** is as **c.** to the unit, and the ratio of **e.** to **b.** is as the unit to **d.**, it will be, by equal proportionality, that the ratio of **f.** to **b.** is as **c.** to **d.** Because this is also the ratio of **a.** to **b.**, then by the first part of the 9th proposition of the Fifth Book, **f.** is equal to **a.** Since, therefore, **e.** measures **f.**, by definition <note>original: "per conceptionē"; refers to a common notion or axiom</note> it will also measure **a.** Thus, **a.** and **b.** are commensurable, for **e.** will measure both, which is what was proposed.

---

### Proposition .7.

For any two square surfaces whose sides are commensurable in length, the ratio of one to the other is as that of a square number to a square number. Conversely, if the ratio of one square surface to another square surface is as the ratio of a square number to a square number, their sides will be commensurable in length. Furthermore, if the ratio of a square surface to another square surface is not as that of a square number to a square number, their sides will be incommensurable in length.
Let **a.** and **b.** be two lines of squares whose areas are **c.** and **d.** I say that if **a.** and **b.** are commensurable in length, the ratio of **c.** to **d.** will be as a square number to a square number, and vice versa. But if the ratio of **c.** to **d.** is not as a square number to a square number, **a.** and **b.** will be incommensurable in length, and vice versa. However, that fourth argument is not proposed here. The first is proven thus: if **a.** and **b.** are commensurable in length, they will be (by the 5th proposition) in the ratio of two numbers, which let be **e.** and **f.**, whose squares are **g.** and **h.** Because the ratio of **c.** to **d.** is the duplicate ratio <note>original: "duplicata"; in Euclidean geometry, the ratio of areas is the "duplicate" (square) of the ratio of the sides</note> of **a.** to **b.** by the 18th proposition of the Sixth Book, it follows that the ratio of **c.** to **d.** is also the duplicate ratio of **e.** to **f.** But by the 11th proposition of the Eighth Book, the ratio of **g.** to **h.** is also the duplicate ratio of **e.** to **f.** Therefore, the ratio of **c.** to **d.** is as **g.** to **h.**, which is the first part. The second is thus: let the ratio of **c.** to **d.** be as the square number **g.** to the square number **h.** I say that **a.** and **b.** will be commensurable in length. Since the ratio of **c.** to **d.** is the duplicate of **a.** to **b.** by the 18th proposition of the Sixth Book, and the ratio of **g.** to **h.** is the duplicate of **e.** to **f.** by the 11th proposition of the Eighth Book, then the simple ratio of **a.** to **b.** is as the simple ratio of **e.** to **f.** by the 6th proposition. Therefore, **a.** and **b.** are commensurable, which is the second part. The third part is evident from the first by the destruction of the consequent <note>original: "a destructione cōsequentis"; a logical term (modus tollens) meaning if the result is false, the premise must be false</note>. Similarly, the fourth is evident from the second by the destruction of the antecedent.

If it should appear that the common diameter <term>diameter: the diagonal of a square</term> of the side <term>costa: the side of a square</term> is not this unequal thing. <note>original: "Si dyametrum communem coste nō hunc disparem esse parere." ...is not like that of square numbers: it follows that the diameter is incommensurable to the side in length. Otherwise, since four is a square number, all even-times-even numbers would be squares, as would infinitely many others which are not squares. Aristotle [Ar.] leads to this absurdity <note>original: "inconveniens"; literally an "inconvenience," but used here in the logical sense of a contradiction or *reductio ad absurdum*.</note> if the diameter is assumed commensurable to the side: that an odd number would be equal to an even one; which is shown thus. For let diameter **a.b.** be commensurable to side **a.c.** By proposition .5., **a.b.** will be to **a.c.** as some number is to another. Let these numbers be **e.** and **f.**, which are the lowest in their ratio; because of this, one of them will be odd. For if both were even, they would not be the lowest. Let their squares also be **g.** and **h.** If, therefore, **e.** is even, it follows from Book IX, proposition 30, that **g.** is also even. Let **k.** be double **h.**; then **k.** will be even by definition. Since therefore **a.b.** is to **a.c.** as **e.** is to **f.**, it follows from Book VI, proposition 8 and Book VIII, proposition 11 that the square of **a.b.** is to the square of **a.c.** as **g.** is to **h.** Thus **g.** is double **h.**, for so the square of **a.b.** is to the square of **a.c.** by the penultimate proposition of the first book <note>This refers to Euclid I.47, the Pythagorean Theorem, which proves the square of the diagonal is equal to the sum of the squares of the sides.</note>; and since **k.** is also double **h.**, it follows by Book V, proposition 9 that the odd number **g.** is equal to the even number **k.** <note>The proof reaches a contradiction: in the ratio of the diagonal to the side, a number is forced to be both even and odd simultaneously.</note> But if **e.** be even and **f.** odd: the ratio of **f.** to half of **e.** (which we call **l.**) will be as **a.c.** is to half of **a.b.** (which we call **a.d.**). Therefore the ratio of the square of **a.c.** to the square of **a.d.** is as the ratio of the number **h.** (which is odd by Book IX, prop. 30) to the square of number **l.** (which we call **m.**). If **k.** is set to be double **m.**, then **k.** will be even by definition. But since the square of **a.c.** is double the square of **a.d.** by the penultimate of the first book, **h.** will be double **m.** Since **k.** is also double **m.**, it follows by Book V, prop. 9 that the odd number **h.** is equal to the even number **k.**, which is what was to be shown.

->Proposition .8.<-

**I**f there are two quantities commensurable with one and the same quantity, it is necessary that they also be commensurable with each other.
Let each of the two quantities **a.** and **b.** be commensurable with quantity **c.** I say that **a.** and **b.** are commensurable. For by proposition .5., **a.** is to **c.** as a number is to a number; similarly, by the same proposition, **c.** is to **b.** as a number is to a number. Therefore, let number **d.** be to number **e.** as **a.** is to **c.**, and number **f.** be to number **g.** as **c.** is to **b.** But let the ratios of **d.** to **e.** and **f.** to **g.** be continued in three terms, which are **h.**, **k.**, and **l.**, as Book VIII, proposition 4 teaches; it will follow by equal proportionality that **a.** is to **b.** as number **h.** is to number **l.** Therefore, by proposition .5., **a.** and **b.** are commensurable <note>original: "communicantes"; used here as a synonym for commensurable.</note>, which is what was proposed.
From this it also follows that if there are two quantities commensurable with one another, whatever one of them is commensurable with, the other is as well; and whatever one is not commensurable with, the other is not either. For let there be two commensurable quantities **a.** and **b.**, and let there be any quantity **c.** with which **a.** is commensurable. I say that **b.** will also be commensurable with the same, which is clear from this eighth proposition since both of them are commensurable with **a.** by hypothesis. Furthermore, if **a.** and **b.** are commensurable as before, and **c.** is any quantity with which **a.** is not commensurable, I say that **b.** will not be commensurable with it either. For if **c.** were commensurable with **b.**, and **a.** was also commensurable with that same **b.** by hypothesis, then by this eighth proposition, **a.** and **c.** would be commensurable. But it was posited that they were not; therefore, what we have said is established.

Furthermore, if the whole composed of them is commensurable with one of them, I say it will be commensurable with the other, and they will be commensurable with each other in the same way. The same is true in the contrary case. For if **a.** and

### Proposition .10.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'O' depicting a floral or circular pattern.</image-desc>**O**f any four proportional quantities, if the first is commensurable to the second, the third will also be commensurable to the fourth. If, however, the first is incommensurable to the second, the third will also be incommensurable to the fourth.

¶ Let there be four proportional quantities **a. b. c. d.** I say that if **a.** is commensurable with **b.**, **c.** will also be commensurable with **d.** For if **a.** is incommensurable to **b.**, **c.** will also be incommensurable to **d.** And if **a.** is commensurable with **b.** in power <term>in potentia: referring to the squares of the lines being commensurable even if the lines themselves are not</term> only, **c.** will also be commensurable with **d.** in power only. However, the author <note>Referring to Euclid.</note> does not propose that [last part] because it is easily shown from the previous demonstrations. For if **a.** is commensurable with **b.**, it will be, by the 5th [proposition] of this book, as a number is to a number. Let it be, therefore, as **c.** is to **f.** Since it is by hypothesis that **a.** is to **b.** as **c.** is to **d.**, **c.** will be to **d.** as the number **c.** is to the number **f.** By the 6th [proposition], therefore, **c.** is commensurable with **d.**, which was the first point. The second is clear from the first by the destruction of the consequence. For if **a.** is incommensurable to **b.**, it is necessary that **c.** be incommensurable to **d.** For if it were commensurable to it, since **c.** is to **d.** as **a.** is to **b.** by hypothesis, it would be by the first part that **a.** is commensurable with **b.**, but it was not; thus the whole that the author proposes is established. Furthermore, regarding what we added—namely, that if **a.** is commensurable with **b.** in power only, then **c.** is commensurable with **d.** in power only—it is shown thus: Since **a.** is not commensurable with **b.** in length, neither will **c.** be commensurable with **d.** in length by the second part of this [proposition]. But since the square of **a.** is commensurable with the square of **b.** by hypothesis, it will be by the 5th [proposition] that the square of line **a.** is to the square of line **b.** as a number is to a number, which let be **e.** and **f.** And because the square of **c.** is to the square of **d.** as the square of **a.** is to the square of **b.**, the square of **c.** will also be to the square of **d.** as the number **e.** is to the number **f.** By the 6th [proposition], therefore, **c.** and **d.** are commensurable in power; and since they are not commensurable in length, the proposition is established.

### Proposition .11.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'P' featuring a foliage pattern.</image-desc>**P**rovided with any straight line, to find two lines incommensurable to it: one in length only, and the other in both length and power <term>potentia: meaning the squares built on the lines are also incommensurable</term>.

¶ Let line **a.** be provided: I wish to find two lines, one of which is commensurable with **a.** in power only, while the other is incommensurable to it in length and in power.

<meta>This page continues the geometric constructions and proofs of Euclid’s Elements, Book X. The previous page discussed the relationships of commensurability between magnitudes and their sums. This page concludes the construction of lines that are incommensurable in length but commensurable in square (power), and moves into Propositions 12 and 13 regarding proportions of lines and their squares.</meta>

I take, therefore, two numbers that do not have the same proportion to one another as any two square numbers. Let these be **b.** and **c.** It is easy to find such numbers, since the proportion of any square number to any non-square number is one that square numbers never share, as confirmed by Proposition 22 of Book VIII <note>Euclid's Elements, Book 8, Proposition 22: "If three numbers are in continued proportion and the first is a square, the third is also a square."</note>. Having taken two such numbers, I find a line **d.** to whose square the square of line **a.** has the same ratio as number **b.** has to number **c.** 

I find this line in the following way: I divide line **a.** into as many equal parts as there are units in number **b.**, which I do easily with the help of Proposition 11 or 12 of Book VI. Then, from the end of line **a.**, I erect a perpendicular line **e.**, which contains the same unit parts of **a.** as many times as there are units in **c.** Therefore, because of the first proposition of Book VI, the proportion of the square of line **a.** to the area <term>superficiem: literally "surface," here referring to the rectangular area</term> formed by lines **a.** and **e.** is as the ratio of line **a.** to line **e.**, and thus as number **b.** to number **c.** 

If line **d.** is placed as the mean proportional <term>medio loco proportionalis: a middle value where a:d = d:e</term> between **a.** and **e.**, as shown in Proposition 9 of Book VI, then by the first part of Proposition 16 of the same book, the square of **d.** will be equal to the area produced by **a.** and **e.** Thus, the proportion of the square of line **a.** to the square of line **d.** will be as number **b.** to number **c.** Wherefore, **a.** and **d.** are commensurable in power <note>original: "commensurabiles in potentia" - meaning their squares have a rational ratio even if the lines themselves do not</note> by the definition and the final part of Proposition 7; but they are incommensurable in length. Thus, line **d.**, which was the first line to be sought, has been found.

I find the second line in this way: I place line **f.** as a mean proportional between **a.** and **d.**, as shown in Proposition 9 of Book VI. By the conclusion of Proposition 17 of Book VI, the square of **a.** to the square of **f.** will be as line **a.** is to line **d.** Thus, by the second part of Proposition 10, the square of **a.** is incommensurable to the square of **f.** Therefore, line **f.** is incommensurable to line **a.** in power, and consequently also in length. Thus, **f.** is the second line that was to be found. And so the proposition is demonstrated.

## Proposition 12.

Of any four proportional lines, if the first is greater than the second by the square of some line commensurable to it in length, it is necessary that the third also be greater than the fourth by the square of some line commensurable to it in length. But if the first is more powerful <term>potentior: "more powerful," meaning the square of the first line exceeds the square of the second</term> than the second by the square of a line incommensurable to it in length, the third will also be more powerful than the fourth by the square of a line incommensurable to it in length. 

Let the four proportional lines be **a., b., c., d.** Let **a.** be greater than **b.**, and **c.** be greater than **d.** Let also the square of **a.** exceed the square of **b.** by the square of line **e.**, and the square of **c.** exceed the square of **d.** by the square of line **f.** I say that <note>original: "dico quod"</note> if **a.** is commensurable with **e.** in length, then **c.** will also be commensurable with **f.** in length. But if **a.** is not commensurable with **e.** in length, neither will **c.** be commensurable with **f.** in length. And if **a.** is commensurable with **e.** in power only, **c.** will also be commensurable with **f.** in power only. 

Yet the author does not propose that last point, because it is easily seen from the previous demonstration. Since the proportion of **a.** to **b.** is as **c.** to **d.**, the square of **a.** to the square of **b.** will be as the square of **c.** to the square of **d.** And because the square of **a.** is equal to the squares of the two lines **b.** and **e.**, and similarly the square of **c.** is equal to the squares of the two lines **d.** and **f.**, the proportion of the squares of the two lines **b.** and **e.** to the square of **e.** will be as the squares of **d.** and **f.** to the square of **f.** Therefore, by division <note>original: "divisim" - a method of manipulating proportions where if a/b = c/d, then (a-b)/b = (c-d)/d</note>, the square of **b.** will be to the square of **e.** as the square of **d.** is to the square of **f.** Therefore, **b.** is to **e.** as **d.** is to **f.** Likewise, by equal proportionality, **a.** will be to **e.** as **c.** is to **f.** Therefore, the first part of this proposition is established by the first part of the previous one, the second part by the second, and the third part by the third added here.

If there are two unequal lines, the longer of which is divided into two commensurable parts by an added area <term>superficies adiuncta: referring to the geometric method of 'application of areas'</term> equal to a quarter part of the square of the shorter line, which area falls short of completing the whole line...

...squares, it is necessary that the longer line be greater in square <term>potentioꝛ: literally "more powerful," referring to the area of the square a line produces</term> than the shorter line by the square of some line commensurable in length with that same longer line. If, however, the longer line is greater in square than the shorter by the square of a line commensurable with it in length, then if an area equal to a quarter of the square of the shorter line is applied to the longer line with a square shape lacking <note>This refers to a specific Euclidean technique of "application of areas" found in Book VI, Proposition 27, where a shape is drawn along a line but falls short by a specific geometric figure, in this case, a square.</note>, it is necessary that the longer line be divided into two commensurable parts.

¶ Let there be two lines, **a.b.** and **c.**, with **a.b.** being the larger. Let a quarter of the square of line **c.** be applied to line **a.b.** such that it is deficient by a square area to complete the line **a.b.** This is possible through Proposition 27 of Book VI, which is easily done in this manner: let **a.b.** be divided into two lines, **a.d.** and **d.b.**, so that between them falls half of line **c.** as a mean proportional <term>continue proportionalis: a middle value in a geometric progression, like a:x = x:b</term>. How this is done will be taught at the end of this demonstration. From Proposition 16 of Book VI, the area of **a.d.** times **d.b.** (which we call **d.e.**) will be equal to the square of half of line **c.** Therefore, from Proposition 4 of Book II, this same area will be one-fourth of the square of line **c.** Furthermore, it lacks a square area to complete line **a.b.**, since **a.d.** is equal to **d.g.** and **d.b.** is equal to **g.e.** I say, therefore, that if the area **d.e.** divides the line **a.b.** into two commensurable parts, line **a.b.** will be greater in square than line **c.** by the square of some line commensurable with it in length, and vice versa. 

Since line **a.b.** is greater than line **c.**, **a.d.** will not be equal to **d.b.** If they were equal, the area **d.e.** would be a square, and since it is equal to the square of half of **c.**, **a.d.** would be equal to half of **c.**, and the whole **a.b.** would equal the whole **c.**, which contradicts our hypothesis. Therefore, **a.d.** is not equal to **d.b.** Thus, from the larger of these, which is **d.b.**, let **d.f.** be cut off equal to **a.d.** By Proposition 8 of Book II, the square of the whole **a.b.** will be equal to four times the area of **d.b.** times **d.a.** plus the square of **f.b.** Consequently, line **a.b.** will be greater in square than line **c.** by the square of line **f.b.**, which must be commensurable with the whole **a.b.** if line **a.d.** is commensurable with line **d.b.** For if this is the case, **d.b.** will be commensurable with **d.f.** (its equal), and therefore by Proposition 9 <note>original: "p .9. b. f. cōicāt cū .f. d." referring to Book X, Proposition 9 regarding commensurability</note>, **f.b.** is commensurable with **f.d.**, and thus with the whole **a.d.**, and because of this with the whole **a.f.**, and finally with the whole **a.b.** Thus the first part is clear. 

The converse is also clear: let **a.b.** be greater in square than **c.** by the square of line **f.b.**, which is commensurable with it in length. I say then that if a quarter of the square of line **c.** is added to line **a.b.** so that a square area is lacking, it will divide line **a.b.** into two commensurable parts. For let **f.a.** be divided into equal parts at **d.**, and let the area **d.e.** be formed from **d.b.** and **d.a.** It will lack a square area to complete line **a.b.** By Proposition 8 of Book II, the square of **a.b.**, being equal to four times the area **d.e.** plus the square of **f.b.**, is equal to the square of **c.** Thus four times the area **d.e.** is equal to the square of **c.**, and so the area **d.e.** is equal to one-fourth of the square of **c.** I say then that **d.b.** is commensurable with **a.d.**, since **f.b.** is commensurable with **a.b.** If this is true, so that **a.d.** is commensurable with **a.b.**, it will also be commensurable with **a.f.** by Proposition 9, and thus with **a.d.** as well as **d.f.** Therefore, **d.b.** is commensurable with **a.d.**, which is the second part.

¶ Now it must be shown how line **a.b.**, when it is placed as greater than line **c.**, can be so divided that half of line **c.** falls between its parts as a mean proportional. When it is divided this way, the area made from one part times the other will be equal to the square of half of line **c.**, and this area will be equal to one-fourth of the square of line **c.** applied to line **a.b.** so that a square area is lacking. This is done as follows: divide **a.b.** equally at **d.**; describe upon it a semicircle **a.f.b.**; and let **b.e.** be a perpendicular to **a.b.**, which is set equal to half of line **c.** Draw **e.f.** parallel to **a.b.** until it cuts the circumference of the semicircle at point **f.** It must cut it, since line **a.b.** is greater than line **c.** Then draw **f.g.** perpendicular to **a.b.** Since by Proposition 34 of Book I it is equal to line **e.b.**, it will also be equal to half of line **c.** Now draw lines **f.a.** and **f.b.** By the first part of Proposition 30 of Book III, the angle **a.f.b.** is a right angle. Therefore, by the first part of the corollary to Proposition 8 of Book VI, line **f.g.** is the mean proportional between **a.g.** and **g.b.** Thus half of line **c.**, which is equal to it, will also be the mean proportional between them, which is what we proposed to show.

### Proposition .14.

If there are two unequal lines, and an area equal to a fourth part of the square of the shorter is applied to the longer line such that it falls short by a square area, and this divides the longer into two incommensurable parts: the square of the longer line will be greater in power <term>potentioꝛ: "more powerful," meaning the area of the square a line produces</term> than the shorter by the square of a line incommensurable in length with that longer line. If, however, the longer line is greater in power than the shorter by the square of a line incommensurable in length with it, and if an area equal to a fourth part of the square of the shorter is applied to it and falls short by a square area, it is necessary that this applied area divide the longer line into two incommensurable portions.

<margin>A marginal geometric diagram showing a vertical line segment and two adjacent rectangles. Points are labeled e, a, b, f, d, and c.</margin>

This 14th proposition follows from the third of the previously sent <note>This refers to the "premises" or propositions immediately preceding this one in Book X.</note> and its arrangement does not differ from the arrangement of that one. Indeed, the method of reasoning is the same in both cases. For if **a.d.** is not commensurable <note>original: "cōicet," meaning to communicate or be commensurable</note> with **d.b.**, then neither will **d.f.** (which is equal to it) be commensurable with that same **d.b.**; thus by the 9th proposition, **d.f.** will not be commensurable with **f.b.**, and therefore neither will **a.f.**; for **a.f.**, **f.f.**, and **f.b.** are commensurable like a numbering and a numbered thing. Therefore, neither will **a.b.** be commensurable with the line **f.b.** But if this is the case—namely, if **a.b.** is not commensurable with **f.b.**—it will not be commensurable with **a.f.**, and thus neither with **a.d.** or **d.f.**; therefore **a.b.** is not commensurable with **d.a.** It can also be demonstrated through the 14th by the preceding one: the first part of this from the second of that, and the second from the first, and by the destruction of the present case. For if **a.d.** and **d.b.** are not commensurable, then neither will **a.b.** and **f.b.** be commensurable; for if **a.b.** and **f.b.** were commensurable, it would be necessary by the second part of the premise that **a.d.** be commensurable with **d.b.**, but it was posited that they are not. In the same way regarding the second part: if **b.a.** and **b.f.** are not commensurable, then **a.d.** and **d.b.** will not be commensurable. For if they were, it follows by the first part of the premise that **a.b.** and **b.f.** would be commensurable, which they are not; therefore the proposition is clear.

### Proposition .15.

Every rectangular area which two lines rational in length contain is proved to be rational.

<margin>A marginal rectangle with corner labels a, b, c, and d.</margin>

Let there be two lines, **a.b.** and **b.c.**, containing a rectangular area **a.c.**, both being rational in length: I say that the area **a.c.** is rational. For once a square has been described on either of them, such as **c.d.** on the line **b.c.**, then by the first proposition of the sixth book, **c.d.** is to **a.c.** as **b.d.** <note>The line **b.d.** here represents the side of the square equal to **b.c.**</note> is to **a.b.** Therefore, since **b.d.** is commensurable in length with **a.b.** by the hypothesis—because **b.c.** (to which it is equal) is rational—it follows by the first part of the 10th proposition that **c.d.** is commensurable with **a.c.** Since, therefore, **c.d.** is rational by definition <note>The square of a rational line is always a rational area.</note>, **a.c.** will also be rational, which is what was proposed.

### Proposition .16.

When a rational rectangular area is applied to a line that is rational in length, or to one commensurable with a rational line, its second side will be rational in length and commensurable in length with the first side.

<margin>A marginal rectangle or square with labels a, b, c, and d positioned at the vertices.</margin>

This is, as it were, the converse of the prior proposition. Thus, if the area **a.c.** is applied to the line **a.b.**, which is rational in length, and the area itself is rational: I say that its second side, which is **b.c.**, will also be rational in length and commensurable with the first side. For let **a.d.** be the square of **a.b.**; it will be rational by definition and because of this it will be commensurable with the rational area **a.c.** Therefore, by the first proposition of the sixth book, as **a.d.** is to **a.c.**, so also is **d.b.** to **b.c.** Since **d.a.** is commensurable with **a.c.**, it follows by the first part of the 10th proposition that **b.d.** is commensurable with **b.c.** Therefore it is commensurable with its equal, but **b.a.** is rational; therefore by the 7th definition, **b.c.** is established as rational; thus the proposition is proved.

### Proposition .17.

To find two lines commensurable in power <term>potentia: the area of their squares</term> only, which are rational, such that the square of the longer is greater than the square of the shorter by the square of a line commensurable with the longer in length.

<margin>A marginal diagram consisting of horizontal and vertical line segments with labels a, b, and c.</margin>

The proposal is to find two rational lines commensurable in square <note>original: "potētia tm̄ cōicātes," communicating in power only</note> such that the longer is greater in power than the shorter by the square of a line commensurable with it in length.

I therefore take a certain rational line **a. b.** upon which I describe a semicircle **a. c. b.** and, having taken any number such as **d. e.**, I divide it into two numbers **d. f.** and **f. e.** such that the ratio <note>original: "pportio"</note> of **d. e.** to **d. f.** is as a square number to a square number, but the ratio of **d. e.** to **f. e.** is not as a square number to a square number. Such a number is any square that is divisible into a square and a non-square, such as 9, which is divided into 4 and 5, and all their equal multiples. 

And I find a line to whose square the square of line **a. b.** has the same ratio as the number **d. e.** to the number **d. f.**; how this is found was stated in the fifth demonstration. This found line, which is necessarily smaller than **a. b.**, I fit within the semicircle **a. c. b.** according to the first [proposition] of the fourth [book], and let it be **a. c.**; then I shall draw the line **c. b.** 

I say that the two lines **a. b.** and **c. b.** are those which we seek. Therefore, by the first part of the 30th [proposition] of the third [book], the angle **c** is a right angle; and thus, by the penultimate [proposition] of the first [book] <note>This refers to the Pythagorean Theorem (Book I, Prop. 47).</note>, the square of **a. b.** is equal to the squares of the two lines **a. c.** and **c. b.** Since the ratio of the square of line **a. b.** to the square of line **a. c.** is as **d. e.** to **d. f.** by the hypothesis, it follows by inverse proportionality that the ratio of the square of line **a. b.** to the square of line **c. b.** is as **d. e.** to **f. e.** 

Therefore, the square of **c. b.** is commensurable <note>original: "cōicat," meaning "communicates" or shares a common measure</note> with the square of **a. b.** by the 6th [proposition] of this [book]. Thus, the square of **c. b.** will be rational by definition, since it is commensurable with a rational area. And because **c. b.** and **a. b.** are incommensurable by the last part of the 7th [proposition], it is established that the two lines **a. b.** and **c. b.** are rational, being commensurable in power only <term>potentia tm̄: "in power only," meaning their squares are commensurable, but the lines themselves are not</term>. And since line **a. b.** is more powerful <term>potentioꝛ: "more powerful," meaning the area of the square it produces is greater</term> than line **c. b.** by the square of line **a. c.**—which, by the second part of the 7th [proposition], is commensurable with it in length—it is clear that the proposition has been achieved.

If, however, it is desired to find more than two lines commensurable in power only, where one is more powerful than any of the others by the square of some line commensurable with it in length: let there be, as before, a rational line **a. b.** in length, upon which a semicircle **a. c. b.** is described. Such numbers present themselves readily, such as 36, which is divisible into 25 and 11; likewise into 16 and 20; again into 9 and 27; and also into 4 and 32. Among these non-squares—which are 11, 20, 27, and 32—there is no ratio of one square number to another.

## Proposition 18

<margin>
<image-desc>A geometric diagram featuring a semicircle with a horizontal diameter labeled a-b. To find two lines that are rational in power only <note>This means the lengths of the lines are irrational, but the areas of the squares built upon them are rational and share a common factor.</note> and commensurable, such that the square of the longer exceeds the square of the shorter by the square of a line that is incommensurable to the longer in length.

In this case also, let the same arrangement and the same hypotheses remain as in the previous proposition, with only this changed: let the ratio of number **d.e.** to neither of the two numbers **d.f.** and **f.e.** be as a square number to a square number. This will be easily done: let **d.e.** be set as any square number divided into two non-square numbers, as if **d.e.** were 9, **d.f.** were 6, and **f.e.** were 3. Arguing as before, with this exception: that **a.b.** and **a.c.** are incommensurable in length according to the last part of the 7th [proposition]. 

And it should be known that two such lines as these and the previous ones taught to be found, when joined together, compose a <term>binomial</term> <note>A line made of two parts that cannot be added into a single simple length.</note>; and when the smaller of them is cut away from the larger, that which remains is called a <term>residue</term> <note>Also known in modern geometry as an apotome.</note>. Note also that lines rational in power only and commensurable can be one rational and the other irrational, just as the square sides <note>original: 'latera tetragonica'</note> of two surfaces, one of which is 25 feet and the other 24, are rational in power only and commensurable; for the side of the first surface is 5, but the side of the second is not a whole number. They can also both be irrational, like the square sides of two surfaces of which one is 24 feet and the other 23; for the side of neither is a whole number, and they are incommensurable in length according to the last part of the seventh [proposition]. But if it is desired to find more than two lines rational in power only and commensurable, such that one is more powerful than any of the others by the square of a line not commensurable with it in length: let such a number be taken that can be divided many times so that the ratio of the whole to none of its parts, nor of any part to another, is as a square number to a square number; just as 25 can be divided into 2, 7, and 16 <note>Note: The text says 23, likely a scribal error for 16 if seeking non-squares, or a general example of partitioning.</note>, or into 5 and 20, and again into 7 and 18. And thus the process is the same as it was in the previous [proposition].

## Proposition 19

<margin>
<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing two adjacent rectangles sharing a vertical side. Points a, b, and d are labeled at the top vertices, and point c is at the bottom. To the left of the diagram, handwritten marginalia reads: "surd surface <note>original: 'superficiē surdā'</note>" and "What a medial surface is <note>original: 'Superficies medialis quid sit'</note>".</image-desc>
</margin>

Every surface <note>meaning "area"</note> contained by two lines that are rational in power only and commensurable is irrational, and it is called a **medial surface**; and its square side—that is, the line which has the power to form it—is irrational and is called a **medial line**.

Let there be two lines **a.b.** and **b.c.** containing the surface **a.c.**, being rational in power only and commensurable; how these are found is manifest from the previous and the one before the previous. I say that the surface **a.c.** is irrational. For let **c.d.** be the square of **b.c.**; it will be rational by hypothesis because the line **b.c.** is rational in power. And because, from the first [proposition] of the sixth [book], the surface **a.c.** is to **c.d.** as the line **a.b.** is to **b.d.**, and **a.b.** does not commute <note>i.e., is not commensurable</note> with **b.d.**, because by hypothesis it does not commute with its equal which is **b.c.**; it follows by the second part of the 10th [proposition] that **a.c.** also does not commute with **c.d.**. Therefore, by definition, the surface **a.c.** is irrational, and thus its square side is also irrational. This surface is called "medial" because it is the mean proportional between two rational surfaces, namely between the squares of the two lines containing it; and the line that can form this surface is called "medial" because it is also the mean proportional between two lines that are rational in power only and commensurable, and these two lines are the sides of the said surface. And this is what we wished to show.

### Proposition 22.

Every difference by which one medial area exceeds another medial area is proved to be irrational.
¶ Let each of two areas, **a. b.** and **a.**, be medial: I say that area **b.**, which is their difference, is <term>irrational<note>In this context, irrational means the area cannot be expressed as a rational number relative to the established unit square.</note></term>. For let line **c. d.** be rational in length, to which is applied area **d. e.** equal to area **a.**, and area **d. f.** equal to the total area **a. b.** How this may be done was taught in the previous proposition. Since, therefore, **d. f.** is equal to **a. b.** and **d. e.** is equal to **a.**, it will be, by conception, that **g. f.** is equal to **b.** If, therefore, area **b.** is not irrational but rational, then **e. f. g.**, which is its equal, will be rational. And since line **e. g.** is rational in length like its equal **c. d.**, it will be by Proposition 16 that line **e. f.** is rational in length and commensurable to line **e. g.** However, by Proposition 20, each of the two lines **c. e.** and **e. f.** is rational in power only and incommensurable to line **c. d.** in length: so that line **e. f.** is incommensurable to line **c. e.** in length. And because by the first proposition of Book 6 <note>original: "primā sexti"</note> the square of line **e. f.** is to the area produced by **e. f.** and **c. e.** as **e. f.** is to **c. e.**, it follows by the second part of Proposition 10 that the square of line **e. f.** is incommensurable to the area made from **e. f.** and **c. e.** Wherefore the square itself will also be incommensurable to double the area of **e. f.** and **c. e.** But the square of **c. e.**, since it is rational, is commensurable with the square of **e. f.**; therefore the whole composed of both will be, by Proposition 9, commensurable with the square of **e. f.** and therefore incommensurable to double the area of **e. f.** and **c. e.** And since by the fourth proposition of Book 2 <note>original: "quartā scđi"</note> the square of line **c. f.** is equal to the two squares of the two lines **c. e.** and **e. f.** and double the area of **c. e.** and **e. f.**—and double the area of **c. e.** and **e. f.** is incommensurable to the sum of the two squares of the two lines **c. e.** and **e. f.**—it follows by those things added in Proposition 9 that the square of **c. f.** is incommensurable to the sum of the two squares of the two lines **c. e.** and **e. f.** But since the sum of these squares is rational, it follows that the square of line **c. f.** is not rational: and therefore line **c. f.** is not rational in power. Because of this, area **d. f.** will not be medial, nor **a. b.** which is equal to it, which is inconsistent since it is the opposite of what was stated. It remains, therefore, that area **b.** is irrational: which is what was proposed.

### Proposition 23.

Every area contained by two medial lines that are commensurable in power only is either rational or medial.
¶ Let there be two medial lines **a. b.** and **b. c.** that are commensurable in power only: I say that the area **a. c.** contained by them is either rational or medial. For let **c. d.** be the square of line **b. c.** and **a. e.** be the square of line **a. b.** These two squares will be commensurable by hypothesis, and by the first proposition of Book 6, area **a. c.** will be the <term>mean proportional<note>A value that holds the same ratio to the first quantity as the third quantity holds to it (e.g., in a:b = b:c, b is the mean proportional).</note></term> between these squares. Therefore, let line **f. g.** be taken which is rational in length, to which is applied area **f. h.** equal to square **a. e.**, and **h. k.** equal to area **a. c.**, and **k. l.** equal to square **d. c.** These three areas **f. h.**, **h. k.**, and **k. l.** will be continuously proportional just as their equals are...

And since areas **f.b.** and **k.l.** are <term>commensurable<note>Commensurable quantities are those that can be measured by the same common unit.</note></term> just as the two squares **a.e.** and **c.d.** are equal to them, it follows by the first [proposition] of the sixth and the 10th [proposition] of this [book] <note>original: ".10.hui⁹"</note> that line **g.b.** is commensurable with **m.l.** Each of them, however, is <term>rational in power<note>A line is "rational in power" if its square is a rational area, even if the line's length itself is irrational.</note></term> by the 20th [proposition] of this [book]. Therefore, the area produced by one into the other is rational; for every area contained by two lines rational in power and commensurable in length is necessarily rational, as is clear from the first [proposition] of the sixth and the first part of the 10th [proposition] of this [book], and from the definition of rational areas. And because, from the first part of the 16th [proposition], the square of line **b.m.** is equal to the area produced by **g.b.** multiplied by **m.l.**, the square of line **b.m.** will be rational. 

If, therefore, line **b.m.** is rational in length (or commensurable with line **k.m.**, which is equal to line **f.g.**), then by the 15th [proposition], area **b.k.** will be rational, and likewise its equal **a.c.** But if line **b.m.** is irrational in length (or incommensurable with line **k.m.**, which is equal to line **f.g.**), since it is at least rational in power—owing to the fact that its square is rational—then by the 19th [proposition], area **b.k.** will be <term>medial<note>A medial area is the "middle" kind of irrationality in Euclid, formed by lines that are only rational in power.</note></term>; wherefore its equal **a.c.** is also medial. Thus the proposition is established. 

¶ And note that if two lines **a.b.** and **b.c.** were medial and commensurable in length, area **a.c.** would be medial only; for area **a.c.** would be commensurable with both squares **a.e.** and **c.d.** by the first [proposition] of the sixth and by the present hypothesis and by the 10th [proposition] of this [book]. And therefore area **b.k.**, being equal to **a.c.**, would be commensurable with both areas **f.b.** and **k.l.** Thus, by the first [proposition] of the sixth and the 10th [proposition] of this [book], line **b.m.** would be commensurable with both lines **g.b.** and **l.m.** Since both of these are rational in power only and not commensurable in length with line **f.g.**, **b.m.** would also be rational in power only and not commensurable in length with line **f.g.**, and therefore not commensurable with line **b.d.** Wherefore, by the 19th [proposition], area **b.k.** will be medial only, and thus also its equal **a.c.** 

But if the two lines **a.b.** and **b.c.** were medial and commensurable neither in length nor in power, area **a.c.** would be neither rational nor medial. For if it were so—namely, that the two lines **a.b.** and **b.c.** were medial and commensurable neither in length nor in power—the two squares **a.e.** and **c.d.** would be incommensurable. Consequently, the two areas **f.b.** and **k.l.** (equal to them) would also be incommensurable. Wherefore the two lines **g.b.** and **m.l.** would be incommensurable by the first [proposition] of the sixth and the second part of the 10th [proposition]. And since each of them is rational only in power by the 20th [proposition], the area of one into the other would be medial by the 19th [proposition]. Since, therefore, the square of line **b.m.** is equal to the said area produced from **g.b.** into **m.l.** by the first part of the 16th [proposition] of the sixth [book], line **b.m.** would be a medial line by the 19th [proposition]. Therefore, by the 15th [proposition], area **b.k.** would not be rational, nor even medial by the 20th [proposition]; wherefore neither would its equal **a.c.** be so.

...[so that the square of] **a** is greater than the square of the shorter line **b** by the square of some line commensurable with it in length. <note>original: "sit.a.possit amplius b2euio2i que sit.b.in quad2ato alicuius linee secum cõmuni/cantis in longitudine"; this refers to the relationship where $a^2 - b^2 = k^2$ and $k$ is commensurable with $a$.</note> I shall set line **c**, according to the teaching of the 9th [proposition] of the sixth [book], <note>Euclid's Elements, Book VI, Prop 9 teaches how to find a part of a line.</note> as the mean proportional between **a** and **b**. Therefore, if the two lines **c** and **d** contain a rational area, they are exactly what we were seeking. To show that they contain a rational area, consider this: since **a** is to **b** as **c** is to **d**, then by permutation **a** is to **c** as **b** is to **d**. But **a** was to **c** as **c** was to **b** <note>Because $c$ was the mean proportional.</note>; therefore **c** is to **b** as **b** is to **d**. But the square of **b** is rational by the hypothesis, since **b** itself is rational in power. Therefore, the area contained by the two lines **c** and **d** is rational; wherefore the proposition is established.
