## Proposition 28.

To find two lines incommensurable in power, containing a rational area, such that both their squares taken together are medial.
Let the arrangement here be exactly the same as in the preceding one. Let the two lines **a.b.** and **c.d.** be such as Proposition 25 proposes; by the same reasoning as the previous one, the two lines **a.e.** and **e.b.** will be such as this 28th proposes. For since line **a.b.** is medial, its square will be medial by the 19th [proposition], and therefore the squares of the two lines **a.e.** and **e.b.** are medial by the second to last [proposition] of the first [book]. And because **a.b.** by **c.d.** contains a rational area, it follows also that **a.b.** by **c.f.**—and therefore by **g.e.**, which is equal to it—contains a rational area. Thus, the area of **a.e.** by **e.b.** is [rational], and what was sought is clearly found. Hence, the two lines which this 28th [proposition] teaches us to find compose a line "powerful" over a rational and a medial [area] <note>That is, the square of the whole line is equal to the sum of a rational and a medial area.</note>, and when the smaller of them is cut away from the greater, the remainder is called the **line which, joined with a rational area, composes a medial whole.**

Therefore, the area of **a.e.** by **e.b.** is medial, since it is equal to the area of **a.b.** by **e.g.** Because line **a.b.** is incommensurable with line **c.d.**, it will also be incommensurable with line **c.f.**, and thus with line **e.g.** Therefore, by the first [proposition] of the sixth and the second part of the 10th of this [book], the area of **a.b.** by **e.g.**—which is equal to the area of **a.e.** by **e.b.**—will be incommensurable with the square of line **a.b.**; and thus also with the squares of the two lines **a.e.** and **e.b.** taken together. Since this is so, it follows also that twice the area of **a.e.** by **e.b.** is incommensurable with the aforementioned squares of the two lines

### Proposition 30.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing a horizontal line segment with three points labeled 'a', 'b', and 'c' from left to right. This illustrates the addition of two line segments.</image-desc>

If two lines **rational in power only** <note>Lines "rational in power only" are those whose squares are commensurable with a standard unit, but the lengths themselves are not. For example, the side of a square of 2 and a square of 3.</note>, being commensurable, are joined in a straight line: the whole line composed of them will be **irrational**; and it is called a **binomial**. <note>original: "binomium". A binomial is the sum of two terms that cannot be simplified into a single rational number, like 1 + √2.</note>
¶ Let there be two lines **a.b.** and **b.c.** joined in a continuous straight line, rational in power only and commensurable: which you will find through [propositions] 17 and 18: I say the whole line **a.c.** composed of them is irrational and is itself called a binomial. For by the fourth [proposition] of the second [book] <note>Euclid II.4 describes the square of a sum: (a+b)² = a² + b² + 2ab.</note>, the square of **a.c.** is equal to the squares of the two lines **a.b.** and **b.c.** and double the area of one of them multiplied by the other: both squares, however, make a **rational** area by the hypothesis: while double the area of one multiplied by the other makes a **medial** area by [proposition] 19. Therefore, both squares taken together make an area incommensurable with double the area of one in the other. Thus, by [proposition] 9, the square of **a.c.** will be incommensurable with the two squares of the two lines **a.b.** and **b.c.** taken together, and is therefore irrational by definition, since those two squares make a rational area. And therefore its square root <note>original: "latus tetragonicū", literally "the side of the square."</note>, which is **a.c.**, is also irrational by definition: thus the proposition is proved.

### Proposition .31.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram consisting of a horizontal line segment a-b-c with a semicircle drawn above it. A perpendicular line rises from point b to intersect the arc of the semicircle.</image-desc>

If two **medial** <note>A medial line is the side of a square equal to a rectangle formed by two rational lines commensurable in power only (e.g., the fourth root of a number).</note> lines, commensurable in power only and containing a **rational area**, are joined directly: the whole line composed of them will be irrational and is called the **first bimedial**. <note>original: "bimediale primum"</note>
¶ Let there be two lines **a.b.** and **b.c.** joined in a continuous straight line, such as are proposed, which you will find through [propositions] 24 and 25: I say the whole line **a.c.** is irrational and is called the **first bimedial**. For double the area of **a.b.** times **b.c.** is rational by the hypothesis, and the two squares of the two lines **a.b.** and **b.c.** taken together make a medial area: since each square is medial by the hypothesis and one of them is commensurable with the other: therefore double the area of one in the other is incommensurable with the two squares taken together: therefore the whole sum from the double area and the two squares—and this is the square of the whole **a.c.** by the fourth [proposition] of the second [book]—is incommensurable with double the area of one in the other by [proposition] 9 of this [book]. Since, therefore, the double area is rational, the square of **a.c.** will be irrational. And thus also the line **a.c.**, which is what was to be shown.

<image-desc>A rectangular area construction with points d, g, h along the top horizontal edge and points e, f on the bottom edge. A vertical line connects point g to f, dividing the large rectangle into two smaller rectangles.</image-desc>

¶ The same [proved] otherwise: let line **d.e.** be rational in length, to which is applied an area **d.f.** equal to the two squares of the two lines **a.b.** and **b.c.** This area **d.f.** will be medial, since each square is medial by the hypothesis and one is commensurable with the other; wherefore by [proposition] 20, line **d.g.** is rational in power only: not commensurable in length with line **d.e.** Again, to line **f.g.**, which is equal to **d.e.**, let an area **f.h.** be applied equal to double the area of **a.b.** in **b.c.**; and **f.h.** will be rational by the hypothesis: wherefore by [proposition] 16, line **g.h.** will be rational in length: thus the two lines **d.g.** and **g.h.** are rational in power and commensurable in that [power] only: therefore by [proposition] 30, the whole line composed of them, which is **d.h.**, is a **binomial** and irrational: wherefore by [proposition] 16, from the destruction of the present, the area **e.h.** is irrational. And because by the fourth [proposition] of the second [book] its square root is line **a.c.**, it will itself be irrational by definition, which was to be demonstrated.

### Proposition .32.

If two **medial** lines, commensurable in power only and containing a **medial area**, are joined in a straight line, the whole line will be irrational and is called the **second bimedial**. <note>original: "bimediale secundum"</note>
¶ Let there be two lines **a.b.** and **b.c.** joined in a continuous straight line as proposed...

These proofs demonstrate how the sum of two lines can result in a new, specific class of irrationality based on whether the area they contain is rational or medial.</summary>

...which can be found through [Proposition] 26: I say that the whole line **a.c.** composed of them is irrational, and it is called the **second bimedial**. <term>Second Bimedial: A line formed by adding two lines that are commensurable in power only, where the sum of their squares is medial and the rectangle they form is also medial and incommensurable with the sum of their squares.</term> For let line **d.e.** be rational in length, to which is applied the surface **d.f.** equal to the two squares of lines **a.b.** and **b.c.** taken together; and because by hypothesis those two squares are commensurable and each is medial, the surface **d.f.** will be medial. Therefore, through [Proposition] 20, the line **d.g.**, which is its second side, is rational in power only and incommensurable in length with line **d.e.** Again, let there be applied to the line **g.f.** (which is equal to line **d.e.**) the surface **f.b.** equal to twice the surface of **a.b.** times **b.c.** The surface **f.b.** will also be medial, for by hypothesis the surface of **a.b.** times **b.c.** was medial. Therefore, its double, to which **f.b.** is equal, will be medial. According to [Proposition] 20, the line **g.b.** is rational in power only and incommensurable in length with line **g.f.** But because **a.b.** and **b.c.** are commensurable in power only, then through the first [proposition] of the sixth [book] and the second part of the tenth [proposition] of this [book], the surface of one multiplied by the other will be incommensurable with the square of either. And since their squares are commensurable by hypothesis, the said surface (and thus its double) will be incommensurable with the two squares taken together. Therefore, the surfaces **d.f.** and **f.b.** are incommensurable. Thus, by the first of the sixth and the second part of the tenth of this book, line **d.g.** will be incommensurable with line **g.b.** Since these are rational in power, the whole line **d.b.** will be a binomial and irrational according to [Proposition] 30. Therefore, by [Proposition] 16, by disproving the consequence, the surface **e.b.** is irrational. And since its square root <note>original: "latus tetragonicum"</note>—by the fourth [proposition] of the second [book]—is the line **a.c.**, it follows by definition that line **a.c.** is irrational; which was the thing proposed to be shown.

### Proposition 33.

<margin><image-desc>Geometric diagram showing a line divided into segments a, b, and c. Below it is a rectangle labeled with g, f, and h.</image-desc></margin>

When two lines incommensurable in power are joined, containing a medial surface, and both their squares taken together are rational: the whole line will be irrational and will be called the **major line**. <term>Major Line: An irrational line composed of two parts whose squares sum to a rational area, but whose rectangle is medial.</term>

Let there be two lines **a.b.** and **b.c.** joined together in a continuous straight line as proposed, which can be found from [Proposition] 27: I say that the line **a.c.** composed of them is an irrational line, and it is called the **major line**. Since both squares taken together are rational, but the surface of one times the other (and thus its double) is medial by hypothesis, the whole sum of the two squares will be incommensurable with twice the surface of one times the other. Therefore, the whole aggregate of the two squares and twice the surface—which is equal to the square of **a.c.** by the fourth [proposition] of the second [book]—will be incommensurable with the two squares of **a.b.** and **b.c.** taken together, according to [Proposition] 9 of this [book]. By definition, therefore, the square of line **a.c.** is irrational and the line **a.c.** is irrational, which is what was proposed. The same may be shown otherwise, as in the previous [propositions]: to the line **d.e.** (which is rational in length) let there be applied the surface **d.f.** equal to the two squares of lines **a.b.** and **b.c.** taken together. It will be rational by hypothesis; therefore, by [Proposition] 16, its second side **d.g.** will also be rational in length and commensurable with line **d.e.** Again, let there be applied to line **f.g.** the surface **f.b.** equal to twice the surface of **a.b.** times **b.c.** It will be medial by hypothesis; therefore, by [Proposition] 20, the line **g.b.** (which is its second side) is rational in power only. By [Proposition] 30, therefore, the line **d.b.** is a binomial and irrational. Therefore, by [Proposition] 16, by disproving the consequence, the surface **e.b.** is irrational, and thus its square root (which by the fourth of the second is **a.c.**) is irrational by definition; which is what we wished to show.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram illustrating the proof of Proposition 34. At the top is a horizontal line segment divided into two parts, with points labeled a, b, and c. When two lines that are incommensurable in power are joined together, containing a rational area, and the sum of their squares is medial: the whole line will be irrational and will be called the **side of a rational plus a medial area**. <note>original: "potens in rationale et mediale." This refers to a line whose square is equal to the sum of a rational area and a medial area.</note>

Let there be, as in the previous propositions, two lines **a.b.** and **b.c.** joined in a continuous straight line as proposed; these are to be taken from [Proposition] 28. I say that the whole line **a.c.** composed of them will be irrational, and it is called the line that is the **side of a rational plus a medial area**. For since the area <note>The "area" here refers to the rectangle formed by the two lines.</note> of **a.b.** times **b.c.** is rational by hypothesis, therefore both its double and the sum of the two squares taken together are medial. It follows from the fourth [proposition] of the second [book] <note>This is the geometric identity $(a+b)^2 = a^2 + b^2 + 2ab$.</note> and the ninth of this book—just as in the previous cases—that the square of the whole line **a.c.** is incommensurable with twice the area of **a.b.** times **b.c.** Therefore, by definition, the square itself is irrational and the line **a.c.** is irrational, which is what was proposed. ¶ The same [is proved] another way: let there be, as before, a line **d.e.** rational in length, and let the area **d.f.** applied to it be equal to the sum of the two squares of lines **a.b.** and **b.c.** taken together. This area will be medial by hypothesis. Therefore, by [Proposition] 20, the line **d.g.** will be rational in power only and not commensurable in length with line **d.e.** And let the area **f.h.** <note>OCR says f.b., likely a typo for f.h. based on the diagram labels.</note> applied to the line **g.f.** be equal to twice the area of **a.b.** times **b.c.** This will be rational by hypothesis, and therefore by [Proposition] 18, its side **g.h.** <note>OCR says g.b.</note> is rational in length. Wherefore, by [Proposition] 30, the line **d.h.** is a **binomial** <term>Binomial: A line composed of two terms that are commensurable in power only, making the whole line irrational.</term> and is irrational. Thus the area **e.h.** is irrational by [Proposition] 18 by way of contradiction. Since the line **a.c.** is its square side <note>original: "latus tetragonicum," meaning the square root.</note>, by the fourth [proposition] of the second [book], it follows that **a.c.** is irrational by definition; thus the proposition is established.

## Proposition .35.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram for Proposition 35. It shows a horizontal line segment with points a, b, and c. Below it, a rectangle is divided into two parts. The left vertical edge has points d, g, and h; the right vertical edge has points e, f, and i.</image-desc>

When two lines are joined that are incommensurable in power and contain a medial area, and the sum of their squares is medial and incommensurable with twice the area of one multiplied by the other: the whole line will be irrational and will be called the **side of the sum of two medial areas**. <note>original: "potens in duo medialia." This line's square is equal to the sum of two medial areas that are incommensurable with each other.</note>

Let there also be two lines here, **a.b.** and **b.c.**, joined in a continuous straight line as proposed, which are to be taken from [Proposition] 29. I say that the line **a.c.** composed of them is irrational, and it is called the **side of the sum of two medial areas**. For let an area **d.f.** be applied to the line **d.e.** (which is rational in length) equal to the sum of the squares of the two lines **a.b.** and **b.c.** taken together. It will be medial by hypothesis, wherefore by [Proposition] 20, the line **d.g.** will be rational in power only and incommensurable with the rational line **d.e.** in length. Again, to the line **g.f.** (which is equal to **d.e.**) let the area **f.h.** be applied, which is equal to twice the area of one [line] times the other. This will also be medial by hypothesis, wherefore by [Proposition] 20, the line **g.h.** will be rational in power only. And since by hypothesis the sum of the squares is incommensurable with twice the area of one times the other, it follows that **d.f.** is incommensurable with **f.h.** Therefore, by the first [proposition] of the sixth [book] and the second part of the tenth [proposition] of this book, the line **d.g.** is incommensurable with **g.h.** By [Proposition] 30, therefore, the line **d.h.** is a **binomial** and irrational. Thus the area **e.h.** is irrational and its square side is **a.c.**, as in the previous cases; wherefore the proposition stands. However, if twice the area of **a.b.** and **b.c.** were not incommensurable with the sum of the squares, the line **a.c.** would be medial. For **d.f.** would be commensurable with **f.h.**, and therefore the line **d.g.** with the line **g.h.** Thus the whole **d.h.** would be rational in power only and incommensurable in length with line **d.e.** By [Proposition] 19, the area **e.h.** would be medial and its square side **a.c.** would be a medial line. # X

¶ If any line is divided into two unequal parts, the squares of both sections taken together are greater than twice the area of one part by the other by as much as the square of the line by which the greater portion exceeds the smaller. <note>This is a geometric way of stating the algebraic identity: $x^2 + y^2 = 2xy + (x-y)^2$. In Euclidean geometry, the "area of one by the other" refers to the rectangle formed by the two segments.</note>
¶ For let the line **a.b.** be divided into two unequal parts at point **c.**, and let **c.b.** be the greater portion, from which **c.d.** is taken equal to **a.c.** I say that the squares of the two lines **a.c.** and **c.b.** are greater than twice the area of one by the other by the square of the line **d.b.** For that which is formed by **a.c.** times **c.b.** twice, together with the squares of the two lines **a.c.** and **c.b.**, is equal to that which is formed by **a.c.** times **c.b.** four times together with the square of **d.b.**, because both these sums are equal to the square of the line **a.b.**—the first by the fourth proposition of the second book, and the second by the eighth proposition of the same book. <note>original: "per quartam secundi scdm vero per .8. eiusdem." Euclid's Elements Book II, Prop. 4 and 8 deal with the squares of divided lines.</note> Therefore, when equals are subtracted from both—namely, twice the area of **a.c.** by **c.b.**—the remainders will be equal: the squares of the two lines **a.c.** and **c.b.** from the first, and twice the area of **a.c.** by **c.b.** plus the square of **d.b.** from the second. Thus the proposition is established. From this it is manifest that if any line is divided into two unequal parts, the squares of both parts taken together are more than double the area of one of them by the other. And this is the reason why we have set this down beforehand.

<image-desc>A square diagram in the right margin, divided into a grid of four rectangles (two squares and two equal rectangles). Labels a, c, d, and b are placed along the base and the vertical divisions. Diagonal lines intersect the interior.</image-desc>

¶ If any line is divided into two unequal parts, and likewise into two other unequal parts, the squares of the more unequal parts taken together are greater than the squares of the less unequal parts taken together by as much as double the square of the line between both divisions and four times the area formed by that same line and the line between the point of the less unequal division and the point that divides the whole line into equal parts.
¶ Let the line **a.b.** be divided into two unequal parts at point **c.**, and likewise by other less unequal parts at point **d.**, and again into equal parts at **e.** I say that the squares of the two more unequal parts, which are **a.c.** and **c.b.**, are greater than the two squares of the two less unequal lines, which are **a.d.** and **d.b.**, by twice the square of line **c.d.** and four times the area formed by **c.d.** times **d.e.** For, by the ninth proposition of the second book, the squares of the two lines **a.c.** and **c.b.** taken together are double the squares of the two lines **b.c.** and **c.e.** taken together. <note>The text here follows the logic of Euclid's lemmas regarding the sum of squares of segments. The "more unequal" the division, the larger the sum of the squares of the segments.</note> But by the same ninth proposition of the second book, the squares of the two lines **a.d.** and **d.b.** taken together are double the squares of the two lines **b.e.** and **e.d.** taken together. Therefore, the squares of the two lines **a.c.** and **c.b.** taken together exceed the squares of the two lines **a.d.** and **d.b.** taken together by the amount that double the square of line **c.e.** exceeds double the square of line **d.e.** This, however, by the fourth proposition of the second book, is double the square of line **c.d.** and four times the area formed by **c.d.** times **d.e.**, which proves the proposition. From this it is manifest that the more unequal the sections of a line are, the greater the sum of their squares will be; and this is why we have set this down beforehand.

## Proposition 36.

It is impossible for a **binomial** <term>binomium: A "two-named" line, formed by adding two rational lines that are commensurable only in their squares (i.e., the square of one could be, for example, 2 and the other 3).</term> to be divided into two other lines besides those terms from which it was joined and named.
¶ Let the line **a.b.** be a binomial; therefore, from [Proposition] 30, it is composed of two lines, **a.c.** and **c.b.**, which are rational in power only and commensurable <note>original: "in potētia tm̄ rōnalibꝰ cōicantibꝰ." This means their lengths are incommensurable, but the areas of the squares built upon them have a ratio of whole numbers.</note>. I say that it is impossible for it to be divided into two other lines under this same condition—namely, that they themselves are rational in power only and commensurable. For if it can be done, let it be divided at **a.d.** and **d.b.**, which are rational in power only and commensurable. Let there also be a line **e.f.**, which is rational in length, to which is applied the area **e.g.** which...

...is equal to the squares of the two lines **a.c.** and **c.b.** taken together. Let the area **f.b.** be equal to the square of line **a.b.**; the area **e.g.** will then be rational, because each of the squares of lines **a.c.** and **c.b.** taken together is rational by hypothesis <note>The hypothesis refers to the definition of a "Binomial" line, where the two parts are rational lines commensurable only in square.</note>. Area **g.b.** is medial by [Proposition] 19, since it is equal to twice the area of **a.c.** times **c.b.** by the fourth [proposition] of the second [book]. <note>original: "per quartam secundi." Since these are different from the two lines **a.c.** and **c.b.**, then by the second of the previously demonstrated lemmas, area **f.k.** will be different from area **e.g.** Let their difference be **k.g.** By the fourth of the second [book], the excess of area **f.b.** over **f.k.** (which we call **k.l.**) is equal to twice the area formed by **a.d.** times **d.b.** Because of this, area **f.k.** will also be rational and area **k.l.** will be medial. Thus, area **k.g.**, since it is the difference between two rational areas (**e.g.** and **f.k.**), will be rational. For a rational area does not differ from another rational area except by a rational amount, as confirmed by the definition and [Proposition] 9 of this book. Yet, since this same area **k.g.** is also the difference between two medial areas (**g.b.** and **k.l.**), it must be irrational by [Proposition] 22, which is impossible. <note>This "reduction to absurdity" is a standard Euclidean proof method: a single area cannot be both rational and irrational at the same time.</note>

->Proposition 37<-

A **first bimedial** line divided at its point of division into two **medial** lines cannot be divided into another two medial lines under the same definition.

Let here also the line **a.b.** be a first bimedial <term>first bimedial: A line composed of two medial lines that are commensurable in square only and whose rectangle is rational.</term> divided into two medial lines **a.c.** and **c.b.** that are commensurable in square only and contain a rational area, as [Proposition] 31 asserts such a line is composed. I say that it is impossible for it to be divided into another two lines under that same definition. If it were possible, let it be divided at point **d.** Having taken a rational line **e.f.**, let area **e.g.** be applied to it equal to the two squares of the lines **a.c.** and **c.b.**, and let area **f.b.** be equal to the square of **a.b.**, and area **f.k.** be equal to the squares of the two lines **a.d.** and **d.b.** By the fourth [proposition] of the second [book], **g.b.** will be equal to twice the area of **a.c.** times **c.b.**, and by the same rule, **k.l.** will be equal to twice the area of **a.d.** times **d.b.** According to the hypothesis, each of the two areas **e.g.** and **k.f.** will be medial, and each of the two lines **g.b.** and **k.l.** <note>The text likely refers to the segments of the areas applied to the rational line.</note> will be rational. But this is impossible: for by the first reasoning, the area **k.g.** would be irrational by [Proposition] 22, but by the second, the same would be rational by definition and [Proposition] 9, which is inconsistent.

->Proposition 38<-

A **second bimedial** line cannot be divided except into the two lines according to its definition.

**The Major line cannot be divided except into the two lines of which it consists at their boundary.**

### Proposition 41.

**The line powering two medial areas cannot be divided into any other two lines at their boundary than those of which it is joined; rather, it is divisible only into the two from which it is composed.**
¶ For this [Proposition] 41, with line **a.b.** divided at point **c.** into those parts of which [Proposition] 35 asserts it is composed, and with the other factors of both figure and position remaining as above, it is proved just like [Proposition] 38. For given the opposite of the proposition, the opposite of [Proposition] 36 follows, which is impossible.

¶ If the greater part of a <term>binomial</term> <note>A binomial line consists of two parts that are commensurable only in square, such as 3 + √5.</note> powers the lesser part by the square of a line commensurable in length to that greater part, and the greater part itself is commensurable in length to the set rational line, it shall be called a **first binomial**.
If, however, the lesser part is commensurable in length to the set rational line, it shall be called a **second binomial**.
But if neither of its parts is commensurable in length to the set rational line, it shall be called a **third binomial**.
Likewise, if the greater part powers the lesser by the square of a line incommensurable in length to that greater part, and the greater part is commensurable in length to the set rational line, it shall be named a **fourth binomial**.
If, however, the lesser part is commensurable in length to the set rational line, it shall be named a **fifth binomial**.
But if neither of its parts is commensurable in length to the set rational line, it will be a **sixth binomial**.

### To investigate the third binomial.
**A** third binomial is found in this way: having placed line **a.** as a rational line in length as before, let **b.** be a prime number. Let **c.** be a square number divisible into a square **d.** and a non-square **e.** Let all other things be as before. I say that the two lines **f.g.** and **g.b.** compose a **third binomial**. However, numbers **b.** and **e.** are not in the ratio of any square numbers, since **b.** is a prime number. For if they were in the ratio of square numbers, it would be necessary (by Proposition 16 of Book VIII and its eighth corollary) for a third number to exist between them in continuous proportionality. Therefore, by Proposition 17 of that same book, number **b.** would be a <term>superficial number</term> <note>A "superficial" or plane number is one that can be formed by multiplying two whole numbers together; a prime number cannot be formed this way, making this result impossible.</note>, which is impossible since it is prime by hypothesis. Therefore, line **g.b.** is incommensurable with the given rational line **a.** according to the last part of 7. That line **f.g.** is more powerful than line **g.b.** by the square of line **f.b.** is clear from Proposition 30 of Book III and the penultimate proposition of Book I; these are commensurable in length by the second part of 7. From the definition of the third binomial, our intention is evident.

**If** a surface is contained by a rational line and a fourth binomial: the side which can produce that surface is a **greater line**.

**W**ith all things remaining as in the preceding proofs, it will result from the hypothesis, the definition of the fourth binomial, and Proposition 19, that each of the two surfaces **d.g.** and **g.e.** (and therefore each of the two **p.m.** and **m.q.**) is medial, and the two squares **l.m.** and **m.n.** taken together are rational, because surface **a.d.** is rational by the definition of the fourth binomial and Proposition 15. And because **d.b.** is divided at point **f.** into two incommensurable parts <note>original: "inōicantia"; literally 'non-naming' or incommensurable</note> by the second part of Proposition 14, surface **a.f.** will be incommensurable with surface **f.b.** Therefore, square **l.m.** is incommensurable with square **m.n.** Thus, the two lines **l.r.** and **r.p.** are incommensurable in power, and since they contain a medial surface **p.m.** and both their squares taken together are rational, it is established by Proposition 33 that line **l.p.** is a **greater line**; which was to be shown.

### Proposition 52.

**If** there be a surface contained by a rational line and a fifth binomial, whatever line can produce that area is necessarily proved to be the **side of a rational and a medial [area]**.

**I**n this case as well, nothing needs to be changed from the previous arrangement and positions: for while they remain, it will result from those things laid down in the definition of the fifth binomial and Proposition 15 that each of the two surfaces **d.g.** and **g.e.** (and thus each of the two **p.m.** and **m.q.**) is rational, and the whole **a.d.** is rational, so that the two squares **l.m.** and **m.n.** taken together are medial by Proposition 19. And since by the second part of Proposition 14, line **f.b.** is incommensurable with line **f.d.**, surface **a.f.** is therefore incommensurable with surface **f.b.**, so that square **l.m.** is incommensurable with square **m.n.** Line **l.r.** will be incommensurable in power with line **r.p.**, and they contain a rational surface **p.m.**, and both their squares taken together are medial. Conclude from Proposition 34 that line **l.p.** is the **side of a rational and a medial [area]** <note>original: "potentem in rationale et mediale"</note>; which is what was promised.

# Proposition 53.

**If a surface is contained by a sixth binomial and a rational line, the line which can produce that area <note>original: "linea que in eam potest"; refers to the square root of the area</note> is proved to be powerful in two medials <note>original: "in duo in medialia potens"; a line whose square is equal to the sum of two medial areas that are incommensurable to one another</note>.**

**I**f this 53rd proposition still allows you to be at leisure from drawing new figures, it is because it is satisfied with the arrangement and positions already laid down. With these remaining as they are, it is necessary from the positions themselves and the definition of the last <note>the sixth</note> binomial, and through Proposition 19, that each of the surfaces **a.d.**, **d.g.**, and **g.c.** [be medial]; on account of which both squares **l.m.** and **m.n.** taken together, as well as the rectangles **p.m.** and **m.q.**, are <term>medial</term> <note>a medial area is one whose side is a medial line; its area is incommensurable with a rational area</note>. Since **b.f.** and **f.d.**—and consequently **a.f.** and **f.h.**—are incommensurable, then the squares **l.m.** and **m.n.** are incommensurable, and thus the lines **b.c.**, **z.r.**, and **p.** will be incommensurable in power. And because they contain a medial surface **p.m.**, and both their squares taken together are a medial area that is double one surface in the other <note>meaning the sum of the squares is incommensurable with twice the rectangle contained by the parts</note>, which is proved because the surface **b.b.** <note>likely a transcription of "h.b." or "g.b." referring to a specific area in the diagram</note> is incommensurable to surface **b.c.** due to the fact that line **d.b.** is incommensurable to line **d.c.**, it follows from Proposition 35 that line **l.p.** is that which is powerful in two medials.

**If one applies a rectangle equal to the square of a binomial to a rational line, its second side will be a first binomial.**

**I**f these six following propositions are the converses of the six preceding ones in their proper order, then this is the intention. From the premises, it is clear that each of the two surfaces **e.l.** and **l.m.**—and therefore the whole surface **e.n.**—is rational. And each of the two equals **n.p.** and **p.g.**—and therefore the whole **m.g.**—is medial. Therefore, by Proposition 16, each of the two lines **f.l.** and **l.n.**, and the whole line **f.n.**, is rational in length and <term>commensurable</term> <note>having a common measure</note> with the given rational line **e.f.**; and by Proposition 20, each of the two **n.q.** and **q.g.**, and the whole **n.g.**, is rational in power only and incommensurable in length to line **m.n.**, and therefore to line **e.f.** (which is equal to it), and consequently to line **f.n.** in length. ->¶ Proposition 55.<-

**IF** a surface equal to the square of a **first bimedial** line is applied to a rational line, its remaining side must be a **second binomial**.
Let line **a.b.** be a first bimedial divided at point **c.** according to its boundary. Let the other elements be as before. I say that line **f.g.** is a second binomial. For the surface **m.g.** will be <term>rational</term> because the parts of a first bimedial contain a rational area. Furthermore, the three surfaces **e.l.**, **l.m.**, and the total **e.n.** are <term>medial</term> <note>a "medial" area is the area of a square whose side is irrational, specifically a medial line</note> and commensurable, because the portions of a first bimedial are medial lines commensurable only in power (according to Proposition 31, by way of 16). Therefore, line **n.g.** will be rational in length and <term>commensurable</term> to the given rational line **e.f.** By Proposition 20, line **f.n.** is rational in power only. Since it is greater than line **n.g.** (from the first of the two preceding demonstrations, the 35th of those added, and the first part of the 6th), its square is greater [than the square of **n.g.**] by the square of a line commensurable with it in length. Therefore, by the first part of the 13th proposition and the definition of line **f.g.**, it is a second binomial, which is what was proposed.

->¶ Proposition 56<-

**If a rectangular surface equal to the square of a second bimedial is applied to a line rational in length, it is necessary that its side be a third binomial.**
If line **a.b.** is a second bimedial divided at its boundary at point **c.**, and all other things remain as before, then line **f.g.** will be a third binomial. For, according to Proposition 32 and our positions, both surfaces **e.n.** and **m.g.** will be medial. Wherefore, by Proposition 20, each of the two lines **f.n.** and **n.g.** will be rational only in power. Since the parts of a second bimedial are commensurable only in power, surface **e.l.** will be commensurable to surface **l.m.**, and thus line **f.l.** will be commensurable in power to line **l.n.** Therefore, by the first part of the 13th proposition, **f.n.** [is more powerful] than **n.g.** by the square of a line commensurable with it in length. Since surfaces **a.b.** and the square **b.b.** <note>likely referring to the squares of the segments</note> are incommensurable because lines **a.c.** and **c.b.** are incommensurable, it follows that both squares taken together are incommensurable to both supplements <note>the rectangles in a square of a binomial</note> taken together. Because the squares are commensurable with each other by hypothesis, and the supplements are equal to each other, it follows that surface **e.n.** is incommensurable to surface **m.g.**, and therefore line **f.n.** is incommensurable to line **n.g.** By the definition, therefore, line **f.g.** is a third binomial, which is what was proposed.

->¶ Proposition 57.<-

Therefore, by Proposition 16, line **f.n.** is rational in length and commensurable to the given rational line **e.f.** But surface **m.g.** will be medial because the portions of a major line contain a medial surface. Thus, by Proposition 20, line **n.g.** is rational only in power. ### Proposition 58.

**If a rectangular area equal to the square of a line that is <term>powerful</term> <note>To be "powerful" over two areas means the square of the line is equal to the sum of those two areas.</note> over a rational and a medial area is applied to a rational line, its other side must be a fifth binomial.**

Let **a. b.** be the proposed line, which is powerful over a medial and a rational area, divided at point **c.** according to its definition; let nothing else be changed from the previous cases. It follows that line **f. g.** is a fifth binomial. For since the parts of this line **a. b.** contain a rational area, it is necessary that the area **g. m.** be rational; therefore, by the 16th proposition, line **n. g.** is rational. And since both squares of the parts of this line taken together are medial, the area **e. n.** will be medial, and by the 20th proposition, line **f. n.** is rational in power only. But because the aforementioned portions of the line are incommensurable in power, the area **e. l.** will be incommensurable to the area **m. l.**, and therefore line **f. l.** is also [incommensurable] to line **l. n.** Thus, by the first part of the 14th proposition, line **f. n.** is greater in power than line **n. g.** by the square of a line incommensurable to itself in length. Therefore, by the definition of the fifth binomial, conclude the proposition.

### Proposition 59.

**Whenever a rectangular area equal to the square of a line that is powerful over two medial areas is applied to a rational line, the other side of that area is proved to be a sixth binomial.**

In this 59th proposition, let line **a. b.** be a line powerful over two medials; let the other elements remain as they were above, and then line **f. g.** will be a sixth binomial. You cannot fail to know this if you are not unmindful of the preceding points and that which is proposed in the 35th proposition; and thus our intention in this matter is clear.

### Proposition 60.

**Every line commensurable with any species of binomial is proved to be a binomial of the same species.**

Let line **a.** be a binomial of any species, and let line **b.** be <term>commensurable</term> <note>Sharing a common measure; having a ratio that can be expressed as a ratio of whole numbers.</note> with it in length. I say that line **b.** is a binomial of the same species as **a.** For let the binomial portions of **a.** be **c.** and **d.**; both will be rational in power only, being commensurable by the 30th proposition. Now let line **b.** be divided at **e.** and **f.** according to the proportion of **c.** to **d.** By converse, eversant, and permutant proportionality <note>These are classical methods of manipulating geometric ratios described in Book V of Euclid.</note>, it will be that **c.** is to **e.** and **d.** is to **f.** as **a.** is to **b.** Since **a.** and **b.** are commensurable, then by the first part of the 10th proposition, **c.** and **e.** are also commensurable, as are **d.** and **f.** If, therefore, **c.** was rational in power only, **e.** will be so as well; but if it was rational in length, **e.** will be as well. In the same way, if **d.** is rational in power only or even in length only, **f.** will be likewise. Similarly, from the 12th proposition, if **c.** is greater in power than **d.** by the square of a line commensurable to it in length—or perhaps incommensurable—then **e.** will be greater in power than **f.** by the square of a line commensurable or incommensurable to it. It is necessary from the definitions of the six species of binomials that **a.** and **b.** be binomials of the same species. However, if line **b.** communicates with binomial **a.** in power only, then line **b.** is also a binomial. But it is not necessary that it be of the same species; indeed, it is impossible for both to fall simultaneously under the first species of binomials, or under the second, fourth, or fifth. However, it is necessary that both fall either under the first three species or both under the last three. For it is impossible for one of them to be in any of the first three species and the other in any of the last three. For since **a.** is commensurable with **b.** in power only, **c.** will also be commensurable with **e.**, and **d.** with **f.**, only in power by the 10th proposition. If, therefore, either of the two lines **c.** or **d.** were rational in length, its counterpart from lines **e.** and **f.** would not be rational in length. It is therefore not possible that **a.** and **b.** fall together under any of those species of binomials in which one of the parts...

...portion of the binomial is rational in length. These species are: the first and second, the fourth and fifth. But truly, since by the 12th proposition, two lines **c.** and **e.** together are more powerful than two lines **d.** and **f.** <note>In this context, being "more powerful" refers to the difference between the squares of the lines being equal to the square of a line commensurable or incommensurable in length with the greater line.</note> in the squares of those lines which are commensurable or incommensurable to them in length: it is necessary that both binomials **a.** and **b.** fall together under the first three species of binomials, or together under the last three, from the definition of those very species. Why do you doubt that line **b.** is a binomial, since **c.** and **e.** are commensurable in power only, just as **d.** and **f.** are? Because they are not commensurable in length, just as their proportionals **c.** and **d.** are not, they undoubtedly compose a binomial by the 30th proposition of this book.

### Proposition 61.

<margin>
<image-desc>A small square diagram with a faint diagonal line and the word "in" <note>likely "in" for "in potentia" or "in length"</note> written inside.</image-desc>

**Every line commensurable with either species of bimedial line is necessarily proven to be a bimedial of the same species.**

The truth of what is said holds whether a line is commensurable <note>original: "communicet"</note> with either bimedial in length, or only in power. For let there be two commensurable lines **a.** and **b.** in either of the two ways mentioned. Let **a.** be a first or second bimedial; I say that **b.** is also a first or second bimedial, according to what **a.** was. For let the bimedial **a.** be divided into its bimedial portions from which it is composed by the 31st and 32nd propositions; let these be **c.** and **d.** Let **b.** likewise be divided into **e.** and **f.** according to the proportion of **c.** to **d.**, as taught by the 12th proposition of the sixth book. Let the area **g.** be contained under **c.** and **d.**, and area **k.** under **e.** and **f.** And let area **h.** <note>The OCR text reads ".b. quadrato .d.", but the logic dictates this refers to the square of a segment, likely 'h'</note> be the square of **d.** and **l.** the square of **f.** By joined, reversed, and permuted proportionality, just as in the preceding proof, **c.** is to **e.** and **d.** is to **f.** as **a.** is to **b.** Therefore, just as by the positioning of **a.** and **b.** they are commensurable (whether in length or in power), so also **c.** and **e.**, and likewise **d.** and **f.**, will similarly be commensurable.

<margin>
<image-desc>A geometric diagram consisting of a rectangle divided into several smaller rectangles labeled with letters: g, h, c, a, d, k, l, b, f, e arranged in a grid-like structure to represent proportional segments and squares of the lines discussed.</image-desc>
</margin>

But because **c.** and **d.** are <term>medial lines</term> <note>A medial line is the side of a square equal to a rectangle contained by two rational lines commensurable only in power.</note> commensurable in power only, it follows from the 21st proposition that **e.** and **f.** are also medial, and from the 10th proposition, commensurable in power only, since they are proportional to **c.** and **d.** by hypothesis. And since by the first proposition of the sixth book, area **g.** is to **h.** as **c.** is to **d.**, and **k.** is to **l.** as **e.** is to **f.**, then **g.** is to **h.** as **k.** is to **l.**, and by permutation **g.** is to **k.** as **h.** is to **l.** Because **h.** is commensurable with **l.**—due to the fact that their two sides **d.** and **f.** are commensurable in length or in power (depending on how **a.** and **b.** are commensurable)—it follows from the 10th proposition that **g.** and **k.** are also commensurable with each other. Therefore, **k.** is rational or medial just as **g.** was, by the definition of a rational surface or the 21st proposition. In this alone does a first bimedial differ from a second bimedial: that the portions of a first bimedial into which it is divided according to its limit contain a rational area, while those of a second bimedial contain a medial area. Therefore, if **a.** was a first bimedial, the area **g.** was rational, whereby **k.** is also rational, and thus **b.** is a first bimedial by the 31st proposition. But if **a.** was a second bimedial, the proposition stands for that as well. The same can be shown otherwise: let there be a rational line **c. d.**, and let **a.** be either of the bimedials and **b.** commensurable to it in length or power. Let area **c. e.** be applied equal to the square of **a.**, and **f. g.** equal to the square of **b.** Areas **c. e.** and **f. g.** will be commensurable because the squares equal to them (the squares of lines **a.** and **b.**) are commensurable by hypothesis. From the first proposition of the sixth book and the 10th of this book, it is necessary that the two lines **d. e.** and **e. g.** be commensurable. And because if **a.** is a first bimedial, line **d. e.** will be a second binomial by the 55th proposition, therefore **e. g.** is also a second binomial by the preceding proposition. Wherefore the <term>tetragonic side</term> <note>The "tetragonic side" is the square root, or the side of a square equal to the given area.</note> of area **f. g.**—which is the line **b.**—is a first bimedial by the 49th proposition. But if **a.** was a second bimedial, line **d. e.** will be a third binomial by the 56th proposition; therefore **e. g.** is a third binomial, and by the preceding proposition its tetragonic side (line **b.**) is a second bimedial by the 50th proposition. It is manifest, therefore, that what was proposed is true.

# BOOK X

<margin>
<image-desc>A geometrical diagram consisting of a larger rectangle divided into sections. A top section is labeled 'm', a middle-left square is labeled 's', and letters 'a', 'b', 'c', and 'd' mark the segments and regions used in the proof of Proposition 62.</image-desc>

**Every line commensurable with a major line is itself a major line.**

This truth holds regardless of which way a line is commensurable with a major line <note>original: "utrolibet modo cōicans," referring to commensurability in length or only in square/power.</note>. Let line **a** be a major line, and let **b** be any line commensurable with it in any way; line **b** will also be a major line. For line **a** is divided into those positions of which it consists according to Proposition 33, which are **c** and **d**, and line **b** is divided according to their proportion into **e** and **f**. Let the area contained under **c** and **d** be **g**, and the area under **e** and **f** be **k**. Let **m** and **b** be the squares of **c** and **d**, while **n** and **l** are the squares of **e** and **f**. Then **m** will be to **b** just as **n** is to **l**, according to the second part of Proposition 18 <note>original: "per scđam ptē. 18."</note>. And together, **m** and **b** are to **b** as **n** and **l** are to **l**; and by permutation, **m** and **b** are to **n** and **l** as **b** is to **l**. Therefore, since **b** is commensurable with **l** (because **d** is commensurable with **f** either in length or in power, just as **a** is commensurable with **b**), it follows that both squares **m** and **b** taken together are commensurable with both squares **n** and **l** taken together. Since the first two squares taken together are rational according to Proposition 33, the latter two will also be rational by definition. And because it is necessary for area **k** to be medial just as **g** is according to Proposition 21, and for lines **c** and **f** to be incommensurable in power just as **c** and **d** are according to Proposition 10, it is concluded by Proposition 33 that line **b** is the line called "major," which is what was proposed. 

**The same proved otherwise:** Since **a** is a major line with which **b** is commensurable, whether in length or in power: take a rational line **c d** and let the area **c e** be applied to it equal to the square of line **a**. Then let **f g** be equal to the square of line **b**. Since the squares of the two lines **a** and **b** are commensurable by hypothesis, the area **c e** will be commensurable with the area **f g**. Therefore, by the first part of Book VI and Proposition 10 of Book X, line **d e** is commensurable with line **e g** in length. And since from Proposition 57 line **d e** is a fourth binomial <term>fourth binomial: a specific type of irrational line where the square of the first term exceeds the square of the second by the square of a line commensurable with the first, and the first term is commensurable with the fixed rational line</term>, line **e g** will also be a fourth binomial by Proposition 60. Therefore, from Proposition 51, line **b**, which is powerful in area **f g** <note>original: "potēs i supficiē," meaning its square is equal to that area</note>, is a major line.

### Proposition 63.

<margin>
<image-desc>A second geometrical diagram showing a set of rectangles and squares labeled 'n', 'k', 'b', 'l', 'e', and 'f', illustrating the relationship between rational and medial areas.</image-desc>
</margin>

**If any line is commensurable with a line powerful in a rational and a medial area, it is proven that it itself is powerful in a rational and a medial area.**

This also holds true however a line is commensurable with a line "powerful in a rational and a medial" <note>This refers to a line whose square is equal to the sum of a rational area and a medial area.</note>, whether in length or in power alone. It is not proved in a double way as before; however, regarding the first method, it is necessary that just as two lines **c** and **d** are incommensurable in power, so too are **e** and **f** by Proposition 10. And just as **g** is a rational area—for such are the portions of a line powerful in a rational and a medial—so too by definition let **k** be rational. And just as the two squares **n** and **l** taken together are medial, just as by Proposition 21 the two squares **n** and **l** taken together will be medial. Therefore, from Proposition 34, **b** is powerful in a rational and a medial area. Regarding the second method, it is necessary from Proposition 58 that line **d e** be a fifth binomial. Thus, by Proposition 60, line **e g** is a fifth binomial. Therefore, by Proposition 52, the square root <note>original: "lat⁹ tetragonicū," literally the 'tetragonal side'</note> of area **f g**, which is **b**, will be a line powerful in a rational and a medial area, which is what was proposed.

### Proposition 64.

<margin>
<image-desc>A third geometrical diagram at the bottom of the margin, featuring larger rectangular regions labeled 'g', 'f', and 'e'.</image-desc>
</margin>

**Every line commensurable with a line powerful in two medial areas is itself powerful in two medial areas.**

With the same arrangement and positions as the previous ones, this will be proven true in the same double way, whether line **b** is commensurable in length or in power with line **a**, which is powerful in two medial areas. For as to the first mode of reasoning, by Proposition 35, area **g** will be medial, and therefore **k** is medial by Proposition 21 since it is commensurable with it. Also, the two squares **n** and **b** taken together will be medial from that same Proposition 35; therefore the two **n** and **l** taken together are medial by Proposition 21. And because the two squares **n** and **b** taken together, from the aforementioned Proposition 35, are incommensurable with double the area **g**, it follows by Proposition 10 and our positions that the two squares **l** and **n** taken together are incommensurable...

### Propositio .65.

<margin>
<image-desc>A vertical geometric diagram consisting of several stacked rectangles. At the top is a rectangle labeled "a". Below it is a rectangle labeled "b". At the bottom is a larger rectangular area bounded by vertical lines "f" (on the left) and "e" (on the right), and a horizontal base line with endpoints "c" and "d". This larger area is bisected horizontally; the line of bisection has the letter "g" at its right end.</image-desc>
</margin>

**If two areas, of which one is rational and the other medial, are joined together: the line powerful in the whole area composed therefrom will be one of four irrational lines: namely, either a binomial, a first bimedial, a major line, or a line powerful in a rational and a medial area.**

Suppose **a** is a rational area and **b** is a medial area. The line powerful in the whole area **a+b** will be one of the four mentioned above. For let the line **c-d** be rational, to which is applied the area **c-e** equal to **a**, and **f-g** equal to **b**. Then, from Proposition 16, the line **d-e** is rational in length and commensurable to the rational line **c-d** already set out. From Proposition 20, the line **e-g** is rational only in power <note>original: "rōnalis in potentia tm̄," meaning its square is rational, but the line itself is irrational.</note>. From Proposition 30, the line **d-g** is a binomial. Since one of the binomial parts, **d-e**, is rational in length and commensurable to the set rational line **c-d**, the line **d-g** must be (by the definition of the types of binomials) either a first, second, fourth, or fifth binomial. By definition, it cannot be a third or sixth. Therefore, from Propositions 48, 49, 51, and 52, the line powerful in the whole area **c-g** (which is equal to areas **a** and **b** combined) will be either a binomial, a first bimedial, a major line, or a line powerful in a rational and a medial area. This is what was proposed. It will not be a second bimedial or a line powerful in two medials; for if it were a second bimedial, then by Proposition 56, line **d-g** would be a third binomial; and if it were powerful in two medials, then by Proposition 59, line **d-g** would be a sixth binomial. But it was neither of these; thus our intention is clear.

### Propositio .66.

**When two incommensurable medial areas are joined together, the line powerful in the whole area will be one of two irrational lines: namely, either a second bimedial or a line powerful in two medial areas.**

Suppose **a** and **b** are two incommensurable medial areas. If they were commensurable, their sum would be a medial area (by Propositions 9 and 21), and thus the line powerful in it would be a medial line (by Proposition 19). I say that the line powerful in the area composed of both will be either a second bimedial or a line powerful in two medial areas. Let the line **c-d** be rational; let the area applied to it **c-e** be equal to **a**, and the area **f-g** be equal to **b**. Then by Proposition 20, line **d-e** and likewise line **e-g** will be rational only in power. Since areas **c-e** and **f-g** are incommensurable just like **a** and **b** which are equal to them, it follows from the first part of the sixth book and Proposition 10 of this book that line **d-g** (by Proposition 30) is a binomial. Since both parts of this binomial, **d-e** and **e-g**, are incommensurable to the set rational line **c-d**, the binomial will be a third or a sixth by the definition of binomials. Therefore, the line powerful in the whole area **c-g** (equal to the sum of **a** and **b**) will be, by Propositions 50 and 53, either a second bimedial or powerful in two medial areas. This is what was proposed.

### Propositio .67.

**When a binomial line and the other irrational lines following it have been established: no one of them will be contained under the term of another.**

This means that if a certain line, such as **a**, is any of the six previously discussed irrational lines—which are the binomial and its five companions—it cannot be any of the others. For if an area equal to its square is applied to the rational line **b-c**, which area is **b-d**: if **a** were a binomial, then by Proposition 54, the line **c-d**...

## Propositio .68.

**If a line is cut off from a line, and both are rational [lines] commensurable in power only: the remaining line will be irrational and will be called a residuum.**

Suppose line **b.c.** is cut off from line **a.b.**, and let both be rational [lines] commensurable only in power <note>original: "rōnales tantū potentia cōicantes"</note>, such as those found by the methods of Propositions 17 and 18; these are the lines that compose a binomial. I say that the remaining line **a.c.** is irrational, and it is called a **residuum**. It is established from the 7th proposition of the second book [of Euclid] that the squares of the two lines **a.b.** and **b.c.** taken together—which compose a rational area by hypothesis and by the definition of a rational area and Proposition 9 of this book—are equal to double the area of **a.b.** and **b.c.** together with the square of **a.c.** And since, from Proposition 19, the area of **a.b.** and **b.c.** is medial, therefore double that area is also medial by Proposition 21, and thus irrational by Proposition 19. It follows that both squares of the two lines **a.b.** and **b.c.** taken together are incommensurable to double the area of one [line] by the other; wherefore by Proposition 9 and the definition of the square of line **a.c.**, it follows that the square of line **a.c.** is irrational, since it is incommensurable to a rational [area], namely the two squares of the two lines **a.b.** and **b.c.** taken together. Therefore, also by definition, the line **a.c.** is irrational, which is what was proposed. For example, in the figure, let the area **e.g.** be equal to the two squares of the two lines **a.b.** and **b.c.** taken together; it will be rational. Likewise, let the area **d.f.** be equal to double the area of one line by the other; it will be medial by Proposition 19, and by the 7th proposition of the second book, the area **f.g.** will be equal to the square of line **a.c.** And since the area **e.g.** is incommensurable to the area **d.f.**, it will be by Proposition 9 incommensurable to **f.g.**; wherefore **f.g.** is irrational, as is its square side <term>latus tetragonicū: the side of a square area</term> **a.c.**

## Propositio .69.

**If a line has been cut off from a line, and both were medial [lines] commensurable in power only and containing a rational area: the remaining line will be irrational and will be called the first medial residuum.**

Suppose line **b.c.** is cut off from line **a.b.**, and let both be such as proposed, which you will find according to Propositions 24 and 25; these are the lines that join to form a first bimedial. I say that the remaining line **a.c.** will be irrational and is called the **first medial residuum**. For both of their squares taken together will be medial, but double the area of one by the other will be rational. Thus both squares taken together are incommensurable to double the area of one by the other. Because both squares taken together are composed of double the area of one by the other and the square of line **a.c.**, it follows by Proposition 9 that the square of line **a.c.** is incommensurable...
